Volume Twenty-Two
The Book of Jurisprudence
Part Two: Prayer

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Bestower of Mercy.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

“Was prayer prescribed for the nations before us as it is for us, in terms of its obligation, times, acts, and manner of performance, or not?”

He—may Allah be pleased with him—replied:

“They had prayers at these times, but their prayers were not identical to ours in their times, manner of performance, and other respects. And Allah knows best.”

He was also asked:

About a man who commits sins and drinks wine, yet performs the five daily prayers, when the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“Any prayer that does not restrain its performer from indecency and wrongdoing only takes him further away from Allah.”

He replied:

“This hadith is not established as a saying of the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Prayer does, however, restrain one from indecency and wrongdoing, as Allah has stated in His Book. In any

However, Ibn ʿAbbās said:

“You have only that portion of your prayer of which you were mindful.”

The Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“A servant may finish his prayer with only half of it recorded for him, or a third, or a quarter,” until he said, “or a tenth.”

When a person performs prayer as commanded, it restrains him from indecency and wrongdoing. If it does not restrain him, this indicates that he is neglecting its due requirements, even though he is acting in obedience. Allah Most High said:

“But there came after them successors who neglected prayer”—to the end of the verse.

Neglecting prayer means failing to fulfil its obligatory requirements, even if one performs it. And Allah knows best.”

He was asked:

Concerning the words of Allah Most High:

“Do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated.”

If a man drinks wine and prays while intoxicated, is his prayer valid or not?

He replied:

The prayer of an intoxicated person who does not know what he is saying is invalid, by agreement. Indeed, he must not even be allowed to enter the mosque, in view of this verse and other evidence, for the prohibition concerns both approaching prayer and approaching places of prayer. And Allah knows best.

translated_text:
Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah have mercy on him—said:

Section

On a “Principle” Concerning Obligations Omitted and Forbidden Acts Committed Before Embracing Islam and Repenting

The principle concerning obligations omitted by someone who was originally a non-Muslim, such as prayer, zakat, and fasting, is that, by consensus, he is not required to make them up after embracing Islam, because he did not believe them to be obligatory. This applies whether or not the message had reached him, and whether his disbelief arose from denial, obstinacy, or ignorance.

In this respect, there is no distinction between a protected non-Muslim (dhimmī) and a belligerent non-Muslim (harbī). This differs from obligations owed by a protected non-Muslim whose fulfilment is required by the covenant of protection, such as repaying debts, returning property entrusted to him, and restoring property wrongfully seized. These obligations are not waived by embracing Islam. This is not because he had accepted them as binding before embracing Islam.

As for someone who is strictly a belligerent non-Muslim, he had undertaken no obligation toward the Muslims, whether concerning acts of worship or other rights. He is therefore not required to discharge any past obligations, whether duties owed to Allah or rights owed to Muslims, even though he would have been punished for neglecting them had he not embraced Islam. For Islam wipes out what came before it.

Likewise, when a non-Muslim commits acts prohibited in Islam but regarded as lawful in his own religion—such as invalid contracts and acquisitions of property, including usurious transactions, gambling, selling wine and pork, marriage without a guardian and without witnesses, and taking Muslims’ property by force or seizure—the legal consequences of those prohibited acts lapse upon his embracing Islam. In his case, they are treated as though they had not been prohibited. By embracing Islam, he is pardoned for entering into such prohibited contracts and taking possession in such prohibited ways. His acts are thus excused, placing him in the position of someone who entered into a contract or took possession in a manner that was not prohibited. They are therefore treated, in his case, like valid transactions among Muslims.

For this reason, when the parties to invalid contracts have already exchanged possession, their ownership of what they received is upheld if they embrace Islam or bring their dispute before us. The same applies to marriage contracts whose grounds of invalidity ceased to exist before adjudication and conversion to Islam. This differs from transactions in which possession has not yet been exchanged: after embracing Islam, they may not take possession in a prohibited manner, just as they may not enter into a prohibited contract. This has been established in its proper place, on the basis of the words of Allah Most High:

“O you who believe, fear Allah and give up what remains of usury, if you are believers.”

He commanded them to relinquish the usury still owed to them, but did not command them to return what they had already received. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever embraces Islam while in possession of something, it remains his.”

He also said:

“Any division made in the pre-Islamic era remains as it was made; any division that comes under Islam must be made according to Islam.”

He also upheld the marriages contracted by people in the pre-Islamic era, even though many of them were not permissible in Islam.

As for Muslim property seized by non-Muslim belligerents who subsequently embrace Islam, it remains theirs, according to the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, the consensus of the early generations, and the position of the vast majority of imams. This is Ahmad’s explicit ruling and the apparent position of his school. As for their submitting a dispute of this kind to us for adjudication, this occurs when they are bound by an agreement granting safe-conduct, a covenant of protection, or a peace treaty. In this case too, we uphold their possession of that property. This concerns rights that accrued to a person in accordance with his beliefs while he was an unbeliever, even if the means by which they arose were prohibited in Islam.

As for punishments, he is not punished for any prohibited act he committed before embracing Islam, whether or not he believed it prohibited. Thus, he is not punished for killing a person, engaging in usury, theft, or anything else, whether he committed these acts against Muslims or against his own coreligionists. If he committed them against Muslims, he believed such acts against them to be permissible. As for his coreligionists, Islamic law permits taking their lives and property, even if he himself believes this forbidden.

For this reason, we say that when unbelievers take one another captive or seize one another’s property as spoils, they are not punished for this after embracing Islam, even if they believed it prohibited. Thus, whenever an act was permissible either in his own religion or in Islam, punishment for it is waived.

وَأَمَّا الْمُسْلِمُ:

translated_text:
But if it was prohibited in both religions—for example, where he had a covenant with another people—then, if his covenant was with Muslims, he would be someone granted safe-conduct, protected under a covenant, or bound by a peace treaty. Such people are liable for Muslim lives they take and property they destroy. They are punished for their transgressions against Muslims and for unlawful sexual intercourse. Regarding drinking wine, there is a well-known disagreement. But if their covenant was with non-Muslims, as in the case of al-Mughīra ibn Shuʿba (1).

Section

As for an apostate, according to the well-known position, he is not required to make up the prayers, zakat, and fasting he omitted during his apostasy. According to the well-known position, however, he remains obliged to make up what he omitted before his apostasy. Another view holds that he must make up the omitted obligations, while a further view holds that he need not do so in either case. Three positions are reported from Ahmad.

As for the prohibited acts he committed, if he was under Muslim control, he is liable for any lives he took or property he destroyed. If he belonged to a group holding out against Muslim authority, there are differing positions reported on the matter.

translated_text:
camels, or omits prayer after embracing Islam because he does not know that it is obligatory for him, or the like—is he required to make up these obligations?

There are two positions within the school. In some cases, a position is expressly transmitted; in others, it is inferred by the school’s jurists. The underlying issue is whether a revealed injunction concerning the detailed rulings of the Sharia becomes binding upon a Muslim before it reaches him. Al-Qādī Abū Yaʿlā mentioned two juristic views on this in a separate treatise. There is also a third view, chosen by some scholars of the school, which distinguishes between an abrogating injunction and an initial injunction: abrogation takes effect only after the abrogating injunction reaches the person, unlike an initial injunction.

They have established, with numerous proofs, that making up the omitted obligations is not required in any of these cases, and that an injunction becomes binding only after it has been conveyed, both generally and in detail. Thus, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, did not instruct Abū Dharr to make up his prayers when he refrained for a time from praying with dry ablution while in a state of major ritual impurity. Nor did he instruct ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb to do so in the incident involving ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir. Nor did he instruct anyone who ate until he could distinguish a white tethering cord from a black one to repeat the fast. There are numerous similar examples in the Sharia.

Indeed, if a disbeliever is pardoned upon embracing Islam for obligations he omitted through lack of belief—even though Allah had imposed them upon him and he is punished for neglecting them—then for Him to pardon a Muslim for obligations he omitted because he did not believe them obligatory, when He does not punish him

translated_text:
for omitting them because of his independent juristic reasoning, his following another scholar, or his excusable ignorance, is all the more fitting and appropriate. Just as Islam wipes away what came before it, repentance wipes away what came before it—especially the repentance of someone who had a valid excuse and then received or understood the text, having previously been unable to hear and understand it. This is abundantly clear. The same applies to contracts he concluded and assets he received without knowing that they were prohibited, owing to excusable ignorance or an interpretation. According to one of the two views, the same ruling applies to him in these matters, with even greater justification.

Thus, if someone enters into a transaction that he believes permissible on the basis of an interpretation—whether involving usury, gambling, the price of wine, an invalid marriage, or something else—and then the truth becomes clear to him and he repents, or he brings his case before us for judgment, or seeks a legal ruling from us, he is allowed to retain what he has received under these contracts. His marriage is also allowed to stand if its invalidating circumstance has ceased to exist. For example, he may have married without a guardian or without witnesses, believing this permissible; married a fifth wife during the fourth wife’s waiting period; entered into a disputed form of marriage intended to make a woman lawful again for her former husband; or done something similar. Even if he subsequently discovers that the marriage was invalid, it is allowed to stand.

If, however, he married on the basis of independent juristic reasoning and subsequently concluded, through independent juristic reasoning, that the marriage was invalid, this rests on the principle that one juristic judgment is not overturned by another, whether in adjudication or in issuing legal opinions. That is a separate basis for the ruling. Our point here, however, concerns the case in which he becomes certain of the prohibition through a definitive text, with a certainty like that of

 لَا يَضْمَنُونَهُ،
 وَعَلَى هَذَا اتَّفَقَ السَّلَفُ كَمَا قَالَ الزُّهْرِيُّ:
 وَقَعَتْ الْفِتْنَةُ وَأَصْحَابُ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ مُتَوَافِرُونَ، فَأَجْمَعُوا
translated_text:
a former unbeliever concerning the truth of Islam. We allow his existing marriage contract to stand and permit him to retain what he received under an invalid contract, provided that the invalidating circumstance no longer exists. This is even more justified than allowing unbelievers, after embracing Islam, to remain in marriages that were prohibited under Islam. Performing obligations and refraining from prohibitions are governed by the same principle, as explained earlier regarding the unbeliever.

This is clear: pardoning a Muslim who acted on an interpretation and allowing his prior arrangements to stand after he abandons that interpretation is more justified than doing so for an unbeliever who acted on an interpretation. Nevertheless, there is disagreement over this within the school and elsewhere. The flaw in the opposing argument lies in focusing on the fact that this is prohibited and that prohibition entails invalidity, while treating all Muslims as one category without distinguishing between those acting on an interpretation and others.

An analogous issue is whether rebels acting on an interpretation are liable for the lives they take and the property they destroy among those on the side of justice. There are two reported opinions.

The first is that they are liable, treating them like armed outlaws and like those who fight out of factional partisanship without relying on an interpretation. This parallels the position of those who treat contracts entered into and assets received on the basis of an interpretation in the same way as those involving no such interpretation.

The second is that they are not liable. The early generations agreed on this, as al-Zuhrī said:

فَصْلٌ:

 كَمَا لَا يَرْفَعُ عُقُوبَةَ الْكَافِرِ:
 وَإِنَّمَا الْكَلَامُ فِي قَضَاءِ مَا تَرَكَهُ مِنْ وَاجِبٍ، وَفِي الْعُقُودِ والقبوض الَّتِي فَعَلَهَا بِتَأْوِيلِ،
translated_text:
that no liability attached to any blood shed, property taken, or sexual relations engaged in on the basis of an interpretation of the Quran.” In another wording: “In this regard, treat them like the people of the pre-Islamic era.” For this reason, “the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) did not hold Usāmah liable for the blood of the man he killed after the man had said, ‘There is no god but Allah,’” because he killed him on the basis of an interpretation. That is, although they regarded what was prohibited as lawful, their ignorance and reliance on an interpretation placed them in the same position as the people of the pre-Islamic era regarding exemption from liability, though they differed from them with respect to Allah’s pardon and mercy. For this community has been pardoned for error and forgetfulness, unlike the unbeliever, who is not forgiven for the disbelief into which he fell through error.

Section

What I have explained concerning obligations a Muslim omits or prohibited acts he commits on the basis of an interpretation derived from independent legal reasoning or following another’s judgment is clear to me. His position in this regard is better than that of an unbeliever acting on an interpretation. This does not prevent me from fighting a rebel acting on an interpretation, flogging someone who drinks intoxicants on the basis of an interpretation, or taking similar measures. An interpretation does not waive worldly punishment in every case, since punishment is intended to avert the harm caused by transgression, just as it does not waive punishment for an unbeliever.

Rather, the issue concerns making up the obligations he omitted, and the contracts he concluded and assets he received on the basis of an interpretation,

translated_text:
and liability for the lives and property he deemed lawful to take on the basis of an interpretation, just as Usāmah deemed it lawful to kill the man he killed after the latter had said, “There is no god but Allah.” Likewise, he is not punished for past conduct when doing so would not deter future misconduct.

As for punishment intended to prevent future wrongdoing, such as fighting a rebel or flogging someone who drinks intoxicants, its purpose is to ensure that obligations are fulfilled and prohibited acts prevented in the future. This is not in question, for in such circumstances it is prescribed, in certain cases, to punish someone acting on an interpretation.

The issue concerns matters relating to the past: making up missed obligations, relinquishing rights acquired during that time, and punishment for what one has done. In these matters—prescribed punishments, rights, and acts of worship—a Muslim acting on an interpretation must be treated more favorably than an unbeliever acting on an interpretation, and is more entitled to such treatment. Repentance wipes away what came before it. The Muslim acting on an interpretation is excused; moreover, he has Islam, through which sins are forgiven, and repentance, which wipes away what preceded it.

Requiring him to make up missed obligations, forfeit rights, and undergo punishments discourages repentance and a return to the truth more than imposing these requirements on an unbeliever would discourage him. For the exposition of Islam and the evidence for it are more compelling than the exposition of these subsidiary rulings and their proofs. The incentive to embrace Islam arising from the force of proof and power may also be greater than the incentive to follow these subsidiary rulings.

I have no doubt about this, although it is disputed. For I know that, had the Sunnah not established such treatment for unbelievers, this analogy would, according to its proponents, have to be applied consistently to an unbeliever as well. Abū Hanīfah’s followers took this into account regarding marriage: they prohibited only those marriages for which there are grounds for admissibility in Islam. Disagreement does not diminish the standing of knowledge and jurisprudence once the supporting proof has become clear.

Section

Two issues, however, require consideration.

The first concerns someone who neglects an obligation or commits a prohibited act, neither on the basis of a belief nor out of excusable ignorance, but out of ignorance coupled with neglect of seeking the knowledge required of him, despite being able to acquire it. Alternatively, he has heard that something is obligatory or prohibited, but fails to commit himself to it out of disregard, not disbelief in the divine message.

These are two frequently occurring cases: someone neglects to seek the general knowledge required of him, consequently neglecting obligations and committing prohibited acts without knowing that they are obligatory or prohibited; or the relevant injunction reaches him, but he does not commit himself to following it, out of partisan attachment to his school or obedience to his desires. Such a person has abandoned the required belief without a valid excuse under Islamic law, just as the unbeliever has failed to embrace Islam. For belief consists in acknowledgment through assent and commitment. He may therefore abandon assent

and commitment alike, for lack of the reflection that leads to assent. Or he may assent in his heart, yet neither acknowledge nor commit himself, because he follows his desires. If such a person repents and acknowledges what is obligatory and prohibited, both assenting and committing himself, is his situation comparable to that of an unbeliever who embraces Islam, since repentance wipes away what preceded it, just as Islam wipes away what preceded it?

The analogy is more remote in this case than in the preceding one. For anyone who requires a person who omitted an obligation on the basis of an interpretation to make it up, and annuls contracts and reverses the taking of possession in the case of someone whose interpretation is excusable, has even stronger grounds for doing so with this person, who sins by abandoning the belief required of him. As for the position we have established and affirmed to be correct, this case requires consideration.

It may be said:

This person is sinful and wrongdoing in neglecting to learn and to commit himself. Pardoning those who err in their interpretation does not necessarily entail pardoning him.

Alternatively, it may be said—and this is more clearly supported by the evidence and analogy:

This person is no worse off than the obstinate unbeliever who abandoned the Quran out of arrogance, envy, and desire, or who heard it, reflected upon it, and became inwardly certain that it was the truth from Allah, yet denied it out of injustice and haughtiness. Such was the case of Pharaoh, most of the People of the Book, and the polytheists: “It is not you they disbelieve; rather, it is Allah’s signs that the wrongdoers deny.” Repentance is like embracing Islam, for the one who said:

“Islam wipes away what came before it,”

is the very one who said:

“Repentance wipes away what came before it,”

and both statements occur in a single hadith

narrated by ‘Amr ibn al-‘Ās and recorded by Ahmad and Muslim. If the unbeliever is pardoned because he has embraced Islam, which wipes away past sins—for good deeds erase evil deeds—and because withholding pardon would deter people from entering Islam by subjecting converts to burdens and shackles lifted through the pronouncement of this Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, then the same reasoning applies to repentance from ignorance and wrongdoing. Acknowledging the truth and returning to it is a good deed through which Allah erases evil deeds. Withholding pardon would greatly discourage repentance and impose heavy burdens and formidable shackles upon those who repent.

It is established in Sahīh Muslim, on the authority of Abū Dharr, that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah replaces every evil deed of His repentant servant with a good deed.”

This accords with the apparent meaning of His words:

“Allah will replace their evil deeds with good deeds.”

If the evil deeds of which he repented have become good deeds, then no evil deed remains to his account after repentance. That taking of possession and that contract therefore fall within the scope of pardon, as does that omission. He is thus not treated as one who has neglected an obligation or committed a prohibited act. In this way, the scriptural evidence is reconciled.

For the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever sleeps through a prayer or forgets it, let him pray it when he remembers it.”

People have differed concerning someone who deliberately omits prayer or fasting: must he make it up?

Our scholars have differed over whether zakat forcibly collected by the ruler inwardly discharges the payer’s obligation. There are two views, although it is not collected from him again. The first is that it does not discharge his obligation, because he lacked the intention despite being capable of forming it. The second is that the ruler’s intention takes the place of the intention of the person refusing to pay, because the ruler represents the Muslims in fulfilling the obligations incumbent upon them.

The first view is more correct. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to accept it from them when they gave it to him, yet the Quran explicitly denies its acceptance because they gave unwillingly. It is therefore clear that if someone gives while disliking giving, it is not accepted from him, just as with someone who prays to be seen by others.

But if a hypocrite or someone who acts to be seen by others repents, is he inwardly obliged to repeat those deeds? Or does his repentance extend retrospectively to his earlier deeds, so that he is rewarded for them? Or is he neither required to repeat them nor rewarded for them?

As for repeating them, the hypocrite is certainly not obliged to do so. A number of hypocrites repented of their hypocrisy during the lifetime of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and he did not command any of them to repeat their deeds.

Moreover, the hypocrite is inwardly a disbeliever. When he comes to believe, his past is forgiven, so he is not required to make up those deeds, just as an open disbeliever is not required to do so upon embracing Islam.

As for whether, upon repenting, he is rewarded for his earlier deeds, his case resembles that of a disbeliever who does good deeds during his disbelief and then embraces Islam: is he rewarded for them? It is reported in the two Sahīh collections that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to Hakīm ibn Hizām:

“You have embraced Islam with the good you did before.”

As for someone who repents of showing off, having believed all along that the deed was obligatory, his case resembles the issue we are discussing: that of someone who has not committed himself to fulfilling what is obligatory, even if he is not inwardly a disbeliever. Requiring him to make up those deeds would be a powerful deterrent to repentance.

A man may spend a long period praying without paying zakat, and perhaps without fasting either. He pays no heed to whether his wealth comes from lawful or unlawful sources, nor does he observe the limits governing marriage, divorce, and other matters. I know some righteous people who wish they had been disbelievers so that they could embrace Islam and have their past forgiven. They consider repentance impossible or exceedingly difficult because of what they have been told, and have come to believe, about its requirements. Moreover, this deters most sinful people from repentance and is akin to making people despair of Allah’s mercy. It places heavy burdens and mighty shackles upon those who repent, whom Allah loves. For Allah loves those who constantly repent and those who purify themselves. Allah rejoices more at His servant’s repentance than someone who recovers the wealth on which his livelihood depends after having despaired of recovering it.

This issue therefore needs careful examination. A disbeliever is not absolved of the obligations he neglected and the forbidden acts he committed on the grounds that he was excused in his disbelief, like a scholar exercising independent judgment; for there is no disagreement that he is not excused. Rather, he is forgiven because embracing Islam is repentance, and repentance wipes away what came before it. Repentance is repentance from neglecting belief and affirmation, as well as from neglecting deeds and actions. It would therefore seem appropriate—and Allah knows best—to treat these people’s condition during their time of ignorance like that of others.

If the speaker meant that Allah commanded them to pray in the sense that He made prayer obligatory upon them, then the second man is correct. But if he meant that they are commanded—that is, that men command them to pray because Allah has commanded those men to instruct them—or that prayer is recommended for children, then the speaker is correct.

As for the statement, “This is not a command from Allah”: if the person means that it is not a command from Allah addressed to children, but rather a command addressed to those who instruct children, then he is correct. But if he means that this is not a command from Allah addressed to anyone, then this is an error which he must retract, and he must seek Allah’s forgiveness. Allah knows best.

No one may delay daytime prayer until night, or nighttime prayer until day, because of any occupation or concern—whether harvesting, ploughing, practising a craft, being in a state of major ritual impurity, the presence of impurity, hunting, amusement, play, serving a master, or anything else. It is therefore not permissible to delay prayer beyond its appointed time because of major or minor ritual impurity, the presence of an impure substance, or any other reason. Rather, one must pray within the appointed time as one’s circumstances allow. Someone in a state of minor ritual impurity who cannot find water or fears harm from using it must perform dry ablution and pray. Likewise, someone in a state of major ritual impurity must perform dry ablution and pray if he cannot find water or fears harm from using it because of illness or cold. Similarly, someone who is naked must pray naked within the appointed time, rather than delay the prayer until after its time has passed in order to pray clothed. Someone who has an impure substance on him that he cannot remove must likewise pray within the appointed time as his circumstances allow. The sick person, too, must pray within the appointed time as his condition permits, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to Imrān ibn Husayn:

“Pray standing; if you cannot, then sitting; and if you cannot, then lying on your side.”

The scholars therefore agree that a sick person must pray within the appointed time, sitting or lying on his side if standing would worsen his illness, rather than pray standing after the time has passed. All of this is because performing prayer within its appointed time is obligatory, and observing that time is the most binding of the obligations of prayer. Likewise, fasting the month of Ramadan is obligatory at its appointed time, and no one may postpone it beyond that time. translated_text:
This further demonstrates that observing prayer at its appointed time is more emphatically required than observing the fast at its appointed time. Allah Most High says:

“Then they were succeeded by generations who neglected prayer and followed their desires.”

Some of the early generations said: “Neglecting it means delaying it beyond its appointed time. Had they abandoned it altogether, they would have been disbelievers.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: “After me there will be rulers who delay prayer beyond its appointed time. So perform the prayer at its appointed time, then regard your prayer with them as voluntary.”

Muslim narrated from Abū Dharr, who said: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: “What will you do when you have rulers over you who delay prayer beyond its appointed time and postpone it beyond its appointed time?”

I said: “What, then, do you command me to do?”

He said: “Perform the prayer at its appointed time. Then, if you happen to join them for it, pray, for it will count as a voluntary prayer for you.”

Ubādah ibn al-Sāmit narrated that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: “You will have rulers over you whose affairs distract them from performing prayer at its appointed time until its time has passed. So perform the prayer at its appointed time.”

A man asked: “Should I pray with them?”

He said: “Yes, if you wish; regard it as a voluntary prayer.” Narrated by Ahmad and Abū Dāwūd.

It was also narrated by Abd Allāh ibn Masʿūd, who said: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: “What will you do when you have rulers over you who perform prayer outside its appointed time?”

I said: “What do you command me to do if I live to see that, O Messenger of Allah?”

He said: “Perform the prayer at its appointed time, and regard your prayer with them as voluntary.”

For this reason, the scholars agree that if a man is without clothing—for example, in the event of the wreck of

the ship he is aboard, or because highwaymen have stripped him of his clothes—he must pray unclothed within the appointed time. Likewise, the scholars agree that a traveler who has no water must perform dry ablution and pray within the appointed time, even if water will be available after that time has passed. Similarly, a traveler in a state of major ritual impurity who has no water must perform dry ablution and pray. The four imams and others agree that he need not repeat the prayer.

Likewise, if the cold is severe and he fears that bathing would make him ill, he must perform dry ablution and pray within the appointed time, rather than delay the prayer until after its time so that he can pray after bathing. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Clean earth is a means of purification for a Muslim, even if he finds no water for ten years. But when you find water, let it touch your skin, for that is better.”

Everything permitted through purification with water is also permitted through dry ablution. Thus, if someone performs dry ablution for an obligatory prayer, he may recite the Quran both within and outside the prayer, even if he is in a state of major ritual impurity. Whoever refuses to pray with dry ablution is of the same kind as the Jews and Christians, for dry ablution is exclusive to the community of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. As the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said in an authentic hadith:

“We have been favored over other people in three ways: our ranks have been made like the ranks of the angels; the earth has been made a place of prayer for me, and its soil a means of purification; and the spoils of war have been made lawful for me, though they were not lawful for anyone before me.”

Another wording states:

“The earth has been made a place of prayer and a means of purification for me. Thus, wherever a man of my community finds himself when prayer is due, he has his place of prayer and his means of purification at hand.”

The scholars have differed over whether dry ablution may be performed before the prayer’s time begins, whether it must be performed for each prayer, and whether it becomes invalid when the prayer’s time ends; or whether one may pray as many prayers as one wishes, just as one does after purification with water

and it is invalidated only by what invalidates ablution or by becoming able to use water? This is the position of Abū Hanīfa and one of the views within the school of Ahmad and others. For the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Clean earth is a means of purification for a Muslim, even if he finds no water for ten years. But when you find water, let it touch your skin, for that is better.”

Al-Tirmidhī graded this hadith sound and authentic.

If someone has a ritual impurity on him and has nothing with which to remove it, he must pray within the appointed time with the impurity still on him, just as ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb prayed while his wound was bleeding, rather than delaying the prayer until its time had passed.

Concerning someone who can find only a ritually impure garment, some scholars say that he should pray unclothed; others say that he should pray in it and repeat the prayer; and still others say that he should pray in it without repeating the prayer. This last view is the most correct scholarly opinion. Allah has not commanded a person to perform an obligatory prayer twice unless, on the first occasion, he failed to fulfil a requirement that he was capable of fulfilling. For example, someone who prays without due composure must repeat the prayer, as related in the report:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, instructed a man who had prayed without due composure to repeat the prayer. He said, ‘Go back and pray, for you have not prayed.’”

Likewise, someone who forgets to purify himself and prays without ablution must repeat the prayer, as related in the report:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, instructed a man who had performed ablution but left a patch on his foot untouched by water to repeat both his ablution and his prayer.”

translated_text:
As for someone who has done what he was commanded to do to the extent of his ability, Allah Most High has said:

“So fear Allah as much as you are able.”

And the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“When I command you to do something, do as much of it as you can.”

If someone is awake during the appointed prayer time, but water is so far away that he cannot reach it until the time has ended, he must pray within the appointed time after performing dry ablution, by agreement of the scholars. Likewise, if the cold is severe, cold water would harm him, and he cannot reach a bathhouse or heat water before the time ends, he must pray within the appointed time after performing dry ablution.

Women and men are alike in this regard. If they are in a state of major ritual impurity and cannot take a ritual bath before the time ends, they must pray within the appointed time after performing dry ablution. If a woman’s menstrual bleeding stops during the appointed prayer time, but she cannot take a ritual bath until after that time has ended, she must perform dry ablution and pray within the appointed time. Whoever thinks that praying after the appointed time with purification using water is better than praying within the appointed time with dry ablution is misguided and ignorant.

If someone wakes up near the end of the dawn prayer’s appointed time, and taking a ritual bath would mean that the sun would rise before he could pray, the majority of scholars say that he should take a ritual bath and pray after sunrise. This is the position of Abū Hanīfa, al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad, and one of the two views in Mālik’s school. According to the other view, however, he should perform dry ablution in this case too and pray before sunrise

as in the cases discussed above, because praying within the appointed time after dry ablution is better than praying afterward with a ritual bath. The correct view, however, is that of the majority, because for someone who has been asleep, the appointed time begins when he wakes up. As the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever sleeps through a prayer or forgets it, let him pray it when he remembers it, for that is its appointed time.”

Thus, for someone who has been asleep, the appointed time begins when he wakes up; the period before that was not its appointed time for him. Accordingly, if he wakes before sunrise but cannot take a ritual bath and pray until after sunrise, he has prayed within his appointed time and has not missed it. This is unlike someone who wakes at the beginning of the appointed time: for him, the appointed time is before sunrise, so he may not let the prayer’s time pass.

Likewise, someone who has forgotten a prayer and then remembers it should take a ritual bath and pray at that point, whatever time it may be, for that is its appointed time for him. If he does not wake until after sunrise—as happened to the Prophet’s Companions, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, when they slept through the prayer in the year of Khaybar—he should pray with complete ritual purification, even if he delays the prayer until the sun passes its zenith. Thus, supposing he is in a state of major ritual impurity, he should enter the bathhouse and take a ritual bath, even if he delays the prayer until nearly that time. He should not pray after dry ablution in this case.

It is recommended that he move away from the place where he slept, just as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his Companions moved away from the place where they had slept. He said:

“This is a place where Satan was present among us.”

Ahmad and others explicitly stated this. If, however, he prays there, his prayer is valid.

translated_text:
If it is asked, “Is this considered making up a missed prayer (qadā’) or performing it within its appointed time (adā’)?” the answer is:

The distinction between these two expressions is merely terminological; it has no basis in the words of Allah and His Messenger. Allah Most High has described performing an act of worship within its appointed time as qadā’, as He says concerning the Friday prayer:

“And when the prayer has been concluded, disperse throughout the land.”

And He Most High says:

“And when you have completed your rites, remember Allah.”

Yet both these acts are performed within their appointed times. In the Arabic language, qadā’ means completing and finishing something, as Allah Most High says:

“And He completed them as seven heavens.”

That is, He completed and finished them. Thus, whoever performs an act of worship in full has completed it—qadā’—even when he performs it within its appointed time.

As far as I know, the scholars agree that if someone believes that the prayer’s appointed time remains and intends it as adā’, but subsequently discovers that he prayed after its time had ended, his prayer is valid. For his prayer would likewise suffice if he believed that its time had ended and intended it as qadā’, but subsequently discovered that its time still remained.

Anyone who performs the act of worship at the time he has been commanded to observe it has fulfilled his obligation in prayer, whether he intended it as adā’ or qadā’. The Friday prayer is valid whether he intends it as adā’ or qadā’, provided that by qadā’ he means the completion mentioned in the Quran.

When someone who has been asleep or has forgotten a prayer prays upon waking or remembering, he has prayed at the time he was commanded to pray, even though he has prayed after the time prescribed for others has ended. Thus, if someone calls this qadā’ in that sense, and in his terminology qadā’ means performing an act of worship after the time prescribed by Islamic law

He replied:

As for the daytime work that Allah does not accept at night, and the nighttime work that Allah does not accept by day, these are the Zuhr and ʿAsr prayers. It is not permissible for a person to delay them until night. Indeed, it is authentically reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever misses the ʿAsr prayer is as though he had been bereft of his family and wealth.”

It is also reported in Sahīh al-Bukhārī that he said:

“Whoever misses the ʿAsr prayer, his deeds are rendered void.”

As for someone who sleeps through a prayer or forgets it, he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever sleeps through a prayer or forgets it should pray it when he remembers it, for that is its appointed time.”

But whoever deliberately lets its time pass has committed one of the gravest major sins. According to the majority of scholars, he must make it up; according to some, performing it as a make-up prayer is not valid at all. Even when he makes it up, he has not discharged his obligation in full, nor does Allah accept it from him in such a way that his punishment is lifted and he becomes entitled to reward. Rather, He lessens his punishment on account of the prayer he has made up, while the sin of deliberately missing its time remains. This is among the sins that require some other means of expiation. He is like someone who owes two duties, fulfils one, and leaves the other unfulfilled.

Allah Most High says:

“So woe to those who pray, who are heedless of their prayer.”

The scholars agree that delaying prayer beyond its appointed time is a form of being heedless of it. Allah Most High also says:

“But they were succeeded by generations who neglected prayer and followed their desires; they will meet with ruin.”

Several of the early generations said that neglecting it means delaying it

He replied:

If someone abandons prayer because he does not believe it to be obligatory, he is a disbeliever according to the scriptural texts and scholarly consensus.  وَنَحْوُهُ. فَإِنَّمَا يَدُلُّ عَلَى وُجُوبِ تَكْمِيلِ الْوُضُوءِ لَيْسَ فِي ذَلِكَ أَمْرٌ بِإِعَادَةِ شَيْءٍ وَمَنْ كَانَ أَيْضًا يَعْتَقِدُ أَنَّ الصَّلَاةَ تَسْقُطُ عَنْ الْعَارِفِينَ، أَوْ عَنْ الْمَشَايِخِ الْوَاصِلِينَ، أَوْ عَنْ بَعْضِ أَتْبَاعِهِمْ، أَوْ أَنَّ الشَّيْخَ يُصَلِّي عَنْهُمْ، أَوْ أَنَّ لِلَّهِ عِبَادًا
translated_text:
—it was clear that what the man had done was not prayer. Yet the Prophet had not known that he was unaware of the obligation to come to rest in the postures of prayer. He therefore initially instructed him to repeat it, then taught him to come to rest when the man said:

“By Him Who sent you with the truth, I cannot do any better than this.”

These, then, are his explicit statements—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—concerning acts prohibited in prayer, fasting and Hajj when committed in ignorance, and those who omit their obligatory elements out of ignorance.

As for his instruction that the person who prayed behind the row repeat his prayer, this was because he had failed to fulfil an obligation while the prayer time still remained. The obligation thus became binding upon him when the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, instructed him, since the time for fulfilling it had not yet ended. He did not instruct him to do this after the time had passed.

As for his instruction that the person who left a patch of his foot untouched by water repeat his ablution and prayer, this was because the man had forgotten and had therefore failed to fulfil an obligation, like someone who forgets to pray. The prayer time also still remained. This was a particular incident involving a specific individual; it could not have occurred both within the prayer time and after it. I mean that he saw a patch on a man’s foot which the water had not reached, so he instructed him to repeat his ablution and prayer. Abū Dāwūd narrated it, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal said, “It is a good hadith.”

As for his words:

“Woe to the heels from the Fire!”

and similar statements, these indicate only that ablution must be completed thoroughly. They contain no instruction to repeat anything.

Likewise, anyone who believes that prayer is no longer obligatory for those with spiritual knowledge, or for shaykhs who have attained spiritual realization, or for some of their followers; or that the shaykh prays on their behalf; or that Allah has servants

original_text:
أَسْقَطَ عَنْهُمْ الصَّلَاةَ، كَمَا يُوجَدُ كَثِيرٌ مِنْ ذَلِكَ فِي كَثِيرٍ مِنْ الْمُنْتَسِبِينَ إلَى الْفَقْرِ وَالزُّهْدِ، وَاتِّبَاعِ بَعْضِ الْمَشَايِخِ وَالْمُعَرِّفَةِ، فَهَؤُلَاءِ يُسْتَتَابُونَ بِاتِّفَاقِ الْأَئِمَّةِ، فَإِنْ أَقَرُّوا بِالْوُجُوبِ، وَإِلَّا قُوتِلُوا، وَإِذَا أَصَرُّوا عَلَى جَحْدِ الْوُجُوبِ حَتَّى قُتِلُوا، كَانُوا مِنْ الْمُرْتَدِّينَ، وَمَنْ تَابَ مِنْهُمْ وَصَلَّى لَمْ يَكُنْ عَلَيْهِ إعَادَةُ مَا تَرَكَ قَبْلَ ذَلِكَ فِي أَظْهَرِ قَوْلَيْ الْعُلَمَاءِ، فَإِنَّ هَؤُلَاءِ إمَّا أَنْ يَكُونُوا مُرْتَدِّينَ، وَإِمَّا أَنْ يَكُونُوا مُسْلِمِينَ جَاهِلِينَ لِلْوُجُوبِ.

 إنَّهُمْ مُرْتَدُّونَ عَنْ الْإِسْلَامِ، فَالْمُرْتَدُّ إذَا أَسْلَمَ لَا يَقْضِي مَا تَرَكَهُ حَالَ الرِّدَّةِ عِنْدَ جُمْهُورِ الْعُلَمَاءِ، كَمَا لَا يَقْضِي الْكَافِرُ إذَا أَسْلَمَ مَا تَرَكَ حَالَ الْكُفْرِ بِاتِّفَاقِ الْعُلَمَاءِ، وَمَذْهَبُ مَالِكٍ وَأَبِي حَنِيفَةَ وَأَحْمَد فِي أَظْهَرِ الرِّوَايَتَيْنِ عَنْهُ، وَالْأُخْرَى يَقْضِي الْمُرْتَدُّ. كَقَوْلِ الشَّافِعِيِّ وَالْأَوَّلُ أَظْهَرُ. فَإِنَّ الَّذِينَ ارْتَدُّوا عَلَى عَهْدِ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ كَالْحَارِثِ ابْنِ قَيْسٍ،
 وَطَائِفَةٍ مَعَهُ أَنْزَلَ اللَّهُ فِيهِمْ:
 
{كَيْفَ يَهْدِي اللَّهُ قَوْمًا كَفَرُوا بَعْدَ إيمَانِهِمْ}
 الْآيَةَ، وَاَلَّتِي بَعْدَهَا. وَكَعَبْدِ اللَّهِ بْنِ أَبِي سَرْحٍ، وَاَلَّذِينَ خَرَجُوا مَعَ الْكُفَّارِ يَوْمَ بَدْرٍ،
 وَأَنْزَلَ فِيهِمْ:
 
{ثُمَّ إنَّ رَبَّكَ لِلَّذِينَ هَاجَرُوا مِنْ بَعْدِ مَا فُتِنُوا ثُمَّ جَاهَدُوا وَصَبَرُوا إنَّ رَبَّكَ مِنْ بَعْدِهَا لَغَفُورٌ رَحِيمٌ}
 فَهَؤُلَاءِ عَادُوا إلَى الْإِسْلَامِ، وَعَبْدُ اللَّهِ بْنُ أَبِي سَرْحٍ عَادَ إلَى الْإِسْلَامِ عَامَ الْفَتْحِ، وَبَايَعَهُ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ وَلَمْ يَأْمُرْ أَحَدًا
translated_text:
whom He has exempted from prayer—as is often found among those who profess spiritual poverty, asceticism, adherence to certain shaykhs, and spiritual knowledge—such people must be called upon to repent, by agreement of the imams. If they acknowledge that prayer is obligatory, that suffices; otherwise, they are to be fought. If they persist in denying its obligation until they are killed, they are counted among the apostates. Whoever among them repents and prays is not required to make up the prayers previously omitted, according to the stronger of the two scholarly views. For these people are either apostates or Muslims unaware that prayer is obligatory.

If it is said that they are apostates from Islam, then, according to the majority of scholars, an apostate who returns to Islam does not make up the prayers omitted during apostasy, just as, by scholarly agreement, a disbeliever who embraces Islam does not make up the prayers omitted during disbelief. This is the position of Mālik, Abū Hanīfa, and Ahmad, according to the stronger of the two reports from him. According to the other report, an apostate must make them up, as al-Shāfiʿī held. The former view is stronger.

For among those who apostatized during the lifetime of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, were al-Hārith ibn Qays and a group with him, concerning whom Allah revealed:

“How will Allah guide a people who disbelieved after having believed?”

—the remainder of the verse and the verse that follows it. Others included ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Sarh and those who went out with the disbelievers on the day of Badr, concerning whom He revealed:

“Then your Lord, for those who emigrated after being put to trial, then strove and remained steadfast—surely your Lord, after that, is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.”

These people returned to Islam. ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Sarh returned to Islam in the year of the Conquest, and the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, accepted his pledge of allegiance. He did not instruct anyone

 وَقَوْلُهُ تَعَالَى:
 
{قُلْ لِلَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا إنْ يَنْتَهُوا يُغْفَرْ لَهُمْ مَا قَدْ سَلَفَ}
 يَتَنَاوَلُ كُلَّ كَافِرٍ.
 وَإِنْ قِيلَ:
 إنَّ هَؤُلَاءِ لَمْ يَكُونُوا مُرْتَدِّينَ، بَلْ جُهَّالًا بِالْوُجُوبِ، وَقَدْ تَقَدَّمَ أَنَّ الْأَظْهَرَ فِي حَقِّ هَؤُلَاءِ أَنَّهُمْ يَسْتَأْنِفُونَ الصَّلَاةَ عَلَى الْوَجْهِ الْمَأْمُورِ، وَلَا قَضَاءَ عَلَيْهِمْ. فَهَذَا حُكْمُ مَنْ تَرَكَهَا غَيْرَ مُعْتَقِدٍ لِوُجُوبِهَا.
 وَأَمَّا مَنْ اعْتَقَدَ وُجُوبَهَا مَعَ إصْرَارِهِ عَلَى تَرْكِ:
 فَقَدْ ذَكَرَ عَلَيْهِ الْمُفَرِّعُونَ مِنْ الْفُقَهَاءِ فُرُوعًا:
translated_text:
of them to make up the prayers they had omitted while in a state of disbelief during their apostasy, just as he did not instruct other disbelievers to do so when they embraced Islam. During his lifetime, many people apostatized and followed al-Aswad al-ʿAnsī, who claimed prophethood in Sanaa, Yemen. Then Allah brought about his death, and those people returned to Islam without being instructed to make up their prayers. Musaylima the Liar also claimed prophethood, and many people followed him. After the Prophet’s death, al-Siddīq and the Companions fought them until they brought the survivors back to Islam. He did not instruct any of them to make up their prayers. The same applies to the other apostates after the Prophet’s death. Most of the desert-dwellers had apostatized and then returned to Islam, yet he did not instruct any of them to make up the prayers they had omitted.

Allah’s words:

“Tell those who disbelieve that if they desist, their past will be forgiven.”

apply to every disbeliever.

If, however, it is said that these people were not apostates but were unaware that prayer was obligatory, it has already been explained that the stronger view concerning them is that they should begin praying in the prescribed manner, without having to make up past prayers. This, then, is the ruling concerning someone who abandons prayer without believing it to be obligatory.

As for someone who believes it to be obligatory yet persists in abandoning it, jurists who elaborate hypothetical cases have set out several cases concerning him:

original_text:
أَحَدُهَا هَذَا،

{لَيْسَ بَيْنَ الْعَبْدِ وَبَيْنَ الْكُفْرِ إلَّا تَرْكُ الصَّلَاةِ}
 رَوَاهُ مُسْلِمٌ.

{الْعَهْدُ الَّذِي بَيْنَنَا وَبَيْنَهُمْ الصَّلَاةُ فَمَنْ تَرَكَهَا فَقَدْ كَفَرَ}
 .
 وَقَوْلِ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ بْنِ شَقِيقٍ:
 كَانَ أَصْحَابُ مُحَمَّدٍ لَا يَرَوْنَ شَيْئًا مِنْ الْأَعْمَالِ فِي تَرْكِهِ كُفْرٌ إلَّا الصَّلَاةَ، فَمَنْ كَانَ مُصِرًّا عَلَى تَرْكِهَا حَتَّى يَمُوتَ لَا يَسْجُدُ لِلَّهِ سَجْدَةً قَطُّ، فَهَذَا لَا يَكُونُ قَطُّ مُسْلِمًا مُقِرًّا بِوُجُوبِهَا، فَإِنَّ اعْتِقَادَ
translated_text:
One of them is this case. A view concerning it is attributed to the majority of them: Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, and Ahmad. If he holds out until he is put to death, is he executed as a disbelieving apostate, or as a sinner like other sinful Muslims? There are two well-known opinions, both reported from Ahmad.

These hypothetical cases were not transmitted from the Companions, and they are unsound. For if he inwardly acknowledges prayer and believes it obligatory, it is impossible for him to persist in abandoning it until he is put to death without praying. Such conduct is unknown among human beings and contrary to their customary behaviour. For this reason, this has never occurred in Islam. No one is known to have believed prayer obligatory and been told, “Unless you pray, we will kill you,” yet persisted in abandoning it while acknowledging its obligation. This has never occurred in Islam.

Whenever a man refuses to pray even at the cost of being put to death, he does not inwardly acknowledge its obligation or commit himself to performing it. Such a person is a disbeliever by the agreement of the Muslims. Numerous reports from the Companions establish his disbelief, as do authentic scriptural texts, such as the Prophet’s words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Nothing stands between a servant and disbelief except abandoning prayer.”

Narrated by Muslim. He also said:

“The covenant between us and them is prayer; whoever abandons it has disbelieved.”

And ʿAbd Allāh ibn Shaqīq said:

“The Companions of Muhammad did not regard abandoning any deed as disbelief except prayer.”

Thus, someone who persists in abandoning prayer until he dies, never once prostrating to Allah, cannot possibly be a Muslim who acknowledges its obligation. For belief in

 وَهُمْ الَّذِينَ جَاءَ فِيهِمْ الْحَدِيثُ الَّذِي فِي السُّنَنِ حَدِيثُ عبادة عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ أَنَّهُ قَالَ:
 
{خَمْسُ صَلَوَاتٍ كَتَبَهُنَّ اللَّهُ عَلَى الْعِبَادِ فِي الْيَوْمِ وَاللَّيْلَةِ مَنْ حَافَظَ عَلَيْهِنَّ كَانَ لَهُ عَهْدٌ عِنْدَ اللَّهِ أَنْ يُدْخِلَهُ الْجَنَّةَ، وَمَنْ لَمْ يُحَافَظْ عَلَيْهِنَّ لَمْ يَكُنْ لَهُ عَهْدٌ عِنْدَ اللَّهِ، إنْ شَاءَ عَذَّبَهُ وَإِنْ شَاءَ غَفَرَ لَهُ.}
 فَالْمُحَافِظُ عَلَيْهَا الَّذِي يُصَلِّيهَا فِي مَوَاقِيتِهَا، كَمَا أَمَرَ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى، وَاَلَّذِي يُؤَخِّرُهَا أَحْيَانًا عَنْ وَقْتِهَا، أَوْ يَتْرُكُ وَاجِبَاتِهَا، فَهَذَا تَحْتَ مَشِيئَةِ اللَّهِ تَعَالَى، وَقَدْ يَكُونُ لِهَذَا نَوَافِلُ يُكَمِّلُ بِهَا فَرَائِضَهُ، كَمَا جَاءَ فِي الْحَدِيثِ.
translated_text:
its obligation, together with the belief that whoever abandons it deserves to be put to death, constitutes a fully sufficient motive for performing it. Such a motive, when accompanied by the ability to act, necessarily brings about the act. Thus, if someone is able to pray yet never does so, it is known that this motive is absent in his case. Firm belief in the punishment for abandoning prayer prompts a person to perform it. Sometimes, however, other factors may counteract this, causing him to delay it, neglect some of its obligatory elements, or occasionally miss it altogether.

As for someone who persists in abandoning prayer, never prays at all, and dies persisting in this abandonment, such a person is not a Muslim. Most people, however, pray at times and abandon prayer at others. They do not observe it consistently and are subject to the threat of punishment. It is they who are referred to in the hadith recorded in the Sunan collections, narrated by Ubādah from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, who said:

“Allah has prescribed five prayers for His servants each day and night. Whoever observes them consistently has a covenant with Allah that He will admit him to Paradise. Whoever does not observe them consistently has no covenant with Allah: if He wills, He will punish him, and if He wills, He will forgive him.”

The one who observes prayer consistently is the one who performs it at its appointed times, as Allah Most High has commanded. Whoever sometimes delays it beyond its appointed time or neglects its obligatory elements is subject to the will of Allah Most High. Such a person may have voluntary prayers through which the deficiencies in his obligatory prayers are made up, as mentioned in the hadith.

وَسُئِلَ:
عَمَّنْ يُؤْمَرُ بِالصَّلَاةِ فَيَمْتَنِعُ، وَمَاذَا يَجِبُ عَلَيْهِ؟
 وَمَنْ اعْتَذَرَ بِقَوْلِهِ:
 
{أُمِرْت أَنْ أُقَاتِلَ النَّاسَ حَتَّى يَقُولُوا لَا إلَهَ إلَّا اللَّهُ}
 هَلْ يَكُونُ لَهُ عُذْرٌ فِي أَنَّهُ لَا يُعَاقَبُ عَلَى تَرْكِ الصَّلَاةِ، أَمْ لَا؟ وَمَاذَا يَجِبُ عَلَى الْأُمَرَاءِ وَوُلَاةِ الْأُمُورِ فِي حَقِّ مَنْ تَحْتَ أَيْدِيهِمْ إذَا تَرَكُوا الصَّلَاةَ؟ وَهَلْ قِيَامُهُمْ فِي ذَلِكَ مِنْ أَعْظَمِ الْجِهَادِ وَأَكْبَرِ أَبْوَابِ الْبِرِّ؟.
فَأَجَابَ:
الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ، مَنْ يَمْتَنِعُ عَنْ الصَّلَاةِ الْمَفْرُوضَةِ فَإِنَّهُ يَسْتَحِقُّ الْعُقُوبَةَ الْغَلِيظَةَ بِاتِّفَاقِ أَئِمَّةِ الْمُسْلِمِينَ،
 بَلْ يَجِبُ عِنْدَ جُمْهُورِ الْأُمَّةِ:
 كَمَالِكِ، وَالشَّافِعِيِّ، وَأَحْمَد، وَغَيْرِهِمْ أَنْ يُسْتَتَابَ، فَإِنْ تَابَ وَإِلَّا قُتِلَ. بَلْ تَارِكُ الصَّلَاةِ شَرٌّ مِنْ السَّارِقِ وَالزَّانِي، وَشَارِبِ الْخَمْرِ، وَآكِلِ الْحَشِيشَةِ. وَيَجِبُ عَلَى كُلِّ مُطَاعٍ أَنْ يَأْمُرَ مَنْ يُطِيعُهُ بِالصَّلَاةِ، حَتَّى الصِّغَارَ الَّذِينَ لَمْ يَبْلُغُوا، قَالَ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ 
{مُرُوهُمْ بِالصَّلَاةِ لِسَبْعِ وَاضْرِبُوهُمْ عَلَيْهَا لِعَشْرِ، وَفَرِّقُوا بَيْنَهُمْ فِي الْمَضَاجِعِ}
 .
translated_text:
He was asked:

What is to be done about someone who is ordered to pray but refuses? If someone invokes the words, “I have been commanded to fight the people until they say, ‘There is no god but Allah,’” as an excuse, does this excuse him from punishment for abandoning prayer, or not? What must rulers and those in authority do regarding those under their authority who abandon prayer? Are their efforts in this regard among the greatest forms of jihad and the foremost avenues of righteousness?

He answered:

Praise be to Allah. Whoever refuses to perform the obligatory prayers deserves severe punishment, by agreement of the leading Muslim scholars. Indeed, according to the majority of the Muslim community, including Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, Ahmad and others, he must be called upon to repent and, if he does not repent, be executed. Indeed, one who abandons prayer is worse than a thief, a fornicator, a wine-drinker or one who consumes hashish.

Everyone in a position of authority must command those who obey him to pray, even children who have not yet reached puberty. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Command them to pray at seven, beat them for neglecting it at ten, and have them sleep in separate beds.”

 كَمَا قَالَ تَعَالَى:
 
{وَقَاتِلُوهُمْ حَتَّى لَا تَكُونَ فِتْنَةٌ وَيَكُونَ الدِّينُ كُلُّهُ لِلَّهِ}
 .
 وَقَدْ قَالَ تَعَالَى:
 
{يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا اتَّقُوا اللَّهَ وَذَرُوا مَا بَقِيَ مِنَ الرِّبَا إنْ كُنْتُمْ مُؤْمِنِينَ}
 
{فَإِنْ لَمْ تَفْعَلُوا فَأْذَنُوا بِحَرْبٍ مِنَ اللَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِ}
 .
translated_text:
Anyone who has a minor in his care—whether a slave, an orphan, or his own child—and fails to command him to pray is to be punished for failing to command the child. The adult is to receive severe disciplinary punishment for this, because he has disobeyed Allah and His Messenger.

Likewise, anyone who has adult slaves, attendants tending horses, camels or falcons, chamber attendants, bābiyya attendants who wash bodies and clothes, servants, a wife, a concubine or female slaves must command all of them to pray. If he does not, he is disobedient to Allah and His Messenger. Such a person does not deserve to belong to the Muslim troops, but rather to the Tatar troops. The Tatars pronounce the two testimonies of faith, yet fighting them is obligatory by the consensus of the Muslims.

Likewise, any group that refuses to abide by even one of the known prescriptions of Islam, whether outward or inward, must be fought.

If they say, “We bear witness, but we will not pray,” they are to be fought until they pray.

If they say, “We will pray, but we will not pay zakat,” they are to be fought until they pay zakat.

If they say, “We will pay zakat, but we will neither fast nor perform Hajj,” they are to be fought until they fast Ramadan and perform the pilgrimage to the House.

If they say, “We will do this, but we will not give up usury, drinking wine or shameful deeds; nor will we fight in Allah’s cause or levy the jizya tax on Jews and Christians,” or anything similar, they are to be fought until they comply.

As the Most High says:

“Fight them until there is no more persecution and all religion is for Allah.”

The Most High also says:

“O you who believe, fear Allah and give up what remains due to you of usury, if you are believers.”

“If you do not, then be warned of war from Allah and His Messenger.”

And usury was the last thing Allah prohibited. The people of al-Tā’if had embraced Islam, prayed and fought in Allah’s cause, yet Allah made clear that if they did not desist from usury, they would be among those who waged war against Allah and His Messenger.

It is related in the two Sahīh collections that when the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, died and some of the Arabs disbelieved, ‘Umar said to Abū Bakr:

“How can you fight the people when the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, ‘I have been commanded to fight the people until they testify that there is no god but Allah and that I am the Messenger of Allah. Once they do so, their lives and property are protected from me, except by right’?”

Abū Bakr replied: “Did he not say, ‘except by right’? By Allah, if they withheld from me an ‘iqāl that they used to render to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, I would fight them over it.”

‘Umar said: “By Allah, as soon as I saw that Allah had opened Abū Bakr’s heart to fighting, I knew that it was right.”

It is also related in the Sahīh that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, mentioned the Khawārij and said:

“Any one of you would consider his own prayer insignificant compared with theirs, his fasting compared with theirs, and his recitation compared with theirs. They recite the Quran, but it does not pass beyond their throats. They pass out of Islam as an arrow passes through its quarry. Wherever you encounter them, kill them, for whoever kills them will have a reward with Allah on the Day of Resurrection.”

He was asked:

People tell a man to pray, but he does not pray. What is incumbent upon him?

He answered:

If he does not pray, he is to be called upon to repent. If he repents, well and good; otherwise, he is to be put to death. And Allah knows best.

He was asked:

If someone deliberately omits a single prayer, intending to make it up after its prescribed time has ended, does his action constitute a major sin?

He answered:

Praise be to Allah. Yes, deliberately delaying a prayer beyond the time when it must be performed is a major sin. translated_text:
said:

“Whoever combines two prayers without a valid excuse has entered one of the gates of major sins.”

He attributed this to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, although that attribution is open to question. Al-Tirmidhī said: “This is the practice followed by the scholars.” The report is well known, and scholars have cited it approvingly, not rejecting it.

In the Sahīh, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever misses the afternoon prayer, his deeds have come to nothing.”

Such a warning—that one’s deeds will come to nothing—is given only for the gravest major sins. Moreover, missing the afternoon prayer is more serious than missing any other prayer, for it is the middle prayer, singled out by the command to observe it diligently. It was prescribed for those before us, but they neglected it; whoever observes it diligently will therefore receive twice the reward. It was also this prayer that Solomon missed, whereupon he did what he did to the horses.

It is also narrated in the Sahīh that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever misses the afternoon prayer, it is as though he has been bereft of his family and wealth.”

Someone bereft of his family and wealth is left deprived, with neither family nor wealth to benefit him. His condition is like that of someone whose deeds have come to nothing.

Furthermore, Allah Most High says:

“So woe to those who pray—those who, with regard to their prayer,

are heedless.”

Thus, He threatens woe to those who neglect prayer until its appointed time has passed, even if they perform it afterward. Likewise, Allah Most High says:

“Then there came after them successors who neglected prayer and followed their desires; so they will meet with ruin.”

When Ibn Mas‘ūd was asked what neglecting prayer meant, he replied: “It means delaying it until its appointed time has passed.” They said: “We thought it meant nothing other than abandoning it.” He replied: “Had they abandoned it, they would have been disbelievers.” Ibn Mas‘ūd would say of certain governors of Kufa in his time, “What has your successor done?” because they used to delay prayer beyond its appointed time.

His words,

“and followed their desires,”

include everyone who pursues what he desires at the expense of observing prayer at its appointed time. This applies whether the desired things are forbidden—such as forbidden food, drink, sexual relations, or things to listen to—or permissible, though excess in them is forbidden, or anything else. Whoever is distracted from performing prayer on time by games, entertainment, conversation with his companions, strolling in his garden, developing his property, conducting his business, or anything else has neglected that prayer and followed his desires.

Allah Most High says:

“O you who believe, let neither your wealth nor your children distract you from the remembrance of Allah. Whoever does so—it is they who are the losers.”

Anyone whose wealth and children distract him from performing the obligatory prayer at its appointed time falls within this warning and is therefore a loser.

Describing those whose conduct is the opposite, Allah Most High says:

“Therein, morning and evening, He is glorified by men

whom neither commerce nor trade distracts from the remembrance of Allah, establishing prayer, and giving zakat.”

Since He, glorified be He, has threatened those who neglect prayer beyond its appointed time and follow their desires with ruin, and since anyone who delays prayer beyond its time because he is occupied with what he desires is neglecting it and following his desires, this shows that doing so is a major sin. Such a warning is issued only for a major sin. This is further supported by His describing such a person as a loser: loss does not result merely from minor sins, which are expiated by avoiding major sins.

Furthermore, no … (1) [one disputes that] whoever deliberately prays without ritual purification or facing a direction other than the qiblah, and intentionally omits bowing and prostration, recitation, or any other requirement, has thereby committed a major sin. Indeed, one may cautiously refrain from declaring him a disbeliever if he does not deem that lawful. If, however, he deems it lawful, he is undoubtedly a disbeliever.

It is well known that observing the appointed time for prayer takes precedence over these obligations and others. Muslims do not dispute that a traveller who has no water, but knows that he will find it after the prayer’s appointed time, may not delay the prayer in order to perform it afterward with ablution or a full ritual bath. Rather, that is what is obligatory. Likewise, regarding someone unable to bow, prostrate, or recite: if he deems it lawful, he is undoubtedly a disbeliever.

translated_text:
It is well known that even if he knows that, after the appointed time, he will be able to pray with full bowing, prostration, and recitation, he must pray within the appointed time, since he is able to do so.

As for the statement of some of our fellow jurists, “It is not permissible to delay prayer beyond its appointed time except for someone who intends to combine it with another prayer or is occupied with fulfilling one of its prerequisites,” no earlier jurist of our school said this, nor did anyone from any other Muslim school—except perhaps some of al-Shāfiʿī’s followers, though I am uncertain about that. There is no doubt that, by Muslim consensus, this statement cannot apply generally and without qualification. Rather, it concerns a familiar kind of case: someone reaches a well and can lower a rope to draw water, but will not finish until after the appointed time; or someone without clothing can sew himself a garment, but will not finish until after the appointed time; and similar cases.

Even so, what this jurist said concerning these cases contradicts the established position of Ahmad and his followers, as well as the position of the body of Muslim scholars among the Hanafīs, Mālikīs, and others. I know of no one who agrees with him on this except some of al-Shāfiʿī’s followers. Whoever holds this view is refuted by the Muslim consensus that merely being occupied with fulfilling a prerequisite does not permit delaying prayer beyond its legally prescribed time.

If the appointed time begins and someone can search for water but will not find it until after that time has ended, he may not delay the prayer, by agreement of the Muslims, even though he is occupied with fulfilling a prerequisite. Likewise, if someone without clothing can go to a village to buy himself a garment, but would not pray until after the appointed time has ended, he may not delay the prayer; there is no disagreement about this.

As for the well-known disagreement among the imams concerning someone who wakes near the end of the appointed time and cannot perform the prayer before sunrise if he first performs ablution: should he pray with dry ablution, or perform ablution and pray after sunrise? There are two well-known views:

The first is Mālik’s view, which gives consideration to the appointed time.

The second is the view of the majority, including Ahmad, al-Shāfiʿī, and Abū Hanīfah. This is the issue that has led some to mistakenly suppose that a prerequisite takes precedence over the appointed time. That is not so, for the appointed time for someone who has been asleep begins when he awakens. As established in an authentic hadith, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever sleeps through a prayer or forgets it should pray it when he remembers it, for that is its appointed time.”

Thus, he made the time at which Allah requires His servant to perform the prayer the time when he remembers or awakens. Accordingly, whoever performs it at that time, attaining the required ritual purity to the extent that he can, has performed it within its appointed time. He has neither been negligent nor neglected the prayer. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“There is no negligence in sleep; negligence occurs only when one is awake.”

This differs from the case of someone who is awake from the beginning of the appointed time, for he is commanded to perform the prayer within that time. Were he not commanded to perform it within that time, he could permissibly delay it while going somewhere to obtain water for purification or a garment to borrow, or attending to something similar. Rather, someone who awakens near the end of the appointed time need only perform ablution just as someone who awakens within that time does. But if he were to delay the prayer because he would find water at midday, for example, that would not be permissible.

Moreover, the scholars have explicitly stated that when the time for prayer arrives and a person does not pray, he is to be put to death, even if he says, “I will make it up later,” just as he is to be put to death if he says, “I will pray without ablution or facing a direction other than the qiblah.” If he deliberately omits any obligatory requirement of prayer upon which there is consensus, he is to be put to death for omitting it, just as he is for abandoning the prayer itself.

If we hold that he is to be put to death when the time remaining for the second or fourth prayer grows short, the matter is as stated. The same applies if we hold that he is to be put to death when the time remaining for the first prayer grows short—which is the correct view—or for the third. This depends on whether he is to be put to death for abandoning one prayer or three; there are two transmitted opinions on this.

If we hold that abandoning one prayer suffices, must one wait until the time of the following prayer, or is it enough that the remaining time for the neglected prayer grows short? There are two juristic views on this.

There is also a third view, which distinguishes between a pair of prayers that may be combined and other prayers.

translated_text:

As for the rulers who used to delay the prayer beyond its appointed time, whom the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, forbade fighting: if it is said that they merely delayed the prayer until the end of its time, there is no issue. But if it is said—and this is the correct view—that they let its time expire, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, commanded the Muslim community to pray within the appointed time, saying:

“Make your prayer with them a voluntary prayer.”

He forbade fighting them, just as he forbade fighting rulers when they appropriated things for themselves, wrongfully withheld people’s rights, and transgressed against them, even though major sins were committed in the course of this.

Anyone who delays the prayer beyond its appointed time is guilty of flagrant sin. Rulers are not to be fought merely because of their sinfulness, even though an individual within the authorities’ power may be put to death for certain forms of sin, such as unlawful sexual intercourse and the like. Not every act punishable by death therefore permits fighting rulers who commit it, for the harm caused by fighting is greater than the harm caused by a major sin committed by the ruler.

For this reason, some scholars among the followers of Ahmad and others explicitly stated that voluntary prayers may be offered behind sinful prayer leaders. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, commanded people to pray behind rulers who delayed the prayer until its time had expired. Such leaders are guilty of flagrant sin, yet he commanded that the prayer be offered behind them as a voluntary prayer.

The point is that incurring the status of a flagrant sinner by allowing a prayer’s time to expire is well recognized among the jurists.

But if someone were to say, “The major sin consists in continually missing prayers, for that constitutes persistence in a minor sin,” the response would be:

The evidence already presented shows that the threatened punishment applies to missing even a single prayer. Furthermore, persistence means resolving to repeat the sin. Someone who commits a minor sin, repents of it, and then returns to it has not thereby committed a major sin.

Moreover, whoever stipulates that prayers must be missed continually needs to provide a precise criterion. If he means continually throughout one’s entire life, those previously mentioned would not fall into this category. If he means a specified period, he must provide evidence for it.

Furthermore, imposing the death penalty for abandoning a single prayer goes further than classifying it as a major sin. And Allah, glorified be He, knows best.

translated_text:
He was asked:

“Does a Muslim who abandons prayer but performs the Friday prayer deserve to be cursed?”

He replied:

All praise is due to Allah. Such a person has incurred punishment by agreement of the Muslims. According to the majority of scholars, including Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, and Ahmad, he must be called upon to repent; if he does not repent, he must be executed.

Cursing those who abandon prayer in general terms is permissible. As for cursing a specific individual, it is preferable to refrain, since he may repent. And Allah knows best.
