translated_text:
at times in their sandals and at times barefoot, as narrated in the Sunan of Abū Dāwūd and Ibn Mājah from ‘Amr ibn Shu‘ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, who said:

“I saw the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, pray both barefoot and in sandals.”

The evidence afforded by praying in sandals is clear. As for praying barefoot, Abū Dāwūd and al-Nasā’ī narrated in their Sunan from ‘Abd Allāh ibn al-Sā’ib, who said:

“I saw the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, praying on the day of the Conquest, having placed his sandals to his left.”

Likewise, the previously mentioned hadith of Abū Sa‘īd in the Sunan of Abū Dāwūd states:

“While the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was leading his Companions in prayer, he took off his sandals and placed them to his left.”

The remainder of the hadith indicates that he was in the mosque, as explained earlier.

The same applies to the hadith of Ibn al-Sā’ib. Muslim, al-Nasā’ī and Ibn Mājah narrated the underlying account from ‘Abd Allāh ibn al-Sā’ib, who said:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, led us in the dawn prayer in Mecca and began reciting Surah al-Mu’minūn. When he reached the mention of Moses and Aaron—or the mention of Moses and Jesus—the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was seized by a cough, so he bowed.”

‘Abd Allāh ibn al-Sā’ib was present on that occasion. This therefore took place in the Sacred Mosque, and he placed his sandals inside the mosque despite knowing that people prayed and circumambulated in that very place. If taking precautions against impurity on the soles of sandals were recommended, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would have been foremost in performing this recommended act to protect the mosque.

Furthermore, Abū Dāwūd narrated in his Sunan from Sa‘īd ibn Abī Sa‘īd, from his father, from Abū Hurayra

from the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, who said:

“If any of you takes off his sandals when praying, he must not inconvenience anyone with them. Let him place them between his feet, or pray in them.”

It also contains a report from Yūsuf ibn Māhak, from Abū Hurayra, that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“When any of you prays, he should not place his sandals to his right, nor to his left, where they would be to someone else’s right—unless there is no one to his left. Let him place them between his feet.”

It has been said that there is some weakness in this hadith’s chain of transmission. Nevertheless, it and the first hadith agree that one should place them between one’s feet. Had taking precautions against their suspected impurity been prescribed, this would not have been the case. Moreover, the first report mentions praying in them, and the second mentions placing them to one’s left when no one is praying there. The stated disapproval of placing them to one’s own right or someone else’s right is not a precaution against impurity, but a matter of etiquette, just as spitting to one’s right is disliked.

In Sahīh Muslim, Khabbāb ibn al-Aratt said:

“We complained to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, about the intense heat of the ground against our foreheads and palms, but he did not grant us relief.”

Some have assumed that this additional wording is in Muslim, but that is not the case. The reason for their complaint was that they would prostrate on the ground, and their foreheads and palms would become hot. They asked him to delay the prayer beyond the delay he already observed to allow the heat to subside, but he did not do so. Some jurists have thought that they asked him

This argument is weak for two reasons:

First, the previously cited hadith of Anas, whose authenticity is agreed upon, states:

“When one of them could not place his forehead firmly on the ground, he would spread out his garment and prostrate on it.”

Prostrating on something attached to one’s person, such as one’s sleeve, hem, or the edge of one’s lower garment or cloak, is a well-known subject of disagreement. Hishām reported from al-Hasan al-Basrī: “The Companions of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would prostrate with their hands inside their clothes, and a man would prostrate on his turban.” This was narrated by al-Bayhaqī.

Al-Bukhārī cited this as supporting evidence in the chapter entitled “Prostrating on a Garment Because of Intense Heat,” saying:

“Al-Hasan said: ‘The people would prostrate on their turbans and caps, with their hands inside their sleeves.’”

He also narrated the previously cited hadith of Anas, who said:

“We used to pray with the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and because of the intense heat, one of us would place his garment where he prostrated.”

translated_text:
the hadith of Abū Sa‘īd al-Khudrī in the two Sahīh collections:

“He saw traces of water and mud on the nose of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and on its tip.”

In another wording, he said:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, led us in prayer, and I saw traces of water and mud on his forehead and the tip of his nose, confirming his dream.”

Al-Bukhārī narrated it with this wording.

Al-Humaydī said: “This hadith is cited as evidence that the forehead should not be wiped during prayer, but rather afterwards, because water was seen on the tip of the Prophet’s nose and on his forehead after he had prayed, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.”

I say: Scholars such as Ahmad and others regarded it as disliked to wipe the forehead during prayer to remove dust and the like that clings to it during prostration. They differed over wiping it after prayer, holding two views, both reported from Ahmad. Similarly, two views are reported from Ahmad concerning drying off the water of ablution with a towel, removing the changed odor of a fasting person’s mouth with a tooth-stick after noon, and other such matters involving the traces left by worship.

Abū Humayd al-Sā‘idī reported:

“When the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prostrated, he would place his forehead firmly on the ground, keep his arms away from his sides, and place his hands level with his shoulders.”

Abū Dāwūd and al-Tirmidhī narrated it, and al-Tirmidhī said: “A sound, authentic hadith.”

Wā’il ibn Hujr said:

“I saw the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prostrating on the ground, placing his forehead and nose on it during his prostration.”

Ahmad narrated it.

Thus, the hadiths and reports indicate that, when free to choose, they would place their foreheads directly on the ground. When necessary, because of heat or the like, they would protect themselves with something they wore: the edge of a garment, a turban or a cap. The most balanced view on this question is therefore that this is permitted when needed, but prostrating on a turban or the like is disliked when there is no need. There are disagreements and further distinctions concerning this question, but this is not the place to discuss them.

The second argument:

Had their request to him been to prostrate on an intervening covering, he would have allowed them to use something separate from themselves on which to prostrate. It is established that he used to pray on a small prayer mat. Maymūnah said:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to pray on a small prayer mat.”

This was narrated by the compilers of the Sahīh collections, such as al-Bukhārī and Muslim, and by the compilers of the three Sunan collections: Abū Dāwūd, al-Nasā’ī and Ibn Mājah. Ahmad also narrated it in al-Musnad, and al-Tirmidhī narrated it from Ibn ‘Abbās.

‘I saw him praying on a mat and prostrating on it.’”

In the two Sahīh collections, Abū Salamah reported that ‘Ā’ishah said:

“I used to sleep in front of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, with my feet in the direction he faced in prayer. When he prostrated, he would nudge me and I would draw my feet back; when he stood up, I would stretch them out again.” She added: “In those days, the houses had no lamps.”

‘Urwah reported from ‘Ā’ishah:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to pray while she lay crosswise between him and the qiblah on his household’s bedding, as a funeral bier is laid.”

In another wording, ‘Irāk reported from ‘Urwah:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to pray while ‘Ā’ishah lay crosswise between him and the qiblah on the bedding on which they both slept.”

All these wordings are from al-Bukhārī. They were cited as evidence in the chapter on praying on bedding. The last wording was cited with a disconnected chain because it serves to explain the report with the connected chain: ‘Urwah had heard it only from ‘Ā’ishah, and he knew best what he had heard from her.

There is no disagreement among scholars that it is permissible to pray and prostrate on floor coverings made from materials of the earth, such as small prayer mats, woven mats and the like. They differed only over whether it is disliked to do so on materials other than those of the earth, such as leather sheets spread out on the ground, made from the hides of livestock, and rugs and dyed woollen carpets. Most scholars permit this as well. This is the position of the scholars of hadith, such as al-Shāfi‘ī and Ahmad, and of the scholars of Kufa, such as Abū Hanīfah and others. translated_text:
the earth, but was made of leather or wool.

Al-Mughīrah ibn Shu‘bah said:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to pray on a woven mat and on a tanned pelt.”

Ahmad and Abū Dāwūd narrated this through Abū ‘Awn Muhammad ibn ‘Ubayd Allāh ibn Sa‘īd al-Thaqafī, from his father, from al-Mughīrah. Abū Hātim al-Rāzī said: “‘Ubayd Allāh ibn Sa‘īd is unknown.”

Ibn ‘Abbās reported:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prayed on a rug.”

Ahmad and Ibn Mājah narrated this. In al-Bukhārī’s al-Tārīkh, Abū al-Dardā’ is reported to have said:

“I would not mind praying on a small prayer mat.”

Since the permissibility of praying on floor coverings is established by the Sunnah and scholarly consensus, it follows that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not prohibit them from using something on which to prostrate to protect themselves from the heat. Rather, they asked him to delay the prayer beyond the delay he already allowed, but he did not grant their request. Some of them would protect themselves from the heat either with something separate from their clothing or with the edge of the garment they were wearing.

If it is said, “The hadith concerning the small prayer mat provides evidence for those who use a prayer rug, as some have indeed argued,” the reply is:

There are several answers to this. First, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not pray on a small prayer mat

It appears that he used it to shield himself from intense heat and for similar purposes, as indicated by the previously mentioned hadith of Abū Sa‘īd, who saw traces of water and mud on his forehead and nose. Thus, this provides no evidence for someone who adopts a prayer rug on which he always prays.

Second, they have mentioned that it covered only the place where he prostrated; it was not like a prayer rug large enough to accommodate his entire body. It appears that he used it to protect himself from the heat. This is what the scholars of uncommon hadith vocabulary have stated. They said:

“A khumrah is like a small mat, made of palm fronds woven together with leather thongs and threads. It is large enough for the face and nose to rest upon; if it is larger than that, it is called a mat. It was given this name because it shields the face and ankles from the heat and cold of the ground.”

It has also been said that it is so named because it covers, or shields, the worshipper’s face; or because its threads are concealed by its palm fronds.

One of them commented on the hadith of Ibn ‘Abbās:

“A mouse came and began dragging the wick in front of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, onto the small mat on which he was sitting, burning an area of it the size of a dirham.”

He said: “This clearly indicates that the term khumrah can also apply to a larger mat of this kind.”

However, the authenticity of this hadith is not known. Moreover, sitting on it does not indicate that it was long enough to pray upon, so this does not contradict what they have stated.

Third, the small prayer mat was not used to avoid or guard against impurities

translated_text:
as those who pray on prayer rugs argue in justification, saying that they do so only to guard against impurity in the mosque, or on its mats and carpets, because so many members of the public tread upon them.

It is established that he prayed in his sandals, that he led his Companions in prayer wearing his sandals while they too wore theirs, and that he instructed people to pray in sandals to differ from the Jews. He also instructed that, if there was any filth on them, they should be rubbed against the earth and then worn in prayer. Sandals obviously come into contact with the ground, and the hadith explicitly states that one may pray in them after rubbing them in this manner, even if filth has soiled them. How, then, could it be recommended to place a barrier between oneself and the ground for fear of impurity, when this is his law and Sunnah?

There are four degrees in this matter. As for those who go to extremes in their obsessive misgivings, they pray neither on the ground nor on coverings spread on the ground for public use, but only on a prayer rug or something similar. How could such people pray in their sandals, when, by their reasoning, that is even less acceptable than praying on the ground? Their sandals have touched the roads along which they have walked and may have encountered impurity; indeed, in some places this may be quite likely.

If they will not pray on the ground with their feet touching it directly—even though the place where they stand is presumed pure, and they touch it only at the time of prayer—then what of sandals that have repeatedly touched roads traversed by animals and human beings, where impurity is likely to be found? For this reason, when these people offer the funeral prayer, they place their feet

 أَنَّ الْخُمْرَةَ لَمْ يَأْمُرْ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ بِهَا الصَّحَابَةَ
translated_text:
on top of their sandals, so that they neither carry impurity nor come into direct contact with it. Some refrain even from this out of scrupulousness, since there is a well-known disagreement over praying on something whose underside is impure; a covering is therefore spread on the ground for such a person. This degree is the furthest removed from the Sunnah.

The second degree:
To pray on a woven mat or the like, rather than on the ground or anything that comes into contact with it.

The third degree:
To pray on the ground, but not in sandals that have repeatedly come into contact with the roads. The patch of ground one carefully selects may be pure, and the likelihood of its having become impure is slight, unlike the soles of sandals.

The fourth degree:
To pray in sandals and, if any filth is found on them, to rub them against the earth, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, instructed. This is the degree established by the Sunnah.

It is therefore clear that, for one whose regular practice was this fourth degree, it could not be recommended to place a prayer rug or some other barrier between himself and the ground to guard against impurity. Thus, the hadith concerning the small prayer mat cannot be interpreted as meaning that he laid it down to avoid impurity. Their use of it as evidence for that practice is therefore invalid. If, however, it was used to protect against the heat, then it should be used when needed for that purpose, and not used when there is no need for it.

Fourth:
The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not instruct the Companions to use the small prayer mat

translated_text:
nor did they each keep a small prayer mat of their own. Rather, they prostrated on earth and pebbles, as mentioned earlier. Had this been recommended or a Sunnah practice, they would have done it, and he would have instructed them to do so. It is thus clear that it was a concession granted because of the need to protect the worshipper from discomfort. They themselves used their clothes and similar things for this purpose. It is well known that the Companions, both during his lifetime and afterward, were better than us, more faithful in following the Sunnah, and more obedient to his commands. Had the purpose been what those who use prayer rugs intend, the Companions would have done so.

Fifth:
The mosque floor was not covered; rather, it consisted of earth and pebbles. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prayed on a woven mat, his wife’s bedding, and similar things. He did not pray there on a small prayer mat, a prayer rug, or anything similar.

If it is said:
“The hadiths of Maymūnah and ʿĀ’ishah indicate that he used to pray on a small prayer mat in his home, for he said, ‘Hand me the small prayer mat from the mosque.’ The previously mentioned hadith of Maymūnah also suggests this.”

The answer is:
Whoever uses a prayer rug to spread over the mosque’s woven mats has no evidence in the Sunnah for this practice. Rather, this innovation is objectionable on several grounds. The first is that such a person avoids praying on the ground for fear that

translated_text:
it is ritually impure, even though praying on the ground is a Sunnah established through mass transmission. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The earth has been made for me a place of prayer and a means of purification. Wherever a man of my community finds himself when prayer becomes due, his place of prayer and means of purification are at hand.”

Avoiding prayer on the ground for this reason is not prescribed.

Indeed, it is established in Sahīh al-Bukhārī that Ibn ʿUmar said:

“Dogs used to come and go in the mosque of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, yet they would not sprinkle water on any of those places.”

Or words to that effect. In Sunan Abī Dāwūd, the wording is:

“They would urinate and come and go, yet they would not sprinkle water on any of those places.”

This hadith has been cited as evidence by those who hold that ground affected by ritual impurity becomes pure through exposure to the sun, wind, and the like. This is one of the two positions within the schools of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad, among others, and it is the position of Abū Hanīfah. They also cite as evidence that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, instructed that a ritually impure sandal be rubbed against the ground and declared earth a means of purifying it. If earth serves to remove impurity from something else, then all the more should it serve to remove impurity from itself.

This position may be held even by those who do not hold that an impure substance becomes pure through transformation. One of the two positions within the schools of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad is that the ground becomes pure by these means, although those holding this position maintain that an impure substance does not become pure through transformation.

translated_text:
Abū Hanīfah, the Zāhirīs, and others—the matter is clearer still according to their view, for they say:

Impure dung becomes pure if it turns into ash or the like. Likewise, blood, carrion, and similar substances that fall into a saltworks become pure if they turn into salt. They all agree that wine becomes pure when Allah, glorified is He, causes it to turn into vinegar. This is also established from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb and other Companions. They therefore judge other substances that undergo transformation by analogy with wine that has been transformed.

Those who distinguish between the two cases justify this by saying that wine became impure through transformation and thus becomes pure through transformation: the juice was pure, then became impure when it turned into wine, and becomes pure when it turns into vinegar. This is a weak argument, for all impure substances likewise became impure through transformation. An animal, while alive, consumes pure food and drink; then it dies and becomes impure. Likewise, pigs, dogs, and beasts of prey—according to those who consider them impure—were created from pure water and earth.

Moreover, this vinegar, salt, and similar things are wholesome, pure substances included in the words of Allah Most High:

“He makes lawful for them what is wholesome and forbids them what is foul.”

Someone who declares these substances forbidden and impure may say that he prohibits them because they are either expressly covered by the revealed text or fall within its meaning. Yet neither is the case, for the text does not cover them

Their origin was indeed impure, but that does not matter, for Allah brings forth the wholesome from the foul and the foul from the wholesome. There is no doubt that this view has stronger support, both in the revealed texts and by analogy.

The question of the purity of graveyards rests on what has already been discussed. Those who regard an old graveyard as impure say that pus and similar discharges from the dead have mingled with the soil and undergone transformation; they therefore regard the soil as impure. According to the view that transformation brings about purification, however, and according to other views, the soil is not impure. This is supported by the report established in the two Sahīh collections:

“The site of the Messenger of Allah’s mosque—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—had been a walled garden belonging to Banū al-Najjār. It contained graves of polytheists, ruins, and date palms. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, ordered that the graves be dug up, the date palms cut down, and the ruins levelled, and a prayer-facing side was established for the mosque.” . . . (1)

Thus, this had been a burial ground for polytheists. Yet when the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, ordered their graves to be dug up, he did not order the removal of the soil that had been in contact with them, or any other soil from the graveyard. Nor did he command that excrement be guarded against.

This is not the place for a detailed discussion of this issue. The purpose, however, is to point out that the practice of most people afflicted with obsessive misgivings—avoiding the ground and declaring it impure—is invalid according to the revealed text, even though some aspects of it are disputed, while others are invalid according to consensus or other evidence of Islamic law.

original_text:
الْوَجْهُ الثَّانِي:
 أَنَّ هَؤُلَاءِ يَفْتَرِشُ أَحَدُهُمْ السَّجَّادَةَ عَلَى مُصَلَّيَاتِ الْمُسْلِمِينَ مِنْ الْحُصْرِ وَالْبُسُطِ وَنَحْوِ ذَلِكَ مِمَّا يُفْرَشُ فِي الْمَسَاجِدِ فَيَزْدَادُونَ بِدْعَةً عَلَى بِدْعَتِهِمْ. وَهَذَا الْأَمْرُ لَمْ يَفْعَلْهُ أَحَدٌ مِنْ السَّلَفِ وَلَمْ يُنْقَلْ عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ مَا يَكُونُ شُبْهَةً لَهُمْ فَضْلًا عَنْ أَنْ يَكُونَ دَلِيلًا؛ بَلْ يُعَلِّلُونَ أَنَّ هَذِهِ الْحُصْرَ يَطَؤُهَا عَامَّةُ النَّاسِ وَلَعَلَّ أَحَدَهُمْ أَنْ يَكُونَ قَدْ رَأَى أَوْ سَمِعَ أَنَّهُ بَعْضَ الْأَوْقَاتِ بَالَ صَبِيٌّ أَوْ غَيْرُهُ عَلَى بَعْضِ حُصْرِ الْمَسْجِدِ أَوْ رَأَى عَلَيْهِ شَيْئًا مِنْ ذَرْقِ الْحَمَامِ. أَوْ غَيْرِهِ فَيَصِيرُ ذَلِكَ حُجَّةً فِي الْوَسْوَاسِ. وَقَدْ عُلِمَ بِالتَّوَاتُرِ أَنَّ الْمَسْجِدَ الْحَرَامَ مَا زَالَ يَطَأُ عَلَيْهِ الْمُسْلِمُونَ عَلَى عَهْدِ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ وَعَهْدِ خُلَفَائِهِ وَهُنَاكَ مِنْ الْحَمَامِ مَا لَيْسَ بِغَيْرِهِ وَيَمُرُّ بِالْمَطَافِ مِنْ الْخَلْقِ مَا لَا يَمُرُّ بِمَسْجِدِ مِنْ الْمَسَاجِدِ فَتَكُونُ هَذِهِ الشُّبْهَةُ الَّتِي ذَكَرْتُمُوهَا أَقْوَى. ثُمَّ إنَّهُ لَمْ يَكُنْ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ وَخُلَفَاؤُهُ وَأَصْحَابُهُ يُصَلِّي هُنَاكَ عَلَى حَائِلٍ وَلَا يَسْتَحِبُّ ذَلِكَ فَلَوْ كَانَ هَذَا مُسْتَحَبًّا كَمَا زَعَمَهُ هَؤُلَاءِ لَمْ يَكُنْ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ وَخُلَفَاؤُهُ وَأَصْحَابُهُ مُتَّفِقِينَ عَلَى تَرْكِ الْمُسْتَحَبِّ الْأَفْضَلِ. وَيَكُونُ هَؤُلَاءِ أَطْوَعَ لِلَّهِ وَأَحْسَنَ عَمَلًا مِنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ وَخُلَفَائِهِ وَأَصْحَابِهِ فَإِنَّ هَذَا خِلَافَ مَا ثَبَتَ فِي الْكِتَابِ وَالسُّنَّةِ وَالْإِجْمَاعِ. وَأَيْضًا فَقَدْ كَانُوا يَطَؤُونَ مَسْجِدَ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ
translated_text:
The second point:

These people lay their prayer rugs over the mats, carpets, and other floor coverings on which Muslims pray in mosques, thereby adding one innovation to another. None of the early generations did this, nor has anything been transmitted from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, that could offer them even a semblance of support, let alone proof. Rather, they justify it by saying that these mats are trodden on by people at large. Perhaps one of them has seen or heard that, on some occasion, a child or someone else urinated on one of the mosque’s mats, or has seen droppings from pigeons or other creatures on it. This then becomes a justification for obsessive misgivings.

Yet it is known through mass-transmitted reports that Muslims regularly walked in the Sacred Mosque during the time of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his caliphs. There are more pigeons there than elsewhere, and more people pass through the area of circumambulation than through any other mosque. Thus, the grounds for suspicion that you mention would be stronger there. Nevertheless, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, his caliphs, and his Companions did not pray there on an intervening covering, nor did they regard doing so as recommended. Had this been recommended, as these people claim, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, his caliphs, and his Companions would not all have neglected the recommended and superior practice. It would also mean that these people were more obedient to Allah and better in their deeds than the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, his caliphs, and his Companions. This contradicts what is established by the Quran, the Sunnah, and scholarly consensus.

Moreover, they used to walk in the mosque of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace

original_text:
بِنِعَالِهِمْ وَخِفَافِهِمْ وَيُصَلُّونَ فِيهِ مَعَ قِيَامِ هَذَا الِاحْتِمَالِ وَلَمْ يُسْتَحَبَّ لَهُمْ هَذَا الِاحْتِرَازُ الَّذِي ابْتَدَعَهُ هَؤُلَاءِ فَعُلِمَ خَطَؤُهُمْ فِي ذَلِكَ.
 وَقَدْ يُفَرِّقُونَ بَيْنَهُمَا بِأَنْ يَقُولُوا:
 الْأَرْضُ تَطْهُرُ بِالشَّمْسِ وَالرِّيحِ وَالِاسْتِحَالَةِ. دُونَ الْحَصِيرِ.
 فَيُقَالُ:
 هَذَا إذَا كَانَ حَقًّا فَإِنَّمَا هُوَ مِنْ النَّجَاسَةِ الْمُخَفَّفَةِ.
 وَذَلِكَ يَظْهَرُ بِ (الْوَجْهِ الثَّالِثِ:
 وَهُوَ أَنَّ النَّجَاسَةَ لَا يُسْتَحَبُّ الْبَحْثُ عَمَّا لَمْ يَظْهَرْ مِنْهَا وَلَا الِاحْتِرَازُ عَمَّا لَيْسَ عَلَيْهِ دَلِيلٌ ظَاهِرٌ لِاحْتِمَالِ وَجُودِهِ فَإِنْ كَانَ قَدْ قَالَ طَائِفَةٌ مِنْ الْفُقَهَاءِ مِنْ أَصْحَابِ أَحْمَد وَغَيْرِهِمْ: أَنَّهُ يُسْتَحَبُّ الِاحْتِرَازُ عَنْ الْمَشْكُوكِ فِيهِ مُطْلَقًا فَهُوَ قَوْلٌ ضَعِيفٌ. وَقَدْ ثَبَتَ عَنْ عُمَرَ بْنِ الْخَطَّابِ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ 
" أَنَّهُ مَرَّ هُوَ وَصَاحِبٌ لَهُ بِمَكَانِ فَسَقَطَ عَلَى صَاحِبِهِ مَاءٌ مِنْ مِيزَابٍ فَنَادَى صَاحِبُهُ: يَا صَاحِبَ الْمِيزَابِ أَمَاؤُك طَاهِرٌ أَمْ نَجِسٌ؟
 فَقَالَ لَهُ عُمَرُ:
 يَا صَاحِبَ الْمِيزَابِ لَا تُخْبِرْهُ فَإِنَّ هَذَا لَيْسَ عَلَيْهِ "
 فَنَهَى عُمَرُ عَنْ إخْبَارِهِ لِأَنَّهُ تَكَلَّفَ مِنْ السُّؤَالِ مَا لَمْ يُؤْمَرْ بِهِ. وَهَذَا قَدْ يَنْبَنِي عَلَى أَصْلٍ.
 وَهُوَ:
 أَنَّ النَّجَاسَةَ إنَّمَا يَثْبُتُ حُكْمُهَا مَعَ الْعِلْمِ فَلَوْ صَلَّى وَبِبَدَنِهِ أَوْ ثِيَابِهِ نَجَاسَةٌ وَلَمْ يَعْلَمْ بِهَا إلَّا بَعْدَ الصَّلَاةِ لَمْ تَجِبْ عَلَيْهِ الْإِعَادَةُ فِي أَصَحِّ قَوْلَيْ الْعُلَمَاءِ وَهُوَ مَذْهَبُ مَالِكٍ وَغَيْرِهِ وَأَحْمَد فِي أَقْوَى الرِّوَايَتَيْنِ وَسَوَاءٌ كَانَ عَلِمَهَا ثُمَّ نَسِيَهَا أَوْ جَهِلَهَا ابْتِدَاءً لِمَا تَقَدَّمَ مِنْ
translated_text:
in their sandals and leather socks, and would pray there despite this possibility. Yet they were not encouraged to take the precaution these people have introduced. Their error in this is therefore clear.

They may distinguish between the two by saying: “The ground becomes pure through sunlight, wind, and transformation, whereas matting does not.”

The response is: Even if this is true, it applies only to lighter impurity.

This becomes clear from the third point: It is not recommended to search for impurity that is not apparent, nor to guard against it merely because it might exist when there is no outward evidence of its presence. Even if some jurists among Ahmad’s followers and others have said that it is recommended to guard against anything doubtful without qualification, this is a weak opinion. It is established that ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb, may Allah be pleased with him,

“He and a companion passed through a place, and water from a gutter fell on his companion. His companion called out, ‘Owner of the gutter, is your water pure or impure?’ ʿUmar said to him, ‘Owner of the gutter, do not tell him, for he is not required to know.’”

Thus, ʿUmar forbade him from answering because his companion had burdened himself with an inquiry he had not been commanded to make. This may rest on a principle: the legal consequences of impurity apply only when one is aware of it. If someone prays with impurity on his body or clothing and only discovers it after the prayer, he is not obliged to repeat it, according to the sounder of the two scholarly opinions. This is the position of Mālik and others, and of Ahmad according to the stronger of the two reports from him. This applies whether he had known about the impurity and then forgotten it, or had been unaware of it from the outset, because of the previously cited report

original_text:
أَنَّ النَّبِيَّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ صَلَّى فِي نَعْلَيْهِ ثُمَّ خَلَعَهُمَا فِي أَثْنَاءِ الصَّلَاةِ لَمَّا أَخْبَرَهُ جِبْرِيلُ أَنَّ بِهِمَا أَذًى وَمَضَى فِي صَلَاتِهِ وَلَمْ يَسْتَأْنِفْهَا مَعَ كَوْنِ ذَلِكَ مَوْجُودًا فِي أَوَّلِ الصَّلَاةِ لَكِنْ لَمْ يَعْلَمْ بِهِ فَتَكَلُّفُهُ لِلْخَلْعِ فِي أَثْنَائِهَا مَعَ أَنَّهُ لَوْلَا الْحَاجَةُ لَكَانَ عَبَثًا أَوْ مَكْرُوهًا. . . 
(١)
. يَدُلُّ عَلَى أَنَّهُ مَأْمُورٌ بِهِ مِنْ اجْتِنَابِ النَّجَاسَةِ مَعَ الْعِلْمِ وَمَظِنَّةٌ تَدُلُّ عَلَى الْعَفْوِ عَنْهَا فِي حَالِ عَدَمِ الْعِلْمِ بِهَا.
 وَقَدْ رَوَى أَبُو دَاوُد أَيْضًا عَنْ أُمِّ جحدر الْعَامِرِيَّةِ أَنَّهَا سَأَلَتْ عَائِشَةَ عَنْ دَمِ الْحَيْضِ يُصِيبُ الثَّوْبَ فَقَالَتْ:
 " 
{كُنْت مَعَ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ وَعَلَيْنَا شِعَارُنَا وَقَدْ أَلْقَيْنَا فَوْقَهُ كِسَاءً فَلَمَّا أَصْبَحَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ أَخَذَ الْكِسَاءَ فَلَبِسَهُ ثُمَّ خَرَجَ فَصَلَّى الْغَدَاةَ ثُمَّ جَلَسَ فَقَالَ رَجُلٌ: يَا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ هَذِهِ لَمْعَةٌ مِنْ دَمٍ فَقَبَضَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ مَا يَلِيهَا فَبَعَثَ بِهَا إلَيَّ مَصْرُورَةً فِي يَدِ غُلَامٍ فَقَالَ: اغْسِلِي هَذَا وأجفيها وَأَرْسِلِي بِهَا إلَيَّ فَدَعَوْت بِقَصْعَتِي فَغَسَلْتهَا ثُمَّ أَجَفَفْتهَا فَأَعَدْتهَا إلَيْهِ فَجَاءَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ نِصْفَ النَّهَارِ وَهِيَ عَلَيْهِ}
. وَفِي هَذَا الْحَدِيثِ لَمْ يَأْمُرْ الْمَأْمُومِينَ بِالْإِعَادَةِ وَلَا ذَكَرَ لَهُمْ أَنَّهُ يُعِيدُ وَأَنَّ عَلَيْهِ الْإِعَادَةَ وَلَا ذَكَرَتْ ذَلِكَ عَائِشَةُ وَظَاهِرُ هَذَا أَنَّهُ لَمْ يُعِدْ. وَلِأَنَّ النَّجَاسَةَ مِنْ بَابِ الْمَنْهِيِّ عَنْهُ فِي الصَّلَاةِ وَبَابُ الْمَنْهِيِّ عَنْهُ
original_footnote: (١) بياض بالأصل
translated_text:
that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prayed in his sandals, then removed them during the prayer when Gabriel informed him that there was filth on them. He continued his prayer without starting it again, although the filth had been present at the beginning of the prayer, but he had not known about it. His taking the trouble to remove them during the prayer—although, had there been no need, doing so would have been pointless or disliked … (1)—indicates that avoiding impurity when aware of it is commanded, and provides grounds for concluding that it is excused when one is unaware of it.

Abū Dāwūd also narrated from Umm Jahdar al-ʿĀmiriyyah that she asked ʿĀ’ishah about menstrual blood getting onto clothing. She replied:

“I was with the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, with our inner covering over us, and we had placed a cloak over it. In the morning, the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, took the cloak, put it on, and went out to perform the dawn prayer. He then sat down, and a man said, ‘Messenger of Allah, here is a patch of blood.’ The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, gathered the cloth around it and sent it to me, bundled up, with a boy, saying, ‘Wash this, dry it, and send it back to me.’ I called for my bowl, washed it, dried it, and returned it to him. The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, came at midday wearing it.”

In this hadith, he did not instruct those who had prayed behind him to repeat the prayer, nor did he tell them that he would repeat it or that he was required to do so. Nor did ʿĀ’ishah mention any such thing. The apparent implication is that he did not repeat it. Another reason is that impurity falls under the category of things prohibited in prayer, and in matters involving prohibitions

مَعْفُوٌّ فِيهِ عَنْ الْمُخْطِئِ وَالنَّاسِي.
 كَمَا قَالَ فِي دُعَاءِ الرَّسُولِ وَالْمُؤْمِنِينَ:
 
{رَبَّنَا لَا تُؤَاخِذْنَا إنْ نَسِينَا أَوْ أَخْطَأْنَا}

 فَإِذَا لَمْ يَكُنْ عَالِمًا بِالنَّجَاسَةِ صَحَّتْ صَلَاتُهُ بَاطِنًا وَظَاهِرًا فَلَا حَاجَةَ بِهِ حِينَئِذٍ عَنْ السُّؤَالِ عَنْ أَشْيَاءَ إنْ أُبْدِيَتْ سَاءَتْهُ قَدْ عَفَا اللَّهُ عَنْهَا. وَهَؤُلَاءِ قَدْ يَبْلُغُ الْحَالُ بِأَحَدِهِمْ إلَى أَنْ يَكْرَهَ الصَّلَاةَ
translated_text:
those who err or forget are excused. As He says, relating the supplication of the Messenger and the believers:

“Our Lord, do not hold us accountable if we forget or make a mistake.”

It is established in the authentic collection, in a hadith narrated by Abū Hurayrah, that Allah answered this supplication. Moreover, the scriptural evidence indicates that speaking and similar acts that invalidate prayer are excused when done forgetfully or in ignorance. This is the position of Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, and Ahmad according to one of the two reports from him.

This is supported by the hadith of Dhū al-Yadayn and similar reports; the hadith of Muʿāwiyah ibn al-Hakam al-Sulamī, who invoked Allah’s mercy upon someone who sneezed during prayer; and the hadith of Ibn Masʿūd concerning the tashahhud, recorded by both al-Bukhārī and Muslim. They initially used to say, “Peace be upon Allah before His servants.” He forbade them to say this, declaring, “Allah Himself is al-Salām (the Source of Peace),” and instructed them to recite the familiar tashahhud, without ordering them to repeat their prayers. The same applies to the hadith of the Bedouin who said in his supplication, “O Allah, have mercy on me and on Muhammad, and do not have mercy on anyone else along with us,” and other such reports. These and similar accounts show that prohibited acts, whether in prayer or otherwise, are excused when committed through forgetfulness, error, or comparable circumstances.

Accordingly, if a person is unaware of the impurity, his prayer is valid both inwardly and outwardly. He therefore has no need to inquire about matters which, if disclosed to him, would distress him, and which Allah has overlooked. Some of these people may reach the point of disliking prayer

translated_text:
except on a prayer rug; indeed, he may even regard praying on anything else as forbidden and avoid it as he would anything unlawful. This resembles the practice of the People of the Book, who would pray only in their places of worship. Someone who prays only on coverings made for prayer resembles someone who prays only in places built for prayer. They may also make this a distinguishing mark of religious people, considering its abandonment a sign of deficient religious commitment and insufficient concern for prayer. They thus regard the practices they have invented, for which no authority has been revealed, as more perfect than the way of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his Companions.

One of them may make a public display of carrying a prayer rug over his shoulder and holding prayer beads in his hand, treating this as an emblem of religion and prayer. Yet it is known through mass-transmitted reports that this was not the distinguishing practice of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his Companions. They would glorify Allah and count on their fingers, as stated in the hadith:

“Count on your fingers, for they will be questioned and made to speak.”

Sometimes one of them would count his glorifications using pebbles or fruit stones.

As for glorifying Allah using prayer beads, some have disapproved of it, while others have permitted it. No one, however, has said that using them is better than counting on the fingers or by other means. Even if this were a recommended practice performed openly, deliberately displaying it and setting oneself apart from others by it is blameworthy. If it is not ostentation, it is an imitation of those who practise ostentation, for many who do this visibly show off. Had it been ostentation involving a prescribed practice, that would have been one of the two evils; but it is ostentation that is not

translated_text:
prescribed.

Allah Most High has said:

“...to test you as to which of you is best in deeds.”

Al-Fudayl ibn ʿIyād, may Allah be pleased with him, said: “The most sincere and the most correct.” They asked: “Abū ʿAlī, what does ‘the most sincere and the most correct’ mean?” He replied: “If a deed is sincere but not correct, it will not be accepted. If it is correct but not sincere, it will not be accepted until it is both sincere and correct. Sincerity means that it is done for Allah, and correctness means that it accords with the Sunnah.”

What al-Fudayl said is agreed upon among Muslims: a deed must be prescribed and commanded, which is what makes it righteous, and one must intend thereby to seek the Face of Allah. As Allah Most High has said:

“So whoever hopes to meet his Lord, let him do righteous deeds and associate no one in the worship of his Lord.”

ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb, may Allah be pleased with him, used to say:

“O Allah, make all my deeds righteous, make them sincerely for Your Face, and let no one else have any share in them.”

Among the verses expressing this meaning is His saying, Most High:

“Yes, whoever submits himself to Allah and does good will have his reward with his Lord. No fear will be upon them, nor will they grieve.”

Allah Most High also said:

“And who is better in religion than one who submits himself to Allah, does good, and follows the faith of Abraham, a man of pure monotheism? And Allah took Abraham as a close friend.”

In Sahīh Muslim, Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, narrated that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah Most High says: ‘I am utterly without need of partners. Whoever does a deed in which he associates someone else with Me, I disavow it, and it belongs entirely to the one he associated with Me.’”

In the Sunan, al-ʿIrbād ibn Sāriyah said:

“The Messenger of Allah admonished us

In the two Sahīh collections, ʿĀ’ishah narrated that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever introduces into this matter of ours something that does not belong to it, it is rejected.”

Another wording reads:

“Whoever performs a deed that does not accord with our way, it is rejected.”

In Sahīh Muslim, Jābir narrated that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to say in his sermon:

“The finest speech is the Book of Allah, and the best guidance is the guidance of Muhammad. The worst matters are those newly introduced, and every innovation is misguidance.”

As for the practice of many people of having mats placed in the mosque on Friday or other days before going there themselves, this is prohibited by the unanimous agreement of Muslims; indeed, it is unlawful. Is a person’s prayer on such a mat valid? Scholars have two opinions on this, because by laying down that mat he has wrongfully appropriated a space in the mosque and prevented other worshippers who arrive before him from praying there.

If someone prays in a space in the mosque while preventing others from praying there, is his prayer like prayer on usurped land? There are two views. As for prayer on land

What is prescribed in the mosque is for people to complete the first row, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

What a person is instructed to do is to go early to the mosque himself. If he sends his mat ahead but delays his own arrival, he has contravened the Sharia in two respects: by arriving late when he is instructed to come early, and by wrongfully appropriating part of the mosque, preventing those who arrive before him from praying there and completing the rows in order, beginning with the first. “Whoever steps over people’s necks will be made a bridge to Hell.”

The second—and correct—opinion is that another person may remove it and pray in its place. The person who arrives first is entitled to pray in that front row and is also instructed to do so. He cannot carry out this instruction and exercise this right without removing the mat. Whatever is necessary to carry out a command is itself commanded. Moreover, the mat was placed there in an act of usurpation, which is a wrong. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever among you sees a wrong, let him change it with his hand. If he cannot, then with his tongue. If he cannot, then with his heart—and that is the weakest faith.”

However, care should be taken that this does not lead to a greater wrong. Allah Most High knows best, and all praise belongs to Allah alone.

“He performed ablution and said, ‘O ‘Ā’ishah, bring me the khumra (mat).’ She brought it, and he prayed on it.”

He replied:

The wording of the hadith is that “he asked for the khumra.” A khumra is something made from palm fronds

and he prostrated on it to protect himself from the ground’s heat and harm. The hadith concerning the khumra is authentic. As for making it large enough to pray on, to protect oneself from impurities and the like, neither the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, nor his Companions used a prayer mat for this purpose. Rather, they prayed both barefoot and wearing sandals, and they prayed directly on earth, woven mats, and other surfaces, without any intervening covering.

It is established in the two Sahīh collections that:

“He used to pray wearing his sandals.”

He also said:

“The Jews do not pray wearing their sandals, so differ from them.”

Once, he prayed wearing his sandals, and his Companions were also wearing theirs. He removed his sandals during the prayer, so they removed theirs. He asked, “Why did you remove your sandals?”

They replied, “We saw you remove yours, so we removed ours.”

He said, “Gabriel came to me and told me that there was filth on them. When any of you comes to the mosque, let him inspect his sandals. If there is filth on them, let him rub them against the earth, for the earth purifies them.”

If the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his Companions prayed wearing their sandals without removing them, but instead walked on the ground in them and prayed in them, how could anyone suppose that he would use a prayer mat, spreading it over a woven mat or another surface and then praying on it? None of the Companions used to do this. It is reported from Mālik that when one of the scholars arrived and spread something of this kind in the Prophet’s mosque, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, he ordered that he be imprisoned, saying, “Did you not know that this is an innovation in our mosque?”

Allah knows best.

لَيْسَ لِلْمُسْلِمِ أَنْ يَتَّخِذَ الْمَسْجِدَ طَرِيقًا فَكَيْفَ إذَا اتَّخَذَهُ الْكَافِرُ طَرِيقًا فَإِنَّ هَذَا يُمْنَعُ بِلَا رَيْبٍ.
translated_text:
He was also asked—may Allah Most High have mercy on him:

“Is it forbidden for someone to reserve a place in the mosque with a prayer mat, a carpet, or something else? If another person prays on any such item without its owner’s permission, is that disliked or not?”

He replied:

No one may reserve any part of the mosque, whether by laying down a prayer mat before arriving, a carpet, or anything else. Nor may another person pray on it without its owner’s permission. Rather, he should remove it and pray in its place, according to the more correct of the two scholarly opinions. Allah knows best.

He was asked:

“Is it permissible for a Christian or a Jew to enter the mosque, with or without a Muslim’s permission, or to use it as a thoroughfare?”

He replied:

A Muslim may not use the mosque as a thoroughfare, so how could a disbeliever do so? This must undoubtedly be prevented.

translated_text:
But if a dhimmī (a non-Muslim under Muslim protection) enters the mosque for a beneficial purpose, scholars hold two opinions, both reported from Ahmad:

The first is that it is not permissible. This is Mālik’s position, because this was the settled practice of the Companions.

The second is that it is permissible. This is the position of Abū Hanīfah and al-Shāfiʿī. There are two opinions within Ahmad’s school and other schools as to whether a Muslim’s permission is required.

He was asked:

“Is prayer valid in a mosque containing a grave, where people gather for congregational prayers and Friday prayer? Should the grave be leveled, or should a barrier or wall be built over it?”

He replied:

Praise be to Allah. The imams agree that a mosque must not be built over a grave, because the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Indeed, those before you used to take graves as places of worship. Beware! Do not take graves as places of worship, for I forbid you to do so.”

He was asked:

A group of people are lodging in the congregational mosque, remaining there day and night. They eat, drink and sleep there, and keep all their belongings and furnishings there. They prevent anyone outside their own group from lodging with them and have monopolized the mosque. Another group then entered some of its enclosed areas to recite the Quran, seeking Allah’s reward, but some of the residents stopped them, saying, “This is our place.” Is this permissible? Give us a ruling, and may you be rewarded.

He replied:

Praise be to Allah. No one has the right to reserve any part of the mosque for himself in such a way that he permanently excludes others from it. Indeed, “the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, forbade habitually occupying one spot as a camel does.”

The scholars said: This means that a man adopts a particular place in the mosque and does not pray

translated_text:
except there. If he has no right to keep to one particular place for prayer, what then of someone who permanently reserves a spot for himself? This applies even if he uses it only for the purposes for which mosques are built, such as prayer, remembrance of Allah and the like. How much more so if he treats the mosque as a home, regularly eating, drinking, sleeping and conducting all his other affairs there, including activities for which mosques were not built!

This is prohibited by agreement of the Muslims. Concessions regarding some of these activities were granted only to those in need, such as the People of the Suffa. A man would arrive in Medina as an emigrant with nowhere to shelter, so he would stay at the Suffa until he could establish a household or find somewhere to stay; then he would move out. Another example is the poor woman who used to shelter in the mosque and sweep it. Likewise, Ibn ʿUmar used to spend the night in the mosque while unmarried, because he had no home to return to until he married.

The same applies to ʿAlī ibn Abī Tālib: when he and Fātima had a disagreement, he went to the mosque and slept there. A distinction must therefore be drawn between occasional, limited use and use by those in need, on the one hand, and frequent, habitual use and use by those without such needs, on the other.

For this reason, Ibn ʿAbbās said, “Do not make the mosque a place for sleeping at night or resting at midday.” This concerned merely sleeping there; what, then, of the other activities mentioned? The scholars even disagreed over whether someone observing a devotional retreat should eat in the mosque or at home, despite his being instructed to remain in the mosque and leave it only out of necessity.

The leading scholars disapproved of private enclosures being set up in the mosque when some rulers introduced them solely for prayer. Yet those rulers only

prayed in them. As for using them as living quarters, sleeping there, and storing clothing and other possessions in them, I know of no Muslim who has allowed this. It turns the mosque into something like an inn with separately enclosed lodgings. The mosque must remain shared by all Muslims; no one may claim exclusive use of any part of it beyond the time he spends there engaged in a prescribed activity. Whoever first occupies a spot in the mosque for prayer, recitation, remembrance of Allah, learning, a devotional retreat or the like has the greater right to it until he finishes that activity. No one may make him leave, for the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, forbade making a man leave his seat; rather, people should make room and allow space.

If his ablution is invalidated and he then returns, he has the greater right to his place, for the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, established this practice, saying:

“When a man leaves his seat and then returns to it, he has the greater right to it.”

As for claiming exclusive use of a place in the mosque to stay and live there, as people have exclusive use of their homes, this is among the gravest wrongs, by agreement of the Muslims.

The most extensive stay in a mosque is that of someone observing a devotional retreat. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, used to observe such retreats in the mosque. He would have a mat set up as an enclosure for him and observe his retreat within it. He also used to observe his retreat in a tent. Likewise, people used to observe devotional retreats in mosques and pitch tents there for themselves. This, however, was only for the duration of the retreat. translated_text:
to engage only in acts that bring him closer to Allah. Someone who makes the mosque his residence is not observing a devotional retreat; rather, his conduct involves both doing what is prohibited and preventing what is prescribed. Someone in this situation prevents people from using that spot for the purposes for which the mosque was built: prayer, recitation and remembrance of Allah. As mentioned in the request for a fatwa, some of them prevent a person from reciting the Quran in that spot as other reciters do. What this wrongdoer has done is objectionable in several respects:

First, he uses the mosque as a place to sleep at night, rest at midday and reside, like rooms in caravanserais and inns.

Second, he prevents someone from reciting the Quran where recitation is prescribed.

Third, he prevents some people but not others. If he argues that those others recite because of the endowment established for them, whereas this person is not among its beneficiaries, that excuse would be even more reprehensible than the exclusion itself. Someone who recites the Quran seeking Allah’s reward is more deserving of assistance than someone who recites because of an endowment. The founder of an endowment has no right to change Allah’s religion. Merely establishing an endowment does not give its beneficiaries any right within the mosque that they did not previously possess.

Thus, if the founder wished to reserve a spot in the mosque for his endowment in such a way as to exclude others from it, he would have no right to do so. Even if he designated a spot in the mosque for the recitation, teaching or similar activities he had stipulated, that particular spot would not become binding, just as it does not become binding in the case of

a vow. If someone vows to pray and observe a devotional retreat in a particular spot in the mosque, that spot does not become binding upon him; according to the scholars generally, he may pray and observe his retreat anywhere else in the mosque. But must he offer expiation for breaking an oath? There are two views within Ahmad’s school. The other three imams do not require expiation.

This is because a vow makes obligatory only something that would constitute obedience even without the vow. A vow does not turn something that is not worship into worship. The person making the vow is obliged to dedicate only what constitutes obedience to Allah, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever vows to obey Allah, let him obey Him; and whoever vows to disobey Allah, let him not disobey Him.”

Thus, if someone vows to do something forbidden or disliked, or something permissible that is neither preferable to perform nor to omit, he is not obliged to fulfil that vow. There are two opinions concerning expiation: Ahmad requires it according to the well-known position reported from him, whereas the other three imams do not.

The same applies to conditions stipulated by the founder of an endowment, a seller or anyone else. As the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“What is the matter with men who stipulate conditions that are not in Allah’s Book? Whoever stipulates a condition that is not in Allah’s Book, it is invalid, even if there are a hundred conditions. Allah’s Book has greater authority, and Allah’s condition is more binding.”

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

Is it permissible to sleep and talk in the mosque, and to walk in sandals in the areas used for prayer?

He replied:

Sleeping there occasionally is permissible for someone who needs to, such as a stranger or a poor person who has no home. People are, however, told not to make it their regular place for sleeping at night and resting at midday.

Speech that Allah and His Messenger love is good in the mosque. Forbidden speech is even more strictly forbidden there, and disliked speech is likewise more objectionable there. Excessive talk, even about permissible matters, is disliked in the mosque.

Walking in sandals is permissible, just as the Companions used to walk in their sandals in the mosque of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. However, when someone comes to the mosque, he should do as the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, instructed: inspect his sandals, and if there is anything unclean on them, rub them against the earth, for the earth purifies them. And Allah knows best.

He was also asked:

Is it permissible to use a tooth-stick and comb one’s beard in the mosque?

He replied:

As for using a tooth-stick in the mosque, I know of no scholar who regarded it as disliked. Indeed, reports indicate that the early generations used tooth-sticks in the mosque. A person may spit or blow his nose into his clothing while in the mosque, by agreement of the imams and according to the reliably established Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Moreover, according to the majority of scholars, performing ablution in the mosque is permissible without being disliked. If ablution is permissible there, even though using a tooth-stick is part of ablution, and prayer is permissible there, even though a tooth-stick is used before prayer, how could using a tooth-stick be disliked? And if spitting and blowing one’s nose into one’s clothing are permissible there, how could using a tooth-stick be disliked?

As for combing the beard, some people regarded it as disliked only on the grounds that human hair, once detached, is ritually impure, and nothing ritually impure may be left in the mosque; or on the grounds that it is like a piece of litter. The majority of scholars, however, hold that human hair detached from the body is ritually pure. This is the position of Mālik and Abū Hanīfa, the apparent position of Ahmad’s school, and one of the two views within al-Shāfiʿī’s school. This is the correct view, for the Prophet

In matters of ritual purity and impurity, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, shares the same rulings as his community. Indeed, the basic principle is that he is their example in all rulings, except where evidence establishes that a ruling applies exclusively to him. Moreover, the correct view, held by the majority, is that the hair of animals that die without lawful slaughter is ritually pure. Indeed, according to one of the two scholarly views—the apparent position of Mālik’s school and one of the two reported positions of Ahmad—all hair is ritually pure, even pig hair. According to either view, there is nothing wrong with combing one’s hair if one gathers the fallen hair and does not leave it in the mosque. Leaving one’s hair in the mosque, however, is disliked even if it is not ritually impure, for the mosque should be kept free even of a speck that might get into someone’s eye. And Allah knows best.

 وَكَذَلِكَ لَا يَجُوزُ أَنْ يُدْفَنُ فِي الْمَسْجِدِ مَيِّتٌ:
 لَا صَغِيرٌ وَلَا كَبِيرٌ وَلَا جَنِينٌ وَلَا غَيْرُهُ. فَإِنَّ الْمَسَاجِدَ لَا يَجُورُ تَشْبِيهُهَا بِالْمَقَابِرِ. وَأَمَّا تَغْيِيرُ الْوَقْفِ لِغَيْرِ مَصْلَحَةٍ؛ فَلَا يَجُوزُ وَلَا يَجُوزُ الِاسْتِنْجَاءُ فِيهَا. وَأَمَّا الْوُضُوءُ فَفِي كَرَاهَتِهِ فِي الْمَسْجِدِ نِزَاعٌ بَيْنَ الْعُلَمَاءِ وَالْأَرْجَحُ أَنَّهُ لَا يُكْرَهُ إلَّا أَنْ يَحْصُلَ مَعَهُ امْتِخَاطٌ أَوْ بُصَاقٌ فِي الْمَسْجِدِ فَإِنَّ الْبُصَاقَ فِي الْمَسْجِدِ خَطِيئَةٌ وَكَفَّارَتُهَا دَفْنُهَا فَكَيْفَ بِالْمُخَاطِ. وَمَنْ لَمْ يَأْتَمِرْ بِمَا أَمَرَهُ اللَّهُ بِهِ وَيَنْتَهِ عَمَّا نَهَى اللَّهُ عَنْهُ؛ بَلْ يَرُدُّ عَلَى الْآمِرِينَ بِالْمَعْرُوفِ وَالنَّاهِينَ عَنْ الْمُنْكَرِ فَإِنَّهُ يُعَاقَبُ الْعُقُوبَةَ الشَّرْعِيَّةَ الَّتِي تُوجِبُ لَهُ وَلِأَمْثَالِهِ أَدَاءَ الْوَاجِبَاتِ وَتَرْكَ الْمُحَرَّمَاتِ.
translated_text:
one who does this, does not obey Allah’s commands, and does not refrain from what he has been forbidden? Even when a scholar gives him a ruling, he insults him. Is the ruler obliged to restrain and stop him and restore the endowment to its former state?

He replied:

No animals may be slaughtered in a mosque, whether sacrificial animals or otherwise. How could this be permissible when prayer in a slaughterhouse specifically set aside for slaughter is deemed objectionable—either prohibited or merely disliked? How, then, can a mosque be made to resemble a slaughterhouse? This would contaminate the mosque with blood, something from which it must be kept free.

Likewise, no deceased person may be buried in a mosque, whether a child, an adult, a fetus, or anyone else. Mosques must not be made to resemble cemeteries. Altering an endowment without any benefit is also impermissible, as is cleansing oneself after relieving oneself in a mosque.

As for performing ablution in a mosque, scholars disagree over whether it is disliked. The stronger view is that it is not disliked unless accompanied by blowing one’s nose or spitting in the mosque. Spitting in a mosque is a sin, and its expiation is to bury the spittle. How much more objectionable, then, is nasal mucus!

Anyone who does not obey what Allah has commanded or refrain from what He has forbidden, but instead rebuffs those who enjoin good and forbid evil, is to receive a punishment prescribed by Islamic law that will compel him and others like him to fulfil their obligations and refrain from prohibited acts.

translated_text:
Nor may the dead be washed in a mosque. If changes are introduced into a mosque that harm those praying there, whatever harms them must be removed, and measures must be taken to serve their interests, either by restoring it to its original condition or by improving upon it. And Allah knows best.

He was asked:

May someone who teaches children in a mosque spend the night there?

He replied:

Praise be to Allah. The mosque must be protected from anything that harms it or disturbs those praying in it, including children raising their voices, soiling its mats, and similar conduct. This is especially so during prayer, for such conduct is among the gravest wrongs.

As for spending the night there, if this is to meet a need—as in the case of a stranger who has no family, a poor stranger who has no home, or someone in similar circumstances—there is no harm, provided he stays there only as long as needed and then moves elsewhere. But taking it as a regular place to sleep at night and rest at midday is not permissible.

translated_text:
He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

In a mosque where Quran recitation and oral instruction take place morning and evening, witnesses at the entrance talk excessively, disturbing those reciting. Is this permissible or not?

He replied:

Praise be to Allah. No one may disturb those in the mosque who are praying, reciting, remembering Allah, supplicating, or engaging in similar activities for which mosques were built. No one may therefore do anything inside a mosque, at its entrance, or nearby that disrupts them. Indeed, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, came out to his Companions while they were praying and reciting aloud, and said:

“O people, each of you is conversing privately with his Lord, so do not raise your voices over one another when reciting.”

If he forbade someone praying from raising his voice over another person praying, how much more does this apply to others? Anyone who does something that disturbs those in the mosque, or does something that leads to such disturbance, must be prevented from doing so. And Allah knows best.

translated_text:
“We have certainly seen the turning of your face toward heaven, and We will surely turn you to a qiblah with which you will be pleased. So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque. And wherever you are, turn your faces toward it.”

Up to His words:

“And wherever you set out from, turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque. And wherever you are, turn your faces toward it.”

Shatrahu means “toward it” or “in its direction,” as the poet said:

Umm Zinbāʿ, turn—turn the pale camels
To face Banū Tamīm.

He also says:

“For everyone there is a direction toward which he turns.”

Wijhah means the same as jihah (direction), just as ʿidah (promise) and zinah (weight) were originally wiʿdah and wiznah. Thus, the qiblah is what one faces, while the wijhah is what one turns toward. Allah, glorified be He, commanded him to turn his face toward the Sacred Mosque. The “Sacred Mosque” means the entire Sacred Precinct, as in His words:

“So let them not approach the Sacred Mosque after this year of theirs.”

This is not restricted to the Kaaba. This bears out the transmitted report: “The Kaaba is the qiblah for the mosque; the mosque is the qiblah for Mecca; Mecca is the qiblah for the Sacred Precinct; and the Sacred Precinct is the qiblah for the earth.”

It is established in the two Sahīh collections that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prayed two units of prayer facing the Kaaba and said: “This is the qiblah.”

It is also established in the two Sahīh collections that he said:

“Do not face the qiblah when defecating or urinating, nor turn your backs toward it; rather, face east or west.”

He thus forbade facing the qiblah when defecating or urinating, and commanded facing it in prayer. Hence, the qiblah which he forbade people to face

 قَالَ التِّرْمِذِيُّ حَدِيثٌ صَحِيحٌ.
 وَهَكَذَا قَالَ غَيْرُ وَاحِدٍ مِنْ الصَّحَابَةِ:
 مِثْلُ عُمَرَ وَعُثْمَانَ وَعَلِيِّ بْنِ أَبِي طَالِبٍ وَابْنِ عَبَّاسٍ وَابْنِ عُمَرَ وَغَيْرِهِمْ. وَلَا يُعْرَفُ عَنْ أَحَدٍ مِنْ الصَّحَابَةِ فِي ذَلِكَ نِزَاعٌ؛ وَهَكَذَا نَصَّ عَلَيْهِ أَئِمَّةُ الْمَذَاهِبِ الْمَتْبُوعَةِ وَكَلَامُهُمْ فِي ذَلِكَ مَعْرُوفٌ. وَقَدْ حَكَى مُتَأَخِّرُو الْفُقَهَاءِ فِي ذَلِكَ قَوْلَيْنِ فِي مَذْهَبِ أَحْمَد وَغَيْرِهِ. وَقَدْ تَأَمَّلْت نُصُوصَ أَحْمَد فِي هَذَا الْبَابِ فَوَجَدْتهَا مُتَّفِقَةً لَا اخْتِلَافَ فِيهَا وَكَذَلِكَ يَذْكُرُ الِاخْتِلَافَ فِي مَذْهَبِ مَالِكٍ وَأَبِي حَنِيفَةَ وَالشَّافِعِيِّ وَهُوَ عِنْدَ التَّحْقِيقِ لَيْسَ بِخِلَافِ؛
 بَلْ مَنْ قَالَ:
 يَجْتَهِدُ أَنْ يُصَلِّيَ إلَى عَيْنِ الْكَعْبَةِ أَوْ فَرْضُهُ اسْتِقْبَالُ عَيْنِ الْكَعْبَةِ بِحَسَبِ اجْتِهَادِهِ فَقَدْ أَصَابَ.
 وَمَنْ قَالَ:
 يَجْتَهِدُ أَنْ يُصَلِّيَ إلَى جِهَةِ الْكَعْبَةِ أَوْ فَرْضُهُ اسْتِقْبَالُ الْقِبْلَةِ فَقَدْ أَصَابَ. وَذَلِكَ أَنَّهُمْ مُتَّفِقُونَ عَلَى أَنَّ مَنْ شَاهَدَ الْكَعْبَةَ فَإِنَّهُ يُصَلِّي إلَيْهَا. وَمُتَّفِقُونَ عَلَى أَنَّهُ كُلَّمَا قَرُبَ الْمُصَلُّونَ إلَيْهَا كَانَ صَفُّهُمْ أَقْصَرَ مِنْ الْبَعِيدِينَ عَنْهَا. وَهَذَا شَأْنُ كُلِّ مَا يُسْتَقْبَلُ. فَالصَّفُّ الْقَرِيبُ مِنْهَا لَا يَزِيدُ طُولُهُ عَلَى قَدْرِ الْكَعْبَةِ. وَلَوْ زَادَ
translated_text:
or turn their backs toward when defecating or urinating is the same qiblah that he commanded worshippers to face in prayer. He, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“What lies between east and west is qiblah.”

Al-Tirmidhī said: “This is an authentic hadith.”

Several Companions likewise stated this, including ʿUmar, ʿUthmān, ʿAlī ibn Abī Tālib, Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn ʿUmar, and others. No disagreement on this matter is known from any of the Companions. The imams of the established schools of law also explicitly stated this, and their statements on the matter are well known.

Later jurists have reported two positions on this matter within the school of Ahmad and other schools. I have examined Ahmad’s statements on this subject and found them consistent, without any disagreement. Differences are likewise reported within the schools of Mālik, Abū Hanīfah, and al-Shāfiʿī, but upon careful examination, these do not constitute a real disagreement.

Rather, whoever says that a person should use his best judgment to pray toward the Kaaba itself, or that his obligation is to face the Kaaba itself according to his best judgment, is correct. Whoever says that a person should use his best judgment to pray in the direction of the Kaaba, or that his obligation is to face the qiblah, is also correct.

This is because they agree that whoever can see the Kaaba must pray facing it. They also agree that the closer worshippers are to it, the shorter their row will be compared with the rows of those farther away. This holds true of anything one faces. Thus, the row close to the Kaaba does not extend beyond its width. If it were longer,

لَكَانَ الزَّائِدُ مُصَلِّيًا إلَى غَيْرِ الْكَعْبَةِ. وَالصَّفُّ الَّذِي خَلْفَهُ يَكُونُ أَطْوَلَ مِنْهُ وَهَلُمَّ جَرَّا. فَإِذَا كَانَتْ الصُّفُوفُ تَحْتَ سَقَائِفِ الْمَسْجِدِ كَانَتْ مُنْحَنِيَةً بِقَدْرِ مَا يَسْتَقْبِلُونَ الْكَعْبَةَ وَهُمْ يُصَلُّونَ إلَيْهَا وَإِلَى جِهَتِهَا أَيْضًا فَإِذَا بَعُدَ النَّاسُ عَنْهَا كَانُوا مُصَلِّينَ إلَى جِهَتِهَا وَهُمْ مُصَلُّونَ إلَيْهَا أَيْضًا وَلَوْ كَانَ الصَّفُّ طَوِيلًا يَزِيدُ طُولُهُ عَلَى قَدْرِ الْكَعْبَةِ صَحَّتْ صَلَاتُهُمْ بِاتِّفَاقِ الْمُسْلِمِينَ وَإِنْ كَانَ الصَّفُّ مُسْتَقِيمًا حَيْثُ لَمْ يُشَاهِدُوهَا. وَمِنْ الْمَعْلُومِ أَنَّهُ لَوْ سَارَ مِنْ الصُّفُوفِ عَلَى خَطٍّ مُسْتَقِيمٍ إلَيْهَا لَكَانَ مَا يَزِيدُ عَلَى قَدْرِهَا خَارِجًا عَنْ مَسَافَتِهَا. فَمَنْ تَوَهَّمَ أَنَّ الْفَرْضَ أَنْ يَقْصِدَ الْمُصَلِّي الصَّلَاةَ فِي مَكَانٍ لَوْ سَارَ عَلَى خَطٍّ مُسْتَقِيمٍ وَصَلَ إلَى عَيْنِ الْكَعْبَةِ فَقَدْ أَخْطَأَ. وَمَنْ فَسَّرَ وُجُوبَ الصَّلَاةِ إلَى الْعَيْنِ بِهَذَا وَأَوْجَبَ هَذَا فَقَدَ أَخْطَأَ وَإِنْ كَانَ هَذَا قَدْ قَالَهُ قَائِلٌ مِنْ الْمُجْتَهِدِينَ فَهَذَا الْقَوْلُ خَطَأٌ خَالَفَ نَصَّ الْكِتَابِ وَالسُّنَّةِ وَإِجْمَاعَ السَّلَفِ؛ بَلْ وَإِجْمَاعَ الْأُمَّةِ. فَإِنَّ الْأُمَّةَ مُتَّفِقَةٌ عَلَى صِحَّةِ صَلَاةِ الصَّفِّ الْمُسْتَطِيلِ الَّذِي يَزِيدُ طُولُهُ عَلَى سَمْتِ الْكَعْبَةِ بِأَضْعَافِ مُضَاعَفَةٍ وَإِنْ كَانَ الصَّفُّ مُسْتَقِيمًا لَا انْحِنَاءَ فِيهِ وَلَا تَقَوُّسَ.
 فَإِنْ قِيلَ:
 مَعَ الْبُعْدِ لَا يُحْتَاجُ إلَى الِانْحِنَاءِ وَالتَّقَوُّسِ كَمَا يُحْتَاجُ إلَيْهِ فِي الْقُرْبِ كَمَا أَنَّ النَّاسَ إذَا اسْتَقْبَلُوا الْهِلَالَ أَوْ الشَّمْسَ أَوْ جَبَلًا مِنْ الْجِبَالِ فَإِنَّهُمْ يَسْتَقْبِلُونَهُ مَعَ كَثْرَتِهِمْ وَتَفَرُّقِهِمْ وَلَوْ كَانَ قَرِيبًا لَمْ يَسْتَقْبِلُوهُ
translated_text:
those extending beyond its width would be praying toward something other than the Kaaba. The row behind it is longer, and so on. Thus, when the rows are beneath the mosque’s covered galleries, they curve sufficiently for the worshippers to face the Kaaba: they are praying toward it and in its direction as well. When people are far from it, they pray in its direction and are also praying toward it. Even if a row extends beyond the width of the Kaaba, their prayer is valid by the agreement of the Muslims, even when the row is straight, provided they cannot see it.

It is evident that, if one were to walk straight ahead toward it from these rows, the portion extending beyond its width would lie outside its alignment. Whoever imagines that a worshipper must pray in such a position that, were he to walk straight ahead, he would reach the Kaaba itself has therefore erred. Whoever interprets the obligation to pray toward the Kaaba itself in this way and makes this obligatory has erred. Even if a jurist exercising independent judgment has held this view, it is erroneous and contrary to the explicit texts of the Quran and Sunnah and the consensus of the early generations—indeed, the consensus of the Muslim community. For the community agrees that the prayer of a long row extending many times beyond the width of the Kaaba is valid, even if the row is straight, without any bend or curvature.

If it is objected:

At a distance, bending and curving are not needed as they are at close range. Similarly, when people face the crescent moon, the sun, or a mountain, they face it even though they are numerous and scattered, whereas if it were close, they could not face it

translated_text:
unless they were few and gathered together. The reply is:

There is no doubt that the bending and curving required at a distance are less than those required nearby. The greater the distance, the less the curvature; the nearer one is, the greater it becomes, until the row nearest the Kaaba has the greatest bend and curvature. Nevertheless, some bending and curving would still be necessary at a distance if the aim were to establish a straight line between the worshipper and the Kaaba, such that, were he to walk along it, he would reach the Kaaba. The curvature, however, would be very slight. It has been said, for example, that if a row were a mile long and situated in Greater Syria, each person’s bend would amount to the measure of a barley grain. This was mentioned by someone who explicitly stated [that] (1) facing the Kaaba itself is obligatory, but said that such slight curvature may be overlooked.

The reply to him is:

This is precisely what we mean when we say that the obligation is to face its direction: one is exempt from having to aim for such bending and curving. The disagreement thus becomes merely verbal, without any substantive difference. The point is that whoever prays in its direction is praying toward the Kaaba itself, even though he is not required to aim for such precision. It should not be said that someone who prays in this manner is mistaken in reality but excused. Rather, he faces the qiblah in reality as well as outwardly, and this is what he has been commanded to do. Thus, when the Companions of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, built mosques in the various cities, some were such that, if a straight line were projected from them toward the Kaaba, it would miss it. Yet the Muslims’ prayers in them were valid by the agreement of the Muslims.

This also clarifies the claim made by those who say:

“For anyone near it or near the mosque of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, the qiblah must lie along a straight line, since the Prophet would not be left in error.”

The reply is:

These people assumed that such an orientation towards the qiblah would be mistaken. It would only be mistaken if the obligation were to seek an alignment along a straight line between the centre of one’s nose and the Kaaba. That is not the case; rather, the texts of the Quran and Sunnah cited above establish the contrary.

A similar example is the statement of some that if people mistakenly perform the standing at ‘Arafah on the tenth day, it suffices for them. The correct view is that this is the Day of ‘Arafah, both in reality and outwardly, and there is no error in that. Rather, the Day of ‘Arafah is the day on which people perform the standing at ‘Arafah. Likewise, the crescent moon only counts as such when people proclaim its sighting; if it rises but they do not proclaim its sighting, it does not count as such. There is, however, a well-known disagreement concerning the crescent: does the term denote what rises, even if its sighting is not proclaimed, or what people proclaim sighting? These are two well-known views within the school of Ahmad and elsewhere, unlike the disagreement concerning facing the Kaaba.

Further evidence for this is that, if it were said that a person must seek an alignment along a straight line between the centre of his nose and forehead and the Kaaba, the reply would be that there must then be a means of knowing this. For Allah has not made anything obligatory without providing evidence by which it may be known. Yet it is well known that only a select few know how to determine this, despite their disagreements and their frequent errors in doing so, whereas the obligation to face the qiblah is general

for all Muslims. The knowledge required of them cannot therefore be obscure, attainable only through a lengthy, difficult and perilous method, when acquiring such knowledge is impossible or difficult in most circumstances.

This is why those who have followed this method speak without knowledge, while disagreeing among themselves about it. Their familiar points of reference are al-Jady and the celestial pole. Some of them say:

“The pole is al-Jady, and it is a faint star.”

This is wrong in three respects: the pole is not al-Jady; al-Jady is not a faint star, but a bright one; and the pole is not a star at all.

Others say:

“Al-Jady is a faint star.”

This too is mistaken. Most of them say that the pole is a faint star, and report two opinions concerning whether the pole revolves or not. This is a confusion of distinct things. The pole, which is the centre of rotation, does not shift from its position, just as the spindle of a millstone does not shift from its position. There is, however, a small, faint star near it. If this star is called the pole, it is so named because it is the nearest star to the pole. This star does revolve: the stars unquestionably revolve, while the centre of rotation, which is their pole, unquestionably does not. Reporting two opinions on this matter is therefore the speech of someone who has failed to distinguish between the two.

The readily visible point of reference is al-Jady. Using it to establish exact alignment with the Kaaba is possible only at certain times, not at all times. the right of someone facing the door. Those whose homeland is aligned with this pole, such as the people of Harrān and others, thus pray towards that corner. Hence their qiblah is said to be the most accurately aligned. Those whose homeland lies west of them—such as the people of Syria—turn slightly eastwards in proportion to their distance from this line: the farther away they are, the more they turn. Those who live east of them—such as the people of Iraq—adjust their qiblah in the opposite direction. Thus, the inhabitants of those lands keep the pole and what lies near it directly behind their heads. The people of Syria turn slightly, keeping it between the left ear and the hollow at the nape, or behind the left ear, depending on how near or far their homeland is from those people. The people of Iraq keep it behind the right ear. It is well known that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and the Companions never instructed anyone to take account of the pole, anything near it, al-Jady, Banāt Na‘sh, or anything else of this kind.

For this reason, Imam Ahmad objected to those who instructed people to take account of these things. He instructed them not to determine the qiblah by al-Jady, saying:

“The hadith makes no mention of al-Jady. Rather, whatever lies between east and west is qiblah.”

This is indeed correct. Had determining the qiblah in this way been obligatory or recommended, the Companions would have known it best and been the first to do so, and the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would have explained it. He left nothing pertaining to the religion unexplained. How, then, could this be so when he expressly stated that whatever lies between east and west is qiblah, and forbade facing the qiblah or turning one’s back towards it when defecating or urinating?
