translated_text:
Muslims that the prohibition in this regard is not limited to the person relieving himself being aligned with the Ka‘bah along a straight line. Rather, the prohibition is broader than that. Facing the qiblah is commanded in one circumstance, just as it is forbidden in another. Although a prohibition may encompass what a command does not, this is consistent with his saying:

“Whatever lies between east and west is qiblah.”

Moreover, making religion dependent on this leads the Muslim community into disputes and disagreements over its religion, whereas Allah has forbidden division and disagreement. Most people have no precise knowledge of this; they merely follow those who have determined it approximately. Exact determination in this matter is either impossible or exceedingly difficult, and the Sharia does not impose such requirements.

Among those who claim expertise in calculation and knowledge of this matter, you will find that most make erroneous statements. When asked for evidence for their claims, they fall back on unverified premises and reports from people whose accounts cannot be trusted. The jurists who have mentioned some of these matters received them from those people without examining them rigorously. Thus, the followers of both groups ultimately rely on others in a way that involves error in many instances. One then claims that the qiblah he has determined is correct, rather than the one determined by the other, while the other claims the opposite. Eventually, people split into factions and groups. All of this is among the things Allah and His Messenger have forbidden.

The reason for this is that they have introduced into their religion what does not belong to it and prescribed religious practices for which Allah has given no permission. They have therefore disagreed over the innovation they themselves prescribed, because it

has no fixed standard, just as those who seek to determine the appearance of the new crescent or the onset of dawn by calculation disagree. There is no consistently valid mathematical proof for this; rather, it is fraught with contradictions and discrepancies. These people have turned away from the latitude afforded by religion and from the proofs of the Sharia, falling into various forms of ignorance and innovation despite their claims to knowledge and expertise. Such is how Allah deals with those who abandon what He has prescribed in favour of innovations and go to excessive lengths in religion.

It is authentically reported in Sahīh Muslim, from al-Ahnaf ibn Qays, from Ibn Mas‘ūd, that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Those who go to extremes are doomed.”

He repeated this three times. Ahmad and Abū Dāwūd also narrated it.

Furthermore, Allah said:

“So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque.”

And He said:

“Everyone has a direction toward which he turns,”

meaning, a direction he faces. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“This is the qiblah.”

The qiblah is that which one faces. He also said:

“Whoever prays as we pray, faces our qiblah, and eats what we slaughter is a Muslim, with the same rights and obligations as us.”

Muslims unanimously agree that, as a general rule, a person praying must face the qiblah. What is commanded, then, is to face the qiblah and turn one’s face toward the Sacred Mosque. It is well known that people are prescribed to turn their faces toward the preacher and are forbidden to face the qiblah when defecating or urinating. In these and similar cases, facing something does not require alignment with the centre of the face and body. Rather, a slight deviation does not mean that one is no longer facing it. If a term has a defined meaning in the Sharia, that meaning is authoritative; otherwise, its meaning in language and customary usage is authoritative. Here, what constitutes facing something is established by the Sharia, language, and customary usage.

As for the Lawgiver, he said:

“Whatever lies between east and west is qiblah.”

It is well known that someone in Medina, Syria, or similar regions who places east to his left and west to his right is facing the Ka'bah with his body, such that a straight line could extend from his face to the Ka'bah, and likewise from his chest and abdomen. That line, however, may not extend from the centre of his face and chest. Thus, facing something with one’s face is broader than facing it with the centre of the face alone. And Allah knows best.

the Muslims in all acts of worship: prayer, purification, zakat, Hajj, fasting, freeing slaves, jihad, and so forth. If a person says something contrary to what he intends in his heart, what counts is his heartfelt intention, not his words. If he speaks without forming an intention in his heart, that does not suffice, by agreement of the imams of the Muslims. Intention is a form of purpose. Hence the Arabs say, “May Allah have good in store for you,” meaning, “May He intend good for you.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Actions are only according to intentions, and each person shall have only what he intended. Whoever emigrates to Allah and His Messenger, his emigration is to Allah and His Messenger; and whoever emigrates for worldly gain or to marry a woman, his emigration is for that for which he emigrated.”

By “intention,” he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, meant the intention in the heart, not on the tongue, by agreement of the imams of the Muslims—the four imams and others.

The occasion of this hadith also indicates this. A man emigrated from Mecca to Medina to marry a woman called Umm Qays, and so he became known as “the emigrant for Umm Qays.” The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, then delivered a sermon from the pulpit and mentioned this hadith. This man’s intention was in his heart.

Stating the intention aloud is neither obligatory nor recommended, by agreement of the Muslims. Rather, anyone who does so believing it to be prescribed by Islamic law is an innovator who contravenes that law. do after the talbiya, not before it. All forms of verbalizing the intention that people have introduced—before the takbīr, before the talbiya, in purification, and in all other acts of worship—are religious innovations that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not prescribe.

Every addition introduced into prescribed acts of worship that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not prescribe is an innovation. Indeed, he consistently refrained from such additions in his worship. Thus, performing them and persisting in them constitutes innovation and misguidance in two respects:

One is the belief that this is prescribed and recommended—that doing it is better than leaving it undone—even though the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, never did it at all. The real implication of this claim is that what we have done is more complete and better than what the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did.

A man once asked Mālik ibn Anas about entering ihrām before reaching the designated boundary. Mālik replied:

“I fear that you may fall into temptation.”

The questioner said, “What temptation is there in that? It is only a few additional miles in obedience to Allah, the Almighty and Majestic.”

He replied, “What greater temptation could there be than to think that you have been singled out for a virtuous deed that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not perform?”

It is established in the two Sahīhs that he said:

“Whoever turns away from my Sunnah is not of me.”

That is, whoever thinks that another way is better than my Sunnah and turns away from what [I have prescribed] (1), believing

that what he has chosen is better than what he has turned away from—is not of me. For the best speech is the speech of Allah, and the best guidance is the guidance of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, as an authentic report states that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would proclaim in his Friday sermons.

Whoever says that someone else’s guidance is better than the guidance of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, has succumbed to temptation; indeed, he is astray. Allah Most High said—honouring him and affirming his proof against all mankind:

“So let those who oppose his command beware, lest a trial befall them or a painful punishment afflict them.”

That is, a punishment that causes pain. He, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, commanded Muslims to follow him, to regard as obligatory what he made obligatory and as recommended what he favoured, and to believe that nothing is better than this. Whoever does not believe this has disobeyed his command. In Sahīh Muslim, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Those who go to excess are ruined.” He said this three times.

That is, those who impose strictness where strictness is unwarranted. Ubayy ibn Kaʿb and Ibn Masʿūd said: “Moderation in following the Sunnah is better than strenuous effort in following an innovation.”

No one may invoke the gathering of people for tarāwīh (Ramadan night prayers) as an argument, saying:

“What an excellent innovation this is!”

For it is an innovation in the linguistic sense, because they did something they had not done in this form during the lifetime of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace; yet it is a Sunnah prescribed in Islamic law. The same applies to expelling Jews and Christians from the Arabian Peninsula and founding towns such as Kūfa

and Basra, compiling the Quran into a single volume, establishing the register of stipends, and other such measures.

The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prescribed the Ramadan night prayers for his community and led them in congregation for several nights. During his lifetime, people prayed both in groups and individually. However, he did not regularly gather them into a single congregation, lest these prayers become obligatory for them. When he died, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, the revealed law became settled.

When ʿUmar—may Allah be pleased with him—became caliph, he gathered them behind a single imam. The one who gathered them was Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, who assembled the people for these prayers at the command of ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb—may Allah be pleased with him. ʿUmar was one of the rightly guided caliphs, concerning whom the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Adhere to my Sunnah and the Sunnah of the rightly guided caliphs after me. Bite firmly upon it with your back teeth.”

That is, the molars, because they exert the greatest force.

In Sahīh Muslim, Ibn ʿUmar is reported to have said:

“The prayer during travel is two rakʿahs. Whoever rejects the Sunnah has disbelieved.”

That is, whoever believes that two rakʿahs do not suffice for a traveller has disbelieved.

The second aspect concerns consistently departing, in acts of worship, from the practice consistently observed by the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. This is an innovation by the agreement of the imams, even if someone supposes that his addition contains some good. An example is the introduction by some earlier people of the call to prayer and the call to commence prayer for the two Eid prayers. They were forbidden to do so, and the imams of the Muslims disapproved of it, just as

 لَمْ يَكْرَهْهُ اللَّهُ وَرَسُولُهُ فَهُوَ غَالِطٌ. فَإِجْمَاعُ أَئِمَّةِ الدِّينِ أَنَّهُ لَا حَرَامَ إلَّا مَا حَرَّمَهُ اللَّهُ وَرَسُولُهُ وَلَا دِينَ إلَّا مَا شَرَعَهُ اللَّهُ وَرَسُولُهُ وَمَنْ خَرَجَ عَنْ هَذَا وَهَذَا فَقَدْ دَخَلَ فِي حَرْبٍ مِنْ اللَّهِ فَمَنْ شَرَعَ مِنْ الدِّينِ مَا لَمْ يَأْذَنْ بِهِ اللَّهُ وَحَرَّمَ مَا لَمْ يُحَرِّمْ اللَّهُ وَرَسُولُهُ فَهُوَ مِنْ دِينِ أَهْلِ الْجَاهِلِيَّةِ الْمُخَالِفِينَ لِرَسُولِهِ الَّذِينَ ذَمَّهُمْ اللَّهُ فِي سُورَةِ الْأَنْعَامِ وَالْأَعْرَافِ وَغَيْرِهِمَا مِنْ السُّورِ حَيْثُ شَرَعُوا مِنْ الدِّينِ مَا لَمْ يَأْذَنْ بِهِ اللَّهُ. فَحَرَّمُوا مَا لَمْ يُحَرِّمْهُ اللَّهُ وَأَحَلُّوا مَا حَرَّمَهُ اللَّهُ فَذَمَّهُمْ اللَّهُ وَعَابَهُمْ عَلَى ذَلِكَ.
 فَلِهَذَا كَانَ دِينُ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ بِاَللَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِ أَنَّ الْأَحْكَامَ الْخَمْسَةَ:
 الْإِيجَابُ

(١) ما بين معقوفتين غير موجود في المطبوع، ولم أقف عليه في كتاب صيانة مجموع الفتاوى من السقط والتصحيف

translated_text:
would be the case if someone prayed two rakʿahs after the ritual walk between Safā and Marwah, by analogy with the two rakʿahs after circumambulation. Some later scholars of al-Shāfiʿī’s school recommended this. Some later scholars of Ahmad’s school also recommended that a pilgrim entering the Sacred Mosque begin with the prayer of greeting the mosque. In doing so, they contradicted the imams and the Sunnah. Rather, the Sunnah is for someone in the state of ihrām to begin with circumambulation, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did when he entered the mosque. This differs from a resident who wishes to pray there without circumambulating: it is good for him to offer the prayer of greeting the mosque.

In short, Allah perfected the religion for the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his community, and through him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, completed His favour upon them. Anyone who declares an act obligatory when Allah and His Messenger have not made it obligatory, or [disliked] (1) when Allah and His Messenger have not deemed it disliked, is mistaken. The imams of the religion unanimously agree that nothing is forbidden except what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden, and nothing belongs to the religion except what Allah and His Messenger have prescribed. Whoever departs from these two principles has brought upon himself war from Allah.

Whoever institutes religious practices that Allah has not authorized and prohibits what Allah and His Messenger have not prohibited follows the religion of the people of pre-Islamic ignorance who opposed His Messenger. Allah condemned them in Surahs al-Anʿām and al-Aʿrāf and elsewhere for instituting religious practices that He had not authorized. They prohibited what Allah had not prohibited and permitted what Allah had forbidden, so Allah condemned and censured them for that.

Thus, those who believe in Allah and His Messenger hold as part of their religion that the five legal rulings—declaring something obligatory

 كَمَا قَالَ بَعْضُ السَّلَفِ:
 لَا تَنْظُرُ إلَى عَمَلِ الْفَقِيهِ وَلَكِنْ سَلْهُ يُصَدِّقْك وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ. وَالْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ.
وَسُئِلَ:
عَمَّنْ يَخْرُجُ مَنْ بَيْتِهِ نَاوِيًا الطَّهَارَةَ أَوْ الصَّلَاةَ. هَلْ يَحْتَاجُ إلَى تَجْدِيدِ نِيَّةٍ غَيْرِ هَذِهِ عِنْدَ فِعْلِ الطَّهَارَةِ أَوْ الصَّلَاةِ؟ أَوْ لَا؟ وَهَلْ التَّلَفُّظُ
translated_text:
, recommended, permissible, disliked, or forbidden—are to be derived only from the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Nothing is obligatory except what Allah and His Messenger have made obligatory, and nothing is lawful except what Allah and His Messenger have made lawful.

On some of these matters the imams of the religion agreed; on others they differed and referred them back to Allah and His Messenger. Allah Most High says:

“O you who believe, obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you. If you disagree over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger, if you believe in Allah and the Last Day. That is better and best in outcome.”

Anyone who speaks ignorantly and in opposition to the imams must be prohibited from doing so and disciplined if he persists, as others like him among the ignorant are treated. No leader of misguidance is to be followed in anything that contravenes the revealed law, even if he is renowned for his knowledge. As one of the early generations said:

“Do not look at the jurist’s conduct; rather, ask him, and he will tell you the truth.”

Allah knows best. All praise is due to Allah.

He was asked:

Does someone who leaves his home intending to purify himself or pray need to renew that intention when he actually purifies himself or prays, or not? And is verbalizing

بِالنِّيَّةِ سُنَّةٌ أَمْ لَا؟ .
فَأَجَابَ:
الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ رَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ، سُئِلَ الْإِمَامُ أَحْمَد عَنْ رَجُلٍ يَخْرُجُ مِنْ بَيْتِهِ لِلصَّلَاةِ هَلْ يَنْوِي حِينَ الصَّلَاةِ؟
 فَقَالَ:
 قَدْ نَوَى حِينَ خَرَجَ وَلِهَذَا قَالَ أَكَابِرُ أَصْحَابِهِ - كالخرقي وَغَيْرِهِ - يُجْزِئُهُ تَقْدِيمُ النِّيَّةِ عَلَى التَّكْبِيرِ مِنْ حِينِ يَدْخُلُ وَقْتُ الصَّلَاةِ وَإِذَا كَانَ مُسْتَحْضِرًا لِلنِّيَّةِ إلَى حِينِ الصَّلَاةِ أَجْزَأَ ذَلِكَ بِاتِّفَاقِ الْعُلَمَاءِ. فَإِنَّ النِّيَّةَ لَا يَجِبُ التَّلَفُّظُ بِهَا بِاتِّفَاقِ الْعُلَمَاءِ. وَمَعْلُومٌ فِي الْعَادَةِ أَنَّ مَنْ كَبَّرَ فِي الصَّلَاةِ لَا بُدَّ أَنْ يَقْصِدَ الصَّلَاةَ وَإِذَا عَلِمَ أَنَّهُ يُصَلِّي الظُّهْرَ نَوَى الظُّهْرَ فَمَتَى عَلِمَ مَا يُرِيدُ فِعْلَهُ نَوَاهُ بِالضَّرُورَةِ وَلَكِنْ إذَا لَمْ يَعْلَمْ أَوْ نَسِيَ شَذَّتْ عَنْهُ النِّيَّةُ وَهَذَا نَادِرٌ وَالتَّلَفُّظُ بِالنِّيَّةِ فِي اسْتِحْبَابِهِ قَوْلَانِ فِي مَذْهَبِ أَحْمَد وَغَيْرِهِ. وَالْمَنْصُوصُ عَنْهُ أَنَّهُ لَا يُسْتَحَبُّ التَّلَفُّظُ بِالنِّيَّةِ.
 قَالَ أَبُو دَاوُد قُلْت لِأَحْمَد:
 يَقُولُ الْمُصَلِّي قَبْلَ التَّكْبِيرِ شَيْئًا؟
 قَالَ:
 لَا.
وَسُئِلَ:
هَلْ يَجِبُ أَنْ تَكُونَ النِّيَّةُ مُقَارِنَةً لِلتَّكْبِيرِ؟ وَالْمَسْئُولُ أَنْ يُوَضِّحَ لَنَا كَيْفِيَّةَ مُقَارَنَتِهَا لِلتَّكْبِيرِ كَمَا ذَكَرَ الشَّافِعِيُّ أَنَّهُ لَا تَصِحُّ الصَّلَاةُ إلَّا
translated_text:
the intention a sunnah practice or not?

He replied:

All praise is due to Allah, Lord of all worlds. Imām Ahmad was asked about a man who leaves his home to pray: must he form his intention at the time of prayer? He replied: “He already formed his intention when he left.”

For this reason, leading scholars among his followers, such as al-Khiraqī and others, said that it suffices to form the intention before the opening takbīr (declaration of Allah’s greatness), as early as the beginning of the prayer’s appointed time. If he keeps the intention consciously in mind until he prays, that suffices by scholarly agreement. Scholars also agree that the intention need not be verbalized.

It is common knowledge that anyone who pronounces the takbīr in prayer necessarily intends to pray. If he knows that he is praying the noon prayer, then he intends the noon prayer. Whenever someone knows what he wishes to do, he necessarily intends it. But if he does not know, or forgets, the intention escapes him; this is rare.

There are two views within Ahmad’s school and elsewhere as to whether verbalizing the intention is recommended. His explicitly stated position is that it is not recommended. Abū Dāwūd said: “I asked Ahmad, ‘Does the worshipper say anything before the takbīr?’ He replied, ‘No.’”

He was also asked:

“Must the intention coincide with the takbīr? Please explain to us how it is to coincide with the takbīr, since al-Shāfi‘ī stated that prayer is not valid unless

أَحَدُهُمَا:

وَالْمُقَارَنَةُ الْمَشْرُوطَةُ:
 قَدْ تُفَسَّرُ بِوُقُوعِ التَّكْبِيرِ عَقِيبَ النِّيَّةِ وَهَذَا مُمْكِنٌ لَا صُعُوبَةَ فِيهِ بَلْ عَامَّةُ النَّاسِ إنَّمَا يُصَلُّونَ هَكَذَا وَهَذَا أَمْرٌ ضَرُورِيٌّ لَوْ كُلِّفُوا تَرْكَهُ لَعَجَزُوا عَنْهُ. وَقَدْ تُفَسَّرُ بِانْبِسَاطِ آخِرِ النِّيَّةِ عَلَى آخِرِ التَّكْبِيرِ. بِحَيْثُ يَكُونُ أَوَّلُهَا مَعَ أَوَّلِهِ وَآخِرُهَا مَعَ آخِرِهِ. وَهَذَا لَا يَصِحُّ؛ لِأَنَّهُ يَقْتَضِي عُزُوبَ كَمَالِ النِّيَّةِ فِي أَوَّلِ الصَّلَاةِ وَخُلُوَّ أَوَّلِ الصَّلَاةِ عَنْ النِّيَّةِ الْوَاجِبَةِ. وَقَدْ تُفَسَّرُ بِحُضُورِ جَمِيعِ النِّيَّةِ مَعَ جَمِيعِ آخِرِ التَّكْبِيرِ وَهَذَا تَنَازَعُوا فِي إمْكَانِهِ.
 فَمِنْ الْعُلَمَاءِ مَنْ قَالَ:
 إنَّ هَذَا غَيْرُ مُمْكِنٍ وَلَا مَقْدُورٍ لِلْبَشَرِ عَلَيْهِ فَضْلًا عَنْ وُجُوبِهِ وَلَوْ قِيلَ بِإِمْكَانِهِ فَهُوَ مُتَعَسِّرٌ فَيَسْقُطُ بِالْحَرَجِ.
original_footnote: (١) بياض بالأصل
translated_text:
the intention coincides with the takbīr. This is difficult.”

He replied:

Regarding the intention’s coinciding with the takbīr, scholars hold two well-known views. The first is that it is not obligatory . . . (1).

The concurrence stipulated as a condition may be understood to mean pronouncing the takbīr immediately after forming the intention. This is possible and presents no difficulty; indeed, this is how people generally pray. It is inevitable: were they required to refrain from doing so, they would be unable to.

It may also be understood as extending the intention so that its end coincides with the end of the takbīr, with its beginning coinciding with the beginning of the takbīr. This is not valid, because it entails the complete intention being absent at the beginning of the prayer, leaving the beginning of the prayer without the required intention.

It may also be understood as keeping the entire intention consciously present throughout the final part of the takbīr. Scholars have disagreed over whether this is possible. Some have said that this is impossible and beyond human capacity, let alone obligatory. Even if it were held to be possible, it would be so difficult that the requirement would be waived on account of hardship.

وَأَيْضًا فَمِمَّا يُبْطِلُ هَذَا وَاَلَّذِي قَبْلَهُ أَنَّ الْمُكَبِّرَ يَنْبَغِي لَهُ أَنْ يَتَدَبَّرَ التَّكْبِيرَ وَيَتَصَوَّرَهُ فَيَكُونُ قَلْبُهُ مَشْغُولًا بِمَعْنَى التَّكْبِيرِ لَا بِمَا يَشْغَلُهُ عَنْ ذَلِكَ مِنْ اسْتِحْضَارِ النِّيَّةِ؛ وَلِأَنَّ النِّيَّةَ مِنْ الشُّرُوطِ وَالشُّرُوطُ تَتَقَدَّمُ الْعِبَادَاتِ وَيَسْتَمِرُّ حُكْمُهَا إلَى آخِرِهَا كَالطَّهَارَةِ وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
وَسُئِلَ:
عَنْ 
" النِّيَّةِ "

فَأَجَابَ:
الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ، نِيَّةُ الطَّهَارَةِ مِنْ وُضُوءٍ أَوْ غُسْلٍ أَوْ تَيَمُّمٍ وَالصَّلَاةِ وَالصِّيَامِ وَالْحَجِّ وَالزَّكَاةِ وَالْكَفَّارَاتِ وَغَيْرِ ذَلِكَ مِنْ الْعِبَادَاتِ لَا تَفْتَقِرُ إلَى نُطْقِ اللِّسَانِ بِاتِّفَاقِ أَئِمَّةِ الْإِسْلَامِ. بَلْ النِّيَّةُ مَحَلُّهَا الْقَلْبُ دُونَ اللِّسَانِ بِاتِّفَاقِهِمْ فَلَوْ لَفَظَ بِلِسَانِهِ غَلَطًا بِخِلَافِ مَا نَوَى فِي قَلْبِهِ كَانَ الِاعْتِبَارُ بِمَا نَوَى لَا بِمَا لَفَظَ وَلَمْ يَذْكُرْ أَحَدٌ فِي ذَلِكَ خِلَافًا إلَّا أَنَّ بَعْضَ مُتَأَخِّرِي أَصْحَابِ الشَّافِعِيِّ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ - خَرَّجَ وَجْهًا فِي ذَلِكَ وَغَلَّطَهُ فِيهِ أَئِمَّةُ أَصْحَابِهِ.
 وَكَانَ سَبَبُ غَلَطِهِ أَنَّ الشَّافِعِيَّ قَالَ:
 إنَّ الصَّلَاةَ لَا بُدَّ مِنْ النُّطْقِ
translated_text:
Moreover, what invalidates both this interpretation and the preceding one is that the person pronouncing the takbīr should reflect upon it and grasp its meaning. His heart should therefore be occupied with the meaning of the takbīr, not distracted from it by consciously calling the intention to mind. Furthermore, intention is a condition of worship, and conditions precede acts of worship and remain legally effective until their completion, as is the case with ritual purity. And Allah knows best.

He was asked:

Does the “intention” required when beginning acts of worship, such as prayer and other observances, need to be spoken aloud—for example, by saying, “I intend to fast” or “I intend to pray”? Is this obligatory or not?

He replied:

Praise be to Allah. The intention for ritual purification—whether through ablution, ritual bathing, or dry ablution—and for prayer, fasting, pilgrimage, zakat, expiations, and other acts of worship does not need to be spoken, by agreement of the imams of Islam. Rather, they agree that the intention resides in the heart, not on the tongue. Thus, if someone mistakenly says something contrary to what he intends in his heart, what counts is his intention, not his words. No one has reported any disagreement on this, except that one of the later scholars of al-Shāfiʿī’s school—may Allah have mercy on him—derived a contrary opinion, but the leading scholars of his school judged him mistaken.

His mistake arose because al-Shāfiʿī said:

“Prayer necessarily requires a spoken utterance

By this, al-Shāfiʿī meant the obligatory opening takbīr. This mistaken scholar, however, thought that al-Shāfiʿī meant stating the intention aloud, and all the scholars of al-Shāfiʿī’s school judged him mistaken.

The scholars did, however, disagree over whether it is recommended to state the intention quietly. The jurists hold two well-known positions on this.

A group of scholars from the schools of Abū Hanīfah, al-Shāfiʿī, and Ahmad held that stating it is recommended because it reinforces the intention.

A group from the schools of Mālik and Ahmad, and others, held that stating it is not recommended, because this is an innovation not reported from the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, or his Companions. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, never commanded anyone in his community to state the intention, nor did he teach any Muslim to do so. Had this been a recognized, prescribed practice, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his Companions would not have neglected it, especially when it concerns something the community encounters every day and night.

This is the soundest position. Indeed, stating the intention betrays a deficiency in both reason and religion. As for religion, it is an innovation. As for reason, it is like someone who wants [to] (1) eat some food and says: “My intention in putting my hand into this vessel is that I want [to] (2) take a morsel from it, put it in my mouth, chew it, and then swallow it to satisfy my hunger.”

This is like someone saying: “I intend to perform, as an obligation, this prayer which is obligatory upon me

وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ -:
عَنْ رَجُلٍ قِيلَ لَهُ:

 ثُمَّ إنَّهُ قَالَ:
 لَنَا بِدْعَةٌ حَسَنَةٌ وَبِدْعَةٌ سَيِّئَةٌ وَاحْتَجَّ بِالتَّرَاوِيحِ
translated_text:
at this time, offering four units in congregation within its prescribed time, for Allah Most High.” All of this is foolishness and ignorance. For intention extends as far as knowledge does: whenever a person knows what he is doing, he necessarily intends it. It is rationally inconceivable for someone to act knowingly without intention; likewise, intention cannot exist without knowledge.

The imams agree that stating the intention aloud and repeating it are not prescribed. Indeed, anyone who habitually does this should be disciplined sufficiently to deter him from worshipping through innovations and disturbing people by raising his voice. For the hadith states:

“O people, each of you is conversing privately with his Lord, so do not raise your voices over one another in recitation.”

What, then, of someone who disturbs people with words other than recitation? Instead, he says: “I intend to pray, to pray such-and-such obligatory prayer at such-and-such a time”—among other practices that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not prescribe.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked about a man who was told: “It is not permissible to state the intention aloud in prayer, nor did the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, command it.”

The man replied: “It is true that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, neither did it nor commanded it. However, he did not forbid it, and the prayer of someone who states it aloud is not invalid.”

He then said: “We have good innovations and bad innovations,” and cited the tarāwīh prayers as evidence

on the grounds that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, neither gathered people for them nor forbade them, and that it was ‘Umar who gathered the people for them and ordered their observance. Is it as he says? Are the practices established by the Rightly Guided Caliphs to be called innovations? May practices instituted by others be judged by analogy with theirs? Is there any basis for what he says and does?

As for his statement, “The prayer of someone who states his intention aloud—for prayer or other acts of worship—is not invalid,” does someone who objects to him sin or not?

He answered:

Praise be to Allah. Stating the intention aloud for prayer is a bad innovation, not a good one. This is agreed upon among Muslims. None of them has said that stating the intention aloud is recommended or that it is a good innovation. Whoever says this has contradicted the Sunnah of the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and the consensus of the four imams and others. Anyone who says this must be called upon to repent. If he repents, well and good; otherwise, he is to be punished as he deserves.

The disagreement concerns only whether uttering the intention quietly is recommended. There are two views on this. The correct view is that uttering it is not recommended, for the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his Companions did not utter it, either quietly or aloud. No one has the right to alter the acts of worship that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prescribed for his community or to introduce innovations into them.

Nor may anyone claim that such things are good innovations, as in the case of the call to prayer that some people introduced for the two Eid prayers. The one who introduced it was Marwān ibn

He replied:

“This is Allah’s religion, with which He sent His messengers, and every Muslim must do this.”

He also recites the Quran aloud behind the imam. Did the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, do this? Did any of the Companions, any of the four imams, or any of the Muslim scholars? If the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, his Companions and the scholars did not do this in prayer, what is required of someone who attributes this to them and practises it himself? Is it permissible for a Muslim to support him with even a single word if he does this, claims that it is part of the religion, and tells those who rebuke him, “Everyone may do whatever he wishes in his religion, and your rebuking me is ignorance”? Are those who rebuke him correct in doing so, or not?

He answered:

Praise be to Allah. Stating the intention aloud is not prescribed according to any of the Muslim scholars. Neither the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, nor any of his caliphs or Companions, nor the early generations of this ummah or its imams, did this. Whoever claims that this is Allah’s religion and that it is obligatory must be instructed in Islamic law and called upon to repent of this statement. If he persists in it, he is to be put to death.

Rather, the intention required for acts of worship—such as ablution, ritual bathing, prayer, fasting, zakat and others—resides in the heart, by agreement of the imams of the Muslims. “Intention” means purpose and resolve, and all rational people agree that purpose and resolve reside in the heart, not the tongue. Thus, if someone forms his intention in his heart, his intention is valid according to the four imams,

and all the other imams of the Muslims, both early and later. There is no disagreement on this among the scholars who are followed and whose views are relied upon in issuing fatwas. Some later followers of the imams, however, claimed that verbalizing the intention is obligatory, though they did not say that stating it aloud is obligatory. Even so, this view is plainly erroneous, contrary to the consensus of the Muslims and to what is necessarily known of the religion of Islam by anyone familiar with the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, the practice of his caliphs, and how the Companions and their successors prayed. Anyone familiar with this knows that they did not verbalize their intentions, nor did the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, command them to do so or teach this to any of the Companions. Rather, it is established in the two Sahīh collections and elsewhere that he said to the Bedouin who prayed incorrectly:

“When you stand to pray, say ‘Allah is the Greatest,’ then recite whatever you can of the Quran.”

In the Sunan collections, it is reported that he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The key to prayer is purification; its inviolable state begins with the declaration ‘Allah is the Greatest’ and ends with the salutation of peace.”

In Sahīh Muslim, it is reported from ʿĀ’ishah, may Allah be pleased with her:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would begin the prayer with the declaration ‘Allah is the Greatest,’ and begin the recitation with ‘All praise is for Allah, Lord of all worlds.’”

It is established through mass transmission and the consensus of the Muslims that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and the Companions would begin the prayer with the declaration “Allah is the Greatest.” No Muslim has transmitted, either from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, or from any of the Companions, that he verbalized his intention before this declaration, whether quietly or aloud, or that he commanded this. It is well known that there would have been ample motivation and incentive to report such a practice if there had been

They said: Had it been recommended, the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would have done it or commanded it. “Pray as you have seen me pray.”

These scholars said: Adding this and similar practices to the manner of performing prayer is like introducing any other innovation into acts of worship—for example, adding the call to prayer and the call to commence prayer to the two Eid prayers, or adding two units of prayer on al-Marwah to the ritual walking between al-Safā and al-Marwah, and similar practices.

translated_text:
to satisfy my hunger,” and “I intend to wear this garment to cover myself,” and similar intentions already present in the heart, which it is unbecoming to articulate. Allah Most High says:

“Are you informing Allah of your religion, when Allah knows whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on earth?”

Concerning His words:

“We feed you only for the sake of Allah,”

some of the early generations said: “They did not say this with their tongues. Rather, Allah knew it from their hearts and reported it on their behalf.”

In short, the intention must be present in the heart; there is no disagreement about this. As for verbalizing it quietly, later scholars disagree over whether this is disliked or recommended. Saying it aloud, however, is disliked, prohibited, and not prescribed, by agreement of the Muslims. Repeating it is still more objectionable. This applies equally to the imam, those praying behind him, and anyone praying alone. By agreement of the Muslims, none of them is prescribed to voice the intention aloud or repeat it; rather, they are forbidden to do so.

Indeed, even someone praying alone is not prescribed to recite aloud if doing so disturbs others. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, came out to his Companions while they were praying and said:

“O people, each of you is conversing privately with his Lord, so do not raise your voices over one another in recitation.”

As for someone praying behind an imam, the Sunnah is for him to recite quietly, by agreement of the Muslims. However, if he occasionally raises his voice

with some words of remembrance, there is no harm in that, just as an imam may occasionally let those behind him hear a verse during a prayer normally recited quietly. It is authentically reported from Abū Qatāda that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace,

“would sometimes let them hear a verse during the noon and afternoon prayers.”

It is also authentically reported that some Companions praying behind the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, recited a supplication aloud at the opening of the prayer or upon rising from bowing, and he did not disapprove of this.

Anyone who persists in practising religious innovations and commending them should receive a discretionary punishment that deters him and others like him from such conduct. Anyone who mistakenly attributes something false to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, must be informed of his error; if he does not desist, he is to be punished. No one may speak about religion without knowledge, nor assist anyone who speaks about religion without knowledge or introduces into it something that does not belong to it.

As for the statement, “Everyone may do whatever he wishes in his religion,” this is a grave statement. Whoever says it must be called upon to repent of it; otherwise, he is to be punished. Indeed, persisting in such a statement warrants execution. No one may practise in religion anything except what Allah and His Messenger have prescribed, rather than whatever he wishes or desires. Allah Most High says:

“And who is more astray than one who follows his own desires without guidance from Allah?”

And He Most High says:

“Indeed, many lead others astray through their desires, without knowledge.”

“Do not follow your desires, lest they lead you astray from the way of Allah.”

And He says:

“Do not follow the desires of a people who went astray before, led many others astray, and strayed from the right way.”

And He Most High says:

“Have you seen the one who has taken as his god

his own desires? Will you then be his guardian?”

“Or do you think that most of them hear or understand? They are only like cattle—rather, they are even further astray.”

And He Most High says:

“But no, by your Lord, they will not believe until they make you judge in their disputes, then find within themselves no unease concerning your judgment and submit wholeheartedly.”

It has been reported that he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“By Him in whose hand is my soul, none of you truly believes until his desires accord with what I have brought.”

He Most High says:

“Have you not seen those who claim to believe in what has been sent down to you and what was sent down before you? They wish to seek judgment from false authorities, although they were commanded to reject them. Satan wishes to lead them far astray.”

“When they are told, ‘Come to what Allah has revealed and to the Messenger,’ you see the hypocrites turn away from you in aversion.”

And He Most High says:

“Or do they have partners who have prescribed for them a religion that Allah has not authorized?”

And He Most High says:

“Alif Lām Mīm Sād.”

“A Book has been sent down to you—so let there be no unease in your heart concerning it—that you may warn by it, and as a reminder to the believers.”

“Follow what has been sent down to you from your Lord, and do not follow any protectors besides Him. How little you take heed!”

And He Most High says:

“If the truth were to follow their desires, the heavens and the earth and all those within them would surely fall into ruin.”

There are many similar passages in the Quran. It is thus clear that a servant must follow the truth with which Allah sent His Messenger, and must not make his religion conform to his desires. And Allah knows best.

translated_text:
He was asked:

Two men disagreed about “intention.” One said, “Do not begin the prayer without an intention,” citing the Prophet’s words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Each person will have only what he intended.”

The other said, “It is valid without an intention.” Give us a ruling, and may you be rewarded.

He replied:

Praise be to Allah. Prayer is not valid without an intention. However, the intention resides in the heart, by the consensus of the Muslims. It consists of purpose and resolve. If someone intends in his heart something different from what he says with his tongue, what counts is what he intended in his heart.

The scholars differed over whether stating one’s intention is recommended, holding two views. They agreed that neither raising one’s voice when stating the intention nor repeatedly stating it is recommended; rather, the imams unanimously agree that these practices are prohibited. If someone does not state his intention verbally, his prayer is valid according to the four imams and others. Only a few outliers among the later scholars dissented.

translated_text:
He—may Allah have mercy on him—was also asked about the saying of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“A person’s intention is more far-reaching than his deeds.”

He replied:

This statement has been made by several people, and some cite it as traced back to the Prophet. Its meaning can be explained in several ways:

First: An intention unaccompanied by action is rewarded, whereas an action unaccompanied by intention is not. The Quran, the Sunnah, and the consensus of the imams establish that whoever performs righteous deeds without sincerity to Allah will not have those deeds accepted. It is also established in both Sahīh collections, through several chains of transmission, that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever intends to do a good deed but does not do it has one good deed recorded for him.”

Second: Whoever intends to do good, does as much of it as he can, but is unable to complete it receives the reward of one who performed it. Thus, it is reported in both Sahīh collections that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“There are men in Medina who have been with you on every journey you have made and in every valley you have crossed.” They asked, “Even though they are in Medina?” He replied, “Even though they are in Medina. A valid excuse has held them back.”

Al-Tirmidhī also graded as authentic the hadith narrated by Abū Kabshah al-Anmārī from the Prophet

It is also reported in both Sahīh collections that he said:

“When a servant falls ill or travels, the deeds he used to perform while healthy and resident are recorded for him.”

There is much evidence supporting this.

Third: The heart is the king of the body, and the limbs are its troops. If the king is upright, his troops are upright; if the king is corrupt, his troops are corrupt. Intention is an act of the king, whereas outward deeds are acts of the troops.

Fourth: According to Ahl al-Sunnah, repentance from a sin is valid even when a person is unable to commit it.

translated_text:
as in the repentance of a man whose penis has been severed from unlawful intercourse, or the repentance of someone whose tongue has been cut out from making accusations of unlawful intercourse and other such sins. The foundation of repentance is the heart’s resolve, and this remains possible despite physical incapacity.

Fifth: Intention is not subject to corruption, unlike outward deeds. Intention is rooted in love for Allah and His Messenger and the desire for His Countenance. This is itself beloved and pleasing to Allah and His Messenger. Outward deeds, however, are subject to many defects and are not accepted unless they are free of them. For this reason, acts of the heart alone are superior to bodily acts alone.

As one of the early Muslims said:

“The believer’s strength lies in his heart, and his weakness in his body; the hypocrite’s strength lies in his body, and his weakness in his heart.”

A detailed discussion of this would be lengthy. Allah knows best.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

A Hanafī man prayed in congregation, keeping his intention private, and then raised his hands with every pronouncement of “Allah is the Greatest.” The congregation’s jurist objected, telling him:

“This is not permissible in your school, and you are introducing an innovation into it. You are wavering: you have neither followed your imam nor taken guidance from your school.”

Does what he did constitute a deficiency in his prayer and a departure from the Sunnah and his imam’s teaching, or not?

He replied:

translated_text:
in that of any of the Muslim imams. Rather, they all agree that stating one’s intention aloud is not prescribed. Whoever does so is mistaken and acts contrary to the Sunnah, by agreement of the imams of the religion. Indeed, the position of Abū Hanīfa, Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, Ahmad, and all the other Muslim imams is that if a person forms the intention in his heart without expressing it verbally, either quietly or aloud, his prayer is valid. Verbalizing the intention is not obligatory, according to either Abū Hanīfa or any of the other imams.

Indeed, when one of al-Shāfiʿī’s later followers put forward an inferred opinion that verbalizing the intention is not obligatory, the other followers declared him mistaken, saying: “Al-Shāfiʿī only required the opening declaration of ‘Allah is the Greatest’ to be spoken, not the intention.” As for Abū Hanīfa and his followers, they never disputed that verbalizing the intention is not obligatory. The same applies to Mālik and his followers, and Ahmad and his followers.

Rather, the scholars differed over whether quietly verbalizing the intention is recommended, holding two views.

A group of the followers of Abū Hanīfa, al-Shāfiʿī, and Ahmad said: “Verbalizing the intention is recommended, but not saying it aloud. Neither verbalizing it nor saying it aloud is obligatory.”

A group of the followers of Mālik and Ahmad, along with others, said: “Rather, verbalizing the intention is not recommended, either quietly or aloud, just as it is not obligatory by agreement of the imams. For the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—and his Companions did not verbalize their intentions, either quietly or aloud.” This is the correct view, supported by the Sunnah.

 وَقَالَ عُقْبَةُ ابْنُ عَامِرٍ:
 لَهُ بِكُلِّ إشَارَةٍ عَشْرُ حَسَنَاتٍ.
translated_text:
As for raising the hands with every declaration of “Allah is the Greatest,” even when prostrating, this is not the Sunnah that the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—practised. The Muslim community does, however, agree that the hands are raised with the opening declaration of “Allah is the Greatest.”

As for raising them when bowing and when standing upright after bowing, most jurists of Kufa, such as Ibrāhīm al-Nakha‘ī, Abū Hanīfa, al-Thawrī, and others, did not know of this practice. Most jurists of the other centres and scholars of transmitted reports, however, knew of it, since reports of this Sunnah from the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—were widely transmitted. These included al-Awzā‘ī, al-Shāfi‘ī, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Ishāq, and Abū ‘Ubayd. It is also one of the two positions reported from Mālik. Indeed, it is established in the two Sahīh collections, through reports from Ibn ‘Umar and others:

“The Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—would raise his hands when beginning the prayer, when bowing, and when raising his head from bowing. He would not do so when prostrating or between the two prostrations.”

This practice is also established from the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—in authentic hadith reports from Mālik ibn al-Huwayrith, Wā’il ibn Hujr, and Abū Humayd al-Sā‘idī, the latter in a gathering of ten Companions of the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—one of whom was Abū Qatāda. It is also known through reports from ‘Alī ibn Abī Tālib, Abū Hurayra, and many other Companions, from the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

Whenever Ibn ‘Umar—may Allah be pleased with them both—saw someone praying without raising his hands during the prayer, he would throw pebbles at him.

‘Uqba ibn ‘Āmir said:

“For each gesture, he is credited with ten good deeds.”

وَالْكُوفِيُّونَ حُجَّتُهُمْ أَنَّ عَبْدَ اللَّهِ بْنَ مَسْعُودٍ - رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ - لَمْ يَكُنْ يَرْفَعُ يَدَيْهِ وَهُمْ مَعْذُورُونَ قَبْلَ أَنْ تَبْلُغَهُمْ السُّنَّةُ الصَّحِيحَةُ؛ فَإِنَّ عَبْدَ اللَّهِ بْنَ مَسْعُودٍ هُوَ الْفَقِيهُ الَّذِي بَعَثَهُ عُمَرُ بْنُ الْخَطَّابِ لِيُعَلِّمَ أَهْلَ الْكُوفَةِ السُّنَّةَ؛ لَكِنْ قَدْ حَفِظَ الرَّفْعَ عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ كَثِيرٌ مِنْ الصَّحَابَةِ رِضْوَانُ اللَّهِ تَعَالَى عَلَيْهِمْ وَابْنُ مَسْعُودٍ لَمْ يُصَرِّحْ بِأَنَّ النَّبِيَّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ لَمْ يَرْفَعْ إلَّا أَوَّلَ مَرَّةٍ؛ لَكِنَّهُمْ رَأَوْهُ يُصَلِّي وَلَا يَرْفَعُ إلَّا أَوَّلَ مَرَّةٍ. وَالْإِنْسَانُ قَدْ يَنْسَى وَقَدْ يُذْهَلُ وَقَدْ خَفِيَ عَلَى ابْنِ مَسْعُودٍ التَّطْبِيقُ فِي الصَّلَاةِ؛ فَكَانَ يُصَلِّي وَإِذَا رَكَعَ طَبَّقَ بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ كَمَا كَانُوا يَفْعَلُونَ أَوَّلَ الْإِسْلَامِ. ثُمَّ إنَّ التَّطْبِيقَ نُسِخَ بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ وَأُمِرُوا بِالرُّكَبِ وَهَذَا لَمْ يَحْفَظْهُ ابْنُ مَسْعُودٍ؛ فَإِنَّ الرَّفْعَ الْمُتَنَازَعَ فِيهِ لَيْسَ مِنْ نَوَاقِضِ الصَّلَاةِ؛ بَلْ يَجُوزُ أَنْ يُصَلِّيَ بِلَا رَفْعٍ وَإِذَا رَفَعَ كَانَ أَفْضَلَ وَأَحْسَنَ.
 وَإِذَا كَانَ الرَّجُلُ مُتَّبِعًا لِأَبِي حَنِيفَةَ أَوْ مَالِكٍ أَوْ الشَّافِعِيِّ أَوْ أَحْمَد:
 وَرَأَى فِي بَعْضِ الْمَسَائِلِ أَنَّ مَذْهَبَ غَيْرِهِ أَقْوَى فَاتَّبَعَهُ كَانَ قَدْ أَحْسَنَ فِي ذَلِكَ وَلَمْ يَقْدَحْ ذَلِكَ فِي دِينِهِ. وَلَا عَدَالَتِهِ بِلَا نِزَاعٍ؛ بَلْ هَذَا أَوْلَى بِالْحَقِّ وَأَحَبُّ إلَى اللَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ مِمَّنْ يَتَعَصَّبُ لِوَاحِدِ مُعَيَّنٍ غَيْرِ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ كَمَنْ يَتَعَصَّبُ لِمَالِكِ أَوْ الشَّافِعِيِّ أَوْ أَحْمَد أَوْ أَبِي حَنِيفَةَ وَيَرَى أَنَّ قَوْلَ هَذَا الْمُعَيَّنِ هُوَ الصَّوَابُ الَّذِي يَنْبَغِي اتِّبَاعُهُ دُونَ قَوْلِ الْإِمَامِ الَّذِي خَالَفَهُ.
translated_text:
The Kufans base their argument on the fact that ‘Abd Allāh ibn Mas‘ūd—may Allah be pleased with him—did not raise his hands. They are excused until the authentic Sunnah reaches them, for ‘Abd Allāh ibn Mas‘ūd was the jurist whom ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb sent to teach the people of Kufa the Sunnah. Nevertheless, many Companions—may Allah Most High be pleased with them—preserved the Prophet’s practice of raising his hands, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Ibn Mas‘ūd did not explicitly state that the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—raised his hands only at the beginning; rather, they saw Ibn Mas‘ūd praying and raising his hands only at the beginning. A person may forget or have a lapse of attention. The matter of pressing the hands together during prayer had also escaped Ibn Mas‘ūd: when praying, he would press his hands together as he bowed, as they used to do in the early days of Islam. This practice was subsequently abrogated, and they were instructed to place their hands on their knees. Ibn Mas‘ūd had not retained this. The disputed raising of the hands does not invalidate the prayer; indeed, one may pray without raising them, though raising them is better and more commendable.

If someone follows Abū Hanīfa, Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī, or Ahmad, then finds another imam’s position stronger on certain issues and follows it, he has acted well. There is no dispute that this does not detract from either his religious commitment or his uprightness. Rather, such a person is closer to the truth and more beloved to Allah and His Messenger—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—than someone who is partisan towards a particular individual other than the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace. This includes someone who is partisan towards Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī, Ahmad, or Abū Hanīfa and considers that particular imam’s position to be the correct one that ought to be followed, rather than the position of the imam who disagreed with him.

original_text:
فَمَنْ فَعَلَ هَذَا كَانَ جَاهِلًا ضَالًّا؛ بَلْ قَدْ يَكُونُ كَافِرًا؛ فَإِنَّهُ مَتَى اعْتَقَدَ أَنَّهُ يَجِبُ عَلَى النَّاسِ اتِّبَاعُ وَاحِدٍ بِعَيْنِهِ مِنْ هَؤُلَاءِ الْأَئِمَّةِ دُونَ الْإِمَامِ الْآخَرِ فَإِنَّهُ يَجِبُ أَنْ يُسْتَتَابَ فَإِنْ تَابَ وَإِلَّا قُتِلَ.
 بَلْ غَايَةُ مَا يُقَالُ:
 إنَّهُ يَسُوغُ أَوْ يَنْبَغِي أَوْ يَجِبُ عَلَى الْعَامِّيِّ أَنْ يُقَلِّدَ وَاحِدًا لَا بِعَيْنِهِ مِنْ غَيْرِ تَعْيِينِ زَيْدٍ وَلَا عَمْرٍو.
 وَأَمَّا أَنْ يَقُولَ قَائِلٌ:
 إنَّهُ يَجِبُ عَلَى الْعَامَّةِ تَقْلِيدُ فُلَانٍ أَوْ فُلَانٍ فَهَذَا لَا يَقُولُهُ مُسْلِمٌ. وَمَنْ كَانَ مُوَالِيًا لِلْأَئِمَّةِ مُحِبًّا لَهُمْ يُقَلِّدُ كُلَّ وَاحِدٍ مِنْهُمْ فِيمَا يَظْهَرُ لَهُ أَنَّهُ مُوَافِقٌ لِلسُّنَّةِ فَهُوَ مُحْسِنٌ فِي ذَلِكَ. بَلْ هَذَا أَحْسَنُ حَالًا مِنْ غَيْرِهِ وَلَا يُقَالُ لِمِثْلِ هَذَا مُذَبْذَبٌ عَلَى وَجْهِ الذَّمِّ.
 وَإِنَّمَا الْمُذَبْذَبُ الْمَذْمُومُ الَّذِي لَا يَكُونُ مَعَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ وَلَا مَعَ الْكُفَّارِ بَلْ يَأْتِي الْمُؤْمِنِينَ بِوَجْهِ وَيَأْتِي الْكَافِرِينَ بِوَجْهِ قَالَ تَعَالَى فِي حَقِّ الْمُنَافِقِينَ:
 
{إنَّ الْمُنَافِقِينَ يُخَادِعُونَ اللَّهَ وَهُوَ خَادِعُهُمْ وَإِذَا قَامُوا إلَى الصَّلَاةِ قَامُوا كُسَالَى يُرَاءُونَ النَّاسَ}
 إلَى قَوْلِهِ: 
{وَمَنْ يُضْلِلِ اللَّهُ فَلَنْ تَجِدَ لَهُ سَبِيلًا}
 . وَقَالَ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ 
{مَثَلُ الْمُنَافِقِ كَمَثَلِ الشَّاةِ الْعَائِرَةِ بَيْنَ الْغَنَمَيْنِ: تُعِيرُ إلَى هَؤُلَاءِ مَرَّةً وَإِلَى هَؤُلَاءِ مَرَّةً}
 . فَهَؤُلَاءِ الْمُنَافِقُونَ الْمُذَبْذَبُونَ هُمْ الَّذِينَ ذَمَّهُمْ اللَّهُ وَرَسُولُهُ وَقَالَ فِي
translated_text:
Thus, whoever does this is ignorant and misguided; indeed, he may even be a disbeliever. For if he believes that people are obliged to follow one particular imam rather than another, he must be called upon to repent; if he does not repent, he is to be put to death.

The most that can be said is that a layperson may, should, or must follow an imam, without prescribing any particular individual—not Zayd or ʿAmr. But to say that ordinary people must follow this or that particular imam is something no Muslim would say. Whoever is loyal to the imams and loves them, following each of them in whatever appears to him to accord with the Sunnah, is doing well. Indeed, his position is better than that of others, and such a person should not be disparaged as “wavering.”

Rather, the blameworthy waverer is someone who is neither with the believers nor with the disbelievers, but presents one face to the believers and another to the disbelievers. Allah Most High said concerning the hypocrites:

“The hypocrites seek to deceive Allah, but He deceives them. When they stand up for prayer, they stand lazily, showing off before people,”

up to His words:

“And whoever Allah leaves astray—you will never find for him a way.”

The Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“The hypocrite is like a sheep wandering between two flocks, going to one at times and to the other at times.”

It is these wavering hypocrites whom Allah and His Messenger condemned, and He said concerning

them:

“When the hypocrites come to you, they say, ‘We testify that you are indeed the Messenger of Allah.’ Allah knows that you are indeed His Messenger, and Allah testifies that the hypocrites are liars.”

He Most High also said concerning them:

“Have you not seen those who take as allies a people with whom Allah is angry? They belong neither to you nor to them, and they knowingly swear to lies.”

These hypocrites who ally themselves with the Jews, with whom Allah is angry, belong neither to the Jews nor to us. Such are those among the Jews, Christians, Tatars, and others who outwardly profess Islam while their hearts remain with their own people. Such a person is neither a true believer nor a disbeliever both outwardly and inwardly. These are the wavering ones whom Allah and His Messenger condemned. Allah has obliged His servants to be believers, neither disbelievers nor hypocrites, but rather to love for Allah’s sake, hate for Allah’s sake, give for Allah’s sake, and withhold for Allah’s sake.

Allah Most High said:

“O you who believe, do not take the Jews and Christians as allies. They are allies of one another. Whoever among you takes them as allies is indeed one of them.”

Then, further on, He says:

“Your allies are none but Allah, His Messenger, and those who believe—those who establish prayer, give zakat, and bow down in worship.”

“Whoever takes Allah, His Messenger, and the believers as allies—then surely the party of Allah will prevail.”

He Most High also said:

“O you who believe, do not take My enemies and your enemies as allies, offering them affection when they have disbelieved in the truth that has come to you,”

and the rest of the verse.

He Most High also said:

“You will not find a people who believe in Allah and the Last Day showing affection to those who oppose Allah and His Messenger, even if they are their fathers, their sons, their brothers, or their kindred.

Those are the ones in whose hearts He has inscribed faith and whom He has strengthened with a spirit from Him.”

He Most High also said:

“The believers are but brothers, so make peace between your brothers.”

In the two Sahīh collections, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is reported to have said:

“The believers, in their mutual love, mercy, and compassion, are like a body: when one limb suffers, the rest of the body responds with fever and sleeplessness.”

In the two Sahīh collections, he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is also reported to have said:

“One believer is to another like a building, each part strengthening the other”—and he interlaced his fingers.

In the two Sahīh collections, he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is also reported to have said:

“A Muslim is the brother of another Muslim: he neither abandons him nor wrongs him.”

The two Sahīh collections also report that he said:

“By Him in whose hand is my soul, none of you believes until he loves for his brother the good that he loves for himself.”

He also said:

“By Him in whose hand is my soul, you will not enter Paradise until you believe, and you will not believe until you love one another. Shall I not tell you something which, if you do it, will make you love one another? Spread the greeting of peace among yourselves.”

Allah Most High has commanded the believers to remain united and in harmony, and has forbidden them to divide and differ. He Most High said:

“O you who believe, fear Allah as He should be feared, and do not die except as Muslims.”

“And hold firmly to the rope of Allah all together, and do not become divided,”

continuing to His words:

“so that you may be guided,”

and then to His words:

“On the Day when some faces will turn white and others black.”

Ibn ‘Abbās, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: “The faces of the people of the Sunnah and the united community will turn white, and the faces of the people of innovation and division will turn black.”

Thus, the imams of the religion follow the path of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them all. The Companions were united and harmonious, even when they disputed certain subsidiary rulings of the Sharia concerning purification, prayer, Hajj, divorce, inheritance, or other matters. Their consensus is conclusive proof.

Whoever is partisan toward one particular imam to the exclusion of the others is like someone who is partisan toward one particular Companion to the exclusion of the rest: like the Rāfidī who champions ‘Alī to the exclusion of the three caliphs and the majority of the Companions, or the Khārijite who disparages ‘Uthmān and ‘Alī, may Allah be pleased with them both. These are the ways of the people of innovation and desires, whom the Quran, the Sunnah, and consensus establish as blameworthy and as departing from the law and path with which Allah sent His Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

Whoever is partisan toward one particular imam bears some resemblance to these people, whether his partisanship is for Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī, Abū Hanīfah, Ahmad, or anyone else. At best, someone who is partisan toward one of them is ignorant of that imam’s standing in knowledge and religion and of the standing of the others. He is therefore both ignorant and unjust. Allah commands knowledge and justice and forbids ignorance and injustice.

He Most High said:

“But man undertook it; indeed, he was unjust and ignorant,”

“so that Allah may punish the hypocritical men and hypocritical women,”

and so on to the end of the surah.

Now Abū Yūsuf and Muhammad were the most devoted followers of Abū Hanīfah and the most knowledgeable about his views

original_text:
وَهُمَا قَدْ خَالَفَاهُ فِي مَسَائِلَ لَا تَكَادُ تُحْصَى لِمَا تَبَيَّنَ لَهُمَا مِنْ السُّنَّةِ وَالْحُجَّةِ مَا وَجَبَ عَلَيْهِمَا اتِّبَاعُهُ وَهُمَا مَعَ ذَلِكَ مُعَظِّمَانِ لِإِمَامِهِمَا.
 لَا يُقَالُ فِيهِمَا مُذَبْذَبَانِ:
 بَلْ أَبُو حَنِيفَةَ وَغَيْرُهُ مِنْ الْأَئِمَّةِ يَقُولُ الْقَوْلَ ثُمَّ تَتَبَيَّنُ لَهُ الْحُجَّةُ فِي خِلَافِهِ فَيَقُولُ بِهَا وَلَا يُقَالُ لَهُ مُذَبْذَبٌ؛ فَإِنَّ الْإِنْسَانَ لَا يَزَالُ يَطْلُبُ الْعِلْمَ وَالْإِيمَانَ. فَإِذَا تَبَيَّنَ لَهُ مِنْ الْعِلْمِ مَا كَانَ خَافِيًا عَلَيْهِ اتَّبَعَهُ وَلَيْسَ هَذَا مُذَبْذَبًا؛ بَلْ هَذَا مُهْتَدٍ زَادَهُ اللَّهُ هُدًى.
 وَقَدْ قَالَ تَعَالَى:
 
{وَقُلْ رَبِّ زِدْنِي عِلْمًا}
 . فَالْوَاجِبُ عَلَى كُلِّ مُؤْمِنٍ مُوَالَاةُ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ وَعُلَمَاءِ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ وَأَنْ يَقْصِدَ الْحَقَّ وَيَتَّبِعَهُ حَيْثُ وَجَدَهُ وَيَعْلَمَ أَنَّ مَنْ اجْتَهَدَ مِنْهُمْ فَأَصَابَ فَلَهُ أَجْرَانِ وَمَنْ اجْتَهَدَ مِنْهُمْ فَأَخْطَأَ فَلَهُ أَجْرٌ لِاجْتِهَادِهِ وَخَطَؤُهُ مَغْفُورٌ لَهُ. وَعَلَى الْمُؤْمِنِينَ أَنْ يَتَّبِعُوا إمَامَهُمْ إذَا فَعَلَ مَا يَسُوغُ؛
 فَإِنَّ النَّبِيَّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ قَالَ:
 
{إنَّمَا جُعِلَ الْإِمَامُ لِيُؤْتَمَّ بِهِ}
 وَسَوَاءٌ رَفَعَ يَدَيْهِ أَوْ لَمْ يَرْفَعْ يَدَيْهِ لَا يَقْدَحُ ذَلِكَ فِي صَلَاتِهِمْ وَلَا يُبْطِلُهَا لَا عِنْدَ أَبِي حَنِيفَةَ وَلَا الشَّافِعِيِّ وَلَا مَالِكٍ وَلَا أَحْمَد. وَلَوْ رَفَعَ الْإِمَامُ دُونَ الْمَأْمُومِ أَوْ الْمَأْمُومُ دُونَ الْإِمَامِ لَمْ يَقْدَحْ ذَلِكَ فِي صَلَاةِ وَاحِدٍ مِنْهُمَا وَلَوْ رَفَعَ الرَّجُلُ فِي بَعْضِ الْأَوْقَاتِ دُونَ بَعْضٍ لَمْ يَقْدَحْ ذَلِكَ فِي صَلَاتِهِ وَلَيْسَ لِأَحَدِ أَنْ يَتَّخِذَ قَوْلَ بَعْضِ الْعُلَمَاءِ شِعَارًا يُوجِبُ اتِّبَاعَهُ وَيَنْهَى عَنْ غَيْرِهِ مِمَّا جَاءَتْ بِهِ السُّنَّةُ؛
 بَلْ كُلُّ مَا جَاءَتْ بِهِ السُّنَّةُ فَهُوَ وَاسِعٌ:
 مِثْلُ الْأَذَانِ وَالْإِقَامَةِ. فَقَدَ
translated_text:
and yet they differed with him on almost countless issues because evidence from the Sunnah and other proofs had become clear to them which they were obliged to follow. Nevertheless, they continued to hold their imam in high esteem. They are not to be called wavering.

Indeed, Abū Hanīfah and the other imams would adopt a view, then discover evidence contrary to it and follow that evidence. Such a person is not called wavering, for a person continues to seek knowledge and faith. When knowledge previously hidden from him becomes clear, he follows it. This is not someone wavering, but someone rightly guided whom Allah has increased in guidance.

Allah Most High said:

“And say, ‘My Lord, increase me in knowledge.’”

Every believer must therefore show loyalty to the believers and their scholars, seek the truth and follow it wherever he finds it, and recognize that whoever among these scholars exercises scholarly judgment and reaches the correct conclusion receives two rewards, while whoever exercises scholarly judgment and errs receives one reward for his effort, and his error is forgiven.

The believers must follow their imam when he does what is permissible, for the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The imam has only been appointed to be followed.”

Whether he raises his hands or does not raise them, this neither impairs nor invalidates their prayer according to Abū Hanīfah, al-Shāfi‘ī, Mālik, or Ahmad. If the imam raises his hands but the person praying behind him does not, or vice versa, this does not impair the prayer of either. Likewise, if a man raises his hands on some occasions but not others, this does not impair his prayer.

No one may make the view of a particular scholar a banner of allegiance, requiring others to follow it and forbidding other practices established by the Sunnah. Rather, there is latitude in all the practices established by the Sunnah, such as the adhān and iqāmah—the call to prayer and the call to commence it. For

it is established in the two Sahīh collections that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace,

“commanded Bilāl to recite the phrases of the adhān twice and those of the iqāmah once.”

It is also established in the two Sahīh collections that he

“taught Abū Mahdhūrah to recite the phrases of the iqāmah twice each, like the adhān.”

Whoever recites the phrases of the iqāmah twice has done well, and whoever recites them once has done well. Whoever makes one form obligatory to the exclusion of the other is mistaken and misguided. Whoever shows allegiance to those who practise one form rather than the other solely on that basis is likewise mistaken and misguided.

Among the reasons Allah gave the Tatars power over the lands of the East was the widespread division and strife among their people over schools of law and other matters. Thus, you find someone affiliated with al-Shāfi‘ī so partisan in favour of his school against that of Abū Hanīfah that he departs from the religion. Someone affiliated with Abū Hanīfah is similarly partisan in favour of his school against that of al-Shāfi‘ī and others, to the point of departing from the religion. Someone affiliated with Ahmad is partisan in favour of his school against one or the other. In the Maghrib, you find someone affiliated with Mālik partisan in favour of his school against one or the other. All this belongs to the division and discord that Allah and His Messenger have forbidden.

All these people who are partisan in falsehood, following conjecture and what their souls desire, and pursuing their own desires without guidance from Allah, deserve blame and punishment.

This is a broad subject that cannot be treated at length in this fatwa. Holding fast to the community and maintaining harmony are fundamental principles of the religion, whereas the disputed subsidiary issue is an obscure matter of detail. How, then, can a fundamental principle be undermined for the sake of upholding a subsidiary matter? Most of these partisans know nothing of the Quran

and the Sunnah, except what Allah wills. Rather, they cling to weak hadiths, unsound opinions, or accounts attributed to certain scholars and shaykhs that may be true or false. Even if they are true, the person concerned is not infallible. They cling to unverified reports from fallible speakers, while claiming authenticated transmission from the infallible speaker—namely, what trustworthy, reliable scholars have transmitted from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and recorded in authentic collections. The transmitters of these reports are deemed trustworthy by the unanimous agreement of the leading religious scholars, and the one from whom they transmit is infallible: he does not speak from his own desire; it is only revelation sent down to him. Allah Most High has required all people to obey and follow him.

Allah Most High says:

“But no, by your Lord, they will not believe until they make you judge in their disputes, then find within themselves no resistance to your decisions and submit completely.”

And Allah Most High says:

“So let those who oppose his command beware, lest a trial afflict them or a painful punishment befall them.”

May Allah Most High guide us and all our fellow believers to the speech, deeds, guidance, and intentions that He loves and is pleased with. Allah knows best. All praise belongs to Allah alone.

He was asked about an imam of the Shāfiʿī school who says, “Allah is greatest,” repeating this declaration many times while the people stand behind him.

He answered:

All praise belongs to Allah. Repeatedly pronouncing the intention and the declaration “Allah is greatest,” as well as pronouncing the intention aloud, is prohibited according to al-Shāfiʿī and all the other leading scholars of Islam. Whoever does this acts wrongly. If he believes this to be part of the religion, he has departed from the consensus of the Muslims. He must be forbidden from doing so. If he is removed from his position as imam when he refuses to desist, there would seem to be grounds for doing so, for it is reported in Sunan Abī Dāwūd:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, ordered that an imam be removed for spitting in the direction of prayer.”

The imam must pray as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to pray. He may not content himself with what suffices for someone praying alone. Rather, he is forbidden to make the prayer excessively long or unduly short. What, then, if he persists in something forbidden to the imam, those following him, and someone praying alone? Allah knows best.

“Whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it as he should, while being a believer—it is they whose striving will be appreciated.”

ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb recited: “Proceed to the remembrance of Allah.” Thus, the striving commanded for Friday prayer means proceeding and going to it.

The word “striving” is originally a generic term. In customary usage, when a term encompasses two categories, people often give one category a distinct name, leaving the general term exclusively for the other. For example, “blood relatives” encompasses all relatives: those who inherit prescribed shares, those who inherit as residuary heirs, and those entitled to neither. Once those entitled to prescribed shares and residuary heirs were distinguished by their own names, “blood relatives,” in the customary terminology of jurists, came to refer exclusively to those entitled to neither.

Likewise, the term jā’iz (“permissible”) encompasses acts and contracts that are obligatory or binding, as well as those that are not. Once certain acts were designated obligatory and certain contracts binding, the term jā’iz, in their customary usage, became restricted to the other category.

Similarly, the term khamr (“wine”) is a general designation for every kind of drink. But once drinks made from things other than grapes were given the distinct name nabīdh, khamr came, in customary usage, to refer exclusively to grape juice. Some scholars consequently thought that the term khamr in the Quran and Sunnah referred exclusively to that. Yet hadiths transmitted from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, through so many independent chains as to establish certainty demonstrate its general scope. There are many similar examples.

translated_text:
This ambiguity arising from later usage has led many people to misunderstand the language of revelation. The word “striving” is a case in point: originally, it encompasses any going or proceeding, and this is the striving commanded in the Quran. One of its two forms may then be given the distinct name “walking,” leaving “striving” restricted to the other. This is the striving that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prohibited when he said:

“When the call to begin the prayer is given, do not come to it running; come to it walking.”

It is reported that ʿUmar used to recite, “Proceed,” and would say, “Had I recited it as ‘strive,’ I would have run until such-and-such happened.” If this report from him is authentic, it would mean that he understood the word “striving” in its restricted sense.

A similar example is the striving between al-Safā and al-Marwah. One jogs only along the valley floor between the two markers, and the term “striving” is used specifically for this. It may also be applied broadly to the entire passage back and forth between al-Safā and al-Marwah. This, however, appears to be because part of it constitutes striving in the restricted sense. And Allah knows best.

He replied:

It is established in the authentic collection that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Will you not form rows as the angels form rows before their Lord?”

They asked, “O Messenger of Allah, how do the angels form rows before their Lord?”

He replied, “They fill the first row, then the next, and stand close together in the row.”

It is also established in the authentic collection that he said:

“If people knew the reward for giving the call to prayer and standing in the first row, and could find no way to obtain it except by drawing lots, they would draw lots for it.”

It is likewise authentically recorded that he said:

“The best of the men’s rows is the first, and the worst is the last.”

These and similar teachings of the Sunnah indicate that worshippers should complete the first row, then the second. Whoever arrives before the others but stands in a row other than the first has acted contrary to Islamic law. If, in addition, he performs the prayer poorly, engages in unnecessary, disliked, or forbidden speech, or commits similar acts from which the mosque should be kept free, then he has failed to honor the religious ordinances and has stepped outside the prescribed bounds of obedience to Allah.

If he does not acknowledge the fault in his conduct and commit himself to following Allah’s command, he deserves a severe punishment that will induce him and others like him to carry out what Allah has commanded and refrain from what Allah has forbidden. And Allah knows best.

He was also asked:

When worshippers do not straighten their rows, but each person prays on his own, is it permissible for them to pray like this in the marketplaces?

He replied:

No one may pray alone behind the row; rather, people must pray in rows. It is reported in the Sunan collections that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The prayer of one who stands alone behind the row is not valid.”

Their prayer in the marketplace is not valid unless the rows are connected. Rather, they must keep the rows close together and fill the first row, then the next. And Allah knows best.

الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ هَذِهِ الْمَسَائِلُ الَّتِي يَقَعُ فِيهَا النِّزَاعُ مِمَّا يَتَعَلَّقُ بِصِفَاتِ الْعِبَادَاتِ أَرْبَعَةُ أَقْسَامٍ:
مِنْهَا:
 مَا ثَبَتَ مِنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ أَنَّهُ سَنَّ كُلَّ وَاحِدٍ مِنْ الْأَمْرَيْنِ وَاتَّفَقَتْ الْأُمَّةُ عَلَى أَنَّ مَنْ فَعَلَ أَحَدَهُمَا لَمْ يَأْثَمْ بِذَلِكَ لَكِنْ قَدْ يَتَنَازَعُونَ فِي الْأَفْضَلِ وَهُوَ بِمَنْزِلَةِ الْقِرَاءَاتِ الثَّابِتَةِ عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ الَّتِي اتَّفَقَ النَّاسُ عَلَى جَوَازِ الْقِرَاءَةِ بِأَيِّ قِرَاءَةٍ شَاءَ مِنْهَا كَالْقِرَاءَةِ الْمَشْهُورَةِ بَيْنَ الْمُسْلِمِينَ فَهَذِهِ يَقْرَأُ الْمُسْلِمُ بِمَا شَاءَ مِنْهَا وَإِنْ اخْتَارَ بَعْضَهَا لِسَبَبِ مِنْ الْأَسْبَابِ.
وَمِنْ هَذَا الْبَابِ الِاسْتِفْتَاحَاتُ الْمَنْقُولَةُ عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ
translated_text:
should he perform tayammum (dry ablution) or not? Does tayammum take the place of ritual ablution in the circumstances mentioned, or not?

When the crescent of Ramadan is obscured, which is better: fasting or not fasting? Or is one free to choose between them? Or is one of them recommended?

Regarding everything that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, consistently practised—in his deeds, circumstances, words, movements and moments of stillness, and in all his affairs, whether acts of worship or everyday habits—is consistently following all of this a sunnah for every member of the Muslim community? Or does this vary according to the different ranks and those occupying them? Please give us your ruling; may you be rewarded.

He replied:

All praise is due to Allah. These disputed questions concerning the manner of performing acts of worship fall into four categories.

One category comprises matters in which it is established that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, instituted both alternatives, and the Muslim community agrees that whoever follows either incurs no sin, although they may disagree over which is preferable. This is comparable to the modes of Quranic recitation established from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, which people agree may be used interchangeably, such as the recitations well known among Muslims. A Muslim may recite according to whichever of these he wishes, even if he prefers some of them for one reason or another.

Also belonging to this category are the opening supplications transmitted from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace

which he used to recite during the night prayer, and the various supplications he would offer in his prayer at the end of the tashahhud (testimony of faith). All these forms established from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, are permissible by the agreement of the Muslims. However, those he commanded are better for us than those he practised without commanding them.

It is recorded in the Sahīh that he said:

“When any of you sits for the tashahhud, let him seek refuge in Allah from four things, saying: ‘O Allah, I seek refuge in You from the punishment of Hell, from the punishment of the grave, from the trials of life and death, and from the trial of the False Messiah.’”

Offering this supplication is better than saying:

“O Allah, forgive my past and future sins, what I have concealed and what I have disclosed, and what You know better than I do. You are the One who brings forward and the One who holds back. There is no god but You.”

It is also authentically established that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to say this at the end of his prayer. However, he commanded the first supplication. A practice whose obligatory status scholars have disputed is more strongly emphasized than one which he did not command and whose obligatory status scholars have not disputed.

Likewise, a supplication that he repeated frequently, such as:

“Our Lord, give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire,”

is more strongly emphasized than one he did not repeat as frequently.

The Second Category

Matters concerning which the scholars agree that either of the two practices leaves a person’s worship valid and entails no sin, but they disagree over which is better and which the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to practise. This category includes qunūt (supplication) in the Fajr and Witr prayers, reciting the basmalah (the invocation “In the name of Allah”) aloud, the wording used to seek refuge in Allah, and similar matters.

They agree that the prayer of someone who recites the basmalah aloud is valid, as is the prayer of someone who recites it quietly. They also agree that the prayer of someone who offers qunūt in Fajr is valid, as is the prayer of someone who does not. The same applies to qunūt in Witr. Their disagreement concerns whether reciting the basmalah is obligatory; the majority hold that it is not. They also disagree over whether reciting it is recommended; the majority hold that it is.

They further disagree about cases in which the imam omits something that a person praying behind him considers obligatory. For example, the imam might omit the basmalah while the follower considers it obligatory; touch his penis without renewing his ablution while the follower considers ablution obligatory after doing so; pray wearing tanned hides from animals that died without lawful slaughter while the follower holds that tanning does not purify them; or undergo cupping without renewing his ablution while the follower considers ablution necessary after cupping.

The correct position, established with certainty, is that the follower’s prayer behind his imam is valid, even if the imam is in fact mistaken. This is because it is established in the Sahīh that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“They lead you in prayer. If they do so correctly, the reward is yours and theirs; if they err, the reward is yours and the blame is theirs.”

Likewise, if a person prays behind someone who offers qunūt in Fajr or Witr, he should offer it with him, whether
