Section

As for food and clothing, the best guidance is the guidance of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. His practice in eating was to eat whatever was readily available if he desired it. He would neither reject what was available nor go to trouble to obtain what was not. If bread and meat were served, he ate them; if fruit, bread, and meat were served, he ate them. If only dates or only bread were served, he ate that. If sweets or honey were served, he ate those too. His favourite drinks were sweet and cool, and he used to eat cucumbers with fresh dates.

When two kinds of food were served, he would not say, “I will not eat two kinds,” nor would he abstain from food because it was delicious or sweet. Sometimes two or three months would pass without a fire being lit in his home, and they would subsist on nothing but dates and water. At times he would tie a stone against his stomach because of hunger. He never found fault with food: if he desired it, he ate it; otherwise, he left it. Food was also eaten at his

table: the meat of a spiny-tailed lizard. He declined to eat it, saying:

“It is not forbidden, but it was not found in the land of my people, so I find it unappealing.”

The same applied to clothing. He wore a shirt and turban, a waist-wrapper and mantle, an outer robe and a farrūj (a type of robe). He wore cotton, wool, and other materials. While travelling, he wore a woollen robe. He also wore clothing brought from Yemen and elsewhere, most of which was made of cotton. They wore garments of Egyptian Coptic cloth, woven from flax. His Sunnah in this regard therefore entails that a man should eat and dress from whatever food and clothing Allah has made readily available in his land. This varies from one region to another.

A group of his Companions had agreed to abstain from eating meat and similar foods, and from marrying women. Allah Most High then revealed:

“O you who believe, do not forbid the good things Allah has made lawful for you, and do not transgress. Indeed, Allah does not love transgressors.”

“And eat of what Allah has provided for you, lawful and good, and fear Allah, in whom you believe.”

The two Sahīh collections report that he learned of some men, one of whom had said, “As for me, I will fast without breaking my fast.” Another said, “As for me, I will stand in prayer without sleeping.” Another said, “As for me, I will not marry women.” Another said, “As for me, I will not eat meat.” He said:

“But I fast and break my fast, pray at night and sleep, marry women, and eat meat. Whoever turns away from my Sunnah is not of me.”

Allah Most High has also said: “O you who believe, eat of the good things We have provided for you, and give thanks to Allah, if you are

worshipping Him alone.”

He thus commanded people to eat of the good things and give thanks to Allah. Whoever forbids the good things is a transgressor, while whoever fails to give thanks is negligent and fails to fulfil Allah’s right.

In Sahīh Muslim, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is reported to have said:

“Indeed, Allah is pleased with a servant who eats a meal and praises Him for it, or takes a drink and praises Him for it.”

Al-Tirmidhī and others report that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The grateful person who eats is of the same standing as the patient person who fasts.”

This way, which the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, followed, is the most balanced and upright of all ways. Deviation from it takes two forms.

Some people indulge excessively in their desires while turning away from fulfilling their obligations. Allah Most High has said:

“Eat and drink, but do not be excessive. Indeed, He does not love those who are excessive.”

Allah Most High has also said:

“But they were succeeded by generations who neglected prayer and followed their desires; they will meet with evil.”

Others forbid the good things and introduce a monasticism that Allah Most High has not prescribed. There is no monasticism in Islam.

Allah Most High has said:

“Do not forbid the good things Allah has made lawful for you, and do not transgress. Indeed, Allah does not love transgressors.”

Allah Most High has also said:

“O messengers, eat of the good things and do righteous deeds. Indeed, I know well what you do.”

It is reported in the Sahīh that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Indeed, Allah has commanded the believers

to do what He commanded the messengers to do. He Most High said:

‘O messengers, eat of the good things and do righteous deeds.’

And He Most High said:

‘O you who believe, eat of the good things We have provided for you.’

Then he mentioned a man who journeys far, dishevelled and dusty, stretching his hands towards heaven: ‘My Lord! My Lord!’ Yet his food is unlawful, his drink is unlawful, his clothing is unlawful, and he has been nourished with what is unlawful. How, then, could his supplication be answered?”

Everything lawful is good, and everything good is lawful, for Allah has made good things lawful for us and forbidden us foul things. What makes something good, however, is that it is beneficial and pleasant.

Allah has forbidden us everything that harms us and permitted us everything that benefits us. This was not so with the People of the Book: because of their wrongdoing, He forbade them good things that had been lawful to them. He thus forbade them good things as a punishment. Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not forbid us any good things.

People’s circumstances differ with regard to food, clothing, hunger and satiety, and even one person’s circumstances vary. Yet the best deeds are those that show the greatest obedience to Allah and bring the greatest benefit to the person performing them. This may be the easier of two deeds, or it may be the harder. Not every difficult deed is superior, nor is every easy deed inferior. Rather, when Islamic law commands us to do something difficult, it commands it because of the benefit it brings, not merely to torment ourselves.

Such is the case with fighting in Allah’s cause, concerning which He Most High said:

“Fighting has been prescribed for you, though it is hateful to you. But perhaps you hate something that is good for you, and perhaps you love something that is bad for you.”

Hajj is the lesser jihad. Hence the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to ‘Ā’ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, concerning ‘umrah:

“Your reward is in proportion to your hardship.”

Allah Most High said concerning fighting in His cause:

“That is because no thirst, fatigue or hunger afflicts them in Allah’s cause, nor do they tread any ground that enrages the disbelievers, nor inflict any loss on an enemy, without a righteous deed being recorded for them on that account. Indeed, Allah does not let the reward of those who do good go to waste.”

Merely tormenting oneself and one’s body without an outweighing benefit, however, has not been prescribed for us. Rather, Allah has commanded us to do what benefits us and forbidden us to do what harms us.

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said in an authentic hadith:

“You have been sent only to make things easy, not to make them difficult.”

When he sent Mu‘ādh and Abū Mūsā to Yemen, he told them:

“Make things easy, not difficult; give glad tidings, and do not drive people away.”

He also said:

“This religion is easy. No one overburdens himself in practising it without being overcome by it. So make use of the early morning, the late afternoon and part of the night. Moderation, moderation, and you will reach your goal.”

It is also reported that he said:

“The religion most beloved to Allah is the upright monotheistic faith marked by ease.”

Thus, if a person experiences heat, cold, hunger or the like while fighting in Allah’s cause, performing Hajj or undertaking other such deeds, this is something for which he is praised. Allah Most High said:

“They said, ‘Do not go forth in the heat.’ Say, ‘The Fire of Hell is far hotter,’ if only they understood.”

Likewise, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Deeds that expiate sins include performing ablution thoroughly

As for merely exposing oneself to heat and cold without any religiously sanctioned benefit, going barefoot, uncovering one’s head, and similar practices that some people regard as striving against the self—if these bring a person no benefit and involve no obedience to Allah, there is no good in them.

Indeed, it is established in an authentic hadith that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, saw a man standing in the sun and asked:

“What is this?”

They replied, “This is Abū Isrā’īl. He has vowed to stand in the sun, not to seek shade or speak, and to fast.”

He said, “Tell him to sit down, seek shade, speak, and complete his fast.”

For this reason, he forbade perpetual silence. Rather, what is prescribed is what the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day should speak good or remain silent.”

Speaking good is better than refraining from it, and refraining from evil speech is better than uttering it.

“When the time for prayer comes, give the call to prayer and the call to commence it, and let one of you lead the other. Pray as you have seen me pray.”

It is also established in an authentic hadith:

“He used to recite between sixty and one hundred verses in Fajr.”

This amounts approximately to between one-third and one-half of a juz’, one of the Quran’s thirty divisions. He would recite the longer surahs of the Mufassal section: Qāf, al-Sajdah, al-Mulk, al-Mu’minūn, al-Sāffāt, and others of similar length. In Zuhr, he would recite less than that—about thirty verses—and in ‘Asr, less still. In Maghrib, he would recite less than that, such as the shorter surahs of the Mufassal.

In ‘Ishā’, he would recite surahs such as “By the sun and its brightness” and “By the night when it covers,” and others of similar length. Sometimes he would prolong the prayer and recite more than this, even reciting al-A‘rāf, al-Tūr, or al-Mursalāt in Maghrib.

Abū Bakr al-Siddīq once recited Sūrat al-Baqarah in Fajr, and ‘Umar used to recite Sūrat Hūd, Sūrat Yūsuf, and others of similar length in Fajr. At times, the Prophet would shorten the prayer, either because he was travelling or for some other reason, as he said:

(may Allah bless him and grant him peace)

“I begin the prayer intending to prolong it, but then I hear a child crying and shorten it, knowing how distressed his mother is for him.”

It is even reported that he recited Sūrat al-Takwīr and Sūrat al-Zalzalah in Fajr. The imam should therefore strive to follow the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. If those praying behind him are unaccustomed to his manner of prayer and might be put off by it, he should introduce them to it gradually. He should not begin with something that would drive them away, but should follow the Sunnah as far as possible. The imam must not prolong the prayer beyond its prescribed length unless they choose that. As established in an authentic hadith, he said, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Whoever leads the people in prayer should keep it brief, for among them are the sick, the elderly, and those with pressing needs.”

This was recorded in the two Sahīh collections. He also said:

“When any of you leads the people in prayer, he should keep it brief; when he prays alone, he may prolong it as much as he wishes.”

He used to prolong the bowing and prostration, as well as the standing after bowing and the sitting between prostrations. It is established in an authentic hadith:

“When he raised his head from bowing, he would remain standing until someone might say, ‘He has forgotten.’ When he raised his head from prostration, he would remain sitting until someone might say, ‘He has forgotten.’”

The Sunan collections report that Anas ibn Mālik likened the prayer of ‘Umar ibn ‘Abd al-‘Azīz to the Prophet’s prayer. ‘Umar would glorify Allah about ten times while bowing and about ten times while prostrating. As for performing ablution whenever it is invalidated, there is the well-known hadith concerning Bilāl, narrated by Buraydah ibn Husayb, who said:

One morning, the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, summoned Bilāl and said:

“Bilāl, how have you preceded me into Paradise? Whenever I have entered Paradise, I have heard you moving ahead of me. Last night I entered Paradise and heard you moving ahead of me. Then I came upon a lofty, square palace made of gold and asked, ‘Whose palace is this?’

“They replied, ‘It belongs to an Arab man.’

“I said, ‘I am an Arab. Whose palace is this?’

“They replied, ‘It belongs to a man of Quraysh.’

“I said, ‘I am a man of Quraysh. Whose palace is this?’

“They replied, ‘It belongs to a man from Muhammad’s nation.’

“I said, ‘I am Muhammad. Whose palace is this?’

“They replied, ‘It belongs to ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb.’”

Bilāl said, “Messenger of Allah, I have never given the call to prayer without praying two units of prayer afterward. Whenever my ablution has been invalidated, I have renewed it immediately and felt bound to offer Allah two units of prayer.”

The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, “Keep to them both.”

This rules out ablution being obligatory, as well as any command to perform it merely for the sake of eating. We know of no one who recommended ablution for eating unless a person is in a state of janābah (major ritual impurity). Scholars differed over whether washing the hands before eating is disliked or recommended. These are two positions, both reported from Ahmad. Those who recommended it cited the hadith of Salmān, in which he said to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“I read in the Torah that washing the hands before and after a meal is among the means of bringing blessing to it.”

Those who disliked it said that it was contrary to the established practice of the Muslims, who did not wash their hands before eating. Rather, this was a Jewish practice, and imitating them is disliked.

As for Salmān’s hadith, some scholars have graded it as weak. It may also be said that this took place in the early days of Islam, when the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, liked to follow the practice of the People of the Book in matters concerning which he had received no command. For this reason, he used to leave his hair unparted in conformity with them, but later parted it. For the same reason, he fasted on ‘Āshūrā’ when he arrived in Medina. Then, before his death, he said:

“If I live until next year, I will certainly fast on the ninth.”

He meant alongside the tenth, in order to differ from the Jews.

Section

As for the questioner’s inquiry about consistently observing the practices that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, maintained in his worship and daily habits: is this a sunnah, or does it vary according to the circumstances of those who observe them regularly?

The answer is that we are commanded to obey Allah and His Messenger. We must therefore obey the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in whatever he commands us to do. Allah has mentioned obedience to him in more than thirty places in His Book. He, Most High, says:

“Whoever obeys the Messenger has indeed obeyed Allah.”

And He says:

“We did not send any messenger except to be obeyed by Allah’s permission.”

He has guaranteed felicity to those who obey him, saying:

“They will be with those whom Allah has blessed: the prophets, the steadfast affirmers of truth, the martyrs and the righteous. What excellent companions they are!”

He has made felicity and misery contingent upon obedience and disobedience to him, saying:

“Whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger, He will admit them into Gardens beneath which rivers flow, to remain there forever. That is the supreme triumph.”

“And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger and transgresses His limits, He will admit him into a Fire, to remain there forever, and he will have a humiliating punishment.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to say in his sermon:

“Whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger

has indeed been rightly guided; whoever disobeys them both harms only himself and will not harm Allah in the least.”

All the messengers called people to worship Allah, fear Him, stand in awe of Him, and obey His messengers. As Noah, peace be upon him, said:

“Worship Allah, fear Him, and obey me.”

Allah, Most High, says:

“Whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger, stands in awe of Allah, and fears Him—it is they who will triumph.”

Noah and each of the prophets said:

“So fear Allah and obey me.”

Obeying the Messenger in what he has commanded us is the foundation upon which every Muslim must rely. It is the means to felicity, just as failing to do so is the cause of misery. All Muslims agree that obeying his commands takes precedence for us over imitating an action in which he has not commanded us to imitate him. The scholars have not disputed that his commands carry greater weight than his actions, for an action of his may be exclusive to him, or it may be recommended. His commands to us, however, are part of the religion Allah has commanded us to follow.

Among his actions are those which we know he commanded us to emulate, as when he said:

“Pray as you have seen me pray.”

And when, after leading them in prayer while on the pulpit, he said:

“I did this only so that you would follow my lead and learn how I pray.”

And when he performed the pilgrimage, he said:

“Learn your pilgrimage rites from me.”

Furthermore, the Book and the Sunnah establish that whatever he did as a matter of ordinary custom is permissible for us, unless there is evidence that it was exclusive to him. As Allah, Glorified and Most High, says:

“When Zayd had ended his marriage to her, We gave her to you in marriage, so that there would be no blame on the believers for marrying the wives of their adopted sons once the latter have ended their marriages to them.”

Thus He permitted him to marry

 فَلَمَّا أَجَابَهُ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ بِفِعْلِهِ دَلَّ ذَلِكَ عَلَى أَنَّهُ يُبَاحُ لِلْأُمَّةِ مَا أُبِيحَ لَهُ؛ وَلِهَذَا كَانَ جُمْهُورُ عُلَمَاءِ الْأُمَّةِ عَلَى أَنَّ اللَّهَ إذَا أَمَرَهُ بِأَمْرِ أَوْ نَهَاهُ عَنْ شَيْءٍ كَانَتْ أُمَّتُهُ أُسْوَةً لَهُ فِي ذَلِكَ مَا لَمْ يَقُمْ دَلِيلٌ عَلَى اخْتِصَاصِهِ بِذَلِكَ.
translated_text:
the wife of his adopted son, to remove any blame from the believers for marrying the wives of their adopted sons. Thus, we know that what he did was permissible for us to do.

When Allah singled him out for certain rulings, He said:

“And a believing woman if she offers herself to the Prophet, if the Prophet wishes to marry her—a privilege exclusively for you, not for the other believers. We know what We have prescribed for them concerning their wives and those whom their right hands possess, so that there may be no hardship for you. And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.”

When He permitted him to marry a woman who offered herself to him, He made clear that this was exclusively for him, not for the other believers. Thus, no one other than him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, may marry a woman without a dower.

In Sahīh Muslim, it is reported:

“A man asked the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, ‘May a fasting person kiss?’ He replied, ‘Ask her,’ referring to Umm Salamah. She told them that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did so. The man said, ‘O Messenger of Allah, Allah has forgiven your past and future sins.’ He replied, ‘By Allah, I am indeed the most mindful of Allah among you and the most fearful of Him.’”

By answering him with his own practice, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, indicated that what was permissible for him was also permissible for his community. Hence, the majority of the community’s scholars held that whenever Allah commands him to do something or forbids him from something, his community is to follow his example in that, unless evidence establishes that it applies exclusively to him.

translated_text:
Among the matters exclusive to him are those peculiar to his prophethood and messengership. No one may follow his example in these, for there is no prophet after him. This includes being obeyed in everything he commands and forbids, even when the grounds for his command are unknown—to the extent that anyone he orders to be killed must be killed. No one after him has this authority. Those in authority, whether scholars or rulers, are to be obeyed provided that they do not command anything contrary to his commands. Hence, Allah made obedience to them subordinate to obedience to him.

Allah Most High said:

“Obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you.”

He said, “and obey the Messenger and those in authority,” because obedience to those in authority is subordinate to obedience to the Messenger. They are not obeyed independently or unconditionally. The Messenger, however, is obeyed unconditionally and independently, for:

“Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah.”

And He Most High said:

“Obey Allah and obey the Messenger.”

Thus, when the Messenger commands us, we must obey him even if we do not know the grounds for his command. Obedience to him is obedience to Allah; unlike obedience to anyone else, obedience to him can never entail disobedience to Allah.

Scholars have discussed matters exclusive to him concerning what was obligatory for him, what was forbidden to him, and the honors conferred upon him. This is not the place to discuss them in detail. Some are agreed upon, while others are disputed.

He, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was the leader of the community. He adjudicated between them, made distributions, led them in military campaigns, carried out the prescribed punishments, secured the fulfillment of rights, and led them in prayer. Following his example in each capacity must therefore accord with that capacity. Thus, the leader of the prayer and the Hajj follows

his example in that capacity; the military commander follows his example in that capacity; and the one who carries out the prescribed punishments follows his example in that capacity. Likewise, whoever adjudicates or issues legal opinions follows his example in that capacity.

People have disagreed about certain things he did: were they exclusive to him, or may the community also do them? Examples include his joining a prayer as its leader after someone else had led the people, and his declining to offer the funeral prayer for someone who had misappropriated war spoils or for a killer.

Furthermore, when he performed an act for a reason known to us, we can follow his example in it. But when we do not know the reason, or when the circumstances were merely incidental, this is a matter over which people disagree. An example is his stopping at a particular place during a journey. Some scholars consider it recommended to stop where he stopped, as Ibn ‘Umar used to do. They maintain that simply doing the same thing as he did is good, even if his action was incidental, whereas we do it with the intention of emulating him.

Other scholars say that following his example is recommended only when we act on the same basis as he did. If his action was merely incidental, it is not prescribed for us to deliberately pursue something he did not intend. For this reason, most of the Emigrants and the Helpers did not do what Ibn ‘Umar used to do.

Moreover, following his example may sometimes concern the particular kind of action, and sometimes its broader category. He may perform an act for a reason that applies both to that particular kind and to others, rather than for a reason exclusive to it. In that case, what is prescribed is the broader practice. An example is his undergoing cupping, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, for this was prompted by his need

translated_text:
to have unhealthy blood removed. Does following his example, then, apply specifically to cupping, or is the aim to remove blood in a beneficial manner? It is well known that following his example is what is prescribed. Thus, in a hot country, where blood moves towards the skin, cupping is beneficial; whereas in a cold country, where blood recedes into the veins, removing it by opening a vein is beneficial.

Likewise, when he applied oil, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was the purpose specifically to apply oil, or was it to groom his hair? If a country has a humid climate and its people bathe in hot water that makes oil unnecessary, while oil harms their hair and skin, then what is prescribed for them is to groom their hair in whatever manner is best for them. It is well known that the second interpretation is more fitting.

Similarly, he used to eat fresh dates, dried dates, barley bread, and other staple foods of his country. Does following his example mean deliberately choosing fresh dates, dried dates, and barley specifically, so that even those living in lands where dates do not grow and barley is not a staple should do so, although their staples are wheat, rice, or other foods? It is well known that the second approach is what is prescribed.

The evidence for this is that when the Companions conquered the various lands, each of them ate the staple foods and wore the clothing of his own country, without deliberately seeking out the foods and clothing of Medina. Had this latter course been better for them, they would have been foremost in choosing what was better.

{فَرَضَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ صَدَقَةَ الْفِطْرِ صَاعًا مِنْ تَمْرٍ أَوْ صَاعًا مِنْ شَعِيرٍ عَلَى كُلِّ صَغِيرٍ أَوْ كَبِيرٍ ذَكَرٍ أَوْ أُنْثَى حُرٍّ أَوْ عَبْدٍ مِنْ الْمُسْلِمِينَ}
 .
 وَهَذِهِ الْمَسْأَلَةُ فِيهَا قَوْلَانِ لِلْعُلَمَاءِ وَهُمَا رِوَايَتَانِ عَنْ أَحْمَد وَأَكْثَرُ الْعُلَمَاءِ عَلَى أَنَّهُ يُخْرِجُ مِنْ قُوتِ بَلَدِهِ وَهَذَا هُوَ الصَّحِيحُ كَمَا ذَكَرَ اللَّهُ ذَلِكَ فِي الْكَفَّارَةِ بِقَوْلِهِ:
 
{مِنْ أَوْسَطِ مَا تُطْعِمُونَ أَهْلِيكُمْ}
 .
 وَمِنْ هَذَا الْبَابِ:
 أَنَّ الْغَالِبَ عَلَيْهِ وَعَلَى أَصْحَابِهِ أَنَّهُمْ كَانُوا يأتزرون وَيَرْتَدُونَ؛ فَهَلْ الْأَفْضَلُ لِكُلِّ أَحَدٍ أَنْ يَرْتَدِيَ ويأتزر وَلَوْ مَعَ الْقَمِيصِ؟ أَوْ الْأَفْضَلُ أَنْ يَلْبَسَ مَعَ الْقَمِيصِ السَّرَاوِيلَ مِنْ غَيْرِ حَاجَةٍ إلَى الْإِزَارِ وَالرِّدَاءِ. هَذَا أَيْضًا مِمَّا تَنَازَعَ فِيهِ الْعُلَمَاءُ وَالثَّانِي أَظْهَرُ وَهَذَا بَابٌ وَاسِعٌ.
 وَهَذَا النَّوْعُ لَيْسَ مَخْصُوصًا بِفِعْلِهِ وَفِعْلِ أَصْحَابِهِ بَلْ وَبِكَثِيرِ مِمَّا أَمَرَهُمْ بِهِ وَنَهَاهُمْ عَنْهُ وَهَذَا سَمَّتْهُ طَائِفَةٌ مِنْ النَّاسِ:
 
" تَنْقِيحُ الْمَنَاطِ "
 وَهُوَ أَنْ يَكُونَ الْحُكْمُ قَدْ ثَبَتَ فِي عَيْنٍ مُعَيَّنَةٍ وَلَيْسَ مَخْصُوصًا بِهَا بَلْ الْحُكْمُ ثَابِتٌ فِيهَا وَفِي غَيْرِهَا فَيُحْتَاجُ أَنْ يُعْرَفَ 
" مَنَاطُ الْحُكْمِ "
.
translated_text:
This is the basis of the scholars’ disagreement concerning zakāt al-fitr (the alms due at the end of Ramadan): if dates and barley are not staple foods in a particular country, should its people give their own staple foods, such as wheat and rice, or should they give dates and barley because the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prescribed them? For in the two Sahīh collections, Ibn ‘Umar reported:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prescribed zakāt al-fitr as one sāʿ-measure of dates or one sāʿ-measure of barley for every Muslim, young or old, male or female, free or enslaved.”

The scholars hold two opinions on this question, both of which are reported from Ahmad. Most scholars hold that a person should give the staple food of his country. This is the correct view, just as Allah stated concerning expiation:

“From the average of what you feed your families.”

Another example is that he and his Companions generally wore waist-wraps and upper wraps. Is it therefore better for everyone to wear an upper wrap and a waist-wrap, even with a shirt? Or is it better to wear trousers with a shirt, without needing a waist-wrap and an upper wrap? This too is a matter over which the scholars have disagreed. The second view is more clearly correct. This is a broad subject.

This kind of reasoning is not confined to his actions and those of his Companions; it also applies to much of what he commanded them to do and forbade them to do. Some have called this “refining the basis of a ruling.” This is where a ruling has been established concerning a particular case but is not exclusive to it; rather, the ruling applies both to that case and to others. It therefore becomes necessary to identify “the basis of the ruling.”

original_text:
مِثَالُ ذَلِكَ أَنَّهُ قَدْ ثَبَتَ فِي الصَّحِيحِ أَنَّ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ 
{سُئِلَ عَنْ فَأْرَةٍ وَقَعَتْ فِي سَمْنٍ فَقَالَ: اُلْقُوهَا وَمَا حَوْلَهَا وَكُلُوا سَمْنَكُمْ}
 فَإِنَّهُ مُتَّفَقٌ عَلَى أَنَّ الْحُكْمَ لَيْسَ مُخْتَصًّا بِتِلْكَ الْفَأْرَةِ وَذَلِكَ السَّمْنِ؛ بَلْ الْحُكْمُ ثَابِتٌ فِيمَا هُوَ أَعَمُّ مِنْهُمَا فَبَقِيَ الْمَنَاطُ الَّذِي عُلِّقَ بِهِ الْحُكْمُ مَا هُوَ؟ فَطَائِفَةٌ مِنْ أَهْلِ الْعِلْمِ يَزْعُمُونَ أَنَّ الْحُكْمَ مُخْتَصٌّ بِفَأْرَةِ وَقَعَتْ فِي سَمْنٍ فَيُنَجِّسُونَ مَا كَانَ كَذَلِكَ مُطْلَقًا وَلَا يُنَجِّسُونَ السَّمْنَ إذَا وَقَعَ فِيهِ الْكَلْبُ وَالْبَوْلُ وَالْعَذِرَةُ وَلَا يُنَجِّسُونَ الزَّيْتَ وَنَحْوَهُ. إذَا وَقَعَتْ فِيهِ الْفَأْرَةُ وَهَذَا الْقَوْلُ خَطَأٌ قَطْعًا. وَلَيْسَ هَذَا مَبْنِيًّا عَلَى كَوْنِ الْقِيَاسِ حُجَّةً. فَإِنَّ الْقِيَاسَ الَّذِي يَكُونُ النِّزَاعُ فِيهِ هُوَ تَخْرِيجُ الْمَنَاطِ وَهُوَ أَنْ يَجُوزَ اخْتِصَاصُ مَوْرِدِ النَّصِّ بِالْحُكْمِ فَإِذَا جَازَ اخْتِصَاصُهُ وَجَازَ أَنْ يَكُونَ الْحُكْمُ مُشْتَرَكًا بَيْنَ مَوْرِدِ النَّصِّ وَغَيْرِهِ.
 احْتَاجَ مُعْتَبِرُ الْقِيَاسِ إلَى أَنْ يَعْلَمَ أَنَّ الْمُشْتَرَكَ بَيْنَ الْأَصْلِ وَالْفَرْعِ هُوَ مَنَاطُ الْحُكْمِ كَمَا فِي قَوْلِهِ:
 
{لَا تَبِيعُوا الذَّهَبَ بِالذَّهَبِ إلَّا مِثْلًا بِمِثْلِ وَلَا تَبِيعُوا الْفِضَّةَ بِالْفِضَّةِ إلَّا مِثْلًا بِمِثْلِ وَلَا تَبِيعُوا الشَّعِيرَ بِالشَّعِيرِ إلَّا مِثْلًا بِمِثْلِ وَلَا تَبِيعُوا الْمِلْحَ بِالْمِلْحِ إلَّا مِثْلًا بِمِثْلِ}
 فَلَمَّا نَهَى عَنْ التَّفَاضُلِ فِي مِثْلِ هَذِهِ الْأَصْنَافِ أَمْكَنَ أَنْ يَكُونَ النَّهْيُ لِمَعْنَى مُشْتَرَكٍ وَلِمَعْنَى مُخْتَصٍّ.
 وَلَمَّا سُئِلَ عَنْ فَأْرَةٍ وَقَعَتْ فِي سَمْنٍ فَأَجَابَ:
 عَنْ تِلْكَ
translated_text:
An example of this is the report established in the Sahīh that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace,

“Was asked about a mouse that had fallen into ghee. He said: ‘Remove it and the ghee around it, and eat the rest of your ghee.’”

There is agreement that the ruling is not exclusive to that particular mouse and that particular ghee; rather, it applies more broadly. The question therefore remains: what is the basis on which the ruling depends? Some scholars claim that the ruling applies exclusively to a mouse falling into ghee. They therefore regard ghee into which a mouse has fallen as impure without qualification, but do not regard ghee as impure when a dog, urine or excrement falls into it. Nor do they regard oil and similar substances as impure when a mouse falls into them. This opinion is unquestionably mistaken.

This does not depend on whether legal analogy is authoritative. The disputed form of analogy involves deriving the basis of the ruling: that is, where it is possible that the ruling applies exclusively to the case addressed by the text. If the ruling could be exclusive to that case, but could also apply both to it and to other cases, someone employing analogy must establish that the feature shared by the original case and the new case is the basis of the ruling. An example is his saying:

“Do not sell gold for gold except in equal amounts; do not sell silver for silver except in equal amounts; do not sell barley for barley except in equal amounts; and do not sell salt for salt except in equal amounts.”

When he prohibited exchanging unequal amounts of commodities such as these, the prohibition could have been based on a shared feature or on a feature peculiar to them.

But when he was asked about a mouse that had fallen into ghee, he gave an answer concerning that

original_text:
الْقَضِيَّةِ الْمُعَيَّنَةِ وَلَا خَفَاءَ أَنَّ الْحُكْمَ لَيْسَ مُخْتَصًّا بِهَا وَكَذَلِكَ سَائِرُ قَضَايَا الْأَعْيَانِ كَالْأَعْرَابِيِّ الَّذِي قَالَ لَهُ:
 إنِّي وَقَعْت عَلَى أَهْلِي فِي رَمَضَانَ فَأَمَرَهُ. أَنْ يَعْتِقَ رَقَبَةً أَوْ يَصُومَ شَهْرَيْنِ مُتَتَابِعَيْنِ أَوْ يُطْعِمَ سِتِّينَ مِسْكِينًا فَإِنَّ الْحُكْمَ لَيْسَ مَخْصُوصًا بِذَلِكَ الْأَعْرَابِيِّ بِاتِّفَاقِ الْمُسْلِمِينَ. لَكِنْ هَلْ أَمَرَهُ بِذَلِكَ لِكَوْنِهِ أَفْطَرَ أَوْ جَامَعَ فِي رَمَضَانَ أَوْ أَفْطَرَ فِيهِ بِالْجِمَاعِ أَوْ أَفْطَرَ بِالْجِنْسِ الْأَعْلَى هَذَا مِمَّا تَنَازَعَ فِيهِ الْعُلَمَاءُ. وَكَذَلِكَ لَمَّا سَأَلَهُ سَائِلٌ عَمَّنْ أَحْرَمَ بِالْعُمْرَةِ وَعَلَيْهِ جُبَّةٌ وَهُوَ مُتَضَمِّخٌ بِالْخَلُوقِ.
 فَقَالَ:
 
{انْزِعْ عَنْك الْجُبَّةَ وَاغْسِلْ عَنْك أَثَرَ الْخَلُوقِ وَاصْنَعْ فِي عُمْرَتِك مَا كُنْت صَانِعًا فِي حَجَّتِك}
 . فَهَلْ أَمَرَهُ بِغَسْلِ الْخَلُوقِ لِكَوْنِهِ طَيِّبًا حَتَّى يُؤْمَرَ الْمُحَرَّمُ بِغَسْلِ كُلِّ طِيبٍ كَانَ عَلَيْهِ أَوْ لِكَوْنِهِ خَلُوقًا لِرَجُلِ؟ وَقَدْ نَهَى أَنْ يَتَزَعْفَرَ الرَّجُلُ فَيَنْهَى عَنْ الْخُلُوقِ لِلرَّجُلِ سَوَاءٌ كَانَ مُحْرِمًا أَوْ غَيْرَ مُحْرِمٍ.
 وَكَذَلِكَ لَمَّا عَتَقَتْ بَرِيرَةُ فَخَيَّرَهَا فَاخْتَارَتْ نَفْسَهَا عِنْدَ مَنْ يَقُولُ:
 إنَّ زَوْجَهَا كَانَ عَبْدًا فَإِنَّ الْمُسْلِمِينَ اتَّفَقُوا عَلَى أَنَّ الْحُكْمَ لَا يَخْتَصُّ بِهَا: لَكِنْ هَلْ التَّخْيِيرُ لِكَوْنِهَا عَتَقَتْ تَحْتَ عَبْدٍ فَكَمَّلَتْ تَحْتَ نَاقِصٍ؟ وَلَا تُخَيَّرُ إذَا عَتَقَتْ تَحْتَ الْحُرِّ أَوْ الْحُكْمُ لِكَوْنِهَا مَلَكَتْ نَفْسَهَا فَتُخَيَّرُ سَوَاءٌ كَانَ الزَّوْجُ حُرًّا أَوْ عَبْدًا؟ هَذَا مِمَّا تَنَازَعُوا فِيهِ. وَهَذَا بَابٌ وَاسِعٌ وَهُوَ مُتَنَاوِلٌ لِكُلِّ حُكْمٍ تَعَلَّقَ بِعَيْنِ مُعَيَّنَةٍ مَعَ الْعِلْمِ بِأَنَّهُ لَا يَخْتَصُّ بِهَا
translated_text:
particular incident, and it is clear that the ruling is not exclusive to it. The same applies to all other rulings concerning particular cases, such as that of the Bedouin who said to him:

“I had intercourse with my wife during Ramadan.”

He instructed him to free a slave, fast for two consecutive months, or feed sixty needy people. Muslims agree that the ruling is not exclusive to that Bedouin. Scholars disagree, however, over whether he instructed him to do this because he had broken his fast, because he had intercourse during Ramadan, because he had broken his fast during Ramadan through intercourse, or because he had broken it through an act belonging to the higher category.

Likewise, someone asked him about a person who had entered the consecrated state for ‘umrah while wearing a robe and smeared with saffron-based perfume. He said:

“Remove your robe, wash off the traces of the saffron-based perfume, and do during your ‘umrah what you would do during your Hajj.”

Did he instruct him to wash off the saffron-based perfume because it was perfume, so that anyone in the consecrated state should be instructed to wash off whatever perfume he was wearing? Or was it because this was saffron-based perfume worn by a man? He had forbidden men to apply saffron to themselves; thus, a man is forbidden to use this perfume whether or not he is in the consecrated state.

Likewise, when Barīrah was freed, he gave her a choice, and she chose to leave her husband—according to those who say that her husband was a slave. Muslims agree that the ruling is not exclusive to her. But was she given the choice because she had been freed while married to a slave, thereby attaining full status while her husband remained of lesser status, so that she would not be given the choice if she were freed while married to a free man? Or was the ruling based on her having gained control over her own person, so that she would be given the choice whether her husband was free or enslaved? This is a matter over which they disagreed.

This is a broad subject, encompassing every ruling attached to a particular case when it is known that the ruling is not exclusive to it.

original_text:
فَيَحْتَاجُ أَنْ يُعْرَفَ الْمَنَاطُ الَّذِي يَتَعَلَّقُ بِهِ الْحُكْمُ وَهَذَا النَّوْعُ يُسَمِّيهِ بَعْضُ النَّاسِ قِيَاسًا؛ وَبَعْضُهُمْ لَا يُسَمِّيهِ قِيَاسًا؛ وَلِهَذَا كَانَ أَبُو حَنِيفَةَ وَأَصْحَابُهُ يَسْتَعْمِلُونَهُ فِي الْمَوَاضِعِ الَّتِي لَا يَسْتَعْمِلُونَ فِيهَا الْقِيَاسَ. وَالصَّوَابُ أَنَّ هَذَا لَيْسَ مِنْ الْقِيَاسِ الَّذِي يُمْكِنُ فِيهِ النِّزَاعُ كَمَا أَنَّ تَحْقِيقَ الْمَنَاطِ لَيْسَ مِمَّا يَقْبَلُ النِّزَاعَ بِاتِّفَاقِ الْعُلَمَاءِ. وَهَذِهِ الْأَنْوَاعُ الثَّلَاثَةُ 
" تَحْقِيقُ الْمَنَاطِ "
 و 
" تَنْقِيحُ الْمَنَاطِ "
 و 
" تَخْرِيجُ الْمَنَاطِ "
 هِيَ جِمَاعُ الِاجْتِهَادِ.
فَالْأَوَّلُ أَنْ يَعْمَلَ بِالنَّصِّ وَالْإِجْمَاعِ؛
 فَإِنَّ الْحُكْمَ مُعَلَّقٌ بِوَصْفِ يَحْتَاجُ فِي الْحُكْمِ عَلَى الْمُعَيَّنِ إلَى أَنْ يَعْلَمَ ثُبُوتَ ذَلِكَ الْوَصْفِ فِيهِ كَمَا يَعْلَمُ أَنَّ اللَّهَ أَمَرَنَا بِإِشْهَادِ ذَوِي عَدْلٍ مِنَّا وَمِمَّنْ نَرْضَى مِنْ الشُّهَدَاءِ وَلَكِنْ لَا يُمْكِنُ تَعْيِينُ كُلِّ شَاهِدٍ فَيَحْتَاجُ أَنْ يَعْلَمَ فِي الشُّهُودِ الْمُعَيَّنِينَ:
 هَلْ هُمْ مِنْ ذَوِي الْعَدْلِ الْمَرْضِيِّينَ أَمْ لَا؟ وَكَمَا أَمَرَ اللَّهُ بِعِشْرَةِ الزَّوْجَيْنِ بِالْمَعْرُوفِ وَقَالَ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ 
{لِلنِّسَاءِ رِزْقُهُنَّ وَكِسْوَتُهُنَّ بِالْمَعْرُوفِ}
 وَلَمْ يُمْكِنْ تَعْيِينُ كُلِّ زَوْجٍ فَيُحْتَاجُ أَنْ يُنْظَرَ فِي الْأَعْيَانِ.
 ثُمَّ مِنْ الْفُقَهَاءِ مَنْ يَقُولُ إنَّ نَفَقَةَ الزَّوْجَةِ مُقَدَّرَةٌ بِالشَّرْعِ وَالصَّوَابُ مَا عَلَيْهِ الْجُمْهُورُ أَنَّ ذَلِكَ مَرْدُودٌ إلَى الْعُرْفِ كَمَا قَالَ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ لِهِنْدِ:
 
{خُذِي مَا يَكْفِيك وَوَلَدَك بِالْمَعْرُوفِ}
 .
translated_text:
so it is necessary to identify the effective cause on which the ruling depends. Some call this form of reasoning analogy, while others do not. Hence Abū Hanīfah and his followers employed it in cases where they did not employ analogy. The correct view is that this does not belong to the kind of analogy that is open to dispute, just as scholars unanimously agree that ascertaining whether the effective cause applies to a particular case is not open to dispute. These three forms—“ascertaining whether the effective cause applies,” “isolating the effective cause,” and “deriving the effective cause”—together encompass independent legal reasoning.

The first consists in applying the revealed texts and scholarly consensus. A ruling is attached to an attribute, and applying it to a particular case requires establishing that the attribute is present in that case. For example, we know that Allah has commanded us to call upright witnesses from among ourselves, whom we find acceptable. Yet every individual witness cannot be specified, so we must determine whether particular witnesses are upright and acceptable.

Likewise, Allah has commanded spouses to live together honorably, and the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Women are entitled to provision and clothing in accordance with what is reasonable.”

Every individual husband cannot be specified, so individual cases must be examined. Some jurists hold that a wife’s maintenance is fixed by Islamic law. The correct view, however, is that of the majority: it is determined by customary practice, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to Hind:

“Take what reasonably suffices for you and your child.”

translated_text:
Likewise, the Most High says:

“Do not approach the orphan’s property except in the best manner.”

It remains to consider whether entrusting it to this particular merchant in return for a share of the profit constitutes dealing with it in the best manner.

Similarly, He says:

“Charitable alms are only for the poor and the needy.”

The question remains whether this particular person belongs to the poor and needy mentioned in the Quran. Likewise, Allah has prohibited intoxicants and usury in general, but the question remains whether a particular drink is an intoxicant.

Muslims—indeed, all rational people—agree on this form of reasoning: the Lawgiver cannot explicitly state the ruling for every individual case; rather, He speaks in general terms. Our Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was granted the gift of concise, comprehensive speech.

(As for the second type, which they call “isolating the effective cause,” this occurs when a ruling is explicitly stated for particular cases, yet we know that the ruling is not confined to them. The correct view is that this does not fall under analogy, since they agree that it is covered by the text. Rather, the text addresses the category to which the particular case belongs, but that category must be identified.

The case of the mouse in the clarified butter belongs here. The ruling is not confined to that particular mouse and that particular clarified butter, nor to the mice and clarified butter of Medina. Rather, someone asked the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, about a mouse that had fallen into clarified butter, and he answered him. This does not mean that the answer applies only to that person or his question, just as he answered others.

The words “mouse” and “clarified butter” were not spoken by the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, such that he himself could be said to have made the ruling dependent on them. Rather, they were spoken by the questioner, who related what had happened to him, just as he was told by

translated_text:
the Bedouin that he had had intercourse with his wife. Had he had intercourse with his concubine, the same would have applied. Likewise, another man told him, “I saw the gleam of her anklet in the moonlight, so I fell upon her.” Had he had intercourse with her without that circumstance, the ruling would have been the same.

The correct view here is that held by the well-known imams: the ruling concerns any foul substance that Allah has forbidden when it falls into clarified butter or similar liquids. Allah has permitted wholesome things for us and forbidden foul things. Thus, when we base the ruling on this consideration, we are following the Book of Allah. When something foul falls into something wholesome, one discards the foul substance and what surrounds it, and eats what remains wholesome, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, commanded.

This response is not the place to discuss such questions at length. We have, however, drawn attention to this because it bears on following the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in his actions. This, then, is a matter that involves people’s juristic reasoning and inference, and whatever understanding, wisdom, and knowledge Allah grants them. Those closest to the truth are those who connect rulings to the considerations to which the Lawgiver connected them.

This is an area in which people have differed in understanding and disputed: is this derived from the Lawgiver’s words, or from considerations underlying analogical reasoning? Some have claimed that most rulings governing people’s actions are not covered by the Lawgiver’s words, but instead require analogy. Others have claimed that all such rulings are established by the revealed texts, and have gone to excess in their adherence to the apparent wording

to the point of denying the clear implications and indications of the wording. An example is the Most High’s saying:

“Do not say to them so much as a word of irritation.”

They said that this indicates only a prohibition on expressing irritation; no prohibition on striking or insulting them can be understood from it. They also rejected “isolating the effective cause” and claimed apparent meanings for words that those words do not convey. Others sometimes give analogy precedence because the text’s indication is incomplete, or because it is a solitary report. Still others set the text and analogy against one another and give precedence to the text, yet fall into inconsistency.

We have explained elsewhere that sound proofs do not contradict one another. Sound rational and scriptural proofs do not conflict, nor does a sound inference from analogy contradict a sound inference from the wording. Sound analogy is, in essence, treating like cases alike. This is the justice with which Allah sent down the Book and sent the messengers. The Messenger does not command anything contrary to justice, nor does he give different rulings for two equivalent cases; nor can one thing be forbidden while its equivalent is lawful.

We have examined most of the cases in which analogy is said to conflict with the text, and the text’s ruling is said to run contrary to analogy. We have found that whenever the Lawgiver singles something out for a ruling different from that of comparable cases, He does so only because it possesses a distinctive attribute that requires this particular ruling. Thus, when needed, estimation takes the place of measurement by volume, just as earth takes the place of water, and carrion takes the place of properly slaughtered meat when needed. The same applies to the statement that lending, leasing, profit-sharing investment partnerships, tending orchards for a share of their produce, sharecropping, and similar transactions run contrary to analogy. If the speaker means that these transactions possess distinctive features requiring their rulings to differ from those governing transactions unlike them, he is correct. Indeed, this is precisely what analogy requires. But if he means that two equivalent acts have been assigned different rulings, this is an error that even those of lesser rank than the prophets are above committing—may Allah’s blessings be upon them.

Rather, it is these opposing analogies that are unsound, such as the analogy of those who said:

“‘Trade is only like usury.’ But Allah has permitted trade and forbidden usury.”

And the analogy of those who said, “Do you eat what you yourselves have killed, yet refuse to eat what Allah has killed?”—meaning carrion. The Most High said:

“Indeed, the devils inspire their allies to dispute with you. And if you obey them, you will surely be polytheists.”

Since this is so, discussing the particular circumstances of a person following the spiritual path requires careful consideration of each case and seeking guidance from Allah. Allah has commanded His servant to say in every prayer:

“Guide us to the straight path—the path of those You have blessed, not those who have incurred Your anger, nor those who have gone astray.”

The servant must therefore strive to attain what he asks for in this supplication, so that he may join those whom Allah has blessed: the prophets, the steadfastly truthful, the martyrs, and the righteous. What excellent companions they are!

translated_text:
Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah have mercy on him—said:

Section: Acts of Worship Prescribed in Different Forms

It has already been explained in several places that when the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, performed an act of worship in different ways, all those forms are prescribed, and none is disliked. Examples include the different forms of the tashahhud (testimony of faith recited while seated in prayer) and the opening supplications; performing Witr prayer at the beginning or end of the night; reciting aloud or quietly during the night prayer; the various readings in which the Quran was revealed; proclaiming Allah’s greatness on Eid; including or omitting tarjīʿ (repetition of the testimonies of faith after reciting them quietly) in the call to prayer; and saying the phrases of the iqāmah (final call to prayer) once or twice.

In our response to the Zarʿiyyah questions and elsewhere, we have explained at length that matters over which scholars differ, and concerning which a person wishes to exercise caution, fall into two categories:

The first consists of matters in which they agree that both alternatives are permissible, but differ as to which is preferable.

translated_text:
The second consists of matters in which they disagree over whether one of the two alternatives is permissible. In many such matters, the Sunnah has sanctioned both alternatives. Hajj is an example. Some have said that converting one’s Hajj into ʿumrah is impermissible; some have even said that tamattuʿ (performing ʿumrah followed by Hajj) is impermissible. Others have said that doing so is obligatory. The correct view is that either course is permissible. During the Farewell Pilgrimage, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, instructed the Companions to convert their Hajj into ʿumrah, although he had previously given them a choice between the three forms of Hajj. The caliphs after him performed Hajj without converting it into ʿumrah, as has been explained at length in its proper place.

The same applies to fasting while travelling. Some have said that it is impermissible and that one must refrain from fasting. The correct view, held by the majority, is that both alternatives are permissible. Many of them then said that fasting is preferable, but the correct view is that not fasting is preferable unless there is an overriding benefit in fasting. No scholar has said that refraining from fasting is impermissible, as some ignorant people suppose. This has been discussed at length in several places.

The point here is that practices established in different forms in the Sunnah—such as the call to prayer, the iqāmah (final call to prayer), prayer in circumstances of fear, and the opening supplications—are to be discussed from two perspectives. The first concerns the permissibility of all these forms, without any being disliked. This is the correct view, and it is the position of Ahmad and others regarding all these matters. Some scholars, however, may regard certain forms as disliked or forbidden because they believe that those forms were not established in the Sunnah or that they were abrogated.

Mahdhūrah to teach him Islam, not to teach him the call to prayer.” The correct view is that he made it part of the call to prayer. This is how Abū Mahdhūrah understood it, and both he and his descendants practised it, with the Muslims accepting their practice in Mecca and elsewhere. Some regarded the call to prayer without tarjīʿ as disliked. This too is mistaken, for the established form of Bilāl’s call to prayer contains no tarjīʿ. Another group regarded tarjīʿ in it as disliked. Some regarded prayer in circumstances of fear as disliked unless performed according to the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar, while others regarded the form prescribed by that group as disliked. The correct view in all these matters is that no form established in the Sunnah is disliked; rather, all are permissible. This has been discussed at length elsewhere.

Our concern here is the second perspective: when the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, practised something in different forms, then—even if some of those forms are considered superior—following his example by practising one form on some occasions and another on others is better than adhering to one and abandoning the other.

An example is the opening supplication. In the two Sahīh collections, Abū Hurayrah said:

“I said, ‘O Messenger of Allah, during your silence between the opening takbīr and the recitation, what do you say?’ He replied, ‘I say: O Allah, distance me from my sins as You have distanced the east from the west. O Allah, cleanse me of my sins as a white garment is cleansed of dirt. O Allah, wash away my sins with snow, water and hail.’”

 وَرَوَى إذَا فَرَغَ مِنْ الْفَاتِحَةِ فَقَالَ طَائِفَةٌ مِنْ أَصْحَابِ الشَّافِعِيِّ وَأَحْمَد:
 يُسْتَحَبُّ ثَلَاثُ سَكَتَاتٍ. وَسَكْتَةُ الْفَاتِحَةِ جَعَلَهَا أَصْحَابُ الشَّافِعِيِّ وَطَائِفَةٌ مِنْ أَصْحَابِ أَحْمَد لِيَقْرَأَ الْمَأْمُومُ الْفَاتِحَةَ. وَالصَّحِيحُ أَنَّهُ لَا يُسْتَحَبُّ إلَّا سَكْتَتَانِ فَلَيْسَ فِي الْحَدِيثِ إلَّا ذَلِكَ وَإِحْدَى الرِّوَايَتَيْنِ غَلَطٌ وَإِلَّا كَانَتْ ثَلَاثًا
translated_text:
this one. It is the strongest evidence for the opening supplication in obligatory prayers, for it explicitly addresses this in the words: “Tell me about your silence between the opening takbīr and the recitation.” This is a question about silence, not about speaking quietly. It is corroborated by the hadith of Samurah and that of Ubayy ibn Ka'b, which state that the Prophet observed two pauses.

There are also several views concerning pauses in prayer.

The first is that there are no pauses, as Mālik held. He did not regard an opening supplication, seeking refuge with Allah, or a pause for the imam’s recitation as recommended.

The second is that there is only one pause, for the opening supplication, as Abū Hanīfah held, since this hadith establishes that pause.

The third is that there are two pauses, as stated in the hadith recorded in the Sunan collections. One version reports that he paused upon completing the recitation, and this is the correct version. Another reports that he paused upon completing al-Fātihah. Accordingly, some followers of al-Shāfi'ī and Ahmad held that three pauses are recommended. The followers of al-Shāfi'ī and some followers of Ahmad considered the pause after al-Fātihah an opportunity for those praying behind the imam to recite al-Fātihah.

The correct view is that only two pauses are recommended, for that is all the hadith mentions. One of the two versions is mistaken; otherwise, there would have been three pauses.

original_text: وَهَذَا هُوَ الْمَنْصُوصُ عَنْ أَحْمَد. وَأَنَّهُ لَا يُسْتَحَبُّ إلَّا سَكْتَتَانِ وَالثَّانِيَةُ عِنْدَ الْفَرَاغِ مِنْ الْقِرَاءَةِ لِلِاسْتِرَاحَةِ وَالْفَصْلِ بَيْنَهَا وَبَيْنَ الرُّكُوعِ. وَأَمَّا السُّكُوتُ عَقِيبَ الْفَاتِحَةِ فَلَا يَسْتَحِبُّهُ أَحْمَد كَمَا لَا يَسْتَحِبُّهُ مَالِكٌ وَأَبُو حَنِيفَةَ وَالْجُمْهُورُ لَا يَسْتَحِبُّونَ أَنْ يَسْكُتَ الْإِمَامُ لِيَقْرَأ الْمَأْمُومُ. وَذَلِكَ أَنَّ قِرَاءَةَ الْمَأْمُومِ عِنْدَهُمْ إذَا جَهَرَ الْإِمَامُ لَيْسَتْ بِوَاجِبَةٍ وَلَا مُسْتَحَبَّةٍ بَلْ هِيَ مَنْهِيٌّ عَنْهَا وَهَلْ تُبْطِلُ الصَّلَاةَ إذَا قَرَأَ مَعَ الْإِمَامِ؟ فِيهِ وَجْهَانِ فِي مَذْهَبِ أَحْمَد فَهُوَ إذَا كَانَ يَسْمَعُ قِرَاءَةَ الْإِمَامِ فَاسْتِمَاعُهُ أَفْضَلُ مِنْ قِرَاءَتِهِ كَاسْتِمَاعِهِ لِمَا زَادَ عَلَى الْفَاتِحَةِ فَيَحْصُلُ لَهُ مَقْصُودُ الْقِرَاءَةِ وَالِاسْتِمَاعِ بَدَلٌ عَنْ قِرَاءَتِهِ فَجَمْعُهُ بَيْنَ الِاسْتِمَاعِ وَالْقِرَاءَةِ جَمْعٌ بَيْنَ الْبَدَلِ وَالْمُبْدَلِ وَلِهَذَا لَمْ يَسْتَحِبَّ أَحْمَد وَجُمْهُورُ أَصْحَابِهِ قِرَاءَتَهُ فِي سَكَتَاتِ الْإِمَامِ إلَّا أَنْ يَسْكُتَ سُكُوتًا بَلِيغًا يَتَّسِعُ لِلِاسْتِفْتَاحِ وَالْقِرَاءَةِ. وَأَمَّا إنْ ضَاقَ عَنْهُمَا فَقَوْلُهُ وَقَوْلُ أَكْثَرِ أَصْحَابِهِ إنَّ الِاسْتِفْتَاحَ أَوْلَى مِنْ الْقِرَاءَةِ بَلْ هُوَ فِي إحْدَى الرِّوَايَتَيْنِ يَأْمُرُ بِالِاسْتِفْتَاحِ مَعَ جَهْرِ الْإِمَامِ فَإِذَا كَانَ الْإِمَامُ مِمَّنْ يَسْكُتُ عَقِيبَ الْفَاتِحَةِ سُكُوتًا يَتَّسِعُ لِلْقِرَاءَةِ فَالْقِرَاءَةُ فِيهِ أَفْضَلُ مِنْ عَدَمِ الْقِرَاءَةِ لَكِنْ هَلْ يُقَالُ الْقِرَاءَةُ فِيهِ بِالْفَاتِحَةِ أَفْضَلُ لِلِاخْتِلَافِ فِي وُجُوبِهَا. أَوْ بِغَيْرِهَا مِنْ الْقُرْآنِ لِكَوْنِهِ قَدْ اسْتَمَعَهَا؟ هَذَا فِيهِ نِزَاعٌ. وَمُقْتَضَى نُصُوصِ أَحْمَد وَأَكْثَرِ أَصْحَابِهِ أَنَّ
translated_text:
and this is the position explicitly stated by Ahmad: only two pauses are recommended, the second coming at the end of the recitation, to rest briefly and separate the recitation from bowing. As for pausing immediately after al-Fātihah, Ahmad does not consider it recommended, nor do Mālik and Abū Hanīfah. The majority do not consider it recommended for the imam to pause so that those praying behind him can recite.

This is because, in their view, recitation by someone praying behind the imam when the imam recites aloud is neither obligatory nor recommended; rather, it is prohibited. Does reciting along with the imam invalidate the prayer? There are two views within Ahmad’s school. If someone can hear the imam’s recitation, listening to it is better than reciting himself, just as he listens to what is recited beyond al-Fātihah. He thereby attains the purpose of recitation, and listening takes the place of his own recitation. Combining listening with recitation therefore combines the substitute with that for which it substitutes.

For this reason, Ahmad and most of his followers did not consider recitation during the imam’s pauses recommended unless the imam pauses long enough to allow both the opening supplication and recitation. If the pause is too short for both, Ahmad and most of his followers hold that the opening supplication takes precedence over recitation. Indeed, according to one of the two reports from him, he instructs the worshipper to offer the opening supplication even while the imam is reciting aloud.

If the imam pauses after al-Fātihah long enough to allow recitation, then reciting during that pause is better than not reciting. But should it be said that reciting al-Fātihah during it is better, because its obligatory status is disputed, or that reciting another passage of the Quran is better, since he has already listened to al-Fātihah? This is disputed. The explicit statements of Ahmad and most of his followers imply that

translated_text:
reciting another passage is better. It is not recommended for him to recite al-Fātihah when he is listening to its recitation. The disapproval expressed by most of the early scholars concerning recitation behind the imam relates to cases in which he recites aloud. Most imams did not pause for long after al-Fātihah, and few worshippers recited while the imam was reciting aloud. This is prohibited by the Quran and Sunnah, and the majority of earlier and later scholars maintain this prohibition. Whether doing so invalidates the prayer is disputed.

Some scholars, however, hold that the worshipper should recite al-Fātihah while the imam recites aloud. Whether his prayer is invalid if he does not recite it is also disputed. Thus, there is disagreement on both sides. Nevertheless, those who prohibit reciting along with the imam constitute the majority of earlier and later scholars, and their position is supported by the Quran and authentic Sunnah. As for those who require the worshipper praying behind the imam to recite in these circumstances, the hadith they rely upon, narrated by Abū Dāwūd, has been judged weak by the leading hadith scholars.

The wording in the hadith of Abū Mūsā, “When he recites, listen attentively,” was graded authentic by Ahmad, Ishāq, Muslim ibn al-Hajjāj and others. Al-Bukhārī considered it defective because of differences in its transmission, but this does not undermine its authenticity. By contrast, the other hadith was not included in the Sahīh, and its weakness is established on several grounds. It is merely a statement of ‘Ubādah ibn al-Sāmit.

Rather, during the imam’s pause, the worshipper should offer the prescribed opening supplication and seek refuge in Allah. If the imam does not pause long enough for this, or the worshipper misses his pause, should he offer the opening supplication and seek refuge in Allah while the imam recites aloud?

There are three reported positions:

The first is that he offers the opening supplication and seeks refuge in Allah while the imam recites aloud, even though he does not recite, because

translated_text:
the purpose of recitation is fulfilled by listening, whereas he does not hear the imam’s opening supplication or his seeking refuge in Allah, since the imam says these silently.

The second position is that he offers the opening supplication but does not seek refuge in Allah, because seeking refuge is prescribed for recitation, and he is not reciting. The opening supplication, however, accompanies the opening takbīr.

The third position is that he neither offers the opening supplication nor seeks refuge in Allah. This is the soundest view and is held by most scholars, including Mālik and al-Shāfi‘ī, and also Abū Hanīfah, as far as I believe. This is because he is commanded to remain silent and listen attentively, so he should not utter anything else. Moreover, since he is prohibited from reciting, he is likewise prohibited from saying these supplications. Many scholars, among Ahmad’s followers and others, say that prohibiting these supplications is all the more warranted, because recitation is obligatory, yet its obligation is waived through listening. In Ahmad’s school, however, the prohibition against recitation is not more emphatic, since he does not consider recitation obligatory for the worshipper praying behind the imam, whether the imam recites silently or aloud. Even if there is disagreement over whether recitation is obligatory for the worshipper praying behind the imam, there is likewise disagreement over whether the opening supplication and seeking refuge in Allah are obligatory. There are two well-known positions on this within his school.

Among the arguments advanced by those who instruct the worshipper to say both while the imam recites aloud is that both are obligatory and no substitute has been prescribed for them, unlike recitation, for which listening has been prescribed as a substitute. The correct view, however, is that these are not obligatory, and only the person who recites is commanded to seek refuge in Allah. إجْمَاعُ الْأُمَّةِ فِيمَا زَادَ عَلَى الْفَاتِحَةِ وَهُوَ قَوْلُ جَمَاهِيرِ السَّلَفِ مِنْ الصَّحَابَةِ وَغَيْرِهِمْ فِي الْفَاتِحَةِ وَغَيْرِهَا وَهُوَ أَحَدُ قَوْلَيْ الشَّافِعِيِّ وَاخْتَارَهُ طَائِفَةٌ مِنْ حُذَّاقِ أَصْحَابِهِ:
 كالرَّازِي وَأَبِي مُحَمَّدٍ بْنِ عَبْدِ السَّلَامِ فَإِنَّ الْقِرَاءَةَ مَعَ جَهْرِ الْإِمَامِ مُنْكَرٌ مُخَالِفٌ لِلْكِتَابِ وَالسُّنَّةِ وَمَا كَانَ عَلَيْهِ عَامَّةُ الصَّحَابَةِ وَلَكِنَّ طَائِفَةً مِنْ أَصْحَابِ أَحْمَد اسْتَحَبُّوا لِلْمَأْمُومِ الْقِرَاءَةَ فِي سَكَتَاتِ الْإِمَامِ وَمِنْهُمْ مَنْ اسْتَحَبَّ أَنْ يَقْرَأَ بِالْفَاتِحَةِ وَإِنْ جَهَرَ وَهُوَ اخْتِيَارُ جَدِّي. كَمَا اسْتَحَبَّ ذَلِكَ طَائِفَةٌ مِنْهُمْ الأوزاعي وَغَيْرُهُ وَاسْتَحَبَّ بَعْضُهُمْ لِلْإِمَامِ أَنْ يَسْكُتَ عَقِبَ الْفَاتِحَةِ لِيَقْرَأَ مَنْ خَلْفَهُ وَأَحْمَد لَمْ يَسْتَحِبَّ هَذَا السُّكُوتَ فَإِنَّهُ لَا يَسْتَحِبُّ الْقِرَاءَةَ إذَا جَهَرَ الْإِمَامُ؛ وَبَسْطُ هَذَا لَهُ مَوْضِعٌ آخَرُ.
 وَالْمَقْصُودُ هُنَا:
 أَنَّ سُكُوتَ الِاسْتِفْتَاحِ ثَبَتَ بِهَذَا الْحَدِيثِ الصَّحِيحِ وَمَعَ هَذَا فَعَامَّةُ الْعُلَمَاءِ مِنْ الصَّحَابَةِ وَمَنْ بَعْدَهُمْ يَسْتَحِبُّونَ الِاسْتِفْتَاحَ بِغَيْرِهِ كَمَا يَسْتَحِبُّ جُمْهُورُهُمْ الِاسْتِفْتَاحَ بِقَوْلِهِ: 
" سُبْحَانَك اللَّهُمَّ "
 وَقَدْ بَيَّنَّا سَبَبَ ذَلِكَ فِي غَيْرِ هَذَا الْمَوْضِعِ وَهُوَ أَنَّ فَضْلَ بَعْضِ الذِّكْرِ عَلَى بَعْضٍ هُوَ لِأَجْلِ مَا اُخْتُصَّ بِهِ الْفَاضِلُ لَا لِأَجْلِ إسْنَادِهِ.
وَالذِّكْرُ ثَلَاثَةُ أَنْوَاعٍ:
 أَفْضَلُهُ مَا كَانَ ثَنَاءً عَلَى اللَّهِ ثُمَّ مَا كَانَ إنْشَاءً مِنْ الْعَبْدِ أَوْ اعْتِرَافًا بِمَا يَجِبُ لِلَّهِ عَلَيْهِ ثُمَّ مَا كَانَ دُعَاءً مِنْ الْعَبْدِ.
translated_text:
the consensus of the Muslim community regarding recitation beyond al-Fātihah. It is also the view of the vast majority of the early generations, including the Companions and others, regarding both al-Fātihah and other passages. It is one of al-Shāfi‘ī’s two positions, adopted by a number of his most accomplished followers, such as al-Rāzī and Abū Muhammad ibn ‘Abd al-Salām. For reciting while the imam recites aloud is reprehensible and contrary to the Quran, the Sunnah, and the practice of the majority of the Companions. Nevertheless, some of Ahmad’s followers recommended that the worshipper praying behind the imam recite during the imam’s pauses. Some recommended reciting al-Fātihah even while the imam recites aloud; this was the position preferred by my grandfather. A number of scholars, including al-Awzā‘ī and others, likewise recommended this. Some also recommended that the imam pause after al-Fātihah so that those behind him could recite. Ahmad did not recommend this pause, since he did not recommend recitation while the imam recites aloud. A detailed discussion of this belongs elsewhere.

The point here is that the pause for the opening supplication is established by this authentic hadith. Nevertheless, the majority of scholars among the Companions and later generations recommend opening with a different supplication, and most recommend opening with the words:

“Glory be to You, O Allah.”

We have explained the reason for this elsewhere: the superiority of one form of remembrance over another rests on the distinctive merits of the superior form, not on its chain of transmission.

Remembrance is of three kinds: the best is praise of Allah; next come declarations made by the servant or acknowledgments of what he owes to Allah; then come supplications made by the servant.

The first kind includes the first half of al-Fātihah, as well as:

“Glory be to You, O Allah, and praise be to You. Blessed is Your name, exalted is Your majesty, and there is no god but You.”

It also includes glorifying Allah when bowing and prostrating.

The second kind includes his words:

“I have turned my face toward Him who created the heavens and the earth,”

and his words when bowing and prostrating:

“O Allah, to You I have bowed and to You I have prostrated,”

as in the hadith of ‘Alī narrated by Muslim.

The third kind includes his words:

“O Allah, put distance between me and my sins,”

and his supplications when bowing and prostrating. For this reason, a group of Ahmad’s followers deemed forms of praise obligatory, just as they deemed the opening supplication obligatory. Two positions on this have been reported from Ahmad, and Ibn Battah and others favoured the view that it is obligatory. A detailed discussion of this belongs elsewhere.

The point here is that occasionally using a less preferred form—such as the opening supplication narrated by Abū Hurayrah, or opening with “I have turned my face” or “Glory be to You, O Allah,” according to those who prefer the alternative—is better than consistently using one form and abandoning another. This is because the best guidance is the guidance of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. As established in an authentic hadith, he used to say in his Friday sermon:

“The best speech is the speech of Allah, and the best guidance is the guidance of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.”

He certainly did not invariably use a single opening supplication, for the hadith of Abū Hurayrah indicates that he used to begin with this one.

 كَانَ يُدَاوِمُ عَلَيْهِ فَكَانَتْ الْمُدَاوَمَةُ عَلَيْهِ أَفْضَلَ قُلْنَا: لَمْ يَقُلْ هَذَا أَحَدٌ مِنْ الْعُلَمَاءِ فِيمَا عَلِمْنَاهُ فَعُلِمَ أَنَّهُ لَمْ يَكُنْ يُدَاوِمُ عَلَيْهِ.

translated_text:
If it is said, “He used to recite it consistently, so consistently reciting it was preferable,” we reply: No scholar, to our knowledge, has said this. Thus we know that he did not recite it consistently.

Moreover, ‘Umar used to recite aloud:

“Glory be to You, O Allah, and praise be to You,”

to teach it to the people. Had the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, not said it in the obligatory prayer, ‘Umar would not have done this with the Muslims’ approval. Similarly, some of them would recite the words of seeking refuge with Allah aloud. It has likewise been said that a number of them recited the basmalah—the formula “In the name of Allah”—aloud to teach people to recite it, just as some recited the words of seeking refuge and the opening supplication aloud, and as Ibn ‘Abbās recited al-Fātihah aloud in the funeral prayer.

The correct view, therefore, is the one explicitly stated by Ahmad: it is recommended to recite these aloud occasionally. Thus, reciting the basmalah aloud on occasion is recommended. Some explicitly reported that Ahmad would recite it aloud when he prayed in Medina. Al-Qādī thought this was because the people of Medina were Shiites who recited it aloud and objected to anyone who did not. For by the time al-Qādī performed Hajj, Shiism had become prominent there, and the Egyptian ‘Ubaydids had gained control over the city and the people of Mecca. They had also prevented pilgrimage from Iraq for a time; al-Qādī himself travelled on pilgrimage from Syria.

The correct explanation, however, is that Ahmad did not instruct people to recite it aloud for that reason. Rather, the people of Medina in his time did not recite it either silently or aloud, in accordance with Mālik’s position. Ahmad therefore wanted it recited aloud, as some of the Companions had done, to teach the Sunnah and make clear that its recitation is recommended in general. Ahmad also recommended, in the case of someone leading people who do not recite the qunūt supplication

in witr and want their imam not to recite it, that he omit it to win their hearts. He thus recommended foregoing what is preferable in order to win their hearts, which accords with al-Qādī’s explanation. Accordingly, reciting the basmalah aloud is recommended when those praying behind the imam prefer this, in order to win their hearts. It is also recommended when doing so makes the Sunnah known, and they learn the Sunnah from him without objecting to his practice.

All of this comes under one comprehensive principle: a less preferable act may become preferable because of an overriding benefit. If something forbidden, such as eating carrion, may become obligatory because of an overriding benefit and the need to avert harm, then a less preferable act may all the more readily become preferable because of an overriding benefit.

The same applies to categories of worship, such as prayer. Prayer, as a category, is superior to Quran recitation and remembrance of Allah. Yet prayer is prohibited at certain times, so recitation, remembrance and supplication at those times are better than prayer. Likewise, supplication at the pilgrimage sites—‘Arafah, Muzdalifah, Minā, al-Safā and al-Marwah—is also better than recitation, as established by textual evidence and scholarly consensus. For the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“I have been forbidden to recite the Quran while bowing or prostrating.”

This appears in al-Sahīh in a hadith narrated by Ibn ‘Abbās. A hadith narrated by ‘Alī also states that the Prophet forbade him to do so. If someone nevertheless recites, does this invalidate his prayer? There are two opinions within Ahmad’s school. Thus, the prohibition of prayer and recitation at the blessed pilgrimage sites … (1).

فَإِنَّ الطَّهَارَةَ شَرْطٌ فِي الصَّلَاةِ وَلَا يُشْتَرَطُ لَهُ الطَّهَارَةُ وَلِكُلِّ مَكَانٍ عِبَادَةٌ تُشْرَعُ وَكَذَلِكَ تَرْكُ الصَّلَاةِ وَقْتَ النَّهْيِ مَشْرُوعٌ فِي كُلِّ زَمَانٍ. وَأَمَّا الطَّوَافُ فَهَلْ تُكْرَهُ فِيهِ الْقِرَاءَةُ؟ فِيهِ قَوْلَانِ مَشْهُورَانِ لِلْعُلَمَاءِ وَهُمَا رِوَايَتَانِ عَنْ أَحْمَد وَالرُّخْصَةُ مَذْهَبُ الشَّافِعِيِّ؛ بَلْ هُوَ يُسْتَحَبُّ فِيهِ الْقِرَاءَةُ وَلَا يُسْتَحَبُّ الْجَهْرُ بِهَا وَلِلْأُخْرَى مُصَنَّفٌ. وَإِذَا كَانَ هَذَا مِنْ أَجْنَاسِ الْعِبَادَاتِ الَّتِي ثَبَتَ فَضْلُ بَعْضِهَا عَلَى بَعْضٍ بِالنَّصِّ وَالْإِجْمَاعِ فَكَيْفَ فِي أَنْوَاعِ الذِّكْرِ لَا سِيَّمَا فِيمَا فِيهِ نِزَاعٌ فَالْأَصْلُ بِلَا رَيْبٍ هَدْيُ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ وَقَدْ ثَبَتَ أَنَّهُ كَانَ يَسْتَفْتِحُ بِهَذَا الِاسْتِفْتَاحِ الَّذِي فِي حَدِيثِ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ فَالْأَفْضَلُ أَنْ يَسْتَفْتِحَ بِهِ أَحْيَانًا وَيَسْتَفْتِحَ بِغَيْرِهِ أَحْيَانًا. وَأَيْضًا فَلِكُلِّ اسْتِفْتَاحٍ حَاجَةٌ لَيْسَتْ لِغَيْرِهِ فَيَأْخُذُ الْمُؤْمِنُ بِحَظِّهِ مِنْ كُلِّ ذِكْرٍ. وَأَيْضًا فَقَدْ يَحْتَاجُ الْإِنْسَانُ إلَى الْمَفْضُولِ وَلَا يَكْفِيهِ الْفَاضِلُ.
 كَمَا فِي:
 
{قُلْ هُوَ اللَّهُ أَحَدٌ}
 فَإِنَّهَا تَعْدِلُ ثُلُثَ الْقُرْآنِ؛ أَيْ يَحْصُلُ لِصَاحِبِهَا مِنْ الْأَجْرِ مَا يَعْدِلُ ثَوَابَ ثُلُثِ الْقُرْآنِ فِي الْقَدْرِ لَا فِي الصِّفَةِ فَإِنَّ مَا فِي الْقُرْآنِ مِنْ الْأَمْرِ وَالنَّهْيِ وَالْقَصَصِ وَالْوَعْدِ وَالْوَعِيدِ لَا يُغْنِي عَنْهُ
translated_text:
For ritual purity is a prerequisite for prayer, but not for that act. Each place has its prescribed form of worship. Likewise, refraining from prayer at the prohibited times is prescribed in every age. As for circumambulation, is Quran recitation during it disliked? Scholars hold two well-known views, both reported from Ahmad. Al-Shāfi‘ī’s position permits it; indeed, he recommends reciting during circumambulation, though not aloud. A treatise is devoted to the other view.

If this applies to categories of worship whose relative superiority is established by textual evidence and scholarly consensus, how much more does it apply to forms of remembrance, especially those concerning which there is disagreement? The standard is undoubtedly the guidance of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. It is established that he used the opening supplication reported in the hadith of Abū Hurayrah. It is therefore best to use this opening supplication sometimes and others at other times. Moreover, each opening supplication meets a need that another does not, so the believer should take his share of every form of remembrance. A person may also need the less preferable act, without the superior act being sufficient for him.

An example is:

“Say, ‘He is Allah, One.’”

This surah is equivalent to one-third of the Quran: that is, whoever recites it receives a reward equivalent to that of one-third of the Quran in amount, but not in kind. For the commands, prohibitions, narratives, promises and warnings contained in the Quran cannot be replaced by

 مَقْصُودِهِ فَلَا يُهْمَلُ مَا شَرَعَهُ مِنْ الْمُسْتَحَبَّاتِ.
 وَإِنْ قِيلَ إنَّ جِنْسَ غَيْرِهِ أَفْضَلُ فَهُوَ فِي زَمَانِهِ وَمَكَانِهِ أَفْضَلُ مِنْ غَيْرِهِ وَالصَّلَوَاتُ الَّتِي كَانَ يَدْعُو فِيهَا بِهَذَا الِاسْتِفْتَاحِ:
 كَانَ دُعَاؤُهُ فِيهَا بِهَذَا الِاسْتِفْتَاحِ أَفْضَلَ مِنْ غَيْرِهِ وَهُوَ دُعَاؤُهُ بِالطَّهَارَةِ وَالتَّنْقِيَةُ مِنْ الذُّنُوبِ التَّبْعِيدُ عَنْهَا مِنْ جِنْسِ الِاسْتِغْفَارِ فِي السَّحَرِ وَكَاسْتِغْفَارِهِ عَقِبَ الصَّلَاةِ وَقَدْ كَانَ يَدْعُو بِمِثْلِ هَذَا الدُّعَاءِ فِي آخِرِ قِيَامِ الِاعْتِدَالِ بَعْدَ التَّحْمِيدِ فَكَانَ يَفْتَتِحُ بِهِ الْقِيَامَ تَارَةً وَيَخْتِمُ بِهِ الْقِيَامَ أَيْضًا. وَقَدْ رُوِيَ عَنْهُ فِي الِاسْتِفْتَاحِ أَنْوَاعٌ وَعَامَّتُهَا فِي قِيَامِ اللَّيْلِ كَمَا ذَكَرَ ذَلِكَ أَحْمَد.
 وَيُسْتَحَبُّ لِلْمُصَلِّي بِاللَّيْلِ أَنْ يَسْتَفْتِحَ بِهَا كُلَّهَا وَهَذَا أَفْضَلُ مِنْ أَنْ يُدَاوِمَ عَلَى نَوْعٍ وَيَهْجُرَ غَيْرَهُ فَإِنَّ هَذَا هَدْيُ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ لَكِنْ يُقَالُ أَيْضًا:
 هَدْيُ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ هُوَ الْأَفْضَلُ وَمِنْ النَّاسِ مَنْ لَا يَصْلُحُ لَهُ الْأَفْضَلُ بَلْ يَكُونُ فِعْلُهُ لِلْمَفْضُولِ

translated_text:
“Say, ‘He is Allah, One.’” Nor is the reward for those passages of the same kind as the reward for this surah, even though the kind of reward for “Say, ‘He is Allah, One’” is superior. The less preferable may therefore be needed where the superior does not suffice, just as a person needs his leg where his eye cannot take its place. The same applies to created things: each has a wisdom for which it was created. So too with acts of worship. Everything prescribed by the Messenger has its wisdom and purpose and brings benefit [in fulfilling] (1) that purpose. Thus, none of the recommended acts he prescribed should be neglected.

Even if another category of worship is said to be superior, a particular act is superior to others at its proper time and place. In those prayers in which he used this opening supplication, his using it was better than using another. This supplication asks for purification, cleansing from sins, and distance from them. It is akin to seeking forgiveness before dawn and to his seeking forgiveness after prayer. He would also offer a similar supplication at the end of his standing upright after bowing, after praising Allah. Thus, he would sometimes begin his standing with it and would also conclude his standing with it. Various opening supplications have been reported from him, most of them in night prayer, as Ahmad mentioned.

It is recommended for someone praying at night to use all these opening supplications. This is better than consistently using one form and abandoning the others, for this was the guidance of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Yet it must also be said: the guidance of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is best, but for some people the best may not be suitable; rather, performing the less preferable act may be

أَنْفَعُ.
 كَمَنْ يَنْتَفِعُ بِالدُّعَاءِ دُونَ الذِّكْرِ أَوْ بِالذِّكْرِ دُونَ الْقِرَاءَةِ أَوْ بِالْقِرَاءَةِ دُونَ صَلَاةِ التَّطَوُّعِ فَالْعِبَادَةُ الَّتِي يَنْتَفِعُ بِهَا فَيَحْضُرُ لَهَا قَلْبُهُ وَيَرْغَبُ فِيهَا وَيُحِبُّهَا أَفْضَلُ مِنْ عِبَادَةٍ يَفْعَلُهَا مَعَ الْغَفْلَةِ وَعَدَمِ الرَّغْبَةِ كَالْغِذَاءِ الَّذِي يَشْتَهِيهِ الْإِنْسَانُ وَهُوَ جَائِعٌ:
 هُوَ أَنْفَعُ لَهُ مِنْ غِذَاءٍ لَا يَشْتَهِيهِ أَوْ يَأْكُلُهُ وَهُوَ غَيْرُ جَائِعٍ.
 فَكَذَلِكَ يُقَالُ هُنَا:
 قَدْ تَكُونُ مُدَاوَمَتُهُ عَلَى النَّوْعِ الْمَفْضُولِ أَنْفَعَ لِمَحَبَّتِهِ وَشُهُودِ قَلْبِهِ وَفَهْمِهِ ذَلِكَ الذِّكْرَ وَنَحْنُ إذَا قُلْنَا التَّنَوُّعُ فِي هَذِهِ الْأَذْكَارِ أَفْضَلُ فَهُوَ أَيْضًا تَفْضِيلٌ لِجِنْسِ التَّنَوُّعِ وَالْمَفْضُولُ قَدْ يَكُونُ أَنْفَعَ لِبَعْضِ النَّاسِ لِمُنَاسَبَتِهِ لَهُ كَمَا قَدْ يَكُونُ جِنْسُهُ فِي الشَّرْعِ أَفْضَلَ فِي بَعْضِ الْأَمْكِنَةِ وَالْأَزْمِنَةِ وَالْأَحْوَالِ فَالْمَفْضُولُ تَارَةً يَكُونُ أَفْضَلَ مُطْلَقًا فِي حَقِّ جَمِيعِ النَّاسِ كَمَا تَقَدَّمَ. وَقَدْ يَكُونُ أَفْضَلَ لِبَعْضِ النَّاسِ لِأَنَّ انْتِفَاعَهُ بِهِ أَتَمُّ وَهَذِهِ حَالُ أَكْثَرِ النَّاسِ قَدْ يَنْتَفِعُونَ بِالْمَفْضُولِ لِمُنَاسَبَتِهِ لِأَحْوَالِهِمْ النَّاقِصَةِ مَا لَا يَنْتَفِعُونَ بِالْفَاضِلِ الَّذِي لَا يَصِلُونَ إلَى أَنْ يَكُونُوا مِنْ أَهْلِهِ.
فَصْلٌ:
وَكَذَلِكَ 
" صَلَاةُ الْخَوْفِ "
 إذَا صَلَّى مَرَّةً عَلَى وَجْهٍ وَمَرَّةً عَلَى وَجْهٍ: كَأَنْ اتَّبَعَ مَنْ حَفِظَ وَجْهًا وَتَرَكَ آخَرَ وَقَدْ يَكُونُ عَلَى وَجْهٍ
translated_text:
more beneficial.

This is like someone who benefits from supplication rather than remembrance, or from remembrance rather than Quran recitation, or from recitation rather than voluntary prayer. Worship from which he benefits—with an attentive heart, eagerness, and love—is better than worship he performs heedlessly and without desire. Likewise, food that a person craves when hungry benefits him more than food he does not crave or eats when he is not hungry.

The same may be said here: consistently practising the less preferable form may benefit him more because he loves it, his heart is attentive, and he understands that remembrance. When we say that varying these forms of remembrance is better, we are likewise giving preference to variation as a general practice. What is less preferable may benefit some people more because it suits them, just as its category may be superior under Islamic law in certain places, times, and circumstances. Thus, what is generally less preferable may sometimes be superior without qualification for everyone, as explained earlier. It may also be superior for certain people because they benefit from it more fully. This is the condition of most people: because the less preferable practice suits their imperfect states, they may derive benefit from it that they do not derive from the superior practice, whose demands they are unable to meet.
