وَسُئِلَ:
هَلْ يَجُوزُ أَنْ يُصَلَّى عَلَى غَيْرِ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ بِأَنْ يُقَالَ:
 اللَّهُمَّ صَلِّ عَلَى فُلَانٍ؟ .
translated_text:
He was asked about the saying of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Whoever invokes blessings upon me once, Allah will bestow blessings upon him ten times. Whoever invokes blessings upon me ten times, Allah will bestow blessings upon him a hundred times. Whoever invokes blessings upon me a hundred times, Allah will bestow blessings upon him a thousand times. Whoever does not invoke blessings upon me will have regrets remaining in his heart, even if he enters Paradise.”

When a servant invokes blessings upon the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, does Allah bestow blessings upon that servant or not?

He answered:

All praise is due to Allah, Lord of all worlds. It is authentically reported in the Sahih from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, that he said:

“Whoever invokes blessings upon me once, Allah will bestow blessings upon him ten times.”

It is also reported from him in the Sunan collections that he said:

“No people gather in a sitting without remembering Allah or invoking blessings upon me therein, except that it will be a cause of sorrow for them on the Day of Resurrection.”

This sorrow means distress and regret. And Allah knows best.

He was asked:

Is it permissible to invoke blessings upon someone other than the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, by saying, “O Allah, bestow blessings upon so-and-so”?

He answered:

All praise is due to Allah.

The scholars have differed over whether someone other than the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, may invoke blessings upon another person independently of invoking blessings upon the Prophet. There are two views:

The first is that this is not permitted. This is the position transmitted from Mālik and al-Shāfi‘ī, and the view preferred by my grandfather, Abū al-Barakāt.

The second is that it is permissible. This is Ahmad’s explicitly stated position and the view preferred by most of his followers, including al-Qādī, Ibn ‘Aqīl, and Shaykh ‘Abd al-Qādir. They cited as evidence the report that ‘Alī said to ‘Umar, “May Allah bestow blessings upon you.”

Those holding the first view cited the statement of Ibn ‘Abbās: “I do not know of anyone upon whom it is fitting for someone to invoke blessings except the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.” Ibn ‘Abbās said this when the Shia emerged and began openly invoking blessings upon ‘Alī to the exclusion of others. This is objectionable and forbidden, as Ibn ‘Abbās stated.

As for what is reported from ‘Alī: if it does not involve exaggeration and this is made a distinctive practice for someone other than the Messenger, then it is a form of supplication, and nothing in the Quran or Sunnah prohibits it. Allah Most High says:

“It is He who bestows blessings upon you, as do His angels.”

The scholars do not disagree that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, may invoke blessings upon others, as in his words:

Shaykh al-Islām, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Section

The well-known, explicitly stated position of Imam Ahmad is that one should supplicate during prayer only with prescribed supplications transmitted in the reports. Al-Athram said:

I asked Ahmad, “What should I supplicate with after the tashahhud?”

He replied, “What has been transmitted in the reports.”

I said to him, “Did the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, not say, ‘Then let him choose whatever supplication he wishes’?”

He replied, “He should choose from what has been transmitted in the reports.”

I asked him again, and he said, “What is in the reports.”

This is the sense of Ahmad’s words.

I say: I have already explained part of the basis for this in light of His words:

“Indeed, He does not love the transgressors.”

translated_text:
contains no transgression. Transgression may lie either in excessive wording or in the meanings expressed, as [one] (1) of the Companions explained when he addressed his son after the latter said:

“O Allah, I ask You for the white palace on the right side of Paradise when I enter it.”

Another said:

“I ask You for Paradise, its palaces and its rivers, and I seek refuge in You from the Fire, its chains and its shackles.”

He said:

“My dear son, ask Allah for Paradise and seek refuge in Him from the Fire, for I heard the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, say: ‘There will be people in this community who transgress in supplication and purification.’”

Transgression may also occur in worship and asceticism.

Ahmad’s statement, “With what has been transmitted in the reports,” is sound. The definite article in “the supplication” refers to supplication that Allah loves, not supplication in general, for some supplications are forbidden.

If it is said, “Whatever supplication is permissible outside prayer is permissible during prayer, such as asking for a house and a beautiful slave girl,” the reply is: “Who says that such a supplication is prescribed outside prayer, or that such wording does not constitute transgression?”

It may then be said: Recommended supplication is supplication prescribed by revelation, for its recommended status can only be established by the Lawgiver. Whatever He has not prescribed cannot be recommended. Rather, one would thereby be instituting as religion something Allah has not authorized, for supplication is among the greatest aspects of religion.

However, if someone offers a supplication without knowing whether it is recommended, or knowing that it is permissible but not recommended, his prayer is not invalidated by that. Prayer is invalidated only by ordinary human speech, and supplication is not a form of ordinary human speech; rather, it is

translated_text:
like praising Allah with a form of praise not prescribed for one. Something of this kind occurred among some of the Companions during the Prophet’s lifetime, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. He did not rebuke the person for offering praise that had not been prescribed for him on that occasion; rather, he denied that he would receive any reward for it.

Some supplications are disliked without invalidating the prayer, while others invalidate it. Supplication thus falls into five categories:

The prescribed categories are the obligatory and the recommended. Permissible supplication is neither recommended nor does it invalidate the prayer. Disliked supplication is objectionable but does not invalidate it, just as turning aside during prayer does not invalidate it, nor does reciting the testimony of faith while standing or reciting the Quran while sitting. Prohibited supplication invalidates it because it constitutes ordinary speech.

This is the precise meaning of Ahmad’s position. He did not regard supplication not transmitted in the reports as invalidating the prayer, but neither did he recommend it, since what is not prescribed cannot be recommended. He explained that the freedom to choose concerns prescribed supplication. Such supplication may follow either the wording of the revealed text or its meaning, since the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not restrict supplication to a single wording, as he did Quranic recitation.

Thus, because the purpose of the funeral prayer is supplication, he did not prescribe a fixed formula for it. And because remembrance of Allah is superior, its wording was more closely regulated, as with the call to prayer, the talbiya (pilgrimage proclamation), and similar forms of remembrance.

As for my grandfather’s statement—may Allah have mercy on him—“except with what has been transmitted in the reports and what concerns his religious affairs,” this is open to question, for Ahmad mentioned only the reports; furthermore,

translated_text:
supplication for worldly benefits is permissible, since it is prescribed, whereas supplication concerning certain religious matters may constitute transgression, as has been related from the Companions, and as when someone asks for the stations of the prophets.

A better formulation would therefore be: “except with prescribed supplication established by the Sunnah,” meaning what has been transmitted in the reports and whatever conveys the same meaning, since, unlike the Quran, we are not required to worship using its exact wording.

We have prohibited reciting the Quran in translation because its wording is itself intended. The same applies to the declaration of Allah’s greatness and similar forms of remembrance. As for supplication, however, no fixed wording has been prescribed, although Ahmad disliked offering it in a language other than Arabic.

There are thus three levels: recitation, remembrance, and supplication using the transmitted wording; then using Arabic wording that conveys the same meaning; then using wording in another language. Ahmad disliked this last practice in prayer, and there is disagreement over whether it invalidates the prayer. It is a form of substitution.

The proponents of juristic reasoning permit translation into a non-Arabic language, despite their strict prohibition of ordinary speech during prayer—to the point that they disapproved of supplication not found in the Quran or in transmitted reports and held that it invalidated the prayer. Thus, they did not regard the use of Arabic as an act of worship in itself, and they permitted the declaration of Allah’s greatness using any wording that conveys magnification. They therefore allowed considerable latitude in substituting a non-Arabic rendering for the Quran and in replacing one form of remembrance with another, but did not allow comparable latitude in supplication. Ahmad and other leading scholars, however,

translated_text:
take the opposite approach: they allow greater latitude in supplication. This is the correct view, because the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Then let him choose whichever supplication he likes best.”

He prescribed no fixed wording for supplication in the funeral prayer, nor did he prescribe a particular supplication for his Companions as he prescribed forms of remembrance for them. How, then, can one restrict the supplication that the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, left unrestricted, while leaving unrestricted the remembrance whose wording he prescribed? Moreover, remembrance is superior to supplication, as we have established elsewhere. For this reason, knowledge-bearing forms of remembrance entail what al-thunā’iyya do not.

This is also why the finest words after the Quran are the enduring righteous words:

“Glory be to Allah; all praise is due to Allah; none has the right to be worshipped but Allah; and Allah is the Greatest.”

The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, instructed those unable to recite the Quran to say these words, and said:

“They are the finest words after the Quran.”

Likewise, the best opening invocation in prayer is the one that incorporates these meanings:

“Glory be to You, O Allah, and all praise is Yours. Blessed is Your name, exalted is Your majesty, and none has the right to be worshipped but You.”

The reasons for this have been explained elsewhere. We have mentioned that this is praise and is therefore superior to supplication. It is praise conveying the meaning of the finest words after the Quran, and this is conducive to having one’s supplication answered. This is illustrated by what al-Bukhārī narrated in his Sahīh from Abū Umāmah, who said: The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Whoever wakes during the night and says, ‘None has the right to be worshipped but Allah alone, without partner. His is the dominion, and all praise belongs to Him, and He has power over all things. All praise is due to Allah; glory be to Allah; Allah is the Greatest; and there is no power or strength except through Allah,’ and then supplicates, his supplication will be answered. If he performs ablution, his prayer will be accepted.”

He thus explained that when someone who wakes during the night begins speaking with these five phrases, this is a means of having his supplication answered and his prayer accepted if he subsequently performs ablution. Beginning the prayer in this manner, praising Allah and extolling Him before supplicating Him, is therefore a means of securing acceptance of the prayer and the supplications it contains.

This is why the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, instructed the man who prayed incorrectly to do this, saying:

“Say ‘Allah is the Greatest,’ then praise Allah and extol Him; then recite whatever you can readily recite of the Quran.”

Other hadiths concerning the opening of prayer also relate that he would say:

“Allah is truly the Greatest! Allah is truly the Greatest! Allah is truly the Greatest! Abundant praise is due to Allah! Abundant praise is due to Allah! Abundant praise is due to Allah!”

This conveys the same meaning. These words are also recommended between the additional takbīrs (declarations of Allah’s greatness) in the Eid prayer, as reported from Ibn Masʿūd. Those takbīrs are of the same kind as the takbīrs that open the prayer.

Another hadith concerning the opening of prayer relates that he would declare Allah’s greatness ten times, praise Him ten times, and glorify Him ten times—or words to that effect. Thus, the agreement of numerous hadiths with the meaning of this opening invocation is like the agreement of the meaning of the testimony recited in prayer as narrated by Abū

When a particular formula of remembrance conveys a meaning shared by most other formulas, it carries greater weight than one supported by only a single hadith. This indicates how frequently the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, intended to express those meanings; whatever he intended and chose more frequently takes precedence over what he chose less frequently.

This is further supported by the fact that these words are also prescribed after the obligatory prayers, as established in authentic hadiths. They therefore belong to the opening and concluding expressions granted to our Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, for he was granted opening expressions, comprehensive words, and concluding expressions. May Allah send blessings and abundant peace upon him and his family.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

Should supplication be offered after the obligatory prayers, after the Sunnah prayers, or after the tashahhud (testimony recited in prayer), within the prayer?

He replied:

The Sunnah that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, practised and instructed others to follow is to supplicate at the tashahhud, before the closing salutation. It is authentically established that he would say after the tashahhud:

“O Allah, I seek refuge in You from the punishment of Hell; I seek refuge in You from the punishment of the grave; I seek refuge in You from the trials of life and death; and I seek refuge in You from the trial of the False Messiah.”

translated_text:
And it is also authentically reported that he instructed people to offer this supplication after the tashahhud. Likewise, it is authentically reported that he would say after the tashahhud, before the closing salutation:

“O Allah, forgive my past and future sins, those I have concealed and those I have made known, and those You know better than I do. You are the One who brings forward and the One who holds back. There is no god but You.”

It is also authentically reported that Abū Bakr said, “O Messenger of Allah, teach me a supplication to offer during my prayer.”

He replied:

“Say: ‘O Allah, I have wronged myself a great deal, and none forgives sins but You. So grant me forgiveness from Yourself and have mercy on me. You are indeed the All-Forgiving, the Most Merciful.’”

Other authentic hadiths also report that he would supplicate after the tashahhud and before the closing salutation. He would supplicate while prostrating and, according to one narration, when he raised his head from bowing. He would also supplicate at the beginning of the prayer. No one, however, reported that he and those praying behind him would supplicate after the closing salutation. Rather, he would remember Allah by declaring that there is no god but Allah, praising Him, glorifying Him, and proclaiming His greatness, as related in the authentic hadiths. And Allah knows best.

He was asked about someone who said:

“It is not permissible to supplicate except by the ninety-nine names. One must not say, ‘O Most Compassionate, O Bestower of Favors,’ nor say, ‘O Guide of the bewildered.’”

Is he entitled to say that?

Praise be to Allah. Although a group of later scholars, such as Abū Muhammad ibn Hazm and others, held this view, the majority of scholars hold otherwise. This was also the position of the early generations of this community and its leading scholars. It is the correct view for several reasons.

First, no authentic hadith from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, specifies which names constitute the ninety-nine.

The best-known report concerning them is the hadith recorded by al-Tirmidhī, narrated by al-Walīd ibn Muslim from Shuayb, from Abū Hamzah. The leading hadith scholars say that this addition consists of names al-Walīd ibn Muslim compiled from his teachers among the hadith scholars. There is a second hadith concerning them, weaker than this one, narrated by Ibn Mājah. Other enumerations besides these two have also been transmitted, compiled by some of the early generations.

The person who restricted Allah’s names to ninety-nine was unable to derive them from the Quran. If there is no binding evidence specifying them, it cannot be said that these alone are the names by which one may supplicate, to the exclusion of all others. For there would be no way to distinguish those one is commanded to use from those one is forbidden to use. Any name whose status is unknown could be among those commanded or among those forbidden.

If it is said, “Supplicate only by a name mentioned in the Book and the Sunnah,” the answer is, “These number more than ninety-nine.”

“Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves.”

And Noah’s words:

“My Lord, I seek refuge in You from asking You for that of which I have no knowledge.”

And Abraham’s words:

“Our Lord, forgive me and my parents.”

And Moses’ words:

“My Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me.”

And the Messiah’s words:

“O Allah, our Lord, send down to us a table spread with food from heaven.”

There are many similar examples. Indeed, it is reported that Mālik and others disliked saying, “O my Master,” preferring instead, “O my Lord,” because this is how the prophets and others supplicated, as Allah has related in the Quran.

The same applies to the name “the Bestower.” In the hadith narrated by the compilers of the Sunan, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, heard a man supplicating:

“O Allah, I ask You by virtue of the fact that dominion belongs to You. You are Allah, the Bestower, the Originator of the heavens and the earth. O Possessor of Majesty and Honour, O Ever-Living, O Sustainer of all!”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“He has indeed called upon Allah by His Greatest Name, by which, when He is invoked, He answers, and when He is asked, He gives.”

This refutes the claim of those who allege that “the Bestower” cannot be among His names.

Imam Ahmad, may Allah be pleased with him, said to a man who was bidding him farewell: “Say: ‘O Guide of the bewildered, guide me to the path of the truthful and make me one of Your righteous servants.’”

A group of speculative theologians, such as al-Qādī Abū Bakr and Abū al-Wafā ibn Aqīl, denied that al-Dalīl (the Guide) was among His names, because they thought that dalīl

meant the evidence by which something is established. The correct view, however, is that of the majority, because dalīl originally denotes that which makes known what it points to. Even if dalīl meant something used as evidence, the servant also takes Him as evidence; thus He is a dalīl in both senses.

Moreover, it is authentically reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah is One and loves what is odd-numbered.”

Yet this name is not among these ninety-nine. It is also authentically reported that he said:

“Allah is Beautiful and loves beauty.”

This name is not among them either. Al-Tirmidhī and others report that he said:

“Allah is Clean and loves cleanliness.”

This name is likewise absent. It is also authentically reported that he said:

“Allah is Pure and accepts only what is pure.”

This name, too, is absent. Pursuing all such examples would take a long time.

Al-Khattābī and others said:

This indicates that He has names which He has kept to Himself. It also indicates that the statement:

“Allah has ninety-nine names; whoever enumerates them will enter Paradise”

means that among His names are ninety-nine which, if a person enumerates them, he will enter Paradise. This is like someone saying, “I have a thousand dirhams that I have set aside for charity,” even though his wealth exceeds that amount.

Allah says in the Quran:

“To Allah belong the Most Beautiful Names, so call upon Him by them.”

He thus commanded that He be called upon by His Most Beautiful Names without restriction. He did not say that His Most Beautiful Names number only ninety-nine. The meaning of the hadith is thus preserved, and Allah knows best.

translated_text:
He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked about a man who said:

“When a servant supplicates, he should not say, ‘O Allah, O Most Merciful.’”

He answered:

Praise be to Allah.

There is no disagreement among Muslims that when a servant supplicates to his Lord, he may say, “O Allah, O Most Merciful.” This is necessarily known to be part of the religion of Islam. As Allah Most High says:

“Say, ‘Call upon Allah or call upon the Most Merciful. Whichever you call upon, to Him belong the Most Beautiful Names.’”

The Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—used to say in his supplication:

“O Allah, O Most Merciful.”

The polytheists then said, “Muhammad forbids us to call upon two gods, yet he calls upon two gods!” So Allah Most High said:

“Say, ‘Call upon Allah or call upon the Most Merciful. Whichever you call upon, to Him belong the Most Beautiful Names.’”

That is, the One being called upon is one God, even though His names are many. As Allah Most High says:

“To Allah belong the Most Beautiful Names, so call upon Him by them, and leave those who deviate concerning His names.”

Whoever denies that one may say, “O Allah, O Most Merciful,” must be called upon to repent. If he repents, that suffices; otherwise, he is to be put to death. And Allah knows best.

“O Allah, I am Your servant and the son of Your servant; my forelock is in Your hand,”

and so forth. She regularly used this wording. She was told, “Say, ‘O Allah, I am Your female servant, the daughter of Your female servant,’” and so forth. Yet she insisted on continuing to use the original wording. Is she correct or not?

He answered:

Rather, she should say:

“O Allah, I am Your female servant, the daughter of Your male servant, the son of Your female servant.”

This is more appropriate and better, although her saying, “Your servant, the son of Your servant,” does have a grammatical justification in Arabic, as with the word zawj (spouse). And Allah knows best.

Rather, someone unaccustomed to grammatical correctness should not strain to achieve it when supplicating. One of the early generations said:

“When attention turns to grammar, humble devotion departs.”

Similarly, forcing rhymed prose into supplication is disliked, but there is nothing wrong with it when it occurs naturally. Supplication originates in the heart, and the tongue follows the heart. Whoever concentrates on correcting his speech while supplicating weakens his heart’s attentiveness. Thus, a person in distress supplicates from his heart with words he is inspired to utter that had not occurred to him before. This is something every believer experiences in his heart.

Supplication is permissible in Arabic and in other languages. Allah, glorified be He, knows the supplicant’s intention and meaning, even if his speech is not grammatically correct. He knows the clamour of voices in their different languages and with their varied needs.

الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ، نَعَمْ يُكْرَهُ هَذَا؛ لِأَنَّ هَذَا بِدْعَةً فَإِنَّ هَذَا
translated_text:
And according to the scholars of Kufa, two salutations are given in all these cases; al-Shāfiʿī agreed with them. The preferred position in the well-known report from Ahmad is that a full prayer comprising standing, bowing, and prostration is concluded with two salutations. As for a prayer consisting of a single physical pillar, such as the funeral prayer, the prostration of recitation, or the prostration of gratitude, the preferred view is that it is concluded with one salutation, as most transmitted reports indicate. Thus, multiple physical pillars are concluded with multiple salutations, and a single physical pillar with a single salutation. The Prophet’s prayer—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—was proportionate: when he lengthened it, he gave each part its share of that length, and when he shortened it, he kept its parts brief overall.

He was asked about a man who, when giving the salutation to his right, says, “Peace be upon you and the mercy of Allah. I ask You to grant me Paradise,” and to his left, “Peace be upon you. I ask You to save me from the Fire.” Is this disliked or not? If it is disliked, what is the evidence for disliking it?

He replied:

Praise be to Allah. Yes, this is disliked, because it is an innovation. For this

translated_text:
Chapter: Remembrance of Allah after Prayer

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked about the following reports:

‘Uqbah ibn ‘Āmir said: “The Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—commanded me to recite the surahs of refuge at the close of every prayer.”

Abū Umāmah said: “It was asked, ‘O Messenger of Allah, which supplication is most readily heard?’ He replied, ‘That offered in the latter part of the night and at the close of the obligatory prayers.’”

Mu‘ādh ibn Jabal reported that the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—took him by the hand and said: “O Mu‘ādh, by Allah, I love you. So never fail to say at the close of every prayer: ‘O Allah, help me to remember You, thank You, and worship You well.’”

Do these hadiths indicate that supplicating after completing the prayer is a Sunnah? Please give us a ruling and explain the matter fully; may you be rewarded.

He replied:

All praise belongs to Allah, Lord of all worlds. The well-known hadiths in the Sahīh, Sunan, and Musnad collections indicate that the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—used to supplicate at the close of his prayer, before completing it, and that he would instruct his Companions to do so and teach them how. No one has reported that, when the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—led the people in prayer, he and those praying behind him would supplicate together after completing the prayer—not at the dawn prayer, the afternoon prayer, or any other prayer. Rather, it is established that he would

face his Companions, remember Allah, and teach them to remember Allah immediately after completing the prayer. It is reported in the Sahīh:

“Before turning away, he would seek forgiveness three times and say: ‘O Allah, You are Peace, and from You comes peace. Blessed are You, Possessor of Majesty and Honor.’”

In the two Sahīh collections, al-Mughīrah ibn Shu‘bah reported that he used to say:

“There is no god worthy of worship except Allah alone, without partner. His is the dominion, and His is all praise, and He has power over all things. O Allah, none can withhold what You give, and none can give what You withhold, nor can the wealth of the wealthy avail them before You.”

It is also reported in the Sahīh, from Ibn al-Zubayr, that the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—used to proclaim Allah’s oneness with these words:

“There is no god worthy of worship except Allah alone, without partner. His is the dominion, and His is all praise, and He has power over all things. There is no might or power except through Allah. There is no god worthy of worship except Allah, and we worship none but Him. All blessings and bounty are His, and to Him belongs all excellent praise. There is no god worthy of worship except Allah, devoting all worship sincerely to Him, even though the disbelievers dislike it.”

It is reported in the Sahīh from Ibn ‘Abbās:

“People used to raise their voices in remembrance of Allah during the lifetime of the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace.”

Another wording states: “We used to know that his prayer had ended by the proclamation of Allah’s greatness.”

The forms of remembrance that the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—used to teach the Muslims to recite immediately after prayer are of several kinds:

translated_text:
The first:

“One says ‘Glory be to Allah’ thirty-three times, ‘Praise be to Allah’ thirty-three times, and ‘Allah is the Greatest’ thirty-three times. That makes ninety-nine, and one completes the hundred by saying: ‘There is no god worthy of worship except Allah alone, without partner. His is the dominion, and His is all praise, and He has power over all things.’”

Muslim narrated this in his Sahīh.

The second: One recites these formulas twenty-five times each, adding “There is no god worthy of worship except Allah.” Muslim also narrated this.

The third: One recites the three formulas thirty-three times. This has two forms: the first is to recite each formula thirty-three times; the second is to recite each formula eleven times. The count of thirty-three is mentioned in the hadith reported in both Sahīh collections.

The fifth: One says “Allah is the Greatest” thirty-four times to complete a hundred.

The sixth: One recites each of the three formulas ten times.

This, then, is the established practice of the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace. This is fitting, because the person praying is conversing privately with his Lord. It is therefore more fitting for him to supplicate to Him and ask of Him while conversing privately with Him than to ask of Him and supplicate to Him after turning away from Him.

As for remembrance after leaving the prayer, it is, as ‘Ā’ishah—may Allah be pleased with her—said, like wiping a mirror after polishing it. Prayer is light: it polishes the heart as a mirror is polished, and remembrance afterwards is like wiping that mirror. Allah Most High says:

“So when you have finished, exert yourself.”
“And direct your longing to your Lord.”

It has been said: When you have finished your worldly occupations, exert yourself in worship and direct your longing to your Lord. This is the better-known of the two interpretations.

Shurayh the judge went out to a group of weavers who were playing on an Eid day. He asked, “Why are you playing?”

They replied, “We have some free time.”

He said, “Is this what someone with free time has been commanded to do?” He then recited the words of Allah Most High:

“So when you have finished, exert yourself.”
“And direct your longing to your Lord.”

This accords with His words:

“O you wrapped in your garment!”
“Stand in prayer through the night, except for a little,”

up to His words:

“Indeed, rising at night brings greater harmony and more upright speech.”
“Indeed, during the day you have lengthy occupations.”

That is, you go about your affairs during the day, whereas at night you are free.

According to the sounder of the two interpretations, rising at night refers specifically to rising after sleep. The verb nasha’a is used when someone rises after sleeping. When a person rises after sleep, his heart is in greater harmony with his tongue, because nothing distracts his heart and sleep has dispelled the effects of the day’s activity. His speech is also more upright.

It has also been said that “So when you have finished” means finished praying; “exert yourself” means in supplication; and “direct your longing to your Lord.” Whether or not this interpretation is correct, it precludes supplication at the end of the prayer, especially since the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—is the one addressed by this command, and he must therefore carry out what Allah has commanded him to do.

{فَإِذَا فَرَغْتَ فَانْصَبْ}
 أَيْ فَرَغْت مِنْ الصَّلَاةِ قَوْلٌ ضَعِيفٌ فَإِنَّ قَوْلَهُ: إذَا فَرَغْت مُطْلَقٌ وَلِأَنَّ الْفَارِغَ إنْ أُرِيدَ بِهِ الْفَارِغُ مِنْ الْعِبَادَةِ فَالدُّعَاءُ أَيْضًا عِبَادَةٌ وَإِنْ أُرِيدَ بِهِ الْفَرَاغُ مِنْ
translated_text:
And his supplications during prayer, as transmitted in the authentic hadith collections and elsewhere, were made only before leaving the prayer. He told his Companions in an authentic hadith:

“When one of you has recited the tashahhud (testimony of faith), let him seek refuge in Allah from four things, saying: ‘O Allah, I seek refuge in You from the punishment of Hell, from the punishment of the grave, from the trials of life and death, and from the trial of the False Messiah.’”

In the authentic hadith of Ibn Masʿūd, after mentioning the tashahhud, he said:

“Then let him choose whatever supplication he likes best.”

ʿĀ’ishah and others also narrated his supplications during his night prayer, and that they were made before leaving the prayer.

Thus, the interpretation, “When you have finished praying, exert yourself in supplication,” resembles the statement in the hadith of Ibn Masʿūd, after the mention of the tashahhud:

“When you have done that, you have completed your prayer. If you wish to stand, then stand; and if you wish to remain seated, then remain seated.”

Whether this addition is among the words of the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—or among the words of someone who interpolated it into the hadith of Ibn Masʿūd, as the hadith authorities who discuss it maintain, it shows that whoever said this regarded that as the completion of the prayer. Likewise, this commentator regarded it as having finished the prayer.

Nevertheless, interpreting His words,

“So when you have finished, exert yourself,”

as meaning “when you have finished praying” is a weak interpretation. For His words “when you have finished” are unqualified. Moreover, if having finished means having finished worship, supplication is itself worship; whereas if what is meant is being free from

worldly occupations through prayer, that is not the case.

This is made clear by the fact that Muslims do not dispute that supplication is made during prayer, just as the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—used to supplicate during it. An authentic hadith establishes that he would say in his opening supplication:

“O Allah, distance me from my sins as You have distanced the east from the west. O Allah, cleanse me of my sins as a white garment is cleansed of dirt. O Allah, wash away my sins with water, snow and hail.”

He would also say:

“O Allah, You are the King; there is no god but You. You are my Lord, and I am Your servant. I have wronged myself and acknowledged my sin, so forgive all my sins, for none forgives sins but You. Guide me to the best character, for none guides to it but You, and turn bad character away from me, for none turns it away from me but You.”

An authentic hadith also establishes that he would supplicate when he raised his head from bowing. His supplications while bowing and prostrating are likewise established, whether in voluntary or obligatory prayer. Mass-transmitted reports establish that he supplicated at the end of the prayer. The two authentic hadith collections relate that Abū Bakr al-Siddīq—may Allah be pleased with him—said:

“O Messenger of Allah, teach me a supplication to say during my prayer.”

He replied:

“Say: ‘O Allah, I have greatly wronged myself, and none forgives sins but You. Grant me forgiveness from Yourself and have mercy on me. You are indeed the All-Forgiving, the Most Merciful.’”

Since supplication is prescribed during prayer, especially at its end, how, then, can he say:

“When you have finished prayer, exert yourself in supplication,” when what he has finished is of the same kind as what he is commanded to do? During prayer, he was already exerting himself in supplication, not free of it.

Furthermore, no Muslim has ever said that supplication after completing prayer is more emphatically prescribed or more powerful than supplication during it. Moreover, if His words meant, “Exert yourself in supplication,” there would have been no need for His words:

“And to your Lord alone direct your longing.”

For it is already known that supplication is to be directed to Allah alone.

It is thus clear that He commanded him to do two things: to strive in worship when free of his occupations, and to direct his longing to his Lord, not to anyone else. This is like His words:

“You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help.”

His words, “You alone we worship,” correspond to His words, “Exert yourself.” And His words, “You alone we ask for help,” correspond to His words, “And to your Lord alone direct your longing.” Similar are His words:

“So worship Him and put your trust in Him.”

And His words:

“He is my Lord; there is no god but Him. In Him I put my trust, and to Him is my return.”

And the words of Shuʿayb—peace be upon him:

“In Him I put my trust, and to Him I turn.”

Another example is the supplication reported for entering the mosque:

“O Allah, make me among the most honoured of those who turn to You, the nearest of those who draw near to You, and the best of those who ask of You and direct their longing to You.”

And the other report:

“To You we direct our longing and our deeds.”

This is because calling upon Allah, as mentioned in the Quran, takes two forms: invocation through worship, and invocation through petition and longing. Thus His words, “Exert yourself,” and “And to your Lord alone direct your longing,” encompass both forms of calling upon Allah. Allah Most High says:

“When the servant of Allah stood up calling upon Him, they almost crowded around him in throngs.”

And Allah Most High says:

“Whoever invokes another god besides Allah, for which he has no proof, his reckoning rests only with his Lord”—to the end of the verse.

There are many similar passages.

" دُبُرَ الصَّلَاةِ "

 وَالنَّاسُ لَهُمْ فِي هَذِهِ فِيمَا بَعْدَ السَّلَامِ ثَلَاثَةُ أَحْوَالٍ:
 مِنْهُمْ مَنْ لَا يَرَى قُعُودَ الْإِمَامِ مُسْتَقْبِلَ الْمَأْمُومِ لَا بِذِكْرِ وَلَا دُعَاءٍ وَلَا غَيْرِ ذَلِكَ وَحُجَّتُهُمْ مَا يُرْوَى عَنْ السَّلَفِ أَنَّهُمْ كَانُوا يَكْرَهُونَ لِلْإِمَامِ أَنْ يَسْتَدِيمَ اسْتِقْبَالَ الْقِبْلَةِ بَعْدَ السَّلَامِ فَظَنُّوا أَنَّ ذَلِكَ يُوجِبُ قِيَامَهُ مِنْ مَكَانِهِ وَلَمْ يَعْلَمُوا أَنَّ انْصِرَافَهُ مُسْتَقْبِلَ الْمَأْمُومِينَ بِوَجْهِهِ كَمَا كَانَ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ يَفْعَلُ يُحَصِّلُ هَذَا الْمَقْصُودَ
translated_text:
As for the expression dubur al-salāh (“the end of prayer”), it may mean either its final part or what immediately follows its final part. A person’s rear, for example, is the hindmost part of the body. The word ʿaqib is similar: it may mean the hindmost part of something, such as a person’s heel, or what immediately follows it.

Thus, supplication described as being “at the end of prayer” may mean supplication during its final part, in agreement with the other hadiths. Alternatively, it may mean what follows its final part, namely, the period after the tashahhud (testimony of faith). This has likewise been called the completion of prayer and finishing it, since nothing remains except the salām (closing salutation), which is incompatible with prayer: deliberately uttering it during prayer invalidates the prayer, whereas the other prescribed remembrances do not invalidate it. Or the expression may be unrestricted or ambiguous. In any event, it cannot be restricted to the period after the salām, because the supplications generally transmitted were offered before that. Nor is it permissible to institute a sunnah on the basis of ambiguous wording that contradicts the mass-transmitted Sunnah conveyed in explicit terms.

People take three positions on this matter concerning the period after the salām:

Some do not approve of the imam remaining seated facing the congregation, whether for remembrance of Allah, supplication, or anything else. Their evidence is the report that the early Muslims disliked the imam continuing to face the direction of prayer after the salām. They assumed that this required him to rise from his place, not realizing that his turning to face the congregation—as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to do—achieves this purpose.

وَهَذَا يَفْعَلُهُ مَنْ يَفْعَلُهُ مِنْ أَصْحَابِ مَالِكٍ. وَمِنْهُمْ مَنْ يَرَى دُعَاءَ الْإِمَامِ وَالْمَأْمُومِ بَعْدَ السَّلَامِ ثُمَّ مِنْهُمْ مَنْ يَرَى ذَلِكَ فِي الصَّلَوَاتِ الْخَمْسِ وَمِنْهُمْ مَنْ يَرَاهُ فِي صَلَاةِ الْفَجْرِ وَالْعَصْرِ كَمَا ذَكَرَ ذَلِكَ مَنْ ذَكَرَهُ مِنْ أَصْحَابِ الشَّافِعِيِّ وَأَحْمَد وَغَيْرِهِمْ وَلَيْسَ مَعَ هَؤُلَاءِ بِذَلِكَ سُنَّةٌ وَإِنَّمَا غَايَتُهُمْ التَّمَسُّكُ بِلَفْظِ مُجْمَلٍ أَوْ بِقِيَاسِ كَقَوْلِ بَعْضِهِمْ مَا بَعْدَ الْفَجْرِ وَالْعَصْرِ لَيْسَ بِوَقْتِ صَلَاةٍ فَيُسْتَحَبُّ فِيهِ الدُّعَاءُ وَمِنْ الْمَعْلُومِ أَنَّ مَا تَقَدَّمَتْ بِهِ سُنَّةُ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ الثَّابِتَةُ الصَّحِيحَةُ بَلْ الْمُتَوَاتِرَةُ لَا يُحْتَاجُ فِيهِ إلَى مُجْمَلٍ وَلَا إلَى قِيَاسٍ.

 وَكَذَلِكَ قَوْلُهُ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ لِمُعَاذِ بْنِ جَبَلٍ:
translated_text:
And this is the practice of some of Mālik’s followers. Others approve of supplication by the imam and those praying behind him after the salām. Some approve of this after all five prayers, while others approve of it after Fajr and ‘Asr, as some followers of al-Shāfi‘ī, Ahmad, and others have mentioned. Yet they have no Sunnah supporting this. At most, they rely on ambiguous wording or analogy, as when some say that the periods after Fajr and ‘Asr are not times for prayer, so supplication is recommended then. It is well known that where the Messenger of Allah’s established, authentic—indeed, mass-transmitted—Sunnah has already provided guidance, there is no need for ambiguous wording or analogy.

As for the statement of ‘Uqbah ibn ‘Āmir:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, commanded me to recite the surahs of refuge at the end of every prayer,”

this refers to after completing the prayer. As for the report of Abū Umāmah:

“It was asked, ‘O Messenger of Allah, which supplication is most readily heard?’ He replied, ‘In the latter part of the night and at the end of the obligatory prayers,’”

this must not be restricted to the period after the salām; rather, it must include the period before the salām.

Even if it is said that it encompasses both before and after the salām, this does not entail that the imam and those praying behind him supplicating together after the salām is a Sunnah, just as it does not entail the same before the salām. Rather, if each person supplicates individually after the salām, this does not conflict with the Sunnah.

Likewise, his words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, to Mu‘ādh ibn Jabal:

“Never fail to say at the end of every prayer: ‘O Allah, help me to remember You, thank You, and worship You well,’”

apply to the period before the salām. They also apply to the period after it, as explained above. Mu‘ādh used to lead his people in prayer, just as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, led the prayer; and the Prophet had sent him to Yemen to teach its people. If this supplication had been prescribed for the imam and those praying behind him collectively, as with the qunūt supplication, he would have said: “O Allah, help us to remember You and thank You.” Since he taught it in the singular, it is clear that it is not prescribed for the imam and those praying behind him to offer it in the plural.

This is further clarified by the report in the Sahīh from al-Barā’ ibn ‘Āzib, who said:

“When we prayed behind the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, we preferred to be on his right, so that he would turn to face us.” He said: “I heard him say: ‘My Lord, protect me from Your punishment on the Day You resurrect Your servants—or on the Day You gather Your servants.’”

This shows that he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, supplicated in the singular, as in the hadith of Mu‘ādh, although both were prayer leaders. It also shows that he would turn to face those praying behind him and that he did not supplicate in the plural.

Some compilers of works on legal rulings have included the hadith of Mu‘ādh among the supplications offered within the prayer before the salām, in keeping with the other hadiths. For example, Muslim and the three Sunan collections report from Abū Hurayrah that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“When any of you has finished the final tashahhud, let him seek refuge with Allah from four things: the punishment of Hell, the punishment of the grave, the trials of life and death, and the trial of the False Messiah.”

“O Allah, I seek refuge in You from the punishment of Hell; I seek refuge in You from the punishment of the grave; I seek refuge in You from the trials of life and death; and I seek refuge in You from the trial of the False Messiah.”

The Sunan collections also relate that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, asked a man: “What do you say during the prayer?”

He replied: “I recite the tashahhud, then say: ‘O Allah, I ask You for Paradise and seek refuge in You from the Fire.’ By Allah, I cannot manage your murmured supplications, nor those of Mu‘ādh.”

He, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, replied: “Our murmured supplications revolve around those two.”

This was reported by Abū Dāwūd and by Abū Hātim in his Sahīh. The apparent meaning is that their murmured supplications, too, came after the tashahhud within the prayer, corresponding to what the man described.

Shaddād ibn Aws reported that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to say during his prayer:

“O Allah, I ask You for steadfastness in religion and firm resolve to follow right guidance. I ask You to enable me to thank You for Your blessings and worship You well. A Jewish woman visited her, mentioned the punishment of the grave, and said to her, “May Allah protect you from the punishment of the grave.” ‘Ā’ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, then asked the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, about the punishment of the grave. “Yes, the punishment of the grave is real.”

‘Ā’ishah said: “After that, I never saw the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, offer a prayer without seeking refuge from the punishment of the grave.”

The hadiths on this subject agree with one another and clarify what has preceded. And Allah knows best.

translated_text:
He was asked:

“Regarding a group of people who glorify Allah, praise Him, and proclaim His greatness: is this sunnah or disliked? Sometimes someone in the group causes hardship by prolonging it unnecessarily.”

He replied:

Glorifying Allah and proclaiming His greatness after prayer is recommended, not obligatory. Anyone who wishes to get up before doing so may do so and should not be reproached. Nor should someone who wishes to perform this recommended act abandon it. However, a person praying behind the imam should not get up until the imam turns away—that is, turns away from the direction of prayer. After the salutation, the imam should remain seated facing the direction of prayer only long enough to seek forgiveness three times and say:

“O Allah, You are Peace, and from You comes peace. Blessed are You, Possessor of majesty and honour.”

Once the imam has turned away, whoever wishes to get up may do so, and whoever wishes to remain seated remembering Allah may do so.

translated_text:
Shaykh al-Islām Ahmad ibn Taymiyyah—may Allah have mercy on him—said:

Section

Counting glorifications of Allah on one’s fingers is sunnah, as the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said to the women:

“Glorify Allah and keep count on your fingers, for they will be questioned and made to speak.”

As for counting them with fruit pits, pebbles, and similar things, this is good. Some of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, used to do so. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, saw the Mother of the Believers counting her glorifications with pebbles and approved of her doing so. It is also reported that Abū Hurayrah used to do this.

As for counting glorifications with beads and similar objects threaded on a string, some people considered it disliked, while others did not. If the intention behind it is good, it is good and not disliked. However, keeping such beads without any need, or displaying them to people—for example, hanging them around one’s neck, wearing them like a bracelet on one’s wrist, or something similar—is either showing off before people or something that invites showing off and resemblance to those who show off, without any need. The first is forbidden, and the second is, at the very least, disliked. For showing off before people in specifically devotional acts, such as prayer, fasting, remembrance of Allah, and recitation of the Quran, is among the gravest sins. Allah says:

the Most High:

“So woe to those who pray,”
“Who are heedless of their prayer,”
“Who show off,”
“And withhold even simple assistance.”

And He, the Most High, says:

“The hypocrites seek to deceive Allah, but He is deceiving them. When they stand for prayer, they stand lazily, showing off before people and remembering Allah only a little.”

As for someone who shows off in obligatory acts of worship, everyone knows how blameworthy his condition is and that Allah will punish him for not worshipping Him with sincere devotion. Allah, the Most High, says:

“They were commanded only to worship Allah with sincere devotion to Him, turning away from falsehood, to establish prayer and to give zakah. That is the upright religion.”

And He, the Most High, says:

“Indeed, We have sent down the Book to you in truth, so worship Allah with sincere devotion to Him. Surely, sincere devotion belongs to Allah alone.”

Such statements occur frequently in the Quran.

As for someone who shows off in voluntary prayers, fasting, remembrance of Allah and recitation of the Quran, no one should suppose that the consequence is merely the nullification of his deeds, leaving him with neither reward nor blame. Rather, he deserves censure and punishment for seeking renown through worship of other than Allah. These are specifically devotional acts: they are valid only when performed by a Muslim, and they may not be performed for any purpose other than drawing near to Allah. This differs from activities that benefit people, such as teaching and leading prayer; scholars disagree over the permissibility of hiring someone to perform these. And Allah knows best.

He was also asked:

Is reciting the Verse of the Throne after every prayer in congregation recommended or not? What was the practice of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, concerning prayer, and what is meant by his words, “after every prayer”?

He answered:

Praise be to Allah. A hadith has been reported concerning reciting the Verse of the Throne after prayer, but it is weak. For this reason, none of the compilers of the authoritative collections reported it, and no ruling of Islamic law can be established on its basis.

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, his Companions and his successors did not recite the Verse of the Throne, or any other passage of the Quran, aloud after prayer. For the imam and those praying behind him to recite it aloud and maintain this practice is undoubtedly a blameworthy innovation. This amounts to instituting a new ritual observance. It is comparable to someone introducing the regular practice of the imam and congregation reciting aloud al-Fātihah, the closing verses of al-Baqarah, the opening verses of al-Hadīd or the closing verses of al-Hashr. It is also comparable to the imam and congregation regularly gathering to perform two units of prayer after the obligatory prayer, and similar practices that are undoubtedly innovations.

وَالِابْتِدَاعِ فَالْأَدْعِيَةُ وَالْأَذْكَارُ النَّبَوِيَّةُ هِيَ أَفْضَلُ مَا يَتَحَرَّاهُ الْمُتَحَرِّي مِنْ الذِّكْرِ وَالدُّعَاءِ وَسَالِكُهَا عَلَى سَبِيلِ أَمَانٍ وَسَلَامَةٍ وَالْفَوَائِدُ وَالنَّتَائِجُ الَّتِي تَحْصُلُ لَا يُعَبِّرُ عَنْهُ لِسَانٌ وَلَا يُحِيطُ بِهِ إنْسَانٌ وَمَا سِوَاهَا مِنْ الْأَذْكَارِ قَدْ يَكُونُ مُحَرَّمًا وَقَدْ يَكُونُ مَكْرُوهًا وَقَدْ يَكُونُ فِيهِ شِرْكٌ مِمَّا لَا يَهْتَدِي إلَيْهِ أَكْثَرُ النَّاسِ وَهِيَ جُمْلَةٌ يَطُولُ تَفْصِيلُهَا. وَلَيْسَ لِأَحَدِ أَنْ يَسُنَّ لِلنَّاسِ نَوْعًا مِنْ الْأَذْكَارِ وَالْأَدْعِيَةِ غَيْرِ الْمَسْنُونِ وَيَجْعَلَهَا عِبَادَةً رَاتِبَةً يُوَاظِبُ النَّاسُ عَلَيْهَا كَمَا يُوَاظِبُونَ عَلَى الصَّلَوَاتِ الْخَمْسِ؛ بَلْ هَذَا ابْتِدَاعُ دِينٍ لَمْ يَأْذَنْ اللَّهُ بِهِ؛ بِخِلَافِ مَا يَدْعُو بِهِ الْمَرْءُ أَحْيَانًا مِنْ غَيْرِ أَنْ يَجْعَلَهُ لِلنَّاسِ سُنَّةً فَهَذَا إذَا لَمْ يُعْلَمْ أَنَّهُ يَتَضَمَّنُ مَعْنًى مُحَرَّمًا لَمْ يَجُزْ الْجَزْمُ بِتَحْرِيمِهِ؛ لَكِنْ قَدْ يَكُونُ فِيهِ ذَلِكَ وَالْإِنْسَانُ لَا يَشْعُرُ بِهِ. وَهَذَا كَمَا أَنَّ الْإِنْسَانَ عِنْدَ الضَّرُورَةِ يَدْعُو بِأَدْعِيَةِ تُفْتَحُ عَلَيْهِ ذَلِكَ الْوَقْتَ فَهَذَا وَأَمْثَالُهُ قَرِيبٌ.
 وَأَمَّا اتِّخَاذُ وِرْدٍ غَيْرِ شَرْعِيٍّ وَاسْتِنَانُ ذِكْرٍ غَيْرِ شَرْعِيٍّ:
 فَهَذَا مِمَّا يُنْهَى عَنْهُ وَمَعَ هَذَا فَفِي الْأَدْعِيَةِ الشَّرْعِيَّةِ وَالْأَذْكَارِ الشَّرْعِيَّةِ غَايَةُ الْمَطَالِبِ الصَّحِيحَةِ وَنِهَايَةُ الْمَقَاصِدِ الْعَلِيَّةِ وَلَا يَعْدِلُ عَنْهَا إلَى غَيْرِهَا مِنْ الْأَذْكَارِ الْمُحْدَثَةِ الْمُبْتَدَعَةِ إلَّا جَاهِلٌ أَوْ مُفَرِّطٌ أَوْ مُتَعَدٍّ.
translated_text:
and innovation. The prophetic supplications and forms of remembrance are the best that anyone seeking to remember Allah and supplicate to Him can pursue. Whoever follows them travels a safe and secure path. No tongue can express, nor any person fully comprehend, the benefits and results they yield. Other forms of remembrance may be forbidden or disliked, and may contain associations of partners with Allah that most people fail to recognize. These are matters whose detailed explanation would be lengthy.

No one may institute for people a form of remembrance or supplication not prescribed in the Sunnah and make it a regular act of worship that they observe as consistently as the five daily prayers. Rather, this is inventing a religion for which Allah has given no permission. This differs from supplications that a person offers occasionally without establishing them as a customary practice for others. If such a supplication is not known to contain a forbidden meaning, it may not be categorically declared forbidden. Nevertheless, it may contain such a meaning without the person realizing it. Similarly, in times of urgent need, a person may offer supplications that he is inspired to utter at that moment. Such cases are relatively straightforward.

As for adopting an unprescribed regular litany and establishing an unprescribed form of remembrance as a customary practice, these are practices that are prohibited. Moreover, prescribed supplications and forms of remembrance encompass the fullest realization of sound aspirations and the loftiest aims. No one turns away from them to newly introduced, innovated forms of remembrance except someone who is ignorant, negligent, or transgressing the bounds.

وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ -:
عَنْ الدُّعَاءِ عَقِيبَ الصَّلَاةِ هَلْ هُوَ سُنَّةٌ أَمْ لَا؟ وَمَنْ أَنْكَرَ عَلَى إمَامٍ لَمْ يَدْعُ عَقِيبَ صَلَاةِ الْعَصْرِ هَلْ هُوَ مُصِيبٌ أَمْ مُخْطِئٌ؟
فَأَجَابَ:
الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ، لَمْ يَكُنْ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ يَدْعُو هُوَ وَالْمَأْمُومُونَ عَقِيبَ الصَّلَوَاتِ الْخَمْسِ كَمَا يَفْعَلُهُ بَعْضُ النَّاسِ عَقِيبَ الْفَجْرِ وَالْعَصْرِ؛ وَلَا نُقِلَ ذَلِكَ عَنْ أَحَدٍ وَلَا اسْتَحَبَّ ذَلِكَ أَحَدٌ مِنْ الْأَئِمَّةِ. وَمَنْ نَقَلَ عَنْ الشَّافِعِيِّ أَنَّهُ اسْتَحَبَّ ذَلِكَ فَقَدْ غَلِطَ عَلَيْهِ وَلَفْظُهُ الْمَوْجُودُ فِي كُتُبِهِ يُنَافِي ذَلِكَ وَكَذَلِكَ أَحْمَد وَغَيْرُهُ مِنْ الْأَئِمَّةِ لَمْ يَسْتَحِبُّوا ذَلِكَ. وَلَكِنَّ طَائِفَةً مِنْ أَصْحَابِ أَحْمَد وَأَبِي حَنِيفَةَ وَغَيْرِهِمَا اسْتَحَبُّوا الدُّعَاءَ بَعْدَ الْفَجْرِ وَالْعَصْرِ.
 قَالُوا:
 لِأَنَّ هَاتَيْنِ الصَّلَاتَيْنِ لَا صَلَاةَ بَعْدَهُمَا فَتُعَوَّضُ بِالدُّعَاءِ عَنْ الصَّلَاةِ. وَاسْتَحَبَّ طَائِفَةٌ أُخْرَى مِنْ أَصْحَابِ الشَّافِعِيِّ وَغَيْرِهِ الدُّعَاءَ عَقِيبَ الصَّلَوَاتِ الْخَمْسِ وَكُلُّهُمْ مُتَّفِقُونَ عَلَى أَنَّ مَنْ تَرَكَ الدُّعَاءَ لَمْ يُنْكَرْ عَلَيْهِ
translated_text:
He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

“Is supplication immediately after prayer a Sunnah practice or not? Is someone who censures an imam for not supplicating after the ‘Asr prayer right or wrong?”

He replied:

Praise be to Allah. It was not the practice of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, to supplicate together with those praying behind him after the five daily prayers, as some people do after Fajr and ‘Asr. Nor has this been transmitted from anyone, and none of the imams considered it recommended. Whoever reports that al-Shāfi‘ī considered it recommended has misrepresented him: the wording found in his books contradicts that. Likewise, Ahmad and the other imams did not consider it recommended. However, a group of followers of Ahmad, Abū Hanīfah, and others considered supplication after Fajr and ‘Asr recommended.

They argued: “Because these two prayers are not followed by any prayer, supplication serves as a substitute for prayer.”

Another group of followers of al-Shāfi‘ī and others considered supplication after the five daily prayers recommended. All of them agree that anyone who refrains from supplication should not be censured.

original_text: وَمَنْ أَنْكَرَ عَلَيْهِ فَهُوَ مُخْطِئٌ بِاتِّفَاقِ الْعُلَمَاءِ فَإِنَّ هَذَا لَيْسَ مَأْمُورًا بِهِ لَا أَمْرَ إيجَابٍ وَلَا أَمْرَ اسْتِحْبَابٍ فِي هَذَا الْمَوْطِنِ وَالْمُنْكِرُ عَلَى التَّارِكِ أَحَقُّ بِالْإِنْكَارِ مِنْهُ؛ بَلْ الْفَاعِلُ أَحَقُّ بِالْإِنْكَارِ فَإِنَّ الْمُدَاوَمَةَ عَلَى مَا لَمْ يَكُنْ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ يُدَاوِمُ عَلَيْهِ فِي الصَّلَوَاتِ الْخَمْسِ لَيْسَ مَشْرُوعًا؛ بَلْ مَكْرُوهٌ كَمَا لَوْ دَاوَمَ عَلَى الدُّعَاءِ قَبْلَ الدُّخُولِ فِي الصَّلَوَاتِ أَوْ دَاوَمَ عَلَى الْقُنُوتِ فِي الرَّكْعَةِ الْأُولَى أَوْ فِي الصَّلَوَاتِ الْخَمْسِ أَوْ دَاوَمَ عَلَى الْجَهْرِ بِالِاسْتِفْتَاحِ فِي كُلِّ صَلَاةٍ وَنَحْوِ ذَلِكَ. فَإِنَّهُ مَكْرُوهٌ وَإِنْ كَانَ الْقُنُوتُ فِي الصَّلَوَاتِ الْخَمْسِ قَدْ فَعَلَهُ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ أَحْيَانًا وَقَدْ كَانَ عُمَرُ يَجْهَرُ بِالِاسْتِفْتَاحِ أَحْيَانًا وَجَهَرَ رَجُلٌ خَلْفَ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ بِنَحْوِ ذَلِكَ فَأَقَرَّهُ عَلَيْهِ فَلَيْسَ كُلُّ مَا يُشْرَع فِعْلُهُ أَحْيَانًا تُشْرَعُ الْمُدَاوِمَةُ عَلَيْهِ. وَلَوْ دَعَا الْإِمَامُ وَالْمَأْمُومُ أَحْيَانًا عَقِيبَ الصَّلَاةِ لِأَمْرِ عَارِضٍ لَمْ يُعَدَّ هَذَا مُخَالِفًا لِلسُّنَّةِ كَاَلَّذِي يُدَاوِمُ عَلَى ذَلِكَ وَالْأَحَادِيثُ الصَّحِيحَةُ تَدُلُّ عَلَى أَنَّ النَّبِيَّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ كَانَ يَدْعُو دُبُرَ الصَّلَاةِ قَبْلَ السَّلَامِ وَيَأْمُرُ بِذَلِكَ. كَمَا قَدْ بَسَطْنَا الْكَلَامَ عَلَى ذَلِكَ وَذَكَرْنَا مَا فِي ذَلِكَ مِنْ الْأَحَادِيثِ وَمَا يُظَنُّ أَنَّ فِيهِ حُجَّةً لِلْمُنَازِعِ فِي غَيْرِ هَذَا الْمَوْضِعِ؛ وَذَلِكَ لِأَنَّ الْمُصَلِّيَ يُنَاجِي رَبَّهُ فَإِذَا سَلَّمَ انْصَرَفَ عَنْ مُنَاجَاتِهِ. وَمَعْلُومٌ أَنَّ سُؤَالَ السَّائِلِ لِرَبِّهِ حَالَ مُنَاجَاتِهِ هُوَ الَّذِي يُنَاسِبُ دُونَ سُؤَالِهِ
translated_text:
and anyone who censures him is mistaken, according to the consensus of the scholars. Such supplication is not enjoined in this situation, whether as an obligation or as a recommendation. The person who censures someone for refraining from it is more deserving of censure than the one who refrains; indeed, the person who practises it is more deserving of censure. Regularly observing a practice in connection with the five daily prayers which the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not regularly observe is not prescribed; rather, it is disliked. This is like regularly supplicating before beginning the prayers, regularly reciting qunūt (the standing supplication) in the first unit of prayer or in all five daily prayers, or regularly reciting the opening supplication aloud in every prayer, and similar practices.

Such regular observance is disliked, even though the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, sometimes recited qunūt in the five daily prayers. ‘Umar would also sometimes recite the opening supplication aloud, and a man praying behind the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, recited something similar aloud, and he approved of it. Not everything that is prescribed on occasion is prescribed as a regular practice.

If the imam and the person praying behind him occasionally supplicate after the prayer because of some circumstance that arises, this would not be considered contrary to the Sunnah, unlike making it a regular practice. The authentic hadiths indicate that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to supplicate at the end of the prayer, before the concluding salutation, and instructed others to do so. We have discussed this at length elsewhere, mentioning the relevant hadiths as well as those thought to provide evidence for the opposing view.

This is because the person praying is conversing intimately with his Lord; once he gives the concluding salutation, he turns away from that intimate conversation. It is well known that the fitting time for a supplicant to ask his Lord is while conversing intimately with Him, rather than asking Him

بَعْدَ انْصِرَافِهِ كَمَا أَنَّ مَنْ كَانَ يُخَاطِبُ مَلِكًا أَوْ غَيْرَهُ فَإِنَّ سُؤَالَهُ وَهُوَ مُقْبِلٌ عَلَى مُخَاطَبَتِهِ أَوْلَى مِنْ سُؤَالِهِ لَهُ بَعْدَ انْصِرَافِهِ.
وَسُئِلَ:
عَنْ هَذَا الَّذِي يَفْعَلُهُ النَّاسُ بَعْدَ كُلِّ صَلَاةٍ مِنْ الدُّعَاءِ:
 هَلْ هُوَ مَكْرُوهٌ؟ وَهَلْ وَرَدَ عَنْ أَحَدٍ مِنْ السَّلَفِ فِعْلُ ذَلِكَ؟ وَيَتْرُكُونَ أَيْضًا الذِّكْرَ الَّذِي صَحَّ أَنَّ النَّبِيَّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ كَانَ يَقُولُهُ وَيَشْتَغِلُونَ بِالدُّعَاءِ؟ فَهَلْ الْأَفْضَلُ الِاشْتِغَالُ بِالذِّكْرِ الْوَارِدِ عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ أَوْ هَذَا الدُّعَاءِ؟ وَهَلْ صَحَّ أَنَّ النَّبِيَّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ كَانَ يَرْفَعُ يَدَيْهِ وَيَمْسَحُ وَجْهَهُ أَمْ لَا؟ .
فَأَجَابَ:
الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ رَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ، الَّذِي نُقِلَ عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ مِنْ ذَلِكَ بَعْدَ الصَّلَاةِ الْمَكْتُوبَةِ إنَّمَا هُوَ الذِّكْرُ الْمَعْرُوفُ.
 كَالْأَذْكَارِ الَّتِي فِي الصِّحَاحِ وَكُتُبِ السُّنَنِ وَالْمَسَانِدِ وَغَيْرِهَا مِثْلَ مَا فِي الصَّحِيحِ:
 أَنَّهُ كَانَ قَبْلَ أَنْ يَنْصَرِفَ مِنْ الصَّلَاةِ يَسْتَغْفِرُ ثَلَاثًا ثُمَّ يَقُولُ: 
{اللَّهُمَّ أَنْتَ السَّلَامُ وَمِنْك السَّلَامُ تَبَارَكْت يَا ذَا الْجَلَالِ وَالْإِكْرَامِ}
 وَفِي الصَّحِيحِ أَنَّهُ كَانَ يَقُولُ دُبُرَ كُلِّ صَلَاةٍ مَكْتُوبَةٍ: {لَا إلَهَ إلَّا اللَّهُ وَحْدَهُ لَا شَرِيكَ لَهُ لَهُ الْمُلْكُ وَلَهُ الْحَمْدُ وَهُوَ عَلَى كُلِّ شَيْءٍ قَدِيرٌ
translated_text:
after turning away, just as someone addressing a king or anyone else is better placed to make a request while still speaking to him than after turning away.

He was asked:

Is the supplication that people offer after every prayer disliked? Has this practice been reported from any of the early generations? They also neglect the remembrance authentically reported from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and occupy themselves with supplication. Is it better to occupy oneself with the remembrance reported from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, or with this supplication? Is it authentically established that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would raise his hands and wipe his face, or not?

He answered:

All praise is due to Allah, Lord of all worlds. What has been transmitted from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, concerning this after the obligatory prayer is only the well-known remembrance, such as the formulas found in the collections of authentic hadith, the Sunan and Musnad collections, and elsewhere. For example, an authentic hadith states that before departing from the prayer, he would seek forgiveness three times, then say:

“O Allah, You are Peace, and from You comes peace. Blessed are You, Possessor of majesty and honour.”

Another authentic hadith states that after every obligatory prayer he would say:

“There is no god but Allah alone, with no partner. To Him belongs sovereignty, and to Him belongs all praise, and He has power over all things.

O Allah, none can withhold what You give, and none can give what You withhold, nor can wealth avail its possessor against You.”

It is reported in an authentic hadith that after the obligatory prayer he would proclaim Allah’s oneness with these words:

“There is no god but Allah alone, with no partner. To Him belongs sovereignty, and to Him belongs all praise, and He has power over all things. There is no might or power except through Allah. There is no god but Allah, and we worship none but Him. To Him belong all blessings and bounty, and to Him belongs all excellent praise. There is no god but Allah; we devote our worship sincerely to Him, even though the disbelievers dislike it.”

It is reported in an authentic hadith that “raising the voice in proclaiming Allah’s greatness after people had finished the obligatory prayer was practised during the lifetime of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.” They would know by this that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, had finished his prayer.

It is reported in an authentic hadith that he said:

“Whoever glorifies Allah thirty-three times after every prayer, praises Him thirty-three times, and proclaims His greatness thirty-three times—making ninety-nine—and completes the hundred by saying, ‘There is no god but Allah alone, with no partner. To Him belongs sovereignty, and to Him belongs all praise, and He has power over all things,’ will have his sins forgiven, even if they are like the foam of the sea.”

It is also reported in an authentic hadith that he would say: “Glory be to Allah, all praise is due to Allah, and Allah is greatest—thirty-three times.”

The Sunan collections contain other forms. Six forms have been transmitted:

original_text:
أَحَدُهَا:
 أَنَّهُ يَقُولُ: هَذِهِ الْكَلِمَاتِ عَشْرًا عَشْرًا عَشْرًا: فَالْمَجْمُوعُ ثَلَاثُونَ.
وَالثَّانِي:
 أَنْ يَقُولَ كُلَّ وَاحِدَةٍ إحْدَى عَشْرَ فَالْمَجْمُوعُ ثَلَاثٌ وَثَلَاثُونَ.
وَالثَّالِثُ:
 أَنْ يَقُولَ كُلَّ وَاحِدَةٍ ثَلَاثًا وَثَلَاثِينَ فَالْمَجْمُوعُ تِسْعٌ وَتِسْعُونَ.
وَالرَّابِعُ:
 أَنْ يَخْتِمَ ذَلِكَ بِالتَّوْحِيدِ التَّامِّ فَالْمَجْمُوعُ مِائَةٌ.
وَالسَّادِسُ 
(١)
: أَنْ يَقُولَ كُلَّ وَاحِدٍ مِنْ الْكَلِمَاتِ الْأَرْبَعِ خَمْسًا وَعِشْرِينَ فَالْمَجْمُوعُ مِائَةٌ. وَأَمَّا قِرَاءَةُ آيَةِ الْكُرْسِيِّ فَقَدْ رُوِيَتْ بِإِسْنَادِ لَا يُمْكِنُ أَنْ يَثْبُتَ بِهِ سُنَّةٌ.
 وَأَمَّا دُعَاءُ الْإِمَامِ وَالْمَأْمُومِينَ جَمِيعًا عَقِيبَ الصَّلَاةِ فَلَمْ يَنْقُلْ هَذَا أَحَدٌ عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ وَلَكِنْ نُقِلَ عَنْهُ أَنَّهُ أَمَرَ مُعَاذًا أَنْ يَقُولَ دُبُرَ كُلِّ صَلَاةٍ:
 
{اللَّهُمَّ أَعِنِّي عَلَى ذِكْرِك وَشُكْرِك وَحُسْنِ عِبَادَتِك}
 وَنَحْوِ ذَلِكَ. وَلَفْظُ دُبُرِ الصَّلَاةِ قَدْ يُرَادُ بِهِ آخِرُ جُزْءٍ مِنْ الصَّلَاةِ. كَمَا يُرَادُ بِدُبُرِ الشَّيْءِ مُؤَخَّرُهُ وَقَدْ يُرَادُ بِهِ مَا بَعْدَ انْقِضَائِهَا كَمَا فِي قَوْله تَعَالَى 
{وَأَدْبَارَ السُّجُودِ}
 وَقَدْ يُرَادُ بِهِ مَجْمُوعُ الْأَمْرَيْنِ وَبَعْضُ الْأَحَادِيثِ
original_footnote:
(١) هكذا بالأصل، ولم يذكر والخامس
قال الشيخ ناصر بن حمد الفهد (ص ١٨٨ - ١٨٩):
وهنا أمران:
الأول: أنه قد سقط من هذا الموضع النوع الخامس كما هو ظاهر، ولعله: (أن يقول كل واحدة ثلاثاً وثلاثين، إلا التكبير فيقوله أربعا وثلاثين). اهـ.
ويدل على هذا كلامه في (٢٢/ ٤٩٤) حيث ذكر الأنواع الستة بترتيب مغاير وهناك التفصيل أكثر.
الثاني: أن هذا السقط حاصل في أصل هذه الفتوى، (الفتوى الكبرى) ١/ ١٨٧.
translated_text:
The first is to say each of these phrases ten times, making thirty in total.

The second is to say each phrase eleven times, making thirty-three in total.

The third is to say each phrase thirty-three times, making ninety-nine in total.

The fourth is to conclude this with the full declaration of Allah’s oneness, making one hundred in total.

The sixth (1) is to say each of the four phrases twenty-five times, making one hundred in total.

As for reciting the Verse of the Throne, this has been reported through a chain of transmission that cannot establish a sunnah practice.

As for the imam and the congregation supplicating together after the prayer, no one has transmitted this from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. However, it has been transmitted that he instructed Muʿādh to say at the close of every prayer:

“O Allah, help me to remember You, thank You, and worship You well,”

and similar supplications. The expression dubur al-salāh (the close of the prayer) may refer to the final part of the prayer, just as the dubur (rear) of a thing means its back part. It may also refer to what comes after the prayer has ended, as in the words of Allah Most High:

“and after prostration.”

It may also encompass both meanings, and some hadiths

original_text:
يُفَسِّرُ بَعْضًا لِمَنْ تَتَبَّعَ ذَلِكَ وَتَدَبَّرَهُ.
 وَبِالْجُمْلَةِ فَهُنَا شَيْئَانِ:
 أَحَدُهُمَا دُعَاءُ الْمُصَلِّي الْمُنْفَرِدِ كَدُعَاءِ الْمُصَلِّي صَلَاةَ الِاسْتِخَارَةِ وَغَيْرِهَا مِنْ الصَّلَوَاتِ وَدُعَاءِ الْمُصَلِّي وَحْدَهُ إمَامًا كَانَ أَوْ مَأْمُومًا. وَالثَّانِي دُعَاءُ الْإِمَامِ وَالْمَأْمُومِينَ جَمِيعًا فَهَذَا الثَّانِي لَا رَيْبَ أَنَّ النَّبِيَّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ لَمْ يَفْعَلْهُ فِي أَعْقَابِ الْمَكْتُوبَاتِ كَمَا كَانَ يَفْعَلُ الْأَذْكَارَ الْمَأْثُورَةَ عَنْهُ إذْ لَوْ فَعَلَ ذَلِكَ لَنَقَلَهُ عَنْهُ أَصْحَابُهُ ثُمَّ التَّابِعُونَ ثُمَّ الْعُلَمَاءُ كَمَا نَقَلُوا مَا هُوَ دُونَ ذَلِكَ؛
 وَلِهَذَا كَانَ الْعُلَمَاءُ الْمُتَأَخِّرُونَ فِي هَذَا الدُّعَاءِ عَلَى أَقْوَالٍ:
 مِنْهُمْ مَنْ يَسْتَحِبُّ ذَلِكَ عَقِيبَ الْفَجْرِ وَالْعَصْرِ كَمَا ذَكَرَ ذَلِكَ طَائِفَةٌ مِنْ أَصْحَابِ أَبِي حَنِيفَةَ وَمَالِكٍ وَأَحْمَد وَغَيْرِهِمْ وَلَمْ يَكُنْ مَعَهُمْ فِي ذَلِكَ سُنَّةٌ يَحْتَجُّونَ بِهَا وَإِنَّمَا احْتَجُّوا بِكَوْنِ هَاتَيْنِ الصَّلَاتَيْنِ لَا صَلَاةَ بَعْدَهُمَا.
 وَمِنْهُمْ:
 مَنْ اسْتَحَبَّهُ أَدْبَارَ الصَّلَوَاتِ كُلِّهَا وَقَالَ: لَا يَجْهَرُ بِهِ إلَّا إذَا قَصَدَ التَّعْلِيمَ. كَمَا ذَكَرَ ذَلِكَ طَائِفَةٌ مِنْ أَصْحَابِ الشَّافِعِيِّ وَغَيْرِهِمْ وَلَيْسَ مَعَهُمْ فِي ذَلِكَ سُنَّةٌ إلَّا مُجَرَّدَ كَوْنِ الدُّعَاءِ مَشْرُوعًا وَهُوَ عَقِبَ الصَّلَوَاتِ يَكُونُ أَقْرَبَ إلَى الْإِجَابَةِ وَهَذَا الَّذِي ذَكَرُوهُ قَدْ اعْتَبَرَهُ الشَّارِعُ فِي صُلْبِ الصَّلَاةِ فَالدُّعَاءُ فِي آخِرِهَا قَبْلَ الْخُرُوجِ مَشْرُوعٌ مَسْنُونٌ
translated_text:
clarify others for anyone who examines and reflects upon them.

In short, two matters must be distinguished here:

The first is an individual worshipper’s supplication, such as that offered by someone performing the prayer for guidance or other prayers, and the supplication a worshipper offers individually, whether leading the prayer or following an imam. The second is the imam and congregation supplicating together. There is no doubt that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not do this second kind after the obligatory prayers, as he did the remembrances transmitted from him. Had he done so, his Companions, then the Successors, then the scholars would have transmitted it from him, just as they transmitted matters of lesser significance.

Hence, later scholars held differing views concerning this supplication:

Some regarded it as recommended after the dawn and afternoon prayers, as mentioned by a number of followers of Abū Hanīfah, Mālik, Ahmad, and others. They had no Prophetic precedent to cite for this; their only argument was that neither of these two prayers is followed by another prayer.

Others regarded it as recommended after all the prayers, saying that it should not be recited aloud unless the intention is to teach. This was mentioned by a number of followers of al-Shāfiʿī and others. They have no Prophetic precedent for this, beyond the general consideration that supplication is prescribed and is more likely to be answered after the prayers. Yet the Lawgiver has already taken this consideration into account within the prayer itself: supplication at its end, before concluding it, is prescribed and established as a sunnah

original_text:
بِالسُّنَّةِ الْمُتَوَاتِرَةِ وَبِاتِّفَاقِ الْمُسْلِمِينَ بَلْ قَدْ ذَهَبَ طَائِفَةٌ مِنْ السَّلَفِ وَالْخَلَفِ إلَى أَنَّ الدُّعَاءَ فِي آخِرِهَا وَاجِبٌ وَأَوْجَبُوا الدُّعَاءَ الَّذِي أَمَرَ بِهِ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ آخِرَ الصَّلَاةِ بِقَوْلِهِ:
 
{إذَا تَشَهَّدَ أَحَدُكُمْ فَلْيَسْتَعِذْ بِاَللَّهِ مِنْ أَرْبَعٍ: مِنْ عَذَابِ جَهَنَّمَ وَمِنْ عَذَابِ الْقَبْرِ وَمِنْ فِتْنَةِ الْمَحْيَا وَالْمَمَاتِ وَمِنْ فِتْنَةِ الْمَسِيحِ الدَّجَّالِ}
 رَوَاهُ مُسْلِمٌ.
 وَغَيْرُهُ وَكَانَ طَاوُوسٌ يَأْمُرُ مَنْ لَمْ يَدْعُ بِهِ أَنْ يُعِيدَ الصَّلَاةَ وَهُوَ قَوْلُ بَعْضِ أَصْحَابِ أَحْمَد وَكَذَلِكَ فِي حَدِيثِ ابْنِ مَسْعُودٍ:
 
{ثُمَّ لِيَتَخَيَّر مِنْ الدُّعَاءِ أَعْجَبَهُ إلَيْهِ}
 وَفِي حَدِيثِ عَائِشَةَ وَغَيْرِهَا أَنَّهُ كَانَ يَدْعُو فِي هَذَا الْمَوْطِنِ وَالْأَحَادِيثُ بِذَلِكَ كَثِيرَةٌ. وَالْمُنَاسَبَةُ الِاعْتِبَارِيَّةُ فِيهِ ظَاهِرَةٌ فَإِنَّ الْمُصَلِّيَ يُنَاجِي رَبَّهُ فَمَا دَامَ فِي الصَّلَاةِ لَمْ يَنْصَرِفْ فَإِنَّهُ يُنَاجِي رَبَّهُ فَالدُّعَاءُ حِينَئِذٍ مُنَاسِبٌ لِحَالِهِ أَمَّا إذَا انْصَرَفَ إلَى النَّاسِ مِنْ مُنَاجَاةِ اللَّهِ لَمْ يَكُنْ مَوْطِنَ مُنَاجَاةٍ لَهُ وَدُعَاءٍ. وَإِنَّمَا هُوَ مَوْطِنُ ذِكْرٍ لَهُ وَثَنَاءٍ عَلَيْهِ فَالْمُنَاجَاةُ وَالدُّعَاءُ حِينَ الْإِقْبَالِ وَالتَّوَجُّهِ إلَيْهِ فِي الصَّلَاةِ. أَمَّا حَالُ الِانْصِرَافِ مِنْ ذَلِكَ فَالثَّنَاءُ وَالذِّكْرُ أَوْلَى.
 وَكَمَا أَنَّ مِنْ الْعُلَمَاءِ مَنْ اسْتَحَبَّ عَقِبَ الصَّلَاةِ مِنْ الدُّعَاءِ مَا لَمْ تَرِدْ بِهِ السُّنَّةُ:
 فَمِنْهُمْ طَائِفَةٌ تُقَابِلُ هَذِهِ لَا يَسْتَحِبُّونَ الْقُعُودَ الْمَشْرُوعَ بَعْدَ الصَّلَاةِ وَلَا يَسْتَعْمِلُونَ الذِّكْرَ الْمَأْثُورَ بَلْ قَدْ يَكْرَهُونَ ذَلِكَ وَيَنْهَوْنَ
translated_text:
by the mass-transmitted Sunnah and the agreement of the Muslims. Indeed, some early and later scholars held that supplication at the end of the prayer is obligatory. They considered obligatory the supplication that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, commanded at the end of the prayer when he said:

“When any of you has recited the tashahhud (testimony of faith), let him seek refuge in Allah from four things: the punishment of Hell, the punishment of the grave, the trials of life and death, and the trial of the False Messiah.”

Reported by Muslim and others. Tāwūs would instruct anyone who had not offered this supplication to repeat the prayer. This is also the view of some of Ahmad’s followers. Likewise, the hadith of Ibn Masʿūd states:

“Then let him choose whichever supplication he likes best.”

The hadith of ʿĀʾishah and others also relates that he used to supplicate at this point. There are many hadiths concerning this.

The rationale for this is clear: the worshipper is conversing intimately with his Lord. As long as he remains in prayer and has not concluded it, he is conversing intimately with his Lord, so supplication is appropriate to his state. Once he turns back to people after conversing intimately with Allah, however, this is no longer the occasion for intimate converse with Him and supplication. Rather, it is an occasion for remembering and praising Him. Intimate converse and supplication belong to the time when one is turning towards Him and directing oneself to Him in prayer. Once one has finished, praise and remembrance are more appropriate.

Just as some scholars have recommended forms of supplication after prayer for which there is no precedent in the Sunnah, another group takes the opposite approach: they do not regard the prescribed sitting after prayer as recommended, nor do they practise the transmitted remembrances. Indeed, they may even dislike this and forbid

original_text:
عَنْهُ فَهَؤُلَاءِ مُفَرِّطُونَ بِالنَّهْيِ عَنْ الْمَشْرُوعِ وَأُولَئِكَ مُجَاوِزُونَ الْأَمْرَ بِغَيْرِ الْمَشْرُوعِ وَالدِّينُ إنَّمَا هُوَ الْأَمْرُ بِالْمَشْرُوعِ دُونَ غَيْرِ الْمَشْرُوعِ.
 وَأَمَّا رَفْعُ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ يَدَيْهِ فِي الدُّعَاءِ:
 فَقَدْ جَاءَ فِيهِ أَحَادِيثُ كَثِيرَةٌ صَحِيحَةٌ وَأَمَّا مَسْحُهُ وَجْهَهُ بِيَدَيْهِ فَلَيْسَ عَنْهُ فِيهِ إلَّا حَدِيثٌ أَوْ حَدِيثَانِ لَا يَقُومُ بِهِمَا حُجَّةٌ وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
وَسُئِلَ:
هَلْ دُعَاءُ الْإِمَامِ وَالْمَأْمُومِ عَقِيبَ صَلَاةِ الْفَرْضِ جَائِزٌ أَمْ لَا؟
فَأَجَابَ:
الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ، أَمَّا دُعَاءُ الْإِمَامِ وَالْمَأْمُومِينَ جَمِيعًا عَقِيبَ الصَّلَاةِ فَهُوَ بِدْعَةٌ لَمْ يَكُنْ عَلَى عَهْدِ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ بَلْ إنَّمَا كَانَ دُعَاؤُهُ فِي صُلْبِ الصَّلَاةِ فَإِنَّ الْمُصَلِّيَ يُنَاجِي رَبَّهُ فَإِذَا دَعَا حَالَ مُنَاجَاتِهِ لَهُ كَانَ مُنَاسِبًا.
 وَأَمَّا الدُّعَاءُ بَعْدَ انْصِرَافِهِ مِنْ مُنَاجَاتِهِ وَخِطَابِهِ فَغَيْرُ مُنَاسِبٍ وَإِنَّمَا الْمَسْنُونُ عَقِبَ الصَّلَاةِ هُوَ الذِّكْرُ الْمَأْثُورُ عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ مِنْ التَّهْلِيلِ وَالتَّحْمِيدِ وَالتَّكْبِيرِ كَمَا كَانَ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ يَقُولُ عَقِبَ الصَّلَاةِ:
 {لَا إلَهَ إلَّا اللَّهُ وَحْدَهُ لَا شَرِيكَ لَهُ لَهُ الْمُلْكُ
translated_text:
it. These fall short by forbidding what is prescribed, whereas the others overstep by enjoining what is not prescribed. Religion consists only in enjoining what is prescribed, not what is unprescribed.

As for the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, raising his hands in supplication, many authentic hadiths report this. As for his wiping his face with his hands, however, only one or two hadiths are reported from him concerning it, and these do not constitute sufficient evidence. And Allah knows best.

He was asked:

Is it permissible for the imam and those praying behind him to supplicate immediately after the obligatory prayer?

He answered:

Praise be to Allah. For the imam and those praying behind him to supplicate together immediately after the prayer is an innovation that did not exist during the time of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Rather, his supplication was made within the prayer itself. The worshipper is conversing intimately with his Lord, so supplicating while conversing intimately with Him is appropriate.

Supplication after he has finished conversing intimately with and addressing his Lord, however, is not appropriate. What the Sunnah prescribes after the prayer is the remembrance transmitted from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: declaring that there is no god but Allah, praising Him, and proclaiming His greatness. Thus, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would say after the prayer:

“There is no god but Allah alone, with no partner. His is the dominion
