the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, who said:

“Allah has angels who roam the earth. When they pass by people remembering Allah, they call to one another, ‘Come to what you seek!’”

He related the hadith, which includes the words:

“We found them glorifying You and praising You.”

However, such gatherings should take place occasionally, at certain times and places. They should not be made a fixed, regularly observed practice, except for what the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prescribed for regular congregational observance, such as the five daily prayers in congregation, Friday prayers, the Eid prayers, and the like.

As for a person maintaining regular devotions consisting of prayer, Quran recitation, remembrance, or supplication at the two ends of the day, during the early hours of the night, or at other times, this is the practice of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and of Allah’s righteous servants, past and present. Whatever is prescribed to be performed collectively, such as the obligatory prayers, should be performed in that manner. Likewise, regular devotions prescribed to be maintained individually should be performed individually.

The Companions—may Allah be pleased with them—would occasionally gather and ask one of their number to recite while the others listened. ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb would say, “Abū Mūsā, remind us of our Lord,” whereupon he would recite while they listened. Some of the Companions would say, “Sit with us, so that we may renew our faith for a while.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, led his Companions in voluntary prayer in congregation on several occasions. He also came out to the Companions who belonged to the people of the Suffah, among whom someone was reciting, and sat with them to listen.

translated_text:
The awe of the heart, tears of the eyes, and trembling of the body that arise from prescribed listening and remembrance are the finest states described in the Quran and Sunnah. As for violent agitation, fainting, death, and cries, if a person is overcome involuntarily, he is not to be blamed, as sometimes happened among the Successors and those after them. This results from the intensity of what the heart experiences, coupled with the heart’s weakness. Strength and composure are better, as exemplified by the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and the Companions. As for remaining unmoved out of hardness and coldness of heart, this is blameworthy and contains no good.

As for the listening mentioned above, its prescribed form—which sets hearts right and serves as their means of drawing near to their Lord by establishing their bond with Him—is listening to the Book of Allah. This is what the best members of this community listen to, especially since the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“He is not one of us who does not recite the Quran melodiously.”

He also said:

“Beautify the Quran with your voices.”

This is the listening praised in the Quran and Sunnah.

But when some members of this community forgot a portion of this listening, of which they had been reminded, enmity and hatred were cast among them. Some introduced listening to poems, clapping, and singing, resembling the whistling and clapping that Allah condemned and imitating what the Christians had innovated. Opposing them were others whose hearts had hardened against the remembrance of Allah and the truth that had been revealed. Their hearts had hardened until they were like stones, or harder still, resembling that for which Allah reproached the Jews.

The balanced religious path is that followed by the best members of this community, past and present. And Allah knows best.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

About some ordinary fuqarā (poor folk) who gather in a mosque, remember Allah, recite some of the Quran, then supplicate, uncover their heads, weep, and plead humbly. They do not intend to show off or gain a reputation, but do this to draw nearer to Allah Most High. Is this permissible or not?

He replied:

Praise be to Allah. Gathering to recite the Quran, remember Allah, and supplicate is good and recommended, provided it is not made a fixed, regular practice—like the prescribed gatherings—and is not accompanied by any reprehensible innovation. Uncovering the head while doing so, however, is disliked, especially if it is treated as an act of worship. In that case, it becomes reprehensible, and it is not permissible to worship Allah in this manner. And Allah knows best.

{وَلِبَاسُ التَّقْوَى ذَلِكَ خَيْرٌ}

{خُذُوا جُنَّتَكُمْ قَالُوا: يَا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ مِنْ عَدُوٍّ حَضَرَ قَالَ: لَا وَلَكِنْ جُنَّتُكُمْ مِنْ النَّارِ: سُبْحَانَ اللَّهِ وَالْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ وَلَا إلَهَ إلَّا اللَّهُ وَاَللَّهُ أَكْبَرُ}

He replied:

Praise be to Allah, Lord of all worlds. This is not disbelief, for this supplication and others like it are intended to seek protection and safety through these words. A person thus shields himself from harm, just as someone shelters in a house from harm, heat, cold, and enemies.

This is like what appears in the well-known hadith from the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—concerning the five injunctions that John son of Zechariah stood before the Children of Israel to deliver. He said:

“I enjoin you to remember Allah. The likeness of this is that of a man pursued by an enemy who enters a fortress and finds protection there from his enemy. Likewise, remembering Allah is the fortress that protects the son of Adam from Satan.”

Or words to that effect. He thus likened remembering Allah, through which a person protects himself from Satan, to a fortress in which he finds protection from an enemy. A fortress has a door, a roof, and walls.

Similarly, righteous deeds, including remembering Allah and other acts, are called a shield and a garment. Thus Allah Most High says:

“But the garment of righteousness—that is best.”

This is according to the better-known of the two interpretations.

Likewise, he said in the hadith:

“Take up your shield.” They asked, “O Messenger of Allah, against an enemy who has come upon us?” He replied, “No, rather your shield against the Fire: ‘Glory be to Allah; praise be to Allah; there is no god but Allah; and Allah is greatest.’”

However, the supplication asked about has not been transmitted. What is prescribed is to use transmitted supplications, for supplication is among the finest acts of worship, and Allah has forbidden us to transgress in it. We should therefore follow what has been prescribed and established in the Sunnah, just as we should in other acts of worship.

Anyone who turns from prescribed supplications to others—even those found in the devotional litanies of certain shaykhs—would do better not to miss out on what is more perfect and excellent: the prophetic supplications. Muslims unanimously agree that these are better and more complete than other supplications, even if some shaykhs have uttered them. How much more so [when] (1) those very supplications may contain error, sin, or something else!

Among those most deserving of blame is someone who adopts a devotional litany not transmitted from the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—even if it belongs to one of the shaykhs, while abandoning the prophetic litanies recited by the master of the children of Adam, the leader of all creation, and Allah’s proof against His servants. And Allah knows best.

Chapter: What Is Disliked in Prayer

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah sanctify his soul—said:

Section: What Allah and His Messenger Have Commanded concerning Establishing Prayer, Performing It Fully, and Maintaining Stillness during It

Allah Most High says in several places in His Book:

“Establish prayer and give zakah.”

And He Most High says:

“Indeed, mankind was created anxious.”
“When evil touches him, impatient,”
“And when good touches him, withholding,”
“Except those who pray.”

And He Most High says:

“Successful indeed are the believers,”
“Those who are humble in their prayer,”
“And those who turn away from idle talk,”
“And those who give zakah,”
“And those who guard their chastity,”
“Except with their spouses or those whom their right hands possess, for then they are free from blame.”
“But whoever seeks beyond that—it is they who are the transgressors.”
“And those who are faithful to their trusts and their pledges,”
“And those who carefully maintain their prayers.”

And He Most High says:

“Seek help through patience and prayer. Indeed, it is burdensome except for the humbly submissive.”

And He Most High says:

“But they were succeeded by generations who neglected prayer and followed their desires; they will therefore meet with ruin.”

And He Most High says:

“When you are secure, establish prayer. Indeed, prayer has been prescribed for the believers at appointed times.”

And He Most High says:

“Carefully maintain the prayers, especially the middle prayer

The significance of these verses will be explained later. Al-Bukhārī and Muslim recorded in their two Sahīh collections—as did the compilers of the Sunan: Abū Dāwūd, al-Tirmidhī, al-Nasā’ī and Ibn Mājah, and the compilers of Musnad collections, such as Ahmad’s Musnad, and other foundational works of Islam—the following report from Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, entered the mosque. A man entered, then came and greeted the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, returned his greeting and said, ‘Go back and pray, for you have not prayed.’

“The man went back and prayed as he had prayed before, then greeted him. The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, ‘And upon you be peace.’ Then he said, ‘Go back and pray, for you have not prayed.’ This happened three times.

“The man said, ‘By Him who sent you with the truth, I do not know how to do any better than this, so teach me.’

“He said, ‘When you stand to pray, proclaim Allah’s greatness, then recite whatever you can of the Quran. Then bow until you are at rest in that position, then rise until you are standing upright. Then prostrate until you are at rest in that position, then sit until you are at rest in that position. Do this throughout your prayer.’”

In a version recorded by al-Bukhārī:

to observe stillness when he stood for prayer, just as he commanded him to bow and prostrate. His unqualified command entails obligation. He also told him:

“For you have not prayed.”

He thus denied that the man’s first performance constituted prayer. An act can only be denied when one of its obligatory elements is missing. If, however, it is performed as Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has required, it cannot rightly be denied merely because some recommended, non-obligatory element is missing.

As for the claim some people make that this is a denial of completeness, as in his saying:

“There is no prayer for one who lives near the mosque except in the mosque,”

the response is: Yes, it denies completeness, but does it deny completeness with respect to the obligatory elements or the recommended elements? The former is correct. The latter, however, is false: nothing of this kind ever occurs in the words of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, or in the words of His Messenger, nor is it true. For if all the obligatory elements of an act are complete, how can the act rightly be denied? Moreover, if that were permissible, it would be permissible to deny the prayer of most people of earlier and later generations, since fulfilling every recommended element is exceedingly rare.

Accordingly, whenever acts are denied in the Quran and Sunnah, this is only because some of their obligatory elements are missing. An example is the saying of the Most High:

“But no, by your Lord, they will not believe until

they make you judge in the disputes between them, then find within themselves no discomfort at what you have decided and submit wholeheartedly.”

And His saying, Most High:

“They say, ‘We believe in Allah and in the Messenger, and we obey.’ Then a group of them turns away thereafter. Those are not believers.”

And His saying, Most High:

“The believers are only those who believe in Allah and His Messenger, then never doubt”—the verse continues.

And His saying:

“The believers are only those who believe in Allah and His Messenger and, when they are with him on a matter of common concern, do not leave until they have sought his permission”—the verse continues. There are many similar examples.

These also include his sayings, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“There is no faith in one who is not trustworthy.”

“There is no prayer without the Opening of the Book.”

“There is no prayer without ablution.”

As for the saying:

“There is no prayer for one who lives near the mosque except in the mosque,”

it has been said that this wording is not reliably preserved from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. ‘Abd al-Haqq al-Ishbīlī mentioned that he narrated it through a chain whose narrators were all trustworthy. In any event, it is reported from ‘Alī, may Allah be pleased with him. A similar report, however, appears in the Sunan collections from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, who said:

“Whoever hears the call and then fails to respond without an excuse has no prayer.”

There is no doubt that this entails that responding to the muezzin’s call and praying in congregation are obligatory, as is established in the Sahīh, where Ibn Umm Maktūm said:

But if someone neglects this obligation, is he punished for it while being rewarded for the prayer he has performed? Or should it be said that his prayer is invalid and he must repeat it, as though he had not performed it at all? Scholars disagree on this.

His saying, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is to be understood in this light:

“When you do this, your prayer is complete. Whatever you omit from this, you diminish your prayer accordingly.”

He thus clarified that the perfection whose absence is asserted is this very completeness mentioned by the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Whoever omits any of these things has left out of his prayer something Allah has made obligatory within it.

The same applies to his saying in the other hadith:

“When he does this, his prayer is complete.”

This is supported by the fact that he commanded him to repeat the prayer. Had what he omitted been merely recommended, he would not have commanded him to repeat it.

Thus, someone who performs his prayer improperly in this way is commanded to repeat it, just as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, commanded this man. But if he does not repeat it and leaves it deficient, should it be said that performing it is equivalent to not performing it, so that he is punished for abandoning it? Or should it be said that he is rewarded for what he performed and punished for what he omitted, such that the obligations he omitted are made up for by the voluntary prayers he performed? There is disagreement on this.

Ziyād—or Ibn Ziyād—and so the man came to Medina and met Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him. He said: ‘He asked about my lineage, and I told him. He then said: “Young man, shall I relate a hadith to you?” I replied: “Yes, may Allah have mercy on you.”’—Yūnus said: ‘I believe he attributed it to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.’—He said:

‘The first of people’s deeds for which they will be called to account on the Day of Resurrection is prayer.’ He continued: ‘Our Lord, Mighty and Majestic, will say to His angels, though He knows best: “Examine My servant’s prayer: did he complete it or leave it deficient?” If it is complete, it will be recorded for him as complete. If he has left any part of it deficient, He will say: “See whether My servant has any voluntary prayers.” If he has voluntary prayers, He will say: “Complete it from his voluntary prayers.” Then the other deeds will be dealt with in the same way.’”

In another wording, Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, said that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The first of a servant’s deeds for which he will be called to account on the Day of Resurrection is his prayer. If it is sound, he will have prospered and succeeded; if it is unsound, he will have failed and lost. If any part of his obligatory prayer is deficient, the Lord will say: ‘See whether My servant has any voluntary prayers.’ The deficiency in his obligatory prayer will then be made up from them. The rest of his deeds will be treated in the same way.”

Al-Tirmidhī narrated it and said: “A sound hadith.”

It was narrated by the compilers of the four Sunan collections. Al-Tirmidhī said: “A sound and authentic hadith.”

This explicitly states that prayer is not valid until a man returns upright after bowing and sits erect after prostration. It thus establishes the obligation to return upright as part of bowing and prostration. Although this question is distinct from that of stillness in prayer, it is closely related to it and inseparable from it.

This hadith explicitly establishes the obligation to return upright. If returning upright is obligatory to complete bowing and prostration, then remaining still in them is all the more obligatory.

His words, “straightens his back in bowing and prostration,” mean when he raises his head from them, for straightening the back is part of completing bowing and prostration. Bowing extends from the moment a person bends down until he returns upright, and prostration extends from the moment he lowers himself from standing or sitting until he returns upright. Lowering and rising are thus the two ends of bowing and prostration, completing each of them. Hence he said:

“He straightens his spine in bowing and prostration.”

This is further clarified by the fact that these two acts of returning upright are obligatory just as completing bowing and prostration is obligatory. This is like his statement in the preceding hadith:

and places his face firmly on the ground until his joints become still and relaxed. Then he says, ‘Allah is the Greatest,’ sits upright on his buttocks, and straightens his spine.”

He thus explained that straightening the spine occurs when rising from prostration, not while lowering oneself. The two preceding hadiths establish the obligation both to return upright in these two positions and to remain still. However, concerning bowing, prostration, and sitting, he said:

“Until you are still while bowing, until you are still while prostrating, and until you are still while sitting.”

Concerning rising from bowing, he said:

“Until you stand upright, and until you stand erect.”

This is because a person standing becomes upright and erect, which necessarily entails stillness. By contrast, someone bowing or prostrating is not erect. Nor can someone sitting be described as completely upright and straight: he may lean to one side, particularly in the tawarruk sitting posture, or forwards, because the limbs on which he sits are bent rather than straight and upright.

Nevertheless, Ibn Mājah narrated that he—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said concerning rising from bowing:

“Until you are still while standing.”

ʿAlī ibn Shaybān al-Hanafī reported:

“We set out and came to the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace. We pledged allegiance to him and prayed behind him. for one who does not straighten his spine in bowing and prostration.’” Narrated by Imam Ahmad and Ibn Mājah. In another version narrated by Imam Ahmad, the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

This shows that straightening the spine means proper alignment in bowing, as we have explained. Some scholars, both from our school and elsewhere, have nevertheless interpreted it as stillness alone. They cited this hadith as evidence for stillness alone, not for returning upright in the two positions. According to our explanation, however, it establishes both.

Imam Ahmad also narrated in al-Musnad that Abū Qatādah—may Allah be pleased with him—reported that the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“The worst thief is the one who steals from his prayer.” They asked, “O Messenger of Allah, how does he steal from his prayer?” He replied, “He does not complete its bowing or prostration.”

Or he said:

“He does not straighten his spine in bowing and prostration.”

This uncertainty over the wording evidently indicates that the intended meaning of the two expressions is the same, and that the doubt concerns only the wording, as in similar reports.

Furthermore, ʿAbd al-Rahmān ibn Shibl—may Allah be pleased with him—said:

“The Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—forbade pecking like a crow, spreading the forearms on the ground like a beast of prey, and settling in a spot in the mosque as a camel does.”

Recorded by Abū Dāwūd, al-Nasā’ī, and Ibn Mājah. He only

grouped these three actions together—despite their differing kinds—because they all involve imitating animals during prayer. He thus forbade imitating the crow, the beast of prey, and the camel, although pecking like a crow is more serious than the other two actions, as indicated by other hadiths concerning it.

In the two Sahīh collections, Qatādah narrates from Anas—may Allah be pleased with him—that the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“Maintain proper alignment in bowing and prostration, and let none of you spread his forearms as a dog does.”

This is especially so since he explained in another hadith:

“It is characteristic of the prayer of the hypocrites.”

Allah Most High has stated in His Book that He will never accept the deeds of the hypocrites. Muslim narrated in his Sahīh from Anas ibn Mālik that the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“That is the prayer of the hypocrite. He delays until the sun is between the two horns of Satan, then rises and pecks through four units of prayer, remembering Allah only a little during them.”

He thus stated that the hypocrite neglects both the prescribed time of the obligatory prayer and its proper performance, pecking through it. This indicates that both are blameworthy, although in either case the person is neglecting an obligation. It is clear evidence that pecking through prayer is impermissible and is a practice of those who have hypocrisy within them. All hypocrisy is forbidden. This hadith is an independent proof in its own right, and it explains the preceding hadith.

Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, the hypocrites seek to deceive Allah, but He deceives them. When they stand for prayer, they stand lazily, showing off to people and remembering Allah only a little.”

This is a stern warning to anyone who pecks through his prayer

translated_text:
you were to die, you would die upon something other than the natural disposition upon which Allah created Muhammad—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—and upon something other than the Sunnah.” Both expressions refer here to religion and the revealed law, not to performing recommended acts, for omitting those does not warrant such censure and warning. Hardly anyone reaches death having observed every recommended practice that the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—performed.

Moreover, in their speech, “natural disposition” and “Sunnah” mean religion and the revealed law. Some people have, however, adopted a technical usage in which “Sunnah” means what is not obligatory, and it may indeed bear that meaning, as in his saying—may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Allah has made fasting Ramadan obligatory upon you, and I have instituted its night prayers for you.”

Nevertheless, the term encompasses the obligatory practices he instituted even more emphatically than the voluntary ones. As reported in the Sahīh, Ibn Mas‘ūd—may Allah be pleased with him—said:

“Allah has prescribed for your Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—the ways of guidance. These congregational prayers are among the ways of guidance. If you were to pray in your homes as this man who stays away prays in his home, you would abandon the Sunnah of your Prophet. If you abandoned the Sunnah of your Prophet, you would go astray. I remember when none of us stayed away except a man known for his hypocrisy.”

Another example is his saying—may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Adhere to my Sunnah and the Sunnah of the rightly guided caliphs who come after me. Hold fast to it and bite onto it with your molar teeth.”

Furthermore, Allah—glorified and exalted be He—has commanded in His Book that prayer be established, and has censured those who pray yet are heedless of their prayer and neglect it. He, the Exalted, says in several places:

“And establish

prayer.” Establishing it entails performing it fully, to the extent possible, as will be seen in the hadith reported by Anas ibn Mālik—may Allah be pleased with him:

“Perform the bowing and prostration properly, for I can see you from behind my back.”

Another version reads:

“Complete the bowing and prostration.”

The significance of this evidence will be explained later.

The evidence for this from the Quran is the saying of Allah—glorified and exalted be He:

“When you travel through the land, there is no blame upon you for shortening the prayer if you fear that those who disbelieve may attack you.”

Allah thus permitted both reducing the number of prayer units and modifying the manner of performing the prayer. This is why He made it conditional upon two circumstances: travel and fear.

Travel permits only a reduction in the number of prayer units, as the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“Allah has relieved the traveller of fasting and half the prayer.”

Accordingly, the practice of Allah’s Messenger—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—which has been mass-transmitted from him, and which the Muslim community has unanimously transmitted, was that:

“He would perform the four-unit prayer as two units when travelling.”

He never performed it as four units while travelling, nor did Abū Bakr or ‘Umar—may Allah be pleased with them both—whether travelling for Hajj, ‘umrah, or jihad.

Fear permits modifying the manner of performing the prayer, as Allah says in the continuation of the passage:

“When you are among them and lead them in prayer, let a group of them stand with you, taking their weapons with them. Once they have prostrated, let them take their positions behind you, and let another group, who have not yet prayed, come forward and pray with you, taking their precautions and their weapons.”

He thus described the prayer in a state of fear, namely the prayer at Dhāt al-Riqā‘, when the enemy was in the direction of the qiblah. In this prayer,

“they would pray behind him. When he rose for the second unit, they would cease following him and complete the second unit on their own, then go to join the ranks of their companions.”

As Allah says:

“Once they have prostrated, let them take their positions behind you.”

He thus attributed the prostration specifically to them, indicating that they perform it individually. He then said:

“And let another group, who have not yet prayed, come forward and pray with you.”

This shows that they perform it. In this prayer, the worshippers are divided into groups: the first group ceases to follow the imam, while the second group rises before the imam’s concluding salutation and completes one unit on its own.

Then Allah Most High said:

“When you have completed the prayer, remember Allah standing, sitting, and lying on your sides. Then, when you are secure, establish the prayer.”

He thus commanded them to establish the prayer once they were safe. This entails performing it fully and forgoing the shortening permitted by fear and travel. It follows that the command to establish the prayer includes the command to perform it fully, to the extent possible.

As for His words concerning prayer in a state of fear:

“And you lead them in prayer,”

‘If you fear that those who disbelieve may attack you’—yet that fear no longer exists today?”

He replied:

“I wondered at the same thing you did, so I mentioned it to the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace. He said: ‘It is a charity Allah has bestowed upon you, so accept His charity.’”

The questioner had assumed that shortening prayer in all cases depended upon the absence of safety. The Sunnah therefore clarified that shortening is of two kinds, each with its own condition. The Sunnah has established that prayer, as prescribed during travel, is complete, for this is how the Prophet commanded people to pray. It is not diminished in reward and recompense, even though it is shortened in form and performance, since the worshipper is sometimes commanded to lengthen the prayer and sometimes to keep it brief.

Furthermore, Allah Most High said:

“Then, when you are secure, establish the prayer. Indeed, prayer has been prescribed for the believers at appointed times.”

The early generations explained “appointed” as meaning “prescribed,” and also as “having a specified time.” What is prescribed is measured out and delimited. Appointing times, determining measures, setting limits, and prescribing are terms close in meaning. This entails that prayer has prescribed measures, limits, and appointed times. This applies both to its timing and to its actions. Just as its timing is delimited, its actions have even greater reason to be delimited and precisely prescribed.

This includes determining its number: Allah made the prayers five, making some of them four units while at home and two while travelling, others three, and others two, whether at home or travelling. It also includes determining the actions performed in prayer. Thus, when there is a valid excuse, it is permissible to combine prayers, which involves a degree of advancing or delaying their timing, just as it is also permissible to reduce the number of their units

Thus, someone combining two prayers may not delay a daytime prayer until night or a nighttime prayer until day. The two daytime prayers are Zuhr and Asr, and the two nighttime prayers are Maghrib and Ishā. The same applies to those with valid excuses who reduce the number of units and simplify the manner of performance: this, too, is subject to prescribed times and limits. The actions must have clearly defined beginnings and endings.

Standing is defined by being upright: if someone voluntarily moves from an upright posture into the bent posture of bowing, he has not fulfilled the requirement of standing.

It is well known that the remembrance recited while standing—namely, Quran recitation—is superior to the remembrance recited while bowing and prostrating. Yet the physical acts of bowing and prostrating are superior to the physical act of standing. For this reason, they constitute worship in their own right and, under our religious law, may never be directed to anyone other than Allah. Other evidence has been discussed elsewhere. That being so, it is clear that these actions have prescribed measures and limits according to one’s ability to perform them.

A person prostrating must reach the ground, which is the furthest extent possible; he may not stop short of it except for a valid excuse. He begins the movement of prostration as soon as he starts bending down, whether he prostrates from a standing or a sitting position. Furthermore, this ensures that bowing and prostration are completed fully.

Moreover, if the actions of prayer have prescribed measures, they must have a definite extent. This requires remaining still. Someone who pecks like a crow gives his action no real duration at all, for a thing’s measure and extent are something beyond its mere existence. Thus, something that continues indefinitely is said to have no measure: a measure applies not to the slightest movement, but to a movement that has some duration.

Furthermore, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has commanded us to establish prayer. To establish something is to make it stand, and something standing is upright and balanced. The actions of prayer must therefore be steady and balanced. This can only be achieved by holding its constituent parts firmly and steadily, which entails remaining still. Someone who pecks like a crow has not properly established his prostration, nor does he complete it if he does not remain firm and settled. The same applies to someone bowing.

This is illustrated by the report in the two Sahīh collections, from Qatāda, from Anas ibn Mālik—may Allah be pleased with them both—who said: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Straighten your rows, for straightening the row is part of perfecting the prayer.”

They also both narrated it on the authority of

ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Suhayb, from Anas ibn Mālik—may Allah be pleased with him—who said: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Complete the rows, for I can see you behind my back.”

In another wording:

“Straighten the rows.”

Al-Bukhārī narrated through Humayd, from Anas, who said:

“The call to commence prayer was given, and the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, turned towards us and said: ‘Straighten your rows and stand close together, for I can see you behind my back.’ Each of us would place his shoulder against his companion’s shoulder and his body against his body.”

If straightening and aligning the row is part of perfecting and establishing prayer—such that, if they abandoned alignment and evenness altogether, with one person’s head level with the lower half of another’s body, they would not constitute a row and would be ordered to repeat their prayer, with even greater reason than the man who prayed alone behind the row and whom the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, ordered to repeat his prayer—then how much more important is it to perform the actions of prayer correctly and in a balanced manner, rather than failing to keep one’s back properly aligned in bowing and prostration?

“Perform bowing and prostration properly, for, by Allah, I can indeed see you behind me”—in another narration, “behind my back”—“when you bow and prostrate.”

{حَافِظُوا عَلَى الصَّلَوَاتِ وَالصَّلَاةِ الْوُسْطَى وَقُومُوا لِلَّهِ قَانِتِينَ}
 أَمْرٌ بِالْقُنُوتِ فِي الْقِيَامِ لِلَّهِ وَالْقُنُوتُ: دَوَامُ الطَّاعَةِ لِلَّهِ عَزَّ وَجَلَّ سَوَاءٌ كَانَ فِي حَالِ الِانْتِصَابِ أَوْ فِي حَالِ السُّجُودِ كَمَا قَالَ تَعَالَى 
{أَمْ مَنْ هُوَ قَانِتٌ آنَاءَ اللَّيْلِ سَاجِدًا وَقَائِمًا يَحْذَرُ الْآخِرَةَ وَيَرْجُو رَحْمَةَ رَبِّهِ}
 وَقَالَ تَعَالَى {فَالصَّالِحَاتُ قَانِتَاتٌ حَافِظَاتٌ لِلْغَيْبِ بِمَا
translated_text:
and prostration, for by Him in whose hand is my soul, I can indeed see you behind my back when you bow and when you prostrate.”

Muslim also narrated it through Hishām al-Dastawā’ī and Ibn Abī ‘Arūba, from Qatāda, from Anas—may Allah be pleased with him—that the Prophet of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Complete your bowing and prostration”—Ibn Abī ‘Arūba’s wording is: “Perform your bowing and prostration properly, for I can see you”—and he related the remainder of the hadith.

This makes clear that performing bowing and prostration properly requires completing them, as expressed in the other wording.

Furthermore, his command to perform bowing and prostration properly entails remaining still in both postures, since it is known that they were already performing the basic act of bending down. Indeed, the command to perform them properly also requires correct alignment in both and completion of their initial and final stages. This refutes those who claim that rising from them is not obligatory, for this command was addressed to those praying behind him, and it is known that they could not finish their prayer before him.

Furthermore, Allah Most High says:

“Guard strictly your prayers, especially the middle prayer, and stand before Allah in devout obedience.”

This is a command to observe qunūt when standing before Allah. Qunūt means constant obedience to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, whether one is standing upright or prostrating. As Allah Most High says:

“Is one who is devoutly obedient during the hours of the night, prostrating and standing, fearing the Hereafter and hoping for his Lord’s mercy…”

And Allah Most High says:

“So righteous women are devoutly obedient, guarding in their husbands’ absence what

Allah has ordained to be guarded.” He also says:

“And whoever among you devoutly obeys Allah and His Messenger…”

And He says:

“To Him belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth; all are devoutly obedient to Him.”

Since this is so, His words, “And stand before Allah in devout obedience,” may be a command to establish prayer generally, as in His words, “Be steadfast in upholding justice.” In that case, the command encompasses all the acts of prayer and requires sustained observance of them. Alternatively, it may mean standing as opposed to sitting. In that case, it encompasses standing both before and after bowing and requires that standing to be prolonged. This is the qunūt that includes supplication, such as qunūt in times of calamity and qunūt in the dawn prayer according to those who consider its regular observance recommended. Once the obligation of this is established, the obligation of remaining still in all the other acts follows all the more strongly.

The first interpretation is supported by the hadith of Zayd ibn Arqam, related from him in the two Sahīh collections. He said:

“One of us used to speak to the man beside him during prayer. Then the verse, ‘And stand before Allah in devout obedience,’ was revealed.” He said: “We were then commanded to remain silent and forbidden to speak.”

He thus stated that they used to speak during prayer. It is well known that refraining from addressing other people is obligatory throughout the prayer. This therefore entails a command to observe qunūt throughout the prayer. The command to observe qunūt indicates that one must refrain from addressing people because qunūt means constant obedience. Thus, someone occupied with addressing other people ceases to occupy himself

translated_text:
Allah:

“Then, when they have fallen onto their sides.”

The basic meaning of wujūb is firmness and stability.

Furthermore, ʿUqbah ibn ʿĀmir (may Allah be pleased with him) reported:

“When ‘So glorify the name of your Lord, the Most Great’ was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) said, ‘Include it in your bowing.’ When ‘Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High’ was revealed, he said, ‘Include it in your prostration.’”

Reported by Abū Dāwūd and Ibn Mājah. The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) thus commanded that these two expressions of glorification be included in bowing and prostration, and his command establishes an obligation. This entails the obligation to bow and prostrate in conjunction with this glorification—which requires remaining still.

Some jurists may say that glorification is not obligatory. This view contradicts the apparent meaning of the Quran and Sunnah, for their apparent meaning indicates that both the action and the utterance are obligatory. Even if evidence establishes that the utterance is not obligatory, this does not preclude the action from being obligatory.

Those who hold that glorification is obligatory cite as evidence the words of the Most High:

“And glorify your Lord with praise before sunrise and before sunset.”

This is a command to perform the prayer as a whole, as established in the two Sahīh collections, from Jarīr ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Bajalī (may Allah be pleased with him), who said:

“We were sitting with the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) when he looked

at the moon on the night of the full moon and said:

‘You will surely see your Lord just as you see this moon, without any difficulty in seeing Him. So if you can avoid being prevented from offering prayer before sunrise and before sunset, then do so.’

Then he recited:

‘And glorify your Lord with praise before sunrise and before sunset.’”

Since Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has called prayer glorification, this indicates that glorification is obligatory. Similarly, when He called it standing in His words, Most High:

“Stand in prayer at night, except for a little,”

this indicated that standing is obligatory. Likewise, when He called it recitation in His words, Most High:

“and the recitation at dawn,”

this indicated that Quran recitation is obligatory within it. And when He called it bowing and prostration in various passages, this indicated that bowing and prostration are obligatory within it.

This is because naming prayer after these actions indicates that they are indispensable to it. Thus, when these actions occur, they constitute indispensable parts of it, just as people refer to a human being by indispensable parts of the body, calling a person a neck, a head, a face, and so forth. An example is the saying of the Most High:

“then the freeing of a slave.”

If prayer could exist without glorification, a command to glorify could not serve as a command to pray. For the expression would then indicate neither its own meaning nor anything that entails that meaning.

Furthermore, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has censured humanity in general, while excepting those who pray and are constant in their prayers. He, Most High, says:

“Indeed, mankind was created anxious.”

“distressed when evil touches him,
and withholding when good touches him,
except those who pray,
who are constant in their prayers.”

The early generations—the Companions and those who came after them—explained being constant in prayer as both observing its appointed times and sustaining its actions with attentive devotion. The verse encompasses both meanings, for He says:

“who are constant in their prayers.”

Someone who is constant in an action is someone who maintains it and performs it continually. When this concerns something performed at separate times, it means performing it every day, rather than doing it on one occasion and omitting it on another. If this is called constancy, then sustaining a single, continuous action has an even greater claim to be called constancy and to fall within the scope of the verse. This indicates that sustaining the actions of prayer is obligatory, because Allah, Mighty and Majestic, censures humanity in general, excepting those who maintain this quality. Whoever fails to sustain its actions is therefore censured by the Lawgiver, and the Lawgiver censures only the omission of an obligation or the commission of something forbidden.

Furthermore, He, Glorified and Exalted, says:

“except those who pray,
who are constant in their prayers.”

This indicates that someone who prays may or may not be constant in prayer, and that one who prays without being constant is blameworthy. This entails censure of anyone who fails to sustain its actions, whether within a continuous prayer or across separate prayers. If sustaining its actions is obligatory, that is precisely what composure in prayer consists of. For this indicates that remaining in bowing, prostration, and the other postures is obligatory. If even less than the lowering mentioned—which is like a crow’s pecking—were sufficient, that would not constitute constancy, nor would it be obligatory to remain in bowing

and prostration—the two fundamental actions of prayer. Thus it is clear that, just as prayer is obligatory, so too is constancy in it, which entails composure and tranquillity in its actions.

Furthermore, Allah Most High says:

“And seek help through patience and prayer. Indeed, it is burdensome except for the humbly devout.”

This entails censure of those who lack humble devotion. Similarly, He Most High says:

“We appointed the direction of prayer which you previously faced only to make evident who follows the Messenger and who turns back on his heels. It was indeed burdensome, except for those whom Allah guided.”

And He Most High says:

“What you call them to is burdensome to the polytheists.”

Thus, the Book of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, indicates that anyone who finds what Allah loves burdensome is religiously blameworthy for this, and that such an attitude incurs His displeasure. Censure or displeasure arises only from neglecting an obligation or committing something forbidden. Since those who lack humble devotion are censured, this indicates that humble devotion is obligatory.

It is clear that the humble devotion mentioned in His saying:

“Indeed, it is burdensome except for the humbly devout”

must include humble devotion within prayer. If what was intended were humble devotion outside prayer, the meaning would be unsound. For if it were said:

“Indeed, prayer

is burdensome except for those who show humble devotion outside it but not within it,” this would imply that prayer is not burdensome for those who lack humble devotion within it, but is burdensome for those who possess it. This would negate the meaning of the verse. It is therefore established that humble devotion is obligatory in prayer.

Its obligatory nature is also indicated by the words of Allah Most High:

“Successful indeed are the believers,”
“those who are humbly devout in their prayers,”
“those who turn away from idle talk,”
“those who pay zakah,”
“those who guard their chastity,”
“except with their wives or those whom their right hands possess, for then they are free from blame.”
“But whoever seeks beyond that—it is they who are the transgressors.”
“And those who faithfully observe their trusts and pledges,”
“and those who diligently maintain their prayers.”
“Those are the inheritors,”
“who will inherit Firdaws, where they will abide forever.”

He, glorified and exalted be He, states that these are the ones who will inherit Firdaws in Paradise. This implies that no others will inherit it, demonstrating that these qualities are obligatory. If any of them were merely recommended, the Garden of Firdaws could be inherited without that quality, since Paradise is attained by fulfilling obligations, without requiring the performance of recommended deeds. This is why He mentioned only obligatory qualities here.

Since humble devotion in prayer is obligatory, and humble devotion encompasses both tranquillity and humility, relevant here is the report from Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, who saw a man fidgeting during his prayer and said:

“Had this man’s heart been humbly devout, his limbs would have been so as well.”

That is, they would have become still

and submissive.

Allah Most High says:

“And among His signs is that you see the earth lying humbled; then, when We send down water upon it, it stirs and swells.”

He thus states that, after being humbled, it stirs—and stirring is movement—and swells, meaning that it rises. This shows that humble devotion involves stillness and lowliness. Hence, while bowing, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, would say:

“O Allah, to You I bow, in You I believe, and to You I submit. My hearing, my sight, my marrow, my mind and my sinews are humbly submissive to You.”

Muslim narrated this in his Sahīh. He thus described himself as humbly submissive while bowing, because one who bows is still and humble. The verse has likewise been explained in this sense.

In the well-known Quranic commentary called Tafsīr al-Wālibī, transmitted from ʿAlī ibn Abī Talha, from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him and his father—the account also transmitted by authors of Quranic commentaries, such as Abū Bakr ibn al-Mundhir, Muhammad ibn Jarīr al-Tabarī and others, through Abū Sālih ʿAbd Allāh ibn Sālih, from Muʿāwiya ibn Abī Sālih, from ʿAlī ibn Abī Talha, from Ibn ʿAbbās—the words of Allah Most High,

“who are humbly devout in their prayers,”

are explained as meaning: “Fearful and still.”

In Quranic commentaries that provide chains of transmission, such as the commentary of Ibn al-Mundhir and others, they narrated through Sufyān al-Thawrī, from Mansūr, from Mujāhid, that he explained “humbly devout” as “being still during prayer.” He said: “Al-Zuhrī said likewise.”

They also narrated through Hishām, from Mughīra, from Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī, that he said: “Humble devotion is in the heart.” He also said: “Still.”

translated_text:
from al-Hasan: “Fearful.”

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated through Abū ʿAbd al-Rahmān al-Maqburī: “Al-Masʿūdī narrated to us that Abū Sinān narrated to us, saying concerning this verse,

‘who are humbly devout in their prayers’:

‘Humble devotion is in the heart; it also involves gentleness toward a fellow Muslim and not turning about during your prayer.’”

Ibn al-Mundhir’s commentary also contains the account found in the commentary of Ishāq ibn Rāhawayh, from Rawh, who said: “Saʿīd narrated to us from Qatāda,” concerning the words,

“who are humbly devout in their prayers.”

He said: “Humble devotion is in the heart, together with fear and lowering the gaze during prayer.”

Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar ibn al-Muthannā, in his book Majāz al-Qurʾān (Quranic Expression), explained

“humbly devout in their prayers”

as meaning: “They neither raise their eyes nor turn about.”

Imam Ahmad narrated an account from Ibn Sīrīn in Kitāb al-Nāsikh wa-l-Mansūkh (The Abrogating and the Abrogated). Ishāq ibn Rāhawayh also narrated it in his commentary, as did Ibn al-Mundhir in his own commentary. He narrated it through al-Thawrī, who said: “Khālid narrated to me from Ibn Sīrīn, who said:

‘The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, used to raise his gaze toward the sky. Then he was commanded to be humbly devout, so he directed his gaze toward his place of prostration.’”

That is, the place where he would prostrate.

Sufyān said: “Someone else also narrated to me from Ibn Sīrīn that this verse was revealed concerning that:

‘Successful indeed are the believers, who are humbly devout in their prayers.’

He said: ‘It means a person’s stillness during prayer.’”

Maʿmar said: “Al-Hasan said: ‘Fearful.’” Qatāda said: “Humble devotion is in the heart.”

This includes humbling the gaze, lowering it and keeping it still, rather than shifting it in different directions, as in the words of Allah Most High:

“So turn away from them

on the Day when the Caller summons to something dreadful. With their eyes humbled, they will emerge from their graves like scattered locusts, rushing toward the Caller. The disbelievers will say, ‘This is a difficult Day.’”

And His words, Most High:

“On the Day when they will emerge from their graves swiftly, as though rushing toward an idol, their eyes humbled, overwhelmed by humiliation. That is the Day they were promised.”

In the other reading: “Khushshaʿan absāruhum (their eyes humbled).”

In these two passages, He describes their bodies as moving swiftly, while describing only their eyes as humbled. This contrasts with the verse about prayer, in which He describes those praying as humbly devout in their whole being, saying:

“Those who are humbly devout in their prayers.”

And His words, Most High:

“Indeed, it is burdensome except for the humbly devout.”

Allah Most High also says:

“On the Day when a shin will be laid bare and they will be called to prostrate but will be unable to do so, their eyes humbled, overwhelmed by humiliation.”

Another example is the humbling of voices, as in His words, Most High:

“And voices will be hushed before the Most Merciful.”

This means that they will become low and fall silent.

Allah Most High says:

“And you will see the wrongdoers, when they see the punishment, saying, ‘Is there any way back?’ And you will see them brought before it, humbled by disgrace, looking with furtive glances.”

Allah Most High also says:

“Some faces that Day will be humbled, labouring and exhausted, entering a scorching Fire, given drink from a boiling spring.”

This will occur on the Day of Resurrection. This is undoubtedly the correct one of the two views.

just as He says of the other group:

“Some faces that Day will be radiant, pleased with their efforts, in a lofty Garden.”

And He, Most High, says:

“And We granted him Isaac, and Jacob as an additional gift, and made each of them righteous. We made them leaders, guiding by Our command, and inspired them to do good deeds, establish prayer, and give zakah. And they were devoted worshippers of Us.”

Since humble devotion in prayer is obligatory and entails stillness and humility, anyone who pecks like a crow has not shown humble devotion in his prostration. Likewise, anyone who does not raise his head from bowing and settle before lowering himself has not attained stillness, for stillness is precisely what is meant by composure. Whoever lacks composure lacks stillness, and whoever lacks stillness has not shown humble devotion in either his bowing or his prostration. Whoever fails to show humble devotion is sinful and disobedient, as we have explained.

Further evidence that humble devotion in prayer is obligatory is that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, threatened those who neglect it, such as someone who raises his gaze towards heaven. Moving and raising his gaze is contrary to the state of one who is humbly devout.

Anas ibn Mālik, may Allah be pleased with him, reported that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“What is the matter with people who raise their eyes during prayer?”

He spoke very sternly about this, then said:

“They must stop doing that, or their sight will surely be snatched away.”

Jābir ibn Samurah reported:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, entered the mosque, where some people were praying with their eyes raised towards heaven. He said: ‘Those men must stop fixing their gaze on heaven, or their sight will not return to them.’”

translated_text:
The first report is in al-Bukhārī, and the second in Muslim. Both also appear in the Sunan collections of Abū Dāwūd, al-Nasā’ī, and Ibn Mājah.

Muhammad ibn Sīrīn said:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to raise his gaze during prayer. But when this verse was revealed, ‘Successful indeed are the believers, those who are humbly devout in their prayer,’ his gaze would no longer go beyond the place of his prostration.”

Imam Ahmad narrated this in The Book of Abrogating and Abrogated Texts.

Since raising one’s gaze towards heaven is incompatible with humble devotion, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, forbade it and issued a warning against it. Looking aside without need, however, diminishes humble devotion without negating it. It therefore detracts from the prayer, as related by al-Bukhārī, Abū Dāwūd, and al-Nasā’ī from ‘Ā’ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, who said:

“I asked the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, about a man looking aside during prayer. He replied: ‘It is something Satan snatches from the servant’s prayer.’”

Shums (“unruly”) is the plural of shamūs, commonly pronounced shamūs with a sād. It describes a horse that swishes its tail to the right and left—a movement without stillness. As for raising the hands when bowing and when rising from bowing, just as they are raised at the opening of the prayer, this is prescribed by agreement of the Muslims. How, then, could the hadith prohibit it?

His words, “Remain still in prayer,” encompass this as well. Thus, one of the imams who did not regard this raising of the hands as prescribed once prayed beside ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Mubārak. When Ibn al-Mubārak raised his hands, he asked him, “Are you trying to fly?” He replied, “If I am flying the first time, then I am flying the second time; otherwise, I am not.” This refutes the reasoning he had put forward.

Moreover, reports from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his Companions establishing this raising of the hands have been mass-transmitted. Thus, the hadith cannot be a prohibition of it, nor can it contradict those reports. Even if they did conflict, the hadiths establishing this raising of the hands are numerous and mass-transmitted, and must be given precedence over a report that is not mass-transmitted, were it to contradict them.

This raising of the hands is accompanied by stillness. His words, “Remain still in prayer,” therefore do not preclude it, just as they do not preclude raising the hands at the opening of the prayer or the other actions of prayer. Rather, his command, “Remain still,” requires stillness in every

part of the prayer. This entails the obligation to remain still when bowing, prostrating, standing after bowing, and sitting between prostrations. This makes clear that stillness is prescribed in all the actions of prayer as far as possible. Thus, one maintains composure even during its transitions, which culminate in movement; stillness in these consists of moving at a measured rather than a rapid pace, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, instructed when walking to prayer. If this applies to movement towards prayer, how much more so to movement within it? He said:

“When you come to prayer, do not come rushing. Come with tranquility. Pray whatever you catch, and make up whatever you miss.”

This also constitutes independent evidence on the issue. Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, said: I heard the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, say:

“When the call to commence prayer is given, do not come rushing. Come walking, with tranquility. Pray whatever you catch, and make up whatever you miss.”

This was narrated by al-Bukhārī, Muslim, Abū Dāwūd, and Ibn Mājah. Abū Dāwūd said—and al-Tirmidhī said likewise—that Ibn Abī Dhi’b, Ibrāhīm ibn Sa‘d, Ma‘mar, and Shu‘ayb ibn Abī Hamzah narrated from al-Zuhrī the wording:

“And complete whatever you miss.”

Ibn ‘Uyaynah narrated from al-Zuhrī the wording, “Make it up.” Muhammad ibn ‘Amr, reporting from Abū Salamah, from Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, and Ja‘far ibn Abī Rabī‘ah, reporting from al-A‘raj, from Abū Hurayrah, related the wording, “Complete it.” Ibn Mas‘ūd also related from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, the wording, “Complete it.” Abū Dāwūd narrated from Abū

Hurayrah, from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, who said:

“Come to prayer with tranquility. Pray whatever you catch, and make up whatever you miss.”

Abū Dāwūd said: Ibn Sīrīn likewise narrated from Abū Hurayrah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—the wording, “Let him make it up.” Abū Rāfi‘ likewise narrated this from Abū Hurayrah. Both “Complete it” and “Make it up” were reported from Abū Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him; the reports from him differed.

Since the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, commanded tranquility when going to prayer and prohibited rushing—which means moving quickly in this context—because going to prayer is a means to performing it, then prayer itself has an even greater claim to tranquility being commanded within it and haste being prohibited. It follows, all the more certainly, that someone bowing or prostrating is commanded to remain tranquil and forbidden to hurry. This is especially so because he commanded tranquility after hearing the call to commence prayer, which obliges a person to go to it, and forbade him to occupy himself instead with voluntary prayer—even if proceeding tranquilly meant missing part of the prayer. He commanded him to remain tranquil and to pray whatever he had missed on his own after the imam’s salutation, giving this precedence over rushing to prayer. This indicates how emphatically rushing to prayer is forbidden; how much more so rushing within it!

{وَعِبَادُ الرَّحْمَنِ الَّذِينَ يَمْشُونَ عَلَى الْأَرْضِ هَوْنًا وَإِذَا خَاطَبَهُمُ الْجَاهِلُونَ قَالُوا سَلَامًا}
 .
 قَالَ الْحَسَنُ وَغَيْرُهُ:
 
" بِسَكِينَةِ وَوَقَارٍ "
 فَأَخْبَرَ أَنَّ عِبَادَ الرَّحْمَنِ هُمْ هَؤُلَاءِ. فَإِذَا كَانَ مَأْمُورًا بِالسَّكِينَةِ وَالْوَقَارِ فِي الْأَفْعَالِ الْعَادِيَّةِ الَّتِي هِيَ مِنْ جِنْسِ الْحَرَكَةِ فَكَيْفَ الْأَفْعَالُ الْعِبَادِيَّةُ؟ ثُمَّ كَيْفَ بِمَا هُوَ فِيهَا مَنْ جِنْسِ السُّكُونِ كَالرُّكُوعِ وَالسُّجُودِ؟ فَإِنَّ هَذِهِ الْأَدِلَّةَ تَقْتَضِي السِّكِّينَةَ فِي الِانْتِقَالِ؛ كَالرَّفْعِ وَالْخَفْضِ وَالنُّهُوضِ وَالِانْحِطَاطِ. وَأَمَّا نَفْسُ الْأَفْعَالِ الَّتِي هِيَ الْمَقْصُودُ بِالِانْتِقَالِ كَالرُّكُوعِ نَفْسِهِ وَالسُّجُودِ نَفْسِهِ وَالْقِيَامِ وَالْقُعُودِ أَنْفُسِهِمَا - وَهَذِهِ هِيَ مِنْ نَفْسِهَا سُكُونٌ - فَمَنْ لَمْ يَسْكُنْ فِيهَا لَمْ يَأْتِ بِهَا وَإِنَّمَا هُوَ بِمَنْزِلَةِ مَنْ أَهْوَى إلَى الْقُعُودِ وَلَمْ يَأْتِ بِهِ كَمَنْ مَدَّ يَدَهُ إلَى الطَّعَامِ وَلَمْ يَأْكُلْ مِنْهُ أَوْ وَضَعَهُ عَلَى فِيهِ وَلَمْ يَطْعَمْهُ.
 وَأَيْضًا:
 فَإِنَّ اللَّهَ تَعَالَى أَوْجَبَ الرُّكُوعَ وَالسُّجُودَ فِي الْكِتَابِ
translated_text:
he forbade him to do in prayer, whether in speech or action, even when praying alone. How, then, should someone actually praying conduct himself with regard to such walking and other actions? If he is forbidden to walk hurriedly and hastily, and commanded to proceed with tranquility—even if he misses part of the prayer with the imam and must make it up—then he is all the more clearly commanded to observe tranquility within the prayer itself.

Further evidence for this is that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, commands tranquility and moderation in movement and walking generally in His Book, saying:

“Be moderate in your pace and lower your voice.”

And He, Most High, says:

“The servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth humbly, and when the ignorant address them, they say words of peace.”

Al-Hasan and others explained this as “with tranquility and dignity.”

Thus, He tells us that these are the servants of the Most Merciful. If a person is commanded to observe tranquility and dignity in ordinary actions involving movement, how much more does this apply to acts of worship? And how much more to those acts within worship that involve stillness, such as bowing and prostration?

These proofs require tranquility during transitions, such as raising and lowering oneself, rising and descending. As for the actual postures that these transitions are intended to reach—bowing itself, prostration itself, and standing and sitting themselves—these are, by their very nature, states of stillness. Whoever does not remain still in them has not performed them. He is merely like someone who lowers himself to sit but never actually sits, or someone who reaches for food without eating any of it, or puts it to his mouth without tasting it.

Moreover, Allah Most High has enjoined bowing and prostration in the Book

and the Sunnah, and both are obligatory by consensus, for Allah Most High says:

“O you who believe, bow and prostrate.”

And He, Most High, says:

“On the Day when a Shin is uncovered and they are called to prostrate but cannot do so, their eyes downcast, humiliation will cover them. They had been called to prostrate while they were sound in body.”

And He, Most High, says:

“What is the matter with them that they do not believe, and when the Quran is recited to them, they do not prostrate?”

And He, Most High, says:

“Only those believe in Our signs who, when reminded of them, fall down in prostration and glorify their Lord with praise, and are not arrogant.”

And He, Most High, says:

“Prostrate and draw near.”

And He, Most High, says:

“Do you not see that to Allah prostrates whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on earth, as do the sun, the moon, the stars, the mountains, the trees, the creatures, and many people? But many others have deserved punishment.”

This indicates that those people who do not prostrate to Allah have deserved punishment. He also says:

“And during the night prostrate to Him, and glorify Him through the long night.”

And He, Most High, says:

“So glorify your Lord with praise and be among those who prostrate.”

And He, Most High, says:

“When they are told, ‘Bow down,’ they do not bow.”

And He, Most High, says:

“Your allies are only Allah, His Messenger, and those who believe—those who establish prayer, give zakah, and bow in worship.”

Since Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has made bowing and prostrating to Him obligatory in His Book, just as He has made prayer itself obligatory, it is the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, who explains to people what has been revealed to them. His Sunnah interprets the Book, clarifies it, points to its meaning, and expresses it.

original_text:
وَفِعْلُهُ إذَا خَرَجَ امْتِثَالًا لِأَمْرِ أَوْ تَفْسِيرًا لِمُجْمَلِ:
 كَانَ حُكْمُهُ حُكْمَ مَا امْتَثَلَهُ وَفَسَّرَهُ. وَهَذَا كَمَا أَنَّهُ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ لَمَّا كَانَ يَأْتِي فِي كُلِّ رَكْعَةٍ بِرُكُوعِ وَاحِدٍ وَسُجُودَيْنِ كَانَ كِلَاهُمَا وَاجِبًا. وَكَانَ هَذَا امْتِثَالًا مِنْهُ لِمَا أَمَرَ اللَّهُ بِهِ مِنْ الرُّكُوعِ وَالسُّجُودِ وَتَفْسِيرًا لِمَا أُجْمِلَ ذِكْرُهُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ وَكَذَلِكَ الْمَرْجِعُ إلَى سُنَّتِهِ فِي كَيْفِيَّةِ السُّجُودِ. وَقَدْ كَانَ يُصَلِّي الْفَرِيضَةَ وَالنَّافِلَةَ وَالنَّاسُ يُصَلُّونَ عَلَى عَهْدِهِ وَلَمْ يُصَلِّ قَطُّ إلَّا بِالِاعْتِدَالِ عَنْ الرُّكُوعِ وَالسُّجُودِ وبالطمأنينة فِي أَفْعَالِ الصَّلَاةِ كُلِّهَا. قَدْ نَقَلَ ذَلِكَ كُلُّ مَنْ نَقَلَ صَلَاةَ الْفَرِيضَةِ وَالنَّافِلَةِ. وَالنَّاسُ يُصَلُّونَ عَلَى عَهْدِهِ وَلَمْ يُصَلِّ قَطُّ إلَّا بِالِاعْتِدَالِ عَنْ الرُّكُوعِ وَالسُّجُودِ وبالطمأنينة. وَكَذَلِكَ كَانَتْ صَلَاةُ أَصْحَابِهِ عَلَى عَهْدِهِ. وَهَذَا يَقْتَضِي وُجُوبَ السُّكُونِ وَالطُّمَأْنِينَةِ فِي هَذِهِ الْأَفْعَالِ كَمَا يَقْتَضِي وُجُوبَ عَدَدِهَا. وَهُوَ سُجُودَانِ مَعَ كُلِّ رُكُوعٍ.
 وَأَيْضًا:
 فَإِنَّ مُدَاوَمَتَهُ عَلَى ذَلِكَ فِي كُلِّ صَلَاةٍ كُلَّ يَوْمٍ مَعَ كَثْرَةِ الصَّلَوَاتِ مِنْ أَقْوَى الْأَدِلَّةِ عَلَى وُجُوبِ ذَلِكَ. إذْ لَوْ كَانَ غَيْرَ وَاجِبٍ لَتَرَكَهُ وَلَوْ مَرَّةً لِيُبَيِّنَ الْجَوَازَ. أَوْ لِيُبَيِّنَ جَوَازَ تَرْكِهِ بِقَوْلِهِ. فَلَمَّا لَمْ يُبَيِّنْ - لَا بِقَوْلِهِ وَلَا بِفِعْلِهِ - جَوَازَ تَرْكِ ذَلِكَ مَعَ مُدَاوَمَتِهِ عَلَيْهِ. كَانَ ذَلِكَ دَلِيلًا عَلَى وُجُوبِهِ.
 وَأَيْضًا:
 فَقَدْ ثَبَتَ عَنْهُ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ فِي صَحِيحِ الْبُخَارِيِّ:
translated_text:
and when an action of his is performed in compliance with a command or to explain something stated without detail, it carries the same ruling as that which it fulfils and explains. Thus, since he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, performed one bow and two prostrations in every unit of prayer, both were obligatory. By doing so, he fulfilled Allah’s command to bow and prostrate and explained what the Quran had mentioned without elaboration. Likewise, his Sunnah is the reference for how to prostrate.

He used to offer obligatory and voluntary prayers, and people prayed during his lifetime. He never prayed without returning to an upright posture after bowing and prostrating and coming to rest in all the postures of prayer. Everyone who transmitted accounts of his obligatory and voluntary prayers reported this. People prayed during his lifetime, and he never prayed without returning to an upright posture after bowing and prostrating and coming to rest. His Companions likewise prayed in this manner during his lifetime. This establishes the obligation to pause and come to rest in these movements, just as it establishes their required number: two prostrations for every bow.

Furthermore, his constant observance of this in every prayer, every day, despite the great number of prayers, is among the strongest proofs that it is obligatory. Had it not been obligatory, he would have omitted it at least once to demonstrate that doing so was permissible, or he would have explained verbally that it could be omitted. Since he never indicated, either by word or deed, that it could be omitted, while consistently observing it himself, this is evidence that it is obligatory.

Furthermore, it is authentically reported from him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in Sahīh al-Bukhārī:

original_text:
أَنَّهُ قَالَ لِمَالِكِ بْنِ الحويرث وَصَاحِبِهِ 
{إذَا حَضَرَتْ الصَّلَاةُ فَأَذِّنَا وَأُقِيمَا وَلْيَؤُمَّكُمَا أَكْبَرُكُمَا. وَصَلُّوا كَمَا رَأَيْتُمُونِي أُصَلِّي}
 فَأَمَرَهُمْ أَنْ يُصَلُّوا كَمَا رَأَوْهُ يُصَلِّي. وَذَلِكَ يَقْتَضِي أَنَّهُ يَجِبُ عَلَى الْإِمَامِ أَنْ يُصَلِّيَ بِالنَّاسِ كَمَا كَانَ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ يُصَلِّي لَهُمْ وَلَا مُعَارِضَ لِذَلِكَ وَلَا مُخَصِّصَ فَإِنَّ الْإِمَامَ يَجِبُ عَلَيْهِ مَا لَا يَجِبُ عَلَى الْمَأْمُومِ وَالْمُنْفَرِدِ. وَقَدْ ثَبَتَ عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ فِي الصَّحِيحَيْنِ عَنْ 
{سَهْلِ ابْنِ سَعْدٍ أَنَّهُ قَالَ: لَقَدْ رَأَيْت رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ قَامَ عَلَى الْمِنْبَرِ وَكَبَّرَ وَكَبَّرَ النَّاسُ مَعَهُ وَرَاءَهُ وَهُوَ عَلَى الْمِنْبَرِ ثُمَّ رَجَعَ فَنَزَلَ الْقَهْقَرَى حَتَّى سَجَدَ فِي أَصْلِ الْمِنْبَرِ ثُمَّ عَادَ حَتَّى فَرَغَ مِنْ آخِرِ صَلَاتِهِ ثُمَّ أَقْبَلَ عَلَى النَّاسِ.
 فَقَالَ:
 يَا أَيُّهَا النَّاسُ إنَّمَا صَنَعْت هَذَا لِتَأْتَمُّوا بِي وَلِتَعْلَمُوا صَلَاتِي}
 وَفِي سُنَنِ أَبِي دَاوُد وَالنَّسَائِي عَنْ سَالِمٍ الْبَرَّادِ قَالَ: {أَتَيْنَا عُقْبَةَ بْنَ عَامِرٍ الْأَنْصَارِيَّ أَبَا مَسْعُودٍ فَقُلْنَا لَهُ: حَدِّثْنَا عَنْ صَلَاةِ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ.
 فَقَامَ بَيْنَ أَيْدِينَا فِي الْمَسْجِدِ فَكَبَّرَ فَلَمَّا رَكَعَ وَضَعَ يَدَيْهِ عَلَى رُكْبَتَيْهِ وَجَعَلَ أَصَابِعَهُ أَسْفَلَ مِنْ ذَلِكَ وَجَافَى بَيْنَ مَرْفِقَيْهِ حَتَّى اسْتَقَرَّ كُلُّ شَيْءٍ مِنْهُ ثُمَّ قَالَ:
 سَمِعَ اللَّهُ لِمَنْ حَمِدَهُ فَقَامَ حَتَّى اسْتَقَرَّ كُلُّ شَيْءٍ مِنْهُ ثُمَّ كَبَّرَ وَسَجَدَ وَوَضَعَ كَفَّيْهِ عَلَى الْأَرْضِ ثُمَّ جَافَى بَيْنَ مَرْفِقَيْهِ حَتَّى اسْتَقَرَّ كُلُّ شَيْءٍ.
translated_text:
that he said to Mālik ibn al-Huwayrith and his companion:

“When the time for prayer comes, give the call to prayer and announce its commencement, and let the older of you lead you both. And pray as you have seen me pray.”

He thus commanded them to pray as they had seen him pray. This entails that the imam must lead people in prayer as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to lead them. Nothing contradicts this or restricts its scope, for the imam has obligations that do not apply to someone following an imam or praying alone.

An authentic report in the two Sahīh collections relates that Sahl ibn Sa‘d said:

“I saw the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, stand on the pulpit and proclaim ‘Allah is the Greatest.’ The people behind him did likewise while he was on the pulpit. He then stepped backwards down from it and prostrated at its base. He then returned and continued until he had finished his prayer. Then he turned towards the people and said, ‘O people, I did this only so that you would follow my example and learn how I pray.’”

In the Sunan collections of Abū Dāwūd and al-Nasā’ī, Sālim al-Barrād said:

“We came to Uqbah ibn Āmir al-Ansārī, Abū Mas‘ūd, and said to him, ‘Tell us about the prayer of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.’ He stood before us in the mosque and proclaimed ‘Allah is the Greatest.’ When he bowed, he placed his hands on his knees, with his fingers below them, and held his elbows apart until every part of his body had come to rest. Then he said, ‘Allah hears whoever praises Him,’ and stood until every part of his body had come to rest. Then he proclaimed ‘Allah is the Greatest’ and prostrated, placing his palms on the ground and holding his elbows apart until every part had come to rest.

original_text:
مِنْهُ ثُمَّ رَفَعَ رَأْسَهُ فَجَلَسَ حَتَّى اسْتَقَرَّ كُلُّ شَيْءٍ مِنْهُ فَفَعَلَ ذَلِكَ أَيْضًا ثُمَّ صَلَّى أَرْبَعَ رَكَعَاتٍ مِثْلَ هَذِهِ الرَّكْعَةِ فَصَلَّى صَلَاتَهُ.
 ثُمَّ قَالَ:
 هَكَذَا رَأَيْنَا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ يُصَلِّي} . وَهَذَا إجْمَاعُ الصَّحَابَةِ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمْ. فَإِنَّهُمْ كَانُوا لَا يُصَلُّونَ إلَّا مُطْمَئِنِّينَ. وَإِذَا رَأَى بَعْضُهُمْ مَنْ لَا يَطْمَئِنُّ أَنْكَرَ عَلَيْهِ وَنَهَاهُ. وَلَا يُنْكِرُ وَاحِدٌ مِنْهُمْ عَلَى الْمُنْكَرِ لِذَلِكَ. وَهَذَا إجْمَاعٌ مِنْهُمْ عَلَى وُجُوبِ السُّكُونِ وَالطُّمَأْنِينَةِ فِي الصَّلَاةِ قَوْلًا وَفِعْلًا. وَلَوْ كَانَ ذَلِكَ غَيْرَ وَاجِبٍ لَكَانُوا يَتْرُكُونَهُ أَحْيَانًا كَمَا كَانُوا يَتْرُكُونَ مَا لَيْسَ بِوَاجِبِ.
 وَأَيْضًا:
 فَإِنَّ الرُّكُوعَ وَالسُّجُودَ فِي لُغَةِ الْعَرَبِ لَا يَكُونُ إلَّا إذَا سَكَنَ حِينَ انْحِنَائِهِ وَحِينَ وَضْعِ وَجْهِهِ عَلَى الْأَرْضِ.
 فَأَمَّا مُجَرَّدُ الْخَفْضِ وَالرَّفْعِ عَنْهُ:
 فَلَا يُسَمَّى ذَلِكَ رُكُوعًا وَلَا سُجُودًا. وَمَنْ سَمَّاهُ رُكُوعًا وَسُجُودًا فَقَدْ غَلِطَ عَلَى اللُّغَةِ.
 فَهُوَ مُطَالَبٌ بِدَلِيلِ مِنْ اللُّغَةِ عَلَى أَنَّ هَذَا يُسَمَّى رَاكِعًا وَسَاجِدًا حَتَّى يَكُونَ فَاعِلُهُ مُمْتَثِلًا لِلْأَمْرِ وَحَتَّى يُقَالَ:
 إنَّ هَذَا الْأَمْرَ الْمُطَالَبَ بِهِ يَحْصُلُ الِامْتِثَالُ فِيهِ بِفِعْلِ مَا يَتَنَاوَلُهُ الِاسْمُ. فَإِنَّ هَذَا لَا يَصِحُّ حَتَّى يَعْلَمَ أَنَّ مُجَرَّدَ هَذَا يُسَمَّى فِي اللُّغَةِ رُكُوعًا وَسُجُودًا وَهَذَا مِمَّا لَا سَبِيلَ إلَيْهِ وَلَا دَلِيلَ عَلَيْهِ.
 فَقَائِلُ ذَلِكَ قَائِلٌ بِغَيْرِ عِلْمٍ فِي كِتَابِ اللَّهِ وَفِي لُغَةِ الْعَرَبِ وَإِذَا حَصَلَ الشَّكُّ:

translated_text:
of his body. Then he raised his head and sat until every part of his body had come to rest. He did the same again, then prayed four units of prayer like this one, completing his prayer. Then he said, ‘This is how we saw the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, pray.’”

This represents the consensus of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them. They would only pray with composure. Whenever any of them saw someone praying without composure, he would rebuke him and forbid him from doing so. None of them objected to anyone who rebuked this. Their words and actions thus establish their consensus that stillness and composure are obligatory in prayer. Had this not been obligatory, they would sometimes have omitted it, just as they sometimes omitted what was not obligatory.

Furthermore, in the Arabic language, bowing and prostration require a person to remain still when bending down and when placing his face on the ground. Merely lowering oneself and rising again is not called bowing or prostration. Whoever calls it bowing and prostration has misunderstood the language. He must therefore provide linguistic evidence that someone doing this is described as bowing and prostrating before that person can be considered to have fulfilled the command, and before it can be said that this required command is fulfilled by performing whatever falls within the scope of those terms.

Such an argument is valid only once it is known that these movements alone are called bowing and prostration in the language. Yet there is no way to establish this, nor any evidence for it. Whoever makes this claim therefore speaks without knowledge concerning the Book of Allah and the Arabic language.

If doubt arises as to whether a person is prostrating or not, he cannot, by unanimous agreement, be regarded as having fulfilled the command. For the obligation is known, whereas the performance of
